The intervention study varies LoRA rank (r=16→256) and adds a DPO phase, revealing a monotonic trade-off between stronger political shift and modest degradation on general benchmarks (e.g., MMLU 59.0→48.6, HellaSwag 83.6→73.8 at r=256), with DPO recovering much of the drop (81.4/57.0) while pushing attitude score to 0.4—evidence the effect is robust to training hyperparameters.

73.key_points: Weakness: Agent, Clarity, Figure, Model, Presentation
73.human_review: I have some confusion about the presentation. I noticed you have three base LLMs to act as agents. In Figure 1/2/3, whose results are reported? I might miss it but it seems to be a little unclear to me.
73.llm_review: Agent, Clarity, Figure, Model, Presentation: (1) Agent confounds: Personas are generated by the same base LLM at temperature=1.0, which can imprint the base prior into the agent descriptions before any debate begins. The Default prompt ("You are an American") conflates cultural priors, safety alignment, and model bias, making the Default an imperfect proxy for a neutral baseline. No human validation of persona ideology is reported. (2) Model/measurement validity: The attitude metric is a 0–10 "severity" rating. For several topics, severity is not isomorphic to partisan stance (e.g., both parties may rate Illegal Immigration as serious but for different causal frames; acknowledging climate change severity differs from endorsing specific policies). The strong claim that partisan lines "never" cross the Default line needs statistical backing beyond visual inspection of means; mixed-effects modeling or trajectory-level tests would help. (3) Clarity/Presentation: Key details (exact metaprompts, full question bank, additional model results) are deferred to the supplement, impeding reproducibility and interpretability in the main text. Choices like 40 runs ("budget" rationale), truncation to nine iterations, and persona-generation procedure lack power analyses or ablations. (4) Figure clarity: Some panels reuse dashed baselines from other figures, and topic-specific semantics of the y-axis are not fully annotated, which makes interpretation harder, especially when comparing pre/post conditions.

74.human_review: For the four subfigures in Figure 1, one of my feelings is: is it possible that LLMs are correcting polarized statements like subfigures 1/2/3? The clear converging trend, in my opinion, is only shown in subfigure 4.
74.llm_review: Figure: The convergence story would benefit from clearer, more self-contained visuals. Concretely: standardize y-axis ranges across topics; annotate the attitude scale with topic-specific semantics (e.g., what higher scores mean per topic); avoid referencing a Default baseline drawn from a different panel—plot each panel’s baseline within-panel; use consistent color/linestyle mapping for agent identities across figures and between solid/dotted (pre/post fine-tune) conditions; add per-run distributional views (violin/box plots at final iteration) or spaghetti plots for a random subset of runs; report effect sizes (e.g., average per-iteration slope and 95% CIs) and significance markers at key iterations; and include a convergence metric (e.g., distance to Default over time) as an inset.

75.key_points: Strength: Comparison, Data, Method, Model, Performance
75.human_review: The paper provides an extensive comparison between GPT and RETRO models, using various PEFT methods and assessing their performance across multiple datasets. This broad scope provides valuable insights into the effectiveness of these techniques in enhancing model performance.
75.llm_review: The paper offers a well-controlled head-to-head comparison between GPT and RETRO under a unified RAG setting, spanning five model scales (823M–48B), three PEFT methods (P-tuning, Adapters, LoRA), and six retrieval-centric datasets. The shared retriever (Dragon+) and consistent prompting/evaluation enable an apples-to-apples methodology across models and sizes. The study surfaces clear performance trends: RETRO is stronger zero-shot, GPT exhibits a higher PEFT-improvement ceiling, medium (≈8B) models provide the best cost–performance balance, and P-tuning lags behind Adapters/LoRA on RETRO.

76.key_points: Strength: Clarity, Data, Detail, Evaluation, Experiment, Metric, Result
76.human_review: The authors meticulously detail their experimental setup, including model configurations, datasets used, and evaluation metrics. This level of detail supports reproducibility and offers clarity on how the results were obtained.
76.llm_review: The experimental setup is clearly described: datasets are appropriate for retrieval-heavy evaluation; metrics match task types (F1 for document QA, exact match for multiple-choice, geometric mean of ROUGE-1/2/L for summarization); and the retrieval pipeline (100-word chunking, top-5 neighbors via Dragon+) is spelled out. The placement of PEFT modules is specified for both architectures. Results are reported per dataset and averaged, with additional figures/tables referenced in the appendix, making the evaluation and findings easy to follow.

77.key_points: Strength: Adaptation, Fine-tuning, Method, Model, Training
77.human_review: By integrating PEFT methods with RAG, the study pioneers a new approach to fine-tuning large language models. This integration is promising for efficient model adaptation without extensive retraining.
77.llm_review: The work carefully adapts multiple fine-tuning methods to distinct model architectures: P-tuning via virtual tokens in the decoder with chunk-aligned padding; Adapters and LoRA inserted in both attention and feed-forward layers; and for RETRO, PEFT layers also placed in the retrieval encoder. Training covers both PEFT and full fine-tuning baselines (for medium models) and includes instruction-tuned RETRO, demonstrating thoughtful coverage of adaptation strategies across models and training regimes.

78.human_review: The specific tuning process and the parameters selected are not detailed.
78.llm_review: The paper does not report precise trainable-parameter accounting for each PEFT method and model size (e.g., LoRA rank/targets, adapter bottleneck widths, number/length of P-tuning virtual tokens), nor the fraction of updated parameters. There is no matched-budget comparison where methods are normalized to the same number of trainable parameters, and compute/memory/throughput footprints are not quantified. This limits interpretability of parameter efficiency claims.

79.human_review: The paper employs a fixed retrieval mechanism, such as Dragon+, but does not discuss the specific reasons for choosing this mechanism or compare it with other retrieval mechanisms (e.g., the latest neural network-based retrievers).
79.llm_review: The comparative scope omits several relevant baselines: important PEFT variants (e.g., QLoRA, IA3, prefix/prompt tuning variants), retrieval-free baselines to isolate the contribution of RAG, and alternative retrievers. The study focuses on a single retriever (Dragon+) and does not include other retrieval-pretrained models beyond RETRO or instruction-tuned GPT comparisons at scale. These omissions weaken the breadth of the comparison and the strength of the "first comprehensive" claim.

80.human_review: The paper lacks a thorough analysis of failure cases or error types for the models on specific tasks. Such analysis is essential for understanding the limitations of the models and for further improvements.
80.llm_review: Analysis of why GPT benefits more from PEFT while RETRO plateaus is largely qualitative. There is no task-level diagnostic (e.g., error typology, retrieval recall/precision, calibration) to explain divergent behaviors across QA vs summarization, nor sensitivity analyses to number/length of retrieved chunks or retriever quality. Model-level probes (e.g., cross-attention utilization in RETRO) are absent, leaving limited guidance on how to improve each model–task pairing.

81.human_review: The article mentions that P-tuning generally underperforms compared to other PEFT methods in RETRO models, but it does not provide a detailed analysis or explanation for this occurrence.
81.llm_review: Several performance claims are descriptive without uncertainty estimates or statistical testing (e.g., the 8B "sweet spot" and small deltas between PEFT methods). There are no multiple-seed runs, learning curves vs data size, or cost–performance plots (latency, GPU hours, memory) to support the trade-off narrative. The explanation for instruction-tuned RETRO’s limited PEFT headroom remains speculative, lacking controlled analyses to disentangle causes (e.g., saturation, over-regularization, or interference).

82.human_review: Novel method: The paper is the first work to integrate multiple prompting methods into the sequence-level distillation and proposes the method to construct the high-quality data, considering two different prompting methods.
82.llm_review: Data, Method, Novelty: The paper proposes a mixed-thought distillation pipeline that is clearly distinct from prior single-path CoT-only distillation. It (i) samples n=20 CoT and n=20 PoT rationales per instance from GPT-3.5-Turbo at temperature 0.7; (ii) filters out non-executable PoT and CoT without answers; (iii) categorizes examples into four types (PoT-only ≈10%, CoT-only ≈10%, both ≈60%, neither ≈20%); and (iv) rebalances by upsampling Type 1/2 and dropping Type 4 to create a well-balanced mixed-thought dataset. On top of this, the method introduces a multi-task loss that supervises both rationale generation and final answers for CoT and PoT, with instance-wise weighting for Type 3. This end-to-end recipe (balanced mixed thought data + adaptive multi-task objective) is novel relative to previous CoT distillation and makes the student explicitly learn both natural-language and program reasoning paths.

83.human_review: The method is intuitive. This paper is well-written and easy to follow the authors' thoughts.
83.llm_review: Method: The training and inference mechanisms are well specified and implementable. Training uses Lpath = E[CE(f(x), r̂ + ŷ)] for each path, and for instances solvable by both, it combines the two path losses as L3 = (1−λ)Lpath_CoT + λLpath_PoT, where λ = n2/(n1+n2) is computed from self-consistency counts (n1 correct CoT samples, n2 correct PoT samples, each out of 20). For Type 1/2, both path losses are applied (L1,2 = Lpath_CoT + Lpath_PoT), encouraging the student to internalize both formats even when one is the sole solver. Inference elicits both paths using path-specific prompts ("Let’s think step by step" vs. "Let’s break down the code step by step"), samples multiple solutions per path, executes PoT with a Python executor, and aggregates answers via majority vote over concatenated ACoT and APoT. The approach plugs into different backbones and fine-tuning regimes (e.g., QLoRA on LLaMA-2/CodeLlama), showing methodological generality.

84.human_review: Experiments are pretty solid and cover nearly every aspect of the methodology to demonstrate its effectiveness.
84.llm_review: Effectiveness, Experiment, Method: Empirical results are strong and consistent across models and tasks. With multi-path inference, Mistral-7B-MD achieves 87.5% (SVAMP), 74.0% (GSM8K), and 77.1% (ASDIV), surpassing the GPT-3.5-Turbo teacher (82.0/77.4/75.8). LLaMA2-7B-MD hits 84.5/53.8/70.2/69.4 on SVAMP/GSM8K/ASDIV/StrategyQA, improving over (i) single-path CoT distillation (69.5/40.1/62.2/67.7) and (ii) PoT distillation (77.0/46.5/65.6/68.0), and even over an ensemble of two separately distilled students (81.0/49.7/69.9/68.1). CodeLlama-7B-MD further reaches 85.5 (SVAMP) and 73.5 (ASDIV), +26.5 and +12.1 over base CodeLlama, respectively. Ablations show scalability with sampling paths: for LLaMA2-7B-MD, multi-path accuracy rises from 66.0% (N=2) to 83.5% (N=14). Mixed distillation also improves single-path abilities (e.g., LLaMA2-7B PoT: 77.0→80.5 on SVAMP; GSM8K: 46.5→51.6). OOD transfer is demonstrated by training on GSM8K and evaluating on SVAMP/ASDIV: LLaMA2-7B-MD + CoT w/ PoT attains 74.5% and 68.9%, outperforming single-path and ensemble baselines. A qualitative case (grape drums) shows CoT-distillation miscomputes 244×146 and PoT-distillation spuriously multiplies by pickers (294×244×146), while MD learns both correct CoT and PoT reasoning, returning the correct 35,624.

85.human_review: Some results are surprising for me and lack enough explanation. For example, in Table 1, when changing CoT to PoT, why can we gain so much improvement (34.5 to 74.0 on SVAMP) on T5 and GPT2. Could authors add more explanation to the result improvement.
85.llm_review: Explanation, Improvement, Result: Several claims require clearer definitions and controlled evidence. (1) The 10/10/60/20 split of PoT-only/CoT-only/both/neither is presented as a fact but appears to be a design target (since the method upsamples Type 1/2 and drops Type 4) rather than an observed distribution; per-dataset distributions before/after balancing are not reported. (2) Filtering criteria are underspecified: what constitutes a "CoT without an answer" (regex patterns? numeric extraction rules?), and how are PoT executor errors (syntax vs. runtime) handled? (3) Results are reported as single-run accuracies with no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, so robustness is unclear. (4) Component attribution is missing: there is no ablation isolating the effects of upsampling, Type-4 removal, or λ-weighted blending versus a 0.5/0.5 baseline. Improvements: report pre/post-balance type histograms per dataset, detailed filtering/executor failure rates, seed variance with significance tests, and targeted ablations (e.g., remove upsampling; fix λ=0.5; train with only Lpath vs. L1,2/L3).

86.human_review: From Figure 9 (Few-shot Template on StrategyQA), I find that the PoT for StrategyQA, the common sense QA task, the code structure is simple and all the reasoning steps is in the docstrings of the function and I'm not so sure why such prompting could bring solid improvement than only using CoT. Could authors also do more explanation for the motivation of their method on the common sense reasoning dataset?
86.llm_review: Data, Improvement, Motivation, Prompt: The mixed-thought corpora rely on a single closed-source teacher (GPT-3.5-Turbo), and the paper does not release the resulting mixed data, prompts, or code, hampering reproducibility and bias auditing. Critical choices lack motivation and sensitivity analyses: temperature=0.7 and n=20 samples per path; the specific balancing strategy (upsampling Type 1/2, dropping Type 4); and the exact prompt templates (e.g., using CoT as code annotations for StrategyQA’s PoT). The study provides no statistics on PoT code length, execution success rate, or failure taxonomy, and no test of prompt phrasing/shot selection (e.g., few-shot exemplars, "Let’s think" vs. alternatives). To strengthen the paper: release mixed-thought data and prompts, report comprehensive data diagnostics (deduplication, average code length/tokens, executor success rates by dataset), run sensitivity to temperature and sample count, ablate few-shot exemplars and prompt phrasings, and assess alternative/open-source teachers to check teacher-specific bias.

87.human_review: I find that in Table 3, only increasing N, we can gain more improvement, especially for PoT but not so much on CoT. Could authors give me more intuition about the gap between CoT and PoT here?
87.llm_review: Improvement, Intuition: The adaptive weight λ = n2/(n1+n2) hinges on self-consistency counts, which can be high for spurious but systematically wrong trajectories. The paper does not analyze when count-based weighting misguides the student or whether λ correlates with instance properties (e.g., numeric magnitude, linguistic ambiguity). A more principled routing could learn a gate over hand-engineered or learned features, or incorporate calibration (e.g., per-path likelihood/entropy, execution success, agreement between intermediate steps and answer). Practical improvements include a cost-accuracy analysis and a learned budgeted router; although Table 3 reports N=2→14 gains (66.0%→83.5%), the method could explicitly optimize the Pareto frontier by stopping early when PoT succeeds or when CoT confidence is high. Providing such intuition- and cost-aware analyses would clarify why and when mixed paths help and how to deploy them efficiently.

88.human_review: The motivation is clear and easy to understand.
88.llm_review: Clear, user-centered motivation: the paper targets a documented gap in referenceless image–text metrics—distinguishing accessibility descriptions (intended to replace images) from captions (intended to supplement). It ties this directly to accessibility impact, showing that the off-the-shelf CLIPScore correlates poorly with blind/low-vision (BLV) judgments (baseline overall correlation 0.08; imaginability 0.10), thereby justifying the need to update CLIP so that descriptions receive higher scores than captions when both are relevant.

89.human_review: The experiments align with the motivation.
89.llm_review: Experiments are well aligned with the motivation: the use of Concadia’s 96,918 (image, description, caption) triplets operationalizes the “purpose” distinction directly. The study contrasts two objectives (behavioral vs. IIT-DAS) and two adaptation methods (full fine-tuning vs. LoRA), evaluates preference for descriptions over captions on Concadia, measures zero-shot transfer on Food101/ImageNet/CIFAR100 to detect capability loss, and correlates model scores with BLV user ratings. Reporting across 5 random seeds with 95% CIs strengthens the connection between the design and the stated accessibility goal.

90.human_review: The fact that the score for description text is higher than for caption text confirms that tuning has provided discriminative power.
90.llm_review: Method description is concrete and traceable: the behavioral objective minimizes a cross-entropy loss to ensure Cθ(x_image, x_description) > Cθ(x_image, x_caption) per triplet. The IIT-DAS objective specifies an interchange intervention applied through a linear subspace Z learned via a randomly initialized orthogonal matrix ρ, pushing the model to separate content similarity from communicative purpose; the formal definition of the intervention operator DII and training details are referenced to Appendix A. Figure 1 visually clarifies a single training step, improving comprehensibility.

91.human_review: The limited drop in accuracy in the label classification task confirms that tuning has not degraded the ability to align text and images.
91.llm_review: Strong accuracy improvements on the targeted axis with quantified magnitudes: the proportion of cases where descriptions outrank captions increases from 49.4% (pretrained CLIP) to 90.3% ± 0.72 (behavioral + LoRA) and 86.6% ± 0.84 (IIT-DAS + LoRA). Alignment with BLV judgments also improves substantially—for example, overall correlation rises from 0.08 (baseline) to 0.36 ± 0.10 (behavioral + LoRA), and imaginability from 0.10 to 0.38 ± 0.12—demonstrating that the optimization target translates into the desired user-centered outcome.

92.human_review: The improved correlation between output scores and human evaluation confirms that the tuning is adapted to the evaluation of the description text.
92.llm_review: Evaluation is multi-faceted and appropriately stress-tests claims: (a) purpose sensitivity on Concadia (Desc > Cap), (b) zero-shot transfer on three downstream classification benchmarks (Food101, ImageNet, CIFAR100) to quantify retention of CLIP’s capabilities, and (c) human relevance via correlations with BLV ratings along multiple dimensions (overall and imaginability reported in the main table). All metrics are reported over 5 seeds with 95% confidence intervals, enabling readers to assess stability and effect sizes.

93.human_review: The finding that LoRa tuning is effective is generalizable and valuable information.
93.llm_review: Generalization and retention are demonstrated quantitatively: LoRA mitigates catastrophic forgetting compared to full fine-tuning, with IIT-DAS + LoRA achieving 73.6% ± 3.22 on Food101 versus 76.4% for baseline CLIP (a small drop), and 45.1% ± 3.96 on ImageNet vs. 53.6% baseline (moderate drop). The fact that the purpose signal is localized to a learned subspace Z suggests a mechanism that can transfer across tasks with reduced interference, as evidenced by better retention than full fine-tuning (e.g., ImageNet 19.5% ± 6.77 for IIT-DAS full).

94.human_review: I felt that the result showing the correlation between the gradients of the IIT-DAS-tuned model and per-token human labels might be useful in evaluating alt-texts.
94.llm_review: Good synergy between model design and evaluation: the IIT-DAS objective not only trades a small amount of purpose sensitivity (86.6% vs. ~90% for behavioral) for better transfer retention, but also yields interpretable structure. Mediated integrated gradients highlight tokens that drive the purpose distinction (e.g., in Figure 2, the proper name “Jimi Hendrix” has positive overall attribution yet negative mediated attribution, consistent with captions favoring named entities while descriptions prioritize visual content). Appendix E further reports that mediated IG correlates with human imageability/concreteness ratings, supporting the interpretability claim.

95.human_review: In the BLV user evaluation, it was understood that the correlation between the output scores of the tuned model and user preferences improved, but it was unclear how good this correlation specifically is for evaluating image-description text pairs.
95.llm_review: Some methodological specifics are underspecified in the main text, limiting reproducibility and interpretability: readers are referred to the appendix for the exact layer(s) where the intervention is applied, the dimensionality and selection of the subspace Z, and sensitivity to the orthogonal initialization ρ. The evaluation omits comparisons to alternative purpose-aware or context-aware metrics (e.g., recent context-conditioned CLIP variants), and lacks ablations isolating the effect of intervention site, subspace size, or LoRA rank—making it hard to attribute gains to specific modeling choices.

96.human_review: I think 5 ~ 10% decrease in transfer tasks is not small.
96.llm_review: Notable performance trade-offs on core tasks and limited task coverage: while IIT-DAS + LoRA preserves Food101 relatively well (73.6% ± 3.22 vs. 76.4% baseline), there are meaningful drops on ImageNet (45.1% ± 3.96 vs. 53.6%) and CIFAR100 (53.7% ± 3.80 vs. 61.5%). Behavioral + LoRA sacrifices even more transfer (e.g., Food101 64.4% ± 8.32). The human-alignment gains, though clear, remain moderate in absolute terms (e.g., overall BLV correlation 0.36 ± 0.10). Moreover, the paper does not evaluate end-to-end tasks directly tied to deployment, such as ranking real-world alt-text candidates, retrieval robustness in the wild, or effects on caption/description generation models.

97.human_review: It is better that the authors provide more analysis to support that tuned-CLIP still performs well for image-description scoring even with these drops.
97.llm_review: Analysis is insightful but could be deeper and better quantified: the mediated IG example in Figure 2 is illustrative, yet the main text provides limited quantitative evidence beyond noting correlations (details in Appendix E). There is no systematic error analysis of cases where captions justifiably should outrank descriptions or where the model fails (e.g., images where named entities are essential for accessibility). The causal interpretation of the IIT-DAS subspace as “purpose” would be stronger with additional validations (e.g., probing classifiers on Z across datasets, invariance tests across seeds/layers, or controlled counterfactuals using the unused Concadia context).

98.human_review: By training on multi-granularity instructions, ToolPlanner more closely mirrors real-world user queries, which often do not specify detailed API parameters.
98.llm_review: Parameter, Training: The paper reports concrete training and optimization details that make the setup reproducible and allow fair comparison. Backbone: LLaMA-7B; context length: 8192 tokens (motivated by long prompts in solution trees); optimizer: Adam; learning rates: 5e-5 (Stage 1 SFT), 2e-5 (Stage 2 RL); warmup ratios: 0.04/0.03; weight decay: 0.0; GPUs: 8×80GB A100; training wall-clock: ~8 hours (Stage 1) and ~30 hours (Stage 2). Data used for training is specified: 75,888 solution steps for SFT and 98,950 mined pairwise responses for RL. The inference/search hyperparameters are also fixed across methods: CoT@N with N=5 for chain decoding; depth-first tree decoding with max 2 children per node and up to 2 trees per reasoning attempt, and a cap of 12 steps per solution (each round = Thought, Action, Action Input). These details, plus the explicit ranking loss Lrank = sum min(0, P(neg) − P(pos)) with β=1 and the reward mapping R(S) ∈ {1, −1, −2, −3}, clearly document the training signals and constraints.

99.human_review: The model shows significant improvements over existing models in key performance metrics such as match rate, pass rate, and win rate.
99.llm_review: Metric, Model, Performance: The evaluation is multi-faceted and tightly aligned with the paper’s goals. A new instruction-following metric (Match) is computed at Category/Tool/API/Hybrid levels, alongside Pass Rate (successful completion within budget with a reasonable answer) and Win Rate (ToolEval preference vs. gold). On the 100-task G3 hybrid test (and multi-granularity variants), ToolPlanner achieves large, specific gains: average Match Rate 55.8% vs. ToolLLaMA-Tree 21.8% and GPT-4-Tree 28.8%; average Pass Rate 84.4% vs. ToolLLaMA-Tree 64.2% and GPT-4-Tree 61.4%; average Win Rate 77.8% vs. ToolLLaMA-Tree 71.2% and GPT-4-Tree 71.6% (Table 1). At the statement level (closest to real use), ToolPlanner attains Pass Rate 88%, exceeding GPT-4-Chain (71%) and GPT-4-Tree (67%) by 17–21 points. A case study (Figure 6) shows GPT-4 failing to perform the air-quality subtask, and ToolLLaMA miscalling a semantically similar but wrong API, while ToolPlanner executes the planned sequence (5 day forecast → Air Quality Forecast) and completes both subtasks—illustrating the benefit of the Match metric and the model’s higher task fidelity. Human instruction evaluation (Table 3) quantitatively supports the realism of coarse instructions (Statement plausibility 2.85, realness 2.94; Category plausibility 2.73, relevance 2.60, realness 2.89 on a 1–3 scale).

100.human_review: The two-stage framework with reinforcement learning allows continuous improvement based on feedback, enhancing the model’s ability to use tools effectively.
100.llm_review: Framework, Improvement, Model: The framework integrates three complementary modules—tag extraction, solution path planning, and solution tree generation—with RL fine-tuning from two feedback channels (task completion and instruction following). Each component’s impact is evidenced by ablations (Table 2): removing instruction-following feedback collapses Match Rate from 55.9% to 11.4% (−44.5 points) while still keeping Pass Rate relatively high (79.2%), proving the feedback’s centrality for adhering to user-specified tools/APIs; removing path planning drops Match Rate by 25.5 points (55.9% → 30.4%); removing tag extraction reduces all metrics (e.g., Pass 84.4% → 70.8%, Win 77.8% → 64.4%). Compared to a standard retriever, the tag extraction module yields higher precision/recall across levels (e.g., API-level F1 0.975 vs. retriever@5 F1 0.68; Hybrid-level F1 0.85 vs. retriever@5 F1 0.60; Table 4/25), supporting the design choice to condition the solver on explicit multi-level tags rather than a top-K API shortlist. Overall, the framework’s modular design and the quantitative deltas substantiate the improvement claims.

101.human_review: While the model is designed to handle a wide range of instructions, there's a risk of overfitting to specific types of queries present in the training dataset.
101.llm_review: Data, Model, Training: The data pipeline relies heavily on ToolBench G3 as seed (4,435 tasks after cleaning) and GPT-4 to generate Category/Tool/API/Statement instructions from Hybrid seeds, resulting in only 36 categories and 240 tools (Table 6), and a small official test set (100 tasks). This raises concerns about coverage and generalization beyond the ToolBench ontology. Moreover, RL pairwise responses (98,950) are mined from solution trees generated by the same SFT model, which can reinforce existing biases and failure modes. Human evaluation of instruction realism uses only 100 samples with 3 annotators and reports no inter-annotator agreement or significance tests. No cross-dataset or unseen-tool evaluation (e.g., APIBench, ToolAlpaca) is provided to demonstrate robustness of the training regime beyond the ToolBench distribution.

102.human_review: The paper mentions that the reasoning process, due to its depth-first nature, can be lengthy, which may affect real-time application efficiency.
102.llm_review: Application, Efficiency: The method is resource- and latency-heavy at inference. The paper notes each instruction may require 4–30 rounds of tool reasoning, with each round emitting Thought, Action, and Action Input and consulting long prompts that necessitate an 8192-token context window. The tree search allows up to 2 children per node and up to 2 full solution trees, potentially inflating token usage and wall-clock time. However, there is no reporting of average decoding time, token counts, or cost per task, nor a comparison to chain-only baselines under a fixed budget. Practical deployment guidance (e.g., pruning heuristics, early stopping, beam budget) is absent, limiting immediate applicability in latency- or cost-sensitive agent settings.

103.human_review: The paper lack sufficient details on the implementation of the reinforcement learning stages, specifically how the feedback mechanisms are integrated and how they influence the learning process dynamically.
103.llm_review: Detail, Implementation: There are inconsistencies and brittle choices that affect reproducibility and validity. (i) Epoch counts conflict: Section 5.2 states Stage 1 is trained for 3 epochs and Stage 2 for 2, whereas Table 5 lists Stage 1 epoch=2 and Stage 2 epoch=3. (ii) The definition of steps/rounds is occasionally confusing (e.g., “maximum number of steps for each solution is 12… Since each round contains 3 steps… the maximum number of steps for each solution is 4”), which mixes steps and rounds. (iii) The reward function’s Match constraint requires that the solution “accesses and only accesses” the specified tags, which can penalize otherwise helpful extra calls and inject label noise; there is no audit of Match/Pass label quality. (iv) Win Rate depends on ChatGPT-based ToolEval comparisons; while a small human study on answers is mentioned (Table 24), comprehensive pairwise human judgments and significance testing are missing. (v) Several crucial prompts and templates are relegated to appendices, and the data/code are promised upon acceptance, limiting current replicability.

104.human_review: Comprehensive analysis of the framework: The authors tested each loss function (subsec 5.1.1~5.1.3) and demonstrated its generalizability by applying it to multiple tasks and backbone models.
104.llm_review: Analysis, Application, Framework: The paper articulates a coherent multi-task framework that operationalizes three desiderata for cross-lingual QA retrieval—cross-lingual consistency, ranking stability, and input-size robustness—within a teacher–student training pipeline. The analysis is thorough: component-wise ablations isolate the contribution of LXLC, Lrank, and LHA; top-k retrieval analyses (R@10, MRR@10) validate ranking stability; and hierarchical (sentence/paragraph) retrieval experiments justify input-size robustness. The application relevance is demonstrated beyond retrieval via a cross-lingual MRC setup with GPT-3.5 as a reader, showing practical downstream gains with reduced token cost at paragraph level. The study also includes cross-encoder generalization (mBERT, XLM-R, mE5), and diagnostic analysis (e.g., tokenizer OOV issue on HI), indicating careful, application-oriented evaluation and reflection.

105.human_review: High performance gain: The framework achieves state-of-the-art results, verified by t-tests.
105.llm_review: Framework, Performance, Result: The proposed multi-consistency framework delivers consistent gains across multiple datasets and metrics. On cross-lingual retrieval (R@1), McCrolin surpasses prior SOTA CL-ReLKT by +1.3 (XORQA), +2.5 (XQuAD), and +1.8 (MLQA) points with significance (p<0.05), reaching a higher micro-averaged score (64.2 vs. 62.4). For top-k retrieval, it attains best average R@10 (82.8) and MRR@10 (70.1), and the inclusion of Lrank over LXLC alone improves both measures consistently. On hierarchical retrieval, it advances sentence-level R@1 from 26.5 (LXLC) to 35.3 and paragraph-level from 46.1 (LXLC) to 55.6, outperforming all baselines. Results generalize across encoders (e.g., mE5 average R@1 from 66.4 to 74.5), supporting the framework’s effectiveness and robustness.

106.human_review: Well-structured: The writing addresses the three main challenges (cross-lingual language consistency, ranking stability, and input size robustness) and provides solutions for each.
106.llm_review: Presentation, Robustness: The paper is generally well-structured, with a clear problem setup, a helpful schematic (Figure 1), and concise formalization of each loss. Experimental reporting separates component-wise and complete-system results and provides language-wise details and additional studies in the appendix. Robustness is addressed along multiple axes: across three standard cross-lingual QA datasets, different input granularities (sentence/paragraph/document), and multiple encoders; significance testing is used where applicable. The out-of-domain and encoder-transfer analyses, together with the downstream MRC study, strengthen claims of robustness and practical utility.

107.llm_review: Clarity, Contribution: While the framework is defined, some details needed for full reproducibility and for isolating the contribution are underspecified. In LXLC (Eq. 2), the roles and relative importance of the four sub-objectives (β1–β4) are not deeply motivated beyond preserving consistency; guidance on setting these weights and τ is deferred to the appendix rather than grounded in principled rationale. The translation protocol for non-English questions (quality control, error rates) and its impact on supervision are only briefly noted. The iterative teacher update scheme lacks a precise stopping criterion and analysis of stability vs. overfitting. These presentation gaps make it harder to fully parse how much each design choice contributes to the overall gains.

108.human_review: It is unclear whether the identification of the three challenges is a novel contribution, or the challenges are well-known but the solution is novel. There is a need to discuss other works according to such challenges to better contextualize this contribution.
108.llm_review: Contribution, Novelty: The core ingredients—distillation/teacher–student transfer from a dominant language, contrastive ranking, and multi-granularity alignment—are individually established in prior work. The proposed losses largely recast standard consistency/distillation and ranking objectives in a combined multi-task setup. Relative to CL-ReLKT and LKT-based approaches, the advances, while effective, appear incremental conceptually. The hierarchical alignment objective for paragraph-level invariance is a reasonable extension, but similar input-size robustness strategies have been explored in multilingual embedding and retrieval literature; the paper would benefit from a crisper positioning that pinpoints what is fundamentally new beyond composing known techniques.

109.human_review: Additionally, the three challenges are not clearly related, which may affect the focus and coherence of the paper's motivation.
109.llm_review: Motivation: The paper motivates the three desired properties, but the necessity of this particular triad and their specific formulations could be better justified against simpler alternatives (e.g., multilingual anchors beyond English, or unified multilingual ranking without explicit teacher–student discrepancy terms). The choice of English as the sole dominant anchor is pragmatic, yet the trade-offs of this asymmetry for low-resource or typologically distant languages are not deeply analyzed. Hyperparameter choices (γ, β, λ, ω, τ) and the fixed number of teacher updates (three) are tuned empirically; a stronger motivational narrative or theoretical intuition for these settings and their sensitivity would clarify why this structure is preferable.

110.human_review: Baseline Selection: The baselines should be chosen based on the answer to the previous question. Current baselines seem to only focus on cross-lingual language consistency (not sure), and that may be the reason that McCrolin achieves SOTA.
110.llm_review: Baseline: The baseline suite, while broad, omits several strong and recent multilingual dense retrievers/rerankers (e.g., mContriever/mContriever-ML, multilingual GTR, ColBERT-X/MuSR-style late interaction, cross-encoder rerankers), and the comparison to mE5 is relegated to a separate section due to data overlap concerns. This makes the main tables less directly comparable to the strongest public baselines. Moreover, fairness concerns arise from different training regimes (e.g., CORA’s end-to-end QA vs. bi-encoder retrieval) and encoder tokenization disparities (the HI OOV issue), which may skew results. A unified, compute-matched re-training of baselines (where feasible), or inclusion of competitive rerankers, would strengthen the empirical case.

111.human_review: The paper introduces a creative way to enhance the performance of large, pre-trained language models without fine-tuning them. By generating focused prompts using a smaller model, the approach maximizes the utility of LLMs in detecting communities.
111.llm_review: The paper proposes a well-scoped model and training strategy: a smaller encoder–decoder LLM (T5-Base) is first fine-tuned to generate "focus areas" and then further optimized with PPO-based reinforcement learning and curriculum learning to steer a frozen, black-box task LLM. The reward design is tailored to the objective (coverage-based community detection accuracy, entity-frequency relevance, informativeness via a learned scorer, and controlled length), and the curriculum stabilizes learning. The approach is modular, reuses strong frozen models without finetuning them, and shows consistent gains across different task LLMs (ChatGPT and Llama 2), underscoring its practicality as a prompting layer rather than a heavy model change.

112.human_review: The method is rigorously evaluated on various tasks, including community detection, bot detection, and news media profiling, using data from different platforms (Reddit and Twitter).
112.llm_review: The work leverages diverse data and evaluations aligned with the method: two Reddit community datasets (Democrats vs. Conservatives; Capitalism vs. Socialism) with temporal splits to model emerging events; a TwiBot-20-derived setup for bot vs. human communities; and a downstream fully-inductive news profiling task (factuality/bias). The evaluation emphasizes out-of-domain/time generalization, includes ablations for each reward, a human study on focus-area quality, and a demonstration that LLM-derived communities improve downstream graph-based profiling. Releasing code/data and testing on multiple LLM backends improve reproducibility and external validity.

113.human_review: Social media has a large community base, and the most important goal is to find similar communities within big data. However, the experiments in the article are not convincing enough. First, the test samples are too small (550, 232, 155), which lacks sufficient persuasive power. In such cases, fluctuations in a small number of data points can greatly impact the metrics. Secondly, the maximum user number set in the article is 6, which is too small for community detection. The authors did not prove their method's effectiveness with larger user numbers. Lastly, the additional time cost of generating focus areas during inference does not significantly improve results with the proposed method.
113.llm_review: Data construction and metrics raise concerns: subreddit membership is proxied by positive upvotes, which may be noisy and not equivalent to community alignment; the 6-user sampling creates a synthetic micro-task that may not reflect real multi-community scenarios; and user summaries are themselves LLM-generated, compounding potential bias and error. The custom Coverage metric forces prediction of a single community among six users and departs from standard community detection metrics (e.g., NMI/AMI/ARI or pairwise F1), making comparability and interpretability difficult. Experimental reporting lacks significance testing and clearer details (e.g., how 1,444 edges are derived/validated in the news task), limiting confidence in the robustness of gains.

114.human_review: The article lacks other baselines, such as using simple similarity methods to cluster user information.
114.llm_review: Baselines and methodological controls are insufficient. The paper does not compare against strong non-LLM alternatives (e.g., content-embedding clustering with SBERT/SimCSE, classical community detection like Louvain/Leiden, or inductive GNNs on user–content graphs) nor against simple LLM prompting baselines (few-shot, self-consistency, chain-of-thought, retrieval-augmented prompts) that could narrow the attribution of gains to the RL-trained prompt generator. The reliance on ChatGPT to create both training summaries and initial "gold" focus areas risks circularity and leakage. Some reward components (e.g., length) are heuristic and could encourage gaming rather than genuine discriminative focus, and the method’s behavior beyond the fixed 6-user setting is not empirically validated.

115.human_review: This paper introduces a novel approach by transitioning from VAE to AE, with a specific focus on modeling a compact latent space and preserving the language model's capabilities.
115.llm_review: The paper proposes a clear and novel approach: replacing the VAE’s fixed prior with an empirical prior estimated online from AE latent features, enabling sampling without KL constraints. The model design—layer-wise latent vectors injected at corresponding decoder layers with orthogonal regularization to encourage distinct semantic subspaces—is simple, stable to train, and directly addresses posterior collapse and prior–posterior mismatch in text VAEs.

116.human_review: The introduction of empirical prior estimation from learned latent vectors is a significant contribution. This method supports sampling during generation and addresses the challenges of simplistic prior distributions in VAE.
116.llm_review: The contribution is well articulated and methodologically supported: an AE objective augmented with orthogonal regularization, an online EMA scheme for estimating per-layer latent statistics, and a memory-style integration of latents via attention that requires no decoder changes. Ablations over regularization strength, number/position of latents, and density-estimation variants (EMA vs. diagonal/full covariance) plus analysis of active units provide evidence that the method better utilizes latent variables and eases optimization.

117.human_review: This paper presents strong empirical results, demonstrating that the proposed AE models outperform SOTA VAE-based models in terms of text quality and diversity on standard benchmarks.
117.llm_review: Benchmarks and results are strong: on Yelp and Yahoo with GPT-2-sized backbones, the method substantially reduces reconstruction perplexity and improves MAUVE and diversity metrics (Self-BLEU, Dist, JS) over strong VAE baselines (e.g., DELLA), with competitive BLEU. A small human evaluation and t-SNE visualizations further support sample quality and semantic structure, and the approach achieves these gains with fewer latent vectors than hierarchical VAE counterparts.

118.human_review: Current baseline methods (2019-2022) are somewhat outdated and lack up-to-date literature for comparison.
118.llm_review: Comparison/method/related work: the paper does not compare against or sufficiently position itself relative to regularized/ex-post density estimation AEs for text (e.g., ARAE, WAE, RAE variants) or stronger non-VAE conditional generators (e.g., tuned nucleus/temperature-controlled GPT-2, diffusion-based priors like Dior-CVAE). The absence of these baselines and a deeper related-work discussion makes it difficult to isolate the benefit of the empirical prior versus general AE design choices.

119.human_review: The methodological details, particularly the orthogonal regularization and empirical prior estimation, could be more clearly explained. Some sections are dense and may be difficult for readers to fully grasp without prior knowledge.
119.llm_review: Detail/method: several implementation specifics are under-specified, limiting reproducibility and assessment of robustness. These include whether EMA tracks per-dimension stats with bias correction or warm-up, handling of encoder drift during training, the exact definition of K in the orthogonality loss and its scaling with latent dimensionality, the precise encoder–decoder layer mapping when depths differ, and the retrieval-based empirical posterior details (pivot selection, M, distance metric, and computational overhead).

120.human_review: In the introduction section, the final part is not detailed enough. It would be useful to illustrate this further by stating which experimental results demonstrate the validity of certain aspects of the study.
120.llm_review: Experiment/result/validation: validation relies mainly on automatic metrics on relatively small datasets (100k), with limited human evaluation and no statistical significance tests. Reconstruction perplexity comparisons between deterministic AE and stochastic VAE may not be apples-to-apples, and results are sensitive to decoding choices (beam vs sampling). The work does not assess controllability/editing or demonstrate scaling to large pretraining, leaving broader impact and generalization claims untested.

121.human_review: The paper studies the important problem of knowledge editing, which is shown to be important in various practical scenarios. The challenge of knowledge editing comes with the unavailability of up-to-date information that is consistently generated in the real world. As such, it becomes paramount to constantly update knowledge in machine learning models, especially LLMs.
121.llm_review: Importance and model contribution: The paper reframes knowledge editing (KE) as alignment and introduces KDPO, a DPO-style objective tailored for sequential factual updates. Two modeling changes are concrete and meaningful for KE: (i) generating the model’s current belief as the negative completion while teacher-forcing on the target prefix y<w, which couples edits at the token level to the intended target; and (ii) optimizing a KL-regularized preference objective against a frozen reference policy to limit drift. The gradient decomposition ∇θ L_KDPO ∝ −∑_k [log πθ(t^w_k|c, y^w_<k) − log πθ(t^l_k|c, y^w_<k)] operationalizes localized push–pull on specific tokens, and the term-cancellation effect when t^l_k = t^w_k directly targets minimal-change edits. Empirically, these design choices materially improve locality without extra parameters or external memory, which is important for sustaining model quality under continual updates.

122.human_review: The paper is carefully organized. The authors include clear figures to illustrate the overall process, which helps readers understand the mechanism.
122.llm_review: Clarity and figures: The exposition is easy to follow, with precise notation and motivating examples. The paper clearly distinguishes cw versus cl conditioning and walks through chain-rule factorization of completions. Figure 1 makes the teacher-forced negative generation concrete via the Messi example, contrasting full autoregression with conditioning on y^w_<k to avoid compounding the model’s old belief. Figure 2 visually explains token-level term cancellations and which tokens are up-/down-weighted in KDPO versus DPO, directly connecting the math to the intended locality benefit. Algorithm 1 concisely summarizes the cycle/step regime for sequential edits, aligning with the text.

123.key_points: Strength: Effectiveness, Evaluation, Experiment, Metric, Performance
123.human_review: The authors conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Moreover, the performance is evaluated under various metrics to demonstrate the capability of the method.
123.llm_review: Effectiveness, evaluation, experiments, metrics, and performance: The empirical study is broad (four KE datasets: ZsRE, WikiBio, WikiData counterfact, WikiData recent; multiple models: GPT-J-6B, Qwen1.5-7B, LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3-8B; 100 and 500 sequential edits) and uses standard KE metrics (edit success, portability, locality, fluency). KDPO consistently improves locality while maintaining strong edit success. For LLaMA3-8B at 100 edits (Table 1): ZsRE locality 40.4 (KDPO) vs 14.5 (FT-L) and 4.5 (FT-M); Wiki recent locality 47.9 (KDPO) vs 24.8 (FT-M) and 21.5 (FT-L); average locality 41.7 (KDPO) vs 12.5 (FT-L) and 10.6 (FT-M). Edit success is also strong, e.g., Wiki recent 96.3 (KDPO) vs 90.4 (FT-M). On LLaMA2-7B at 100 edits, KDPO achieves average locality 50.8 vs 32.8 (FT-M) and 13.1 (FT-L), with comparable or better edit success (e.g., ZsRE 91.4). At 500 edits (Table 2), KDPO maintains advantages where baselines degrade: for LLaMA3-8B, locality 31.4 (KDPO) vs 3.5 (FT-M) and portability 44.9 (KDPO) vs 29.2 (FT-M); for LLaMA2-7B, locality 45.4 (KDPO) vs 27.3 (FT-M). General capabilities are preserved: after 500 counterfact edits on LLaMA2-7B (Table 3, right), KDPO averages 61.86 on HellaSwag/Winogrande/MMLU vs the base model’s 62.76, while vanilla DPO drops to 58.68 and ROME to 29.96, evidencing KDPO’s better retention.

124.human_review: The authors mainly use relatively small LLMs for performance evaluation. I understand that the proposed method is proposed for white-box LLMs and requires parameter updates, which makes it difficult to generalize to larger models without sufficient computational resources. This appears as a crucial disadvantage of the work, as its capability in larger models is still not validated. Especially when the black-box LLMs are unavailable, the authors should be more concerned about performance on larger models, as it is not prevalent in practice to deploy a 7-b model and update it.
124.llm_review: Evaluation, generalization, and model coverage: (1) Missing or underpowered baselines: IKE (Zheng et al., 2023) and several recent KE approaches are not included in Tables 1–2, and the paper notes some baselines failed to converge (Supp. B.1), which complicates fairness. Including IKE (non-parametric editing) would test whether KDPO’s gains persist when no weights are changed. (2) Assumptions in the method may limit generalization: the training describes K := K_w = K_l and constructs the negative with teacher-forcing on y^w_<k (Sec. 3.4–3.5). This setup presumes availability of a target completion and comparable length, and may not reflect edits that require variable-length, multi-sentence, or compositional changes. (3) Model diversity: results focus on decoder-only base models (GPT-J, Qwen1.5, LLaMA2/3). There is no evaluation on instruction-tuned chat variants (e.g., LLaMA-2-Chat) or encoder–decoder architectures (e.g., T5), reducing evidence that KDPO generalizes across commonly deployed model families. (4) Sequential edit protocol: datasets were filtered to remove repeated-subject edits; thus, the study does not stress-test conflicting or revisited entities, which are common in real maintenance scenarios.

125.human_review: As mentioned in Weakness 1, the method is not applicable to black-box LLMs, which limits its application scope.
125.llm_review: Application and deployment: KDPO requires a full reference copy (Sec. 7), doubling memory footprint—prohibitive for large models in production. The online negative generation per cycle (yl = argmax πθ(cw), then s optimization steps) adds decoding and training latency per edit, yet the paper does not report wall-clock, throughput, or GPU-hours. The reliance on target completions (for teacher forcing) assumes clean, well-formed edit strings; in realistic workflows, updates often come as structured triples or noisy text, and the paper does not evaluate robustness to such inputs. Finally, handling operational issues—conflicting edits, rollback, provenance, or safety constraints—is not discussed, limiting immediate deployability despite the strong metrics.

126.human_review: Similar to a concurrent work [1], the authors find that consistent directions exists for refusal or acceptance of a prompt.
126.llm_review: Prompt: The paper clearly defines and curates distinct prompt sets—100 harmless and 100 harmful anchors—to anchor the representation space, and it provides an explicit taxonomy of jailbreak prompts (initial, failed, succeeded). This prompt design enables an interpretable acceptance/refusal direction and supports consistent visualization and measurement across multiple attack types (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR) and several LLMs, making the prompt-centric analysis concrete and replicable.

127.human_review:
This insight is then used to propose a method to find this direction which can enhance and complement other whitebox jailbreak attacks. - This mainly involves moving the representation of current attack in the direction of the acceptance direction.

[1] Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717
127.llm_review: Method: The proposed objective—maximizing the projection of a prompt’s representation along the acceptance direction—is simple, well-specified, and orthogonal to existing white-box attacks, allowing drop-in replacement of the loss in methods like GCG and AutoDAN. The anchoring procedure and early-stopping strategy (string-matching plus LLM-based judge) are described with sufficient operational detail, improving reproducibility and offering a transparent link between geometric intuition and attack optimization.

128.human_review: The analysis mainly applies for models whose weights are accessible and thus excludes some of the frontier models.
128.llm_review: Analysis, Application, Model: The analysis hinges on last-token representations and a 2D PCA projection anchored by relatively small (100/100) prompt sets; sensitivity to the choice of layer, dimensionality, and anchor composition is not explored, raising concerns about overfitting and omitted confounders. Application-wise, the approach requires white-box access to hidden states, limiting practical utility for API-only models where jailbreaks are most consequential. Model-wise, conclusions are uneven across architectures (e.g., Gemma’s weaker separation and inconsistent trends), and the work does not demonstrate that the acceptance direction generalizes beyond the studied families or supports actionable defensive applications.

129.human_review: The optimization based approach to move the representation in the acceptance direction can lead to the prompt being unfaithful to the original intent of the i initial jailbreaking prompt and requires powerful LLM as a judge to avoid such drift in semantics.
129.llm_review: Approach, Prompt: The projection-based optimization can induce semantic drift toward off-topic prompts, and mitigation relies on heuristic early stopping using keyword matching plus a specific LLM judge, which may couple evaluation and training choices and introduce bias. Prompt-wise, the acceptance/refusal direction is learned from small, curated anchor sets and tested predominantly on AdvBench; these prompt sources may not span the diversity of real-world harmful/harmless requests or jailbreak styles, risking a narrow definition of harmfulness that limits external validity.

130.human_review: The  improvements over baseline for some models/attacks appear less significant based on the empirical results presented.
130.llm_review: Improvement, Result: Reported improvements are not uniform—while gains for GCG are substantial, AutoDAN sees mixed or degraded performance on some models (e.g., Gemma), transfer gains are minimal, and defenses (especially paraphrasing) sharply reduce ASR. Results lack uncertainty estimates or statistical tests, and key ablations (e.g., anchor set size/composition, PCA dimensionality, layer choice) are missing, making it hard to assess the robustness and generality of the claimed improvements.

131.human_review: Empirical results in section 4 do suggest there exists optimal mixture ratio for CPT, and the it aligns with expectation that the optional mixture ratio is supposed to be larger for lager models due to higher capacity. This offers confidence and insights for data mixture when continual pre-training.
131.llm_review: Data, model, and results are well-aligned and concretely supported. Data: the study pre-trains on a 220B-token general corpus (≈44% Chinese, 36% English, 20% code) and conducts CPT with an additional 20B tokens, while each domain dataset (Finance, Academic Papers) contains at least 20B tokens—enabling robust loss estimation across mixtures. Models: four Llama-like scales are covered (460M, 940M, 1.6B, 3.1B), allowing size-wise trends to be observed. Results: clear empirical patterns are reported—domain loss decreases monotonically with R, general loss first increases then decreases (Fig. 3–4), and CMR increases with model size. Using their fits, the paper predicts CMRs at Tmax=20B as 29.8% (460M), 34.9% (940M), 41.4% (1.6B), and 47.8% (3.1B) (Fig. 5). The study also shows that with R=1/4 all models satisfy the CPT objective, but with R=1/3 only 940M+ models do (Fig. 2), directly evidencing the size–CMR relationship.

132.human_review: I find the problem setup is valuable and complete. It establish a novel framework to investigate the trade-off between domain performance and general performance, and to compare various CPT strategies.
132.llm_review: A principled framework plus demonstrated predictive performance. The authors formalize CPT as minimizing F(S,R,T,λ)=LCPT_dom+λ(LCPT_gen−L_gen−ϵ) (Eq. 3), define feasible ratios via slope-based conditions ∂LΔgen/∂LΔdom≈−1/λ (Eq. 5), and identify the Critical Mixture Ratio as the maximum feasible R. They fit loss vs. mixture ratio with L(R)=α·R^s+β (Fig. 3) and loss vs. tokens with LΔdom(T)=α1·T^s1+β1 and LΔgen(T)=α2·T^s2+α3·T^s3+β2 (Eq. 6; Fig. 4), then derive T0(R,λ) to test feasibility (Eq. 7) and fit R_CMR=α4·T^s4+β3 (Eq. 8; Fig. 5). Reported fit quality includes very small ratio-prediction errors (≤0.05% in Table 2) and high R^2/low MSE for token fits (Table 3), supporting the framework’s predictive utility.

133.human_review: The paper also documents that general loss usually first increases and then decreases as the training proceeds.
133.llm_review: Training is systematically controlled to isolate the effects of the mixture ratio. Pre-training for all models uses the same 200B tokens, max LR 3e-4, batch size 512, seq length 4096, and 100k steps; CPT uses a fixed 20B-token budget (10k steps) with max LR 3e-5 and a warmup-constant schedule. Mixture ratios are swept over {1/8, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2} for Finance and extended to {1/8, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 3/4} for Academic Papers. This controlled setup, combined with consistent architectures across 460M–3.1B, enables clean cross-sectional analyses (Fig. 1–2) and reliable fitting of non-monotonic general-loss dynamics (Fig. 4).

134.human_review: The claim on the predictability of CMR is not sufficiently supported. The investigation of the fitted scaling law falls into the in-sample realm despite that generalization evaluation is conducted on academic paper domain. Different models are likely to behavior differently during CPT, but the same model on different domains is more likely behaves similarly. Therefore, the generalization evaluation reported in the paper is an easy one. However, the most valuable application of the scaling law is the generalization ability across LLMs, so that researchers can confidently apply the law to guide their CPT. Such generalization evaluation is unfortunately missed in the paper.
134.llm_review: Evaluation relies solely on validation loss; there are no downstream or task-oriented metrics to confirm that the proposed CMR actually preserves general ability and improves domain utility (e.g., no baseline comparisons on public benchmarks for general ability or domain tasks). Generalization is thin: the second domain (Academic Papers) is tested only on the 460M model, so the reported size–CMR trend (e.g., 29.8%→47.8% from 460M to 3.1B) is not validated beyond Finance. The model scale tops at 3.1B, which limits confidence in extrapolating to contemporary LLMs (7B–70B+). Moreover, Fig. 1 omits mixture ratios >1/2 in Finance, and for some curves at R=1/3 the feasibility is argued via subtle slope behavior deferred to Appendix B.2, leaving the practical detectability of such feasible trajectories underexplored.

135.human_review: The proposed scale law and reported empirical observation doesn't consider the domain heterogeneity. The domain loss and the impact on general loss can heavily depend on the target domain and composition of pre-training data.
135.llm_review: Data transparency and practical adoption are limited. The domain corpora are not released and key curation details (filtering, deduplication, licensing) are sparse, hampering reproducibility. Impact is constrained by the sensitivity of the method to hyperparameters that are not well operationalized: the tolerance ϵ is fixed at 0.05 without ablation; λ needs to be very large (authors mention solving with λ in [100, 7000]) to detect small general-loss changes; early-stopping at T0 is not demonstrated in practice. Training scope further narrows applicability: the main Finance results use a single CPT budget (20B tokens), while larger T (e.g., T=250 units ≈500B tokens in Fig. 5) is only extrapolated, not measured; the mixture grid is relatively coarse ({1/8,1/4,1/3,1/2}), leaving behavior at very low/high R underexplored under the primary setting.

136.human_review: The analyses are very well thought out, and technically sound.
136.llm_review: Analysis: The study offers a systematic mixed-methods analysis of 90 multi-turn conversations (617 turns) spanning three state-of-the-art models. It clearly operationalizes a set of nine observable steering strategies, quantifies their prevalence, reports per-model success rates, and complements the quantitative breakdown with concrete, end-to-end exemplars that trace how strategies accumulate across turns to resolve failures.

137.human_review: Having both empirical findings and theoretical findings about guiding strategies when it comes to coding is interesting and very useful for the community. It is helpful to guide code generation, and dialogue community.
137.llm_review: Findings and Theory: Empirically, the paper shows that expert Socratic feedback can convert 58% of initially failed code-generation attempts into accepted LeetCode solutions, and identifies which strategies (e.g., pointing out specific errors, specific approach instruction) are used most often. Theoretically, it frames these behaviors within Socratic Questioning (definition, elenchus, maieutic, counterfactual, dialectic), offering a coherent lens for interpreting how targeted, stage-aware feedback scaffolds model reasoning in code tasks.

138.llm_review: Presentation: The manuscript is readable and well-structured, with clear problem framing, an overview figure of the study, helpful conversation snippets, and a detailed multi-turn case study that illustrates the methodology. The inclusion of prompt templates and explicit success criteria (LeetCode acceptance) improves transparency and makes the study easy to follow.

139.human_review: The major downside of the overall work for me is that I do not see any real-world implications of this. Because the paper is using socratic strategies to guide LLMs to better code. But presents no way of making the LLMs better in the long run, nor making coders better in coding. So I do not understand overall the purpose or the main motivation behind this analysis. It is a fascinating analysis, but I am struggling to understand why it is important to advocate about how users should learn how to use LLMs and steer them towards an idea instead of the other way around, where LLMs can become more helpful tools.
139.llm_review: Analysis and Model: The comparative model analysis is undermined by confounds and missing controls (e.g., GPT-4’s ability to run code vs. Opus not executing code), unclear initial-failure filtering across models, and absent reporting of key configuration details (e.g., temperature, sampling settings, deterministic retries). The study does not provide inter-annotator agreement for coding transcripts, does not test statistical significance of differences (strategy frequencies, success rates), and does not analyze order effects or robustness across problem types, limiting the strength of model-level conclusions.

140.human_review: Overall having only an analysis without a novel algorithm or a dataset is underwhelming for an ACL-related audience. It may be more influential to pursue this paper at an HCI venue, or a cognitive science venue.
140.llm_review: Algorithm, Analysis, and Data: There is no algorithmic contribution or intervention beyond a descriptive taxonomy; the mapping from observed behaviors to Socratic categories appears post hoc and is not validated with reliability metrics. The dataset is small (8 experts, 30 problems, 90 interactions), potentially biased by expert selection and problem filtering, and lacks a novice/control group. Without causal analysis or ablations (e.g., non-Socratic guidance, scripted templates), the findings remain correlational, and the limited data/annotation detail (e.g., no released corpus or coding guide/IAA) constrains reproducibility and generalizability.

141.human_review: The paper has some strong results on the prompt-extraction benchmarks as compared with the baseline logit2prompt.
141.llm_review: Benchmark, Prompt, Result: The paper evaluates prompt inversion across both user-prompt and system-prompt regimes with concrete, large-scale, and cross-model benchmarks. For user prompts, on Instructions-2M with Llama-2 Chat (7B), output2prompt achieves 96.7 ±0.1 cosine similarity, BLEU 56.8 ±1.1, exact match 21.1 ±1.3, token F1 79.5 ±0.6 (Table 1), and maintains strong transfer without any finetuning to GPT-3.5 (93.0 ±0.2 CS), Mistral 7B Instruct (93.4 ±0.2 CS), and Gemma 2B (92.4 ±0.2 CS) with 64 outputs per prompt (Table 2). For system prompts, trained on Synthetic GPTs with GPT-3.5, zero-shot CS is 98.1 ±0.3 on in-domain, 89.9 ±0.9 on Real GPTs, and improves on Awesome-ChatGPT-Prompts from 83.9 ±0.4 to 92.0 ±0.4 after 50-shot finetuning (Table 4). Cross-LLM transfer for system prompts is also strong without finetuning: CS of 97.2 (GPT-4), 97.9 (Llama-3-70B-chat), 98.4 (Mixtral-8x22B), 97.3 (Qwen-110B) (Table 5). The paper further provides sensitivity analyses: performance increases with the number of outputs (Fig. 2), beating logit2text in cosine with only 2 outputs and in BLEU at 32 outputs, and shows robustness to prompt length with CS ≥97.4 across average lengths from 108 to 433 tokens (Table 6). Generalization to ShareGPT and Unnatural Instructions is quantified (Table 3), with Unnatural Instructions improving from 83.3 CS zero-shot to 94.6 after only 50 finetuning samples.

142.human_review: The paper addresses an important practical and commercial problem - prompt inversion. The problem is already known, but the authors have proposed a method to do it at lower complexity than one of their competing baselines logit2prompt, and lower cost than Sha and Zhang which requires all answers to be concatenated, and hence may be costly for token inference.
142.llm_review: Complexity, Method: Methodologically, the paper contributes a black-box inversion approach that needs only normal outputs (no logits, no adversarial/jailbreak queries) and introduces a sparse encoder that encodes each output independently, reducing encoder complexity from O(n^2 l^2) to O(n l^2). This design choice enables practical training: T5-base (222M) with bf16 on a single A40 (48G) completes in ~4 hours over 3 epochs using ~30k samples for user prompts (vs. logit2text’s 2M samples and 100 epochs). The method is simple to implement (concatenate per-output encodings, standard cross-attention decoding) and operationally grounded with concrete settings (N=64 outputs, temperature=1.5 for Llama-2 user prompts; four non-adversarial query templates and temperature=0.8 for system prompts). Despite the efficiency, accuracy remains high, e.g., 96.7 CS on Llama-2 Chat and strong cross-model transfer for both user and system prompts.

143.human_review: Cosine similarity as the metric of choice leaves a possibility for a large number of false positives. This artificially can inflate the metric, in my opinion. See for example Line 2 in Table 4 where BLEU is ~2, but CS is 83.9.
143.llm_review: Metric: The main evidence relies on cosine similarity using OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 and a binary LLM-as-judge metric (a GPT-4o YES/NO question about functional similarity). While CS is high (e.g., 96.7 on Llama-2 Chat; 97–98 across several LLMs for system prompts), exact match is low or drops sharply in transfer (e.g., 21.1% on Llama-2 Chat falls to 9.0% on GPT-3.5 and 6–7% on Mistral/Gemma in Table 2), and BLEU degrades on cross-model cases (31–33). Moreover, LLM Eval appears unstable: on Awesome-ChatGPT-Prompts, finetuning raises CS from 83.9 to 92.0 but LLM Eval drops from 77.2 to 57.4 (Table 4). There is no human evaluation or task-level behavioral assessment to validate that high CS reliably reflects functional cloning, risking overinterpretation of embedding-based similarity.

144.human_review: The cosine similarity of 98.2 in table 5 makes me wonder whether this is a good metric at all?
144.llm_review: Metric: Although standard errors are reported, there is no hypothesis testing across methods/models or calibration analysis mapping cosine or token F1 to downstream equivalence. Important practical questions remain unanswered, e.g., what CS threshold corresponds to acceptable cloning on held-out tasks, or how robust results are to changes in embedding model (only ada-002 is used). For user prompts on out-of-domain datasets (Table 3), BLEU is extremely low (e.g., 2.5 on ShareGPT zero-shot; 4.4 on Unnatural Instructions zero-shot), yet CS remains >80, highlighting a mismatch between surface-form and the claimed functional similarity. Without complementary metrics (task success, preference judgments, safety parity), the evidence for real functional fidelity is incomplete.

145.human_review: The inversion process is not clear. For example, there is no algorithm, or no methodology section. Please add a paragraph or algorithm on what exactly the sparse encoding method is.
145.llm_review: Algorithm, Method: The approach assumes access to many diverse outputs per prompt (N=64) and uses high temperatures (1.5 for Llama-2 Chat) plus fixed query templates for system prompts (four prompts that elicit 64 total outputs). In realistic deployments, temperature is often low/deterministic and rate-limited, and output lengths may be constrained, which could reduce diversity and degrade inversion quality (Fig. 2 shows a clear dependence on number of outputs). The method frequently produces paraphrases rather than exact reconstructions (acknowledged in Limitations), missing control tokens or in-context examples, which can be crucial for faithfully cloning behavior. The sparse encoder assumes independence across outputs; if there are cross-output dependencies (e.g., stylistic correlations), the architecture may leave performance on the table. Finally, greedy decoding is used; there is no analysis of whether more robust decoding (e.g., beam search) improves fidelity or overfits spurious phrasing.

146.human_review: Given Morris 2023a, where one is able to extract inputs from text-embedding vectors, and Morris 2023b where logits are used, given Sha and Zhang, can you add a section on the novelty. Can you compare the results with say Sha and Zhang, which I believe is a valid baseline?
146.llm_review: Baseline, Comparison, Novelty, Result: Comparisons focus on logit2text (requires logits) and jailbreak-style prompts, which sit in different threat models, making head-to-head fairness challenging. Contemporary black-box baselines like PRSA (noted as concurrent) are not reproduced, nor are simpler non-logit baselines such as retrieval over a prompt bank followed by paraphrase generation. In several transfer settings, improvements are modest or mixed (e.g., Table 2 shows CS staying >92 but BLEU ~31–33 and exact match 6–9%), which tempers claims about strong reconstruction. Without broader baselines and upper/lower bounds (e.g., oracle similarity when only 2–4 outputs are available), the incremental novelty of applying a seq2seq inverter with a sparse encoder may be under-appreciated by readers.

147.human_review: No ablations for Table 3, and Table 4.
147.llm_review: Ablation, Table: Core design choices are not fully dissected in the main text. The claimed memory/time benefits of the sparse encoder are not quantified with wall-clock/GB numbers in a consolidated table; the main comparison to full attention is relegated to the appendix, and there is no ablation on training-time parameters (number of outputs per prompt, temperature), data size (e.g., 10k vs 30k), or decoding (greedy vs beam). While Fig. 2 studies inference-time outputs, training-time ablations and query-template sensitivity (for system prompts) are missing. A compact ablation table summarizing accuracy vs. compute/memory would make the efficiency and robustness claims more convincing.

148.human_review: The researchers conduct extensive experiments across multiple models, datasets, and sampling strategies
148.llm_review: Data, experiment, and model choices are clearly specified and well-aligned. The study evaluates cross-modality transfer on two public meme benchmarks (FHM dev_seen: 246 hateful/254 non-hateful; MAMI test: 500 non-hateful, hateful count implied) and uses a large, diverse text dataset (Latent Hatred: 7,100 implicit + 1,089 explicit hate; 13,921 non-hate) as the text support set. It tests two independent 7B instruction-tuned LLMs (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and Qwen2-7B-Instruct), multiple shot counts (4/8/16), and multiple retrieval strategies (random; TF-IDF and BM25 over text vs. over rationales). To standardize inputs, all memes are captioned with the same OFA captioner, and greedy decoding is used to minimize randomness. Metrics include Accuracy and F1, and tables report 0 invalid generations in all settings, aiding reproducibility.

149.human_review: The findings suggest that text-based hate speech examples can significantly enhance multimodal hate speech detection, which could be valuable for improving content moderation systems.
149.llm_review: Findings are supported by concrete, cross-model improvements. Using the Latent Hatred (text) support set, best F1 substantially exceeds zero-shot: Mistral–MAMI rises from 0.568 (0-shot) to 0.701 (16-shot BM25 Text; +0.133), and Mistral–FHM from 0.594 to 0.658 (8-shot BM25 Text; +0.064). Qwen shows similar gains: MAMI 0.574 → 0.674 (8-shot BM25 Text or 16-shot BM25 Rationale; +0.100) and FHM 0.609 → 0.653 (8-shot BM25 Text; +0.044). Text-based demonstrations are competitive or superior to vision-language demonstrations: for Mistral, best text-support F1 beats best FHM-support F1 on both datasets (FHM: 0.658 vs. 0.635; MAMI: 0.701 vs. 0.680). For Qwen, text support beats FHM support on FHM (0.653 vs. 0.636) and matches it on MAMI (both 0.674).

150.human_review: The study provides detailed information about the models, datasets, and experimental setup, enhancing reproducibility.
150.llm_review: The design isolates the effect of support-set modality while keeping the model and input interface fixed. By converting memes to captions with a single captioner (OFA), both text and vision-language support sets enter the LLM as text, allowing direct comparison of demonstrations. Retrieval is systematically varied (TF-IDF vs. BM25; over meme text/captions vs. over rationales), and shot budgets probe scaling. Examples of controlled contrasts: on Mistral–MAMI, BM25 Text consistently dominates BM25 Rationale at the same shot count (e.g., 16-shot 0.701 vs. 0.659), and on Qwen–FHM, BM25 Text 8-shot (0.653) outperforms TF-IDF Text 8-shot (0.632), supporting conclusions about retrieval choices.

151.human_review: The study only evaluates two 7B parameter models, which may not fully represent the capabilities of larger or more diverse language models
151.llm_review: Evaluation and model baselines are too narrow for a claims-bearing study on multimodal hate detection. Only text-only LLMs are evaluated, with no comparisons to strong multimodal or task-specific baselines (e.g., fine-tuned FHM baselines, CLIP/ALBEF/ViLBERT variants, or contemporary VLMs like LLaVA/BLIP-2 for in-context inference). Without these yardsticks, it is difficult to contextualize the reported F1 gains (e.g., Mistral–MAMI +0.133) against the state of the art. Moreover, no statistical significance testing or variance analysis is provided; several settings degrade below zero-shot, underscoring the need for significance and robustness checks (e.g., Qwen–FHM 8-shot Random F1=0.581 vs. 0-shot 0.609).

152.human_review: The experiments are limited to large language models and do not include evaluations using large vision-language models, which could potentially perform better on multimodal tasks
152.llm_review: Some experimental details may confound conclusions about the contribution of demonstrations and rationales. Rationales used for retrieval and in-context exemplars are generated by Mistral and then reused for Qwen, potentially biasing retrieval in favor of Mistral’s explanation style. Retrieval over rationales often underperforms retrieval over text/captions (e.g., Mistral–MAMI 16-shot BM25 Text 0.701 vs. BM25 Rationale 0.659; Qwen–FHM 4-shot BM25 Rationale 0.587 vs. 0-shot 0.609), but there is no ablation on whether including rationales in the prompt helps or hurts. The prompt template, rationale format, and retrieval hyperparameters (e.g., k, preprocessing) are not systematically ablated. There is also no per-category analysis (e.g., FHM type-wise, MAMI subtypes) or error analysis to illuminate failure modes.

153.human_review: The study relies on a limited number of datasets, which may not fully represent the diversity of hate speech across different platforms and contexts
