153.llm_review: Data clarity and coverage issues limit interpretability and reproducibility. The paper reports inconsistent FHM counts: dev_seen is stated as 246 hateful/254 non-hateful for evaluation, yet the vision-language support set is also described as “FHM dev_seen” with 3,007 hateful and 5,493 non-hateful—numbers that resemble full training data, not dev_seen. MAMI counts also contain a likely typo (“120500 hateful and 500 non-hateful”), making the hateful count unclear. Beyond bookkeeping, coverage is narrow: FHM includes synthetic memes, and MAMI is restricted to misogyny; broader targets and real-world multimodal diversity are not evaluated. The captioner (OFA trained on MSCOCO) is out-of-domain for hateful content and may omit crucial visual cues; processed captions and rationales are not clearly slated for release.

154.human_review: The approach of converting visual information into image captions may lead to loss of important visual cues for hate speech detection
154.llm_review: The approach reframes multimodal detection as text-only classification via captioning, which weakens the central claim of cross-modality transfer. Because all inputs to the LLM are text (meme OCR text + OFA captions), the method does not test whether demonstrations help models reason over image-text interactions; it tests whether demonstrations help on a caption-augmented text proxy. Observed gains may reflect textual similarity and dataset biases rather than genuine cross-modal reasoning. Methodological novelty is limited (retrieval-augmented few-shot ICL), and it remains unclear if the conclusions hold when using actual in-context prompting of vision-language models or when visual features contradict captions.

155.human_review: This proposed method combines training on adversarial samples and in-loop repairing adversarial samples to realize better defense capability. Such an idea can enjoy the benefits from both aspects, and the single backbone model helps to reduce the computational cost.
155.llm_review: Adversarial/Method/Model/Training: The paper proposes a two-phase defense that is technically coherent and tailored to textual attacks. Phase #1 jointly trains a victim classifier and an in-model adversarial detector with an aggregated loss L = Lc + Ld + La + λ||θ||² (Eq. 2): Lc is computed only on clean data (labels for adversaries are set to ∅), Ld trains a binary adversary detector, and La is computed only on adversarial examples to avoid the well-known clean-performance degradation of adversarial training. Adversarial examples for detector training are sampled from three distinct word-level attacks (BAE, PWWS, TextFooler), enabling the detector to capture multiple perturbation patterns (Eq. 1). Phase #2 repairs only inputs flagged as adversarial (ŷ2 = 1) via perturbation defocusing: it re-injects controlled substitutions with an attacker A_PD (PWWS for efficiency and semantic stability), then selects among k = 3 candidates using feature-space cosine similarity aggregation (Eq. 6). This design both reduces unnecessary processing of natural inputs and leverages the model’s own robustness to restore labels. Empirically, RAPID achieves high detection and defense rates on BERT across datasets: e.g., on SST2, DTA = 98.62 and DFA ≈ 99.86 against TextFooler; on Amazon, DFA reaches 99.99 against TextFooler/BAE, and RPA ≈ 93.96–94.42 across attacks (Table 2). Against strong baselines, RAPID consistently yields higher repaired accuracy, e.g., on SST2 under TextFooler, RS&V’s RPA is 39.70 versus RAPID’s 89.72, and on Amazon under TextFooler, RS&V’s RPA is 55.70 versus RAPID’s 93.96 (Table 2). The authors also report a ≈2% false positive rate on clean inputs and nearly 50% reduction in defense-time cost by pre-detecting adversaries (Appendix/Table 15), underscoring practical efficiency. The method transfers to DeBERTa (Table 6), where higher inherent robustness correlates with stronger detection/defense (e.g., AGNews DTA ≈ 96.47, DFA ≈ 98.47 with PWWS), supporting the model-agnostic, plug-in claim.

156.key_points: Strength: Clarity, Description, Discussion, Experiment, Motivation
156.human_review: The paper is well-written, the description is clear and the idea is easy to follow. Sufficient discussions have been made in the Introduction section to illustrate its motivation. Extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate the difference between variants and the influence of some hyper-parameters.
156.llm_review: Clarity/Description/Discussion/Experiment/Motivation: The paper is well structured around two clearly articulated bottlenecks—semantic repair and efficiency—and explains how detection-gated repair addresses both. The workflow diagram (Figure 3) and equations (Eqs. 1–6) make the pipeline concrete: multi-attack sampling, loss decomposition, gating on ŷ2, repair via PWWS, and k = 3 candidate selection by cosine similarity. The evaluation protocol is explicit, with five metrics (NTA, ATA, DTA, DFA, RPA) computed on full test sets rather than sampled subsets. Experiments span four datasets (SST2, Amazon, AGNews, Yahoo), multiple training-time and test-time attacks (BAE, PWWS, TextFooler), generalization to unseen attacks (PSO, IGA, DEEPWORDBUG, CLARE; Table 5), and adaptive attacks using EOT (Table 4). The ablation in Table 3 quantifies the contribution of pseudo-similarity filtering (e.g., RPA drops by 1–4 points without it, such as Yahoo-PWWS: −4.02), and the DeBERTa study (Table 6) discusses dependence on base-model robustness. The paper also provides qualitative semantic analyses via cosine-similarity distributions (Figures 1 and 4) and a click-to-run demo/API, improving interpretability and reproducibility.

157.human_review: I still have some concerns about the filter strategy for repaired samples, as this strategy is equivalent to selecting the semantic center of these samples, despite it may indeed show promising performance.
157.llm_review: Performance: While strong overall, performance is not uniform across settings. On the 10-way Yahoo dataset, repaired accuracy after defense remains moderate, typically ≈69–73% (e.g., PWWS: 69.40; TF: 70.50; BAE: 73.06; Table 2), leaving a sizable robustness gap. Under adaptive attacks, RPA notably declines: on AGNews, OA→AA drops are 92.36→85.82 (PWWS), 93.64→86.61 (BAE), and 92.14→89.13 (TF); on Amazon, 99.42→93.43 (PWWS), 93.89→88.51 (BAE), and 93.96→88.75 (TF) (Table 4). Generalization to CLARE is weak across all datasets, with DTA ≈60–65% and RPA ≈52–65% (e.g., AGNews RPA 64.78, Yahoo 52.47, SST2 65.30, Amazon 62.94; Table 5). Even when detection is high, RPA on multi-class remains far from clean NTA, tempering the claim of broadly restoring semantics.

158.human_review: We can assume that different perturbations add some noises to the original texts in a fixed target direction and noises are distributed uniformly. Selecting the semantic center of these samples can eliminate the effects of these noises, or in other words, lower the diversity. I think it is not an ideal way to obtain a more robust model
158.llm_review: Model/Robustness: The method hinges on the base model’s ability to recover correct predictions once malicious perturbations are “defocused.” This assumption breaks under more subtle, grammar-preserving or semantics-preserving attacks (e.g., CLARE), where DTA and RPA both collapse (Table 5). Robustness appears tied to the attack distribution used during detector training; CLARE is not included in training and becomes a clear failure mode. The repair procedure uses a single attack algorithm (PWWS) and a small candidate set (k=3), which may be insufficient for complex edits that require sentence-level or paraphrase-level changes; adversaries could target this bottleneck by producing perturbations that PWWS cannot counteract with minimal substitutions. Although DeBERTa improves some metrics (Table 6), gains are not universal (e.g., Yahoo TF RPA ≈ 69.96 is still modest), indicating that simply upgrading the base model does not eliminate vulnerabilities.

159.human_review: I admire that the authors have added a simulated human evaluation on the repaired samples using GPT-3.5. However, RAPID seems to have limited improvement in terms of naturalness, especially compared with the semantic similarity results in Figure 4.
159.llm_review: Evaluation/Figure: The primary evidence for “semantic repair” relies on cosine similarity in the victim model’s feature space (Figures 1 and 4), which risks circularity; improvements could stem from model-specific embedding geometry rather than true semantic fidelity. No human evaluation or external semantic encoders (e.g., STS or task-agnostic LMs) are used to validate meaning preservation. Some important comparisons are missing: the paper does not report TextShield (Shen et al., 2023) results due to reproducibility, leaving out a close methodological baseline. Statistical significance is not reported. Efficiency claims (≈50% cost reduction) and LLM-based attack results are deferred to the appendix, limiting visibility of practical trade-offs in the main text. Figures (box plots) lack details like sample sizes and confidence intervals, and axis labeling ties them to the victim model’s representations, reducing the generality of the semantic claims.

160.human_review: The paper introduces PEARL, a novel black-box method to address the issue of paraphrase divergence in large language models (LLMs). PEARL takes a approach by aligning the input questions with the LLM's preferences for expressions.
160.llm_review: Approach/Method/Model/Novelty: The paper reframes paraphrase divergence as aligning inputs to a target model’s “expression preferences” and instantiates this with a black-box paraphrase generator (PEARL) trained to convert non-preferred into preferred formulations using only input–output signals from the target LLM. Concretely: (i) a seq2seq generator (FLAN-T5-L, 770M) is trained on pairs built via a Cartesian product of preferred vs non-preferred paraphrases, where preference is determined by whether the target LLM answers correctly; (ii) paraphrase-type prompting (following Wahle et al., 2023) is used during training-set construction to diversify edit operations (e.g., Change of format, Semantic-based, Change of order); (iii) semantic fidelity is enforced by BLEURT filtering with threshold θ=0.4; and (iv) identical sentence pairs are injected at ratio λ=0.2 so the generator can abstain when the input already matches model preference. The method is strictly black-box (no parameter access), composable with retrieval/prompting baselines, and provides interpretable analyses of learned preferences via paraphrase-type distributions (Figure 3), where models show marked sensitivity to Change of format and word-order changes.

161.key_points: Strength: Data, Effectiveness, Experiment, Performance, Result
161.human_review: The paper presents extensive experiments across six datasets spanning three tasks: open-domain QA, commonsense reasoning, and math word problems. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of PEARL, outperforming existing black-box tuning methods and even approaching the performance of a white-box method like LoRA.
161.llm_review: Data/Effectiveness/Experiment/Performance/Result: The evaluation spans six datasets across three tasks—open-domain QA (CompQ, WebQSP, CWQ), commonsense reasoning (CSQA, SiQA), and math word problems (SVAMP)—with greedy decoding, max new tokens=256. Against manual prompts, PEARL yields consistent absolute EM/accuracy gains on all datasets (Table 2): CompQ 27.00→29.88 (+2.88 EM), WebQSP 43.20→44.97 (+1.77), CWQ 32.71→34.78 (+2.07), CSQA 25.55→26.78 (+1.23 acc), SiQA 34.75→35.52 (+0.77 acc), SVAMP 26.00→27.20 (+1.20 EM), averaging 31.54→33.19 (+1.65 absolute; 5.23% relative). PEARL composes effectively: UPRISE improves from 33.84→35.55 on CWQ (+1.71) and 36.54→39.66 on SiQA (+3.12), and EPR from 46.31→49.24 on WebQSP (+2.93) and 33.75→36.25 on CompQ (+2.50), with average relative gains of 5.32% (UPRISE) and 5.27% (EPR). On some datasets PEARL-enhanced black-box methods meet or exceed LoRA: EPR+PEARL outperforms LoRA on CompQ (36.25 vs 32.25) and CWQ (46.46 vs 40.58), and Manual+PEARL beats LoRA on SVAMP (27.20 vs 26.30). Transferability (Table 3) shows average improvements when applying a generator trained on MPT-7B to other models: TinyLlama-1.3B 30.24→30.76 (+1.72% rel), RedPajama-3B 24.57→25.80 (+5.01%), BLOOMz-7B 24.26→27.20 (+12.12%), and MPT-30B 46.47→47.30 (+1.79%). Ablations (Table 4) substantiate design choices: removing type instructions, filtering, or identity-pair augmentation drops the average to 32.41 (−0.78), 30.58 (−2.61), and 30.96 (−2.23), respectively, with large per-dataset declines (e.g., CWQ 34.78→30.12 without filtering, −4.66). Further, Table 6 shows identity-pair augmentation halves counterproductive paraphrases (e.g., CompQ 7.88%→3.75%).

162.human_review: The paper compares PEARL with existing black-box tuning methods like UPRISE and EPR, as well as a white-box method like LoRA. However, it does not provide a comparison with other dedicated paraphrasing methods, which could be more relevant baselines for the specific task of paraphrase generation. A comparison with state-of-the-art paraphrasing techniques would help better contextualize the performance and advantages of PEARL.
162.llm_review: Baseline/Comparison/Performance: The comparison omits widely used black-box prompting baselines that often improve QA/reasoning robustness, such as chain-of-thought (CoT) and self-consistency; all target LLMs are decoded greedily without CoT, potentially understating baseline strength on CSQA/SiQA/SVAMP. Evaluation relies solely on EM/accuracy; open-domain QA typically reports F1 or alias-aware metrics to account for near-miss answers, so gains like WebQSP 43.20→44.97 (+1.77 EM) and CSQA 25.55→26.78 (+1.23 acc) may not be statistically meaningful—yet no significance testing is reported. On SVAMP, EPR is acknowledged as a mismatched baseline and performs poorly (21.60 EM), which limits the informativeness of the EPR→EPR+PEARL gain (to 23.50). Transfer experiments report average improvements but include notable per-dataset regressions (Table 3), e.g., RedPajama-3B SVAMP 12.60→10.90 (−1.70) and TinyLlama-1.3B CSQA 28.58→27.35 (−1.23), tempering the generality of the transfer claim.

163.human_review: The paper's approach is a bit strange. Instead of generating many paraphrased versions of the question and then aligning the model's predictions with them, it aims to enhance the model's ability to answer related questions by generating paraphrases. The idea behind the paper is not very intuitive.
163.llm_review: Approach/Model/Novelty: The notion of “model preference” is operationalized via correctness under paraphrases and summarized using paraphrase-type distributions, but it lacks a principled objective or theoretical grounding; e.g., Figure 3 highlights mismatches between learned and actual preferences (SVAMP: generator emphasizes Synthetic/analytic substitution while the model shows little sensitivity; CSQA exhibits the opposite), indicating imperfect preference capture. The training data construction may introduce noise and imbalance: pairs are formed via a Cartesian product P+×P− based on single-answer correctness labels and a BLEURT filter at θ=0.4, yet there is no sensitivity analysis for θ or λ=0.2, nor reporting of pair counts, raising concerns about label noise and over-representation of certain types. Despite being black-box relative to the target LLM, training one 770M generator per task (3 epochs, batch 32) is non-trivial for deployment, and no wall-clock or cost analysis is provided. Even after augmentation, counterproductive paraphrases remain non-negligible (Table 6: 3.75% on CompQ, 7.53% on CSQA, 7.7% on SVAMP), and transfer still produces regressions on some model–dataset pairs (Table 3), suggesting the learned preferences are not robustly generalizable. Overall, the novelty is incremental relative to existing input rewriting/prompt optimization paradigms, with open questions about scalability and reliability.

164.human_review: CasCoD introduces a two-step learning process that significantly mitigates the issue of spurious correlations, a common limitation in current distillation practices.
164.llm_review: The paper isolates a concrete failure mode of standard CoT distillation with specific evidence: when both are trained on the same BBH-train data, Answer-SFT outperforms Std-CoT on OOD datasets by clear margins (e.g., AGIEval 31.2 vs 21.6, ARC-E 71.6 vs 59.6, ARC-C 53.7 vs 45.1 in Table 1). Motivated by this, the authors propose a simple but well-justified reformulation—decomposing training into rationale learning (q→r) and answer learning conditioned on the rationale (q⊕r→a)—and align the inference procedure to match the two-step training. This clear problem diagnosis and targeted objective redesign make the contribution easy to understand and reproduce.

165.human_review: The method is shown to enhance the generalizability of reasoning for SLMs across various datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in both IND and OOD settings.
165.llm_review: Data/Generalization/Method: The method is evaluated in-domain on BBH (with a 4:1 BBH-train/test split) and out-of-domain on three families: BB-sub (61 BB subtasks filtered to multiple-choice/reasoning and capped at 100 instances/subtask), AGIEval (English multiple-choice subsets), and ARC-E/ARC-C (test sets). CasCoD* consistently improves over Std-CoT on OOD: BB-sub 37.0 vs 28.7 (+8.3), AGIEval 28.3 vs 21.6 (+6.7), ARC-E 70.6 vs 59.6 (+11.0), ARC-C 52.7 vs 45.1 (+7.6). It also improves in-domain on BBH-test (59.4 vs 54.2, +5.2). Against answer-only SFT, CasCoD* is comparable on OOD (e.g., better on BB-sub: 37.0 vs 33.2; slightly worse on AGIEval: 28.3 vs 31.2; ARC-E: 70.6 vs 71.6; ARC-C: 52.7 vs 53.7) while preserving the ability to generate rationales—an attractive trade-off for practitioners who need explanations.

166.human_review: The methodology is rigorously validated through extensive experiments, showing clear improvements over baseline models and previous approaches.
166.llm_review: Experiment/Method/Model/Validation: The empirical study is unusually thorough. (i) Two-step vs single-step: a CasCoD-single variant that tries to compress both objectives into one forward pass underperforms the full two-step CasCoD across all five datasets (Figure 4), showing the cascade matters. (ii) Weighting: varying α shows robust OOD gains across models even at high α, with best ranges around 0.01–0.3 (Figure 5); the main results use α=0.3 (CasCoD*). (iii) Data efficiency: CasCoD surpasses Std-CoT on OOD using only 12.5% of BBH-train by 5–7% and improves BB-sub by +6.3% with just 25% of the data (Figure 6). (iv) Model size and architecture: Gains hold for TinyLLaMA-1.1B, LLaMA2-7B/13B (Figure 3) and for CodeLLaMA-7B, LLaMA3-8B, and Mistral-7B-v0.2 (Table 3), with the 13B student on BB-sub reaching 92.7% of the teacher’s Zero-shot-CoT score. (v) Hypothesis validation: Under the “preset answer” probe, CasCoD lowers the negative impact (A) and raises the positive impact (B) relative to Std-CoT across OOD tasks, e.g., on BB-sub A: 73.3 vs 79.7 and B: 57.4 vs 47.5, reducing C from 32.2 to 15.9 (Table 2). (vi) Faithfulness: LAS measured with ChatGPT and GPT-4 simulators is higher for CasCoD than baselines (Table 4), indicating rationales more predictive of answers.

167.human_review: The success of the method heavily depends on the quality of CoTs generated by teacher models, which if flawed, could propagate errors to the student models.
167.llm_review: Method/Model: The novelty over prior multi-objective CoT distillation (e.g., Step-by-step and MT-CoT) is modest—primarily the explicit conditioning of the answer objective on the rationale and cascaded optimization. The approach depends on rule-based CoT splitting using a fixed delimiter (e.g., “Therefore, the answer is”), which may be brittle across datasets, styles, or languages, and assumes teacher CoTs adhere to this format. Training the answer step on teacher-forced rationales while inferring with model-generated rationales can introduce a distribution mismatch and cascading errors. Inference also requires two passes (q→r and q⊕r→a), increasing latency; yet the paper provides no runtime or throughput comparison against single-step baselines.

168.human_review: The selection of datasets for evaluation could inherently favor the proposed method, especially if the datasets share similar characteristics that are particularly suited to the cascading learning process.
168.llm_review: Data/Evaluation: The OOD benchmark BB-sub is constructed via keyword filtering and subsampling (61 subtasks, up to 100 instances each), which may not represent the full distribution of BIG-Bench or broader OOD reasoning. All evaluations focus on multiple-choice; generalization to open-ended or program-of-thought settings is untested. The training data retains only teacher CoTs that match ground-truth answers, creating selection bias toward “easy-to-explain” items and potentially inflating faithfulness. The paper reports single accuracies without confidence intervals or significance tests, does not vary seeds, and uses greedy decoding only, leaving robustness and stability underexplored.

169.human_review: The performance of CasCoD might be sensitive to the tuning of hyperparameters such as the loss weighting factor α, which can affect the balance between learning rationales and answers.
169.llm_review: Parameter/Performance: The method introduces an extra hyperparameter (α) and a two-stage inference pipeline, increasing tuning and compute complexity. Although α is somewhat robust on OOD, Figure 5 suggests larger models (e.g., 13B) are sensitive on in-domain performance as α approaches 0.9. The efficiency–accuracy trade-off is not quantified: CasCoD entails two forward passes per example during training and inference, but there is no report of wall-clock time, memory, or tokens/sec. Finally, while CasCoD* clearly beats Std-CoT, it does not consistently surpass Answer-SFT on OOD (AGIEval: 28.3 vs 31.2; ARC-E: 70.6 vs 71.6; ARC-C: 52.7 vs 53.7 in Table 1), raising questions about practical value when explanations are not required.

170.human_review: Novel design. Leverages visual and interaction feedback from the environment to train a reward model and applies preference optimization techniques to train LLMs using the generated reward signals.
170.llm_review: Model/Novelty/Training: The paper introduces a two-level hierarchical agent where separate LLMs handle (i) subgoal prediction and (ii) low-level actions, both expressed in a constrained, language-parameterized format (h, kh) and (l, kl). The core novelty is Environment Preference Optimization (EPO), which (a) trains an LLM-based reward model R_ρ(F, T, P) on multimodal environment feedback F (object detections, segmentations, captions, and binary interaction outcomes) unified into language, then (b) ranks candidate subgoals/actions to construct preference pairs, and (c) combines a DPO-style objective with an additional token-level alignment term: LEPO(θ) = E[−log πθ(ȗp|T)] + LD, where LD maximizes the log-probability gap between chosen and rejected responses relative to a supervised reference πsup. This explicit token-level alignment addresses format stability issues of soft-only preference optimization and is an architectural/training contribution not present in prior hierarchy-based ALFRED agents. The joint use of the same preference pipeline to train both the high-level and low-level modules is also a clean, unified training story.

171.human_review:
Extensive experiments. Demonstrates effectiveness in scenarios with limited annotated data by leveraging unannotated datasets and
shows superior performance compared to supervised fine-tuning, especially as the ratio of unannotated to annotated data increases.
171.llm_review: Data/Effectiveness/Experiment/Performance: On the ALFRED public leaderboard, the method attains SOTA across seen/unseen splits and PLW metrics. For example, Success Rate (Unseen) = 0.6235 vs. CAPEAM 0.5036 (+0.1199 absolute), and PLW-SR (Unseen) = 0.5199 vs. best prior 0.2159, indicating markedly higher efficiency. Goal-conditioned metrics also improve (e.g., PLW-GC Unseen = 0.6415 vs. Prompter 0.2622). Data-efficiency is demonstrated via labeled/unlabeled splits: in 10/90, EPO reaches 0.5091 (Unseen) vs. SFT 0.4689; in 90/10, 0.5445 vs. 0.5286, with gains persisting even at full data (0.5481 vs. 0.5383). Component ablations are informative: replacing a hand-coded low-level program with the LLM interaction module plus reward modeling and EPO yields higher Unseen SR (0.5542 vs. 0.5383) and higher Seen SR (0.50 vs. 0.40). Reward-model inputs matter: using both interaction and visual feedback improves Unseen SR to 0.5334 from 0.4397 (baseline), with interaction-only (0.5383) outperforming visual-only (0.4738), supporting the claim that multimodal feedback contributes and that interaction signals are especially discriminative.

172.llm_review: Data: The framework leverages unlabeled task specifications by converting environment observations into language (detections/segmentations via RCNN/Mask-RCNN, captions via BLIP-2 at actionable viewpoints, and binary action outcomes), enabling the LLM reward model to score candidate outputs without human labels. This yields a preference dataset at both hierarchy levels and reduces dependence on fully annotated demonstrations. The 10/90 split shows meaningful gains over SFT (0.5091 vs. 0.4689 Unseen), indicating practical scalability when annotations are scarce. Notably, the approach explicitly avoids semantic voxel maps and instead uses exploration (Appendix B) to infer object locations, increasing applicability to settings where simulator metadata is unavailable.

173.human_review: According to Table 4, visual augmentation contributed to a very limited performance gain (even worse). Further analysis is needed.
173.llm_review: Analysis/Performance: Despite strong aggregate scores, the paper lacks granular analyses that would substantiate where the gains come from. (i) No breakdown by ALFRED task families (e.g., clean/heat/cool/slice/examine/pick-place) or by subgoal type (Pickup/Put/Toggle/MoveNav), making it hard to attribute improvements to high-level decomposition vs. low-level interaction. (ii) No sensitivity or robustness tests to noisy feedback (e.g., degraded object detection, captioning errors), even though the reward model depends directly on these signals. (iii) No calibration/accuracy report for the reward model (AUC, precision/recall on positive/negative pairs), nor analysis of how preference errors affect downstream policy quality. (iv) Results are presented without variance or confidence intervals, and there are no learning curves or seed sensitivity studies, so statistical reliability and sample efficiency remain unclear.

174.human_review: Figure 3 gives a good example of using a hierarchical approach, with one LLM for subgoal decomposition and another for low-level actions. I am wondering if any quantitative evaluation on how many steps are within each task on average and how many percentage of failed (sub)tasks could be corrected in the end.
174.llm_review: Approach/Evaluation/Figure/Task: The method assumes a discrete, language-annotated action space and explicit symbolic subgoals, limiting immediate applicability to continuous-control or unstructured action spaces; this is acknowledged in Limitations but not empirically examined. Figures 1–2 are high-level and omit essential training specifics: the candidate set size n used for ranking, how negatives are constructed beyond random sampling, the precise architecture and prompting templates for R_ρ, the value of β in Eq. (3), and how πsup is obtained and used during training. The paper evaluates only on ALFRED; despite claims of generality, there is no test on other embodied simulators or real robots. Details on how exploration trajectories are generated and how exploration-induced feedback is integrated into training are deferred to the appendix, reducing reproducibility from the main text.

175.human_review: There are limited descriptions of baselines. I am not sure if it is fair to compare baselines to the proposed EPO.
175.llm_review: Baseline/Comparison: While the leaderboard table includes established ALFRED baselines (HLSM, FILM, EPA, Prompter, CAPEAM), key ablations for fair comparison are missing. There is no DPO-only variant (token-level term ablated) to isolate the marginal benefit of the proposed alignment term. No comparisons to RLHF/RLAIF or self-rewarded LMs, nor to LLM-guided agents like ELLM under matched sensing/tooling. The method benefits from object detectors, segmentation, and BLIP-2 captions and uses exploration; it is unclear whether competing baselines are allowed comparable auxiliary tools or whether information budgets are matched, which complicates fairness claims about SOTA.

176.human_review: I recommend releasing the code repository and datasets (including generated reward signals for the unannotated dataset) for reproducibility.
176.llm_review: Data: Reward-model training constructs negatives by randomly sampling incorrect outputs given (F, T), which likely yields many easy negatives; the absence of hard-negative mining (e.g., same object class family or visually/semantically similar objects) can overestimate reward-model quality and downstream EPO effectiveness. The paper does not report the size of the preference dataset (pairs per instance), the unlabeled corpus scale, or the detector/captioner noise rates, nor does it quantify label leakage risk from the labeled subset into the reward model. BLIP-2 captions are only taken at interaction viewpoints, which may bias feedback toward easy, close-range observations; the impact of this selection bias is untested. Finally, the label space mismatch issue (e.g., correcting "dog" to "statue") is shown qualitatively, but the frequency of such cases and the reward model’s reliability under label-space gaps are not measured.

177.human_review: The experiment results are explicitly effective and demonstrate the paper’s analysis, such as the correlation between the first token and the prefixed key.
177.llm_review: Analysis, Effectiveness, Experiment, Result: The paper offers a clear analytical decomposition of ROME’s update into numerator and denominator and pinpoints a concrete failure mode—mixed use of prefixed and unprefixed keys—that drives extremely small denominators in collapse cases. The experimental evidence aligns with the analysis: measuring intermediate quantities shows numerators are comparable while denominators shrink drastically in collapse cases, and enforcing key consistency (C-ROME) stabilizes models. Coupled with the simple test-time prefixing for first-token subjects, the method prevents collapse while retaining the intended edit effect for GPT-2-XL and GPT-J, demonstrating practical effectiveness supported by targeted experiments and reproducible results across multiple models.

178.human_review: C-ROME is capable of dealing with collapse cases effectively. The experiment result exemplifies that C-ROME has a significant restorative effect on the edit efficacy metric.
178.llm_review: Experiment, Metric, Result: The study employs appropriate and sensitive metrics: ME-PPL50 perplexity to detect collapse and standard CounterFact metrics (efficacy, generalization, locality) to evaluate editing quality. Experiments are run on collapse and normal subsets (HardCF and random COUNTERFACT samples), yielding consistent patterns: original ROME exhibits massive perplexity spikes on collapse cases, while C-ROME maintains near-original perplexity; adding test-time prefixes restores high efficacy on collapse cases for GPT-2-XL and GPT-J with strong locality. These results are coherent across settings and make a compelling empirical case.

179.human_review: The relationship between collapse cases and the token length of the edit question’s subject is quite interesting, which was neglected in the previous analysis.
179.llm_review: Analysis: The causal story is well-supported by a sequence of analyses: (i) algebraic inspection of the ROME update reveals the role of inconsistent keys; (ii) t-SNE visualizations highlight distributional divergence between prefixed and unprefixed keys specifically in collapse cases; (iii) identifying the first-token representation as an outlier in autoregressive models explains why collapse concentrates on single-token, sentence-initial subjects; and (iv) additional checks (e.g., Llama2’s <s> token and T5’s bidirectional encoder) corroborate the architectural link. The reasoning is coherent and traces from implementation detail to representational properties of the models.

180.human_review: The experiment of unprefixed k* and prefixed k* lacks of innovation, because the difference in their distributions is intuitive. The representations of k* with prefixes will be integrated with the random-sampled prefixes in the self-attention module. Even if their next token prediction results may be similar at the last layer, their representations still show significant differences in distribution at ROME’s edit layer (17th layer for GPT2-XL with 48 layers).
180.llm_review: Experiment: The experimental scope is limited. Most analyses and validations center on GPT-2-XL and GPT-J, with only light treatment of Llama2-7b and no evaluation on larger or more recent LLMs. The study focuses exclusively on single-edit scenarios, leaving sequential or multi-edit collapse untested. There are few ablations (e.g., prefix length/content, layers/blocks edited), limited quantitative robustness checks beyond t-SNE visuals, and no statistical significance reporting. Evaluation is also confined to COUNTERFACT/HardCF without downstream tasks, constraining external validity.

181.human_review: Compared to method ROME, method C-ROME does not present any novel changes over method ROME, indicating that this paper may lack sufficient workload.
181.llm_review: Comparison, Novelty: The core bug—mixed prefixed/unprefixed keys—was concurrently identified by prior work, and the proposed mitigation (consistent keys and test-time prefixing) is incremental rather than conceptually novel. Comparative breadth is limited: the paper does not benchmark against alternative editing methods or recent stabilizing strategies, nor does it compare to other simple fixes (e.g., regularizing the update magnitude, alternative value fitting objectives, or MEMIT-like formulations). As a result, the contribution feels more like a careful diagnosis and patch than a new editing paradigm.

182.human_review: The analysis based on Llama is not sufficiently convincing. The experimental results do not demonstrate the improvements of C-ROME on Llama, and the analysis of Llama in the paper is also questionable.
182.llm_review: Analysis, Experiment, Improvement, Result: While the first-token hypothesis is compelling, the evidence relies largely on qualitative t-SNE plots; more quantitative measures (e.g., cosine distance distributions, layer-wise divergence, CKA) would strengthen the claim. The improvement is partial: although collapse is avoided and efficacy is restored with test-time prefixing for GPT-2-XL/J, generalization gains are limited and Llama2-7b’s efficacy remains low in collapse cases. The reliance on test-time prompt modification limits practicality and may be tokenizer/model dependent. Future work should provide deeper mechanistic analysis (e.g., attention/contextualization differences for position 0, layer-wise effects), broaden model coverage, and explore training-time or objective-level fixes that improve generalization without requiring prompt engineering.

183.human_review: well written, easy to read, easy to follow, introducing the method and experiment to reader fluently.
183.llm_review: Clarity/Method/Experiment/Presentation: The paper articulates a clear hypothesis—compound syntax harms ABSA—and supports it with targeted diagnostics and a coherent method. Section 3.2 defines simple vs. compound sentences and quantifies their prevalence (e.g., Rest16: 32.63% simple / 67.37% compound) and difficulty (ASQP Rest16 recall 57.87 on simple vs. 50.21 on compound; Table 1). The approach is presented cleanly as a two-stage pipeline (Figure 3): (1) SFT to distill LLM splitting with (s, Q) supervision and LLM filtering (K=2), and (2) DPO-based preference alignment using p+/p− pairs computed via sentence-level F1 from the target ABSA model. Experiments are tied back to the hypothesis with (i) oracle-style evidence that more split candidates increase F1 (Figure 2), (ii) end-task gains across ASQP/ACOS and models (Table 2), (iii) aspect-level error analysis showing improved aspect detection (e.g., MvP Rest15 aspect-F1 76.35→77.62; Table 4), and (iv) per-sentence-type results isolating improvements on compound inputs (Table 5). The narrative is easy to follow and well cross-referenced to figures/tables.

184.human_review: the ideal is simple yet efficient, fully utilized the LLMs to enhance existing models by providing ABSA models with simplified, clearer sentences as input, the paper demonstrates that ATOSS significantly improves the performance of sentiment quadruplet extraction tasks, such as ASQP and ACOS. This highlights the substantial impact that sentence structure can have on the effectiveness of sentiment analysis.
184.llm_review: Efficiency/Model: ATOSS is plug-and-play and does not require updating ABSA model parameters; it wraps existing models (Paraphrase, MvP) and closed LLMs (GPT-3.5/4) with a lightweight T5-base splitter. This yields practical deployment flexibility: for example, GPT-4-turbo on ACOS Rest16 improves from F1 28.99 to 30.20 with ATOSS(Specific), and MvP on ASQP Rest16 improves from 61.82 to 62.25 (Table 2) without touching the ABSA models. The K=2 post-filtering keeps the splitter output concise, and the same trained splitter generalizes across tasks in a cross-task setting (ASQP-trained splitter applied to TASD shows F1 gains, e.g., ASQP→TASD on Rest16 from 71.23 to 71.33; Table 3), indicating low integration overhead and broad compatibility.

185.human_review: ATOSS is designed as a "play-and-plug" module that can be seamlessly integrated with various ABSA models, including both fine-tuned and large language models (LLMs). This allows the benefits of the sentence simplification to be leveraged without requiring any modifications to the underlying ABSA models.
185.llm_review: Complexity/Model: The model targets the specific failure mode of long-distance dependencies and coordination in compound sentences by splitting around aspect terms. This is validated with targeted analyses: compound-only F1 improves after ATOSS for multiple backbones (e.g., Paraphrase ACOS Rest16 compound F1 58.20→60.82; MvP ASQP Rest15 compound 45.72→47.31; GPT-4-turbo ASQP Rest16 compound 34.35→36.14; Table 5). Improvements are also evident in aspect identification (e.g., GPT-4-turbo ACOS Rest16 aspect-F1 62.83→63.36; Table 4), consistent with the claim that disentangling aspect–opinion scopes simplifies quad extraction. Preference alignment further tailors split formats to each model/dataset, often converting neutral or mixed effects from the general splitter into positive gains (e.g., MvP ACOS Rest16 F1 58.95 with General vs. 60.61 with Specific; Table 2).

186.human_review: the Direct preference optimization (DPO) part leads to the decrease of the generalizability of this method, a model-specific training procedure is requirement when it comes a new model. Thus the "play-and-plug" is not applicable on this method.
186.llm_review: Generalization/Training: The distillation stage conditions the teacher LLM on gold quads ("By providing the LLM with (s, Q), we guide it to split s based on ground-truth aspect terms"; §4.1), which risks overfitting to annotation schemes and creates a train–test mismatch when gold quads are unavailable at inference. Preference selection relies on sentence-level F1 from the target model to define p+/p−, entangling the splitter with specific model biases and datasets. Empirical coverage is limited to four English datasets in two domains (restaurants, laptops); there are no out-of-domain, cross-genre, or multilingual tests. Ablations are partial: while General vs. Specific is reported, there is no ablation of the gold-guided prompting, the LLM filtering (K=2), or DPO choices across datasets. Multi-seed variability and significance tests are absent, further limiting generalization claims.

187.human_review: Besides, It doesn't look like DPOs have a very big performance advantage, and their complexity is higher, also limits the generalizability of the method. I think it was there simply because the authors want to make the whole method more complex.
187.llm_review: Complexity/Generalization/Performance: The pipeline adds multiple components—LLM generation (10 candidates), LLM-based filtering, and DPO alignment—but runtime/latency and token costs are not quantified. The authors acknowledge cost concerns in §7, yet the main results lack throughput/latency measurements or cost-per-instance accounting. Performance gains are often modest and sometimes regress: e.g., Paraphrase ACOS Rest16 F1 59.46→59.14 with General (Table 2), MvP ACOS Rest16 F1 59.52→58.95 with General before improving to 60.61 with Specific, GPT-3.5 ASQP Laptop16 F1 8.35→8.18 with Specific, and GPT-4 ACOS Rest16 Pre-processing yields small increments (28.99→30.20). Many improvements are within likely noise given single-seed evaluation and no statistical testing. This raises concerns about robustness and external validity of the reported gains.

188.human_review: the method is pretty easy and simple, the workload is small too. This article is more suitable as a short paper.
188.llm_review: Complexity/Method: The method hinges on heuristic and LLM-mediated steps whose semantic faithfulness is not evaluated. LLM filtering uses hand-written criteria (Appendix B) and preferred/dispreferred selection includes tie-breaking heuristics (e.g., when scores are equal, choose the output with the most conjunctions), which have unclear theoretical justification. There is no human evaluation or automatic test to ensure that splits preserve polarity scope, negation, or coordination semantics—critical for ABSA—despite the motivating example in Figure 1 where splitting could plausibly alter the perceived sentiment of "mediocre" or the scope of "never to return." DPO hyperparameters and safeguards against semantic drift are only briefly described, limiting reproducibility and leaving open whether improvements stem from better structure or inadvertent content changes.

189.human_review: The motivation and method are sound. The expression on KGs indeed differs from daily communications. Thus, adapting the KG subgraphs via an adapter is more reasonable than simply verbalizing them via the labels. Training the adapter with DPO sounds reasonable.
189.llm_review: Motivation and Training: The paper targets a concrete gap in KGQA RAG: existing KR methods (Triple, KG-to-Text, Summary) either include irrelevant triples or miss crucial edges and rarely align the rewritten context to the question’s reasoning path. CoTKR directly addresses this by interleaving reasoning and summarization—explicitly generating xt,r (reasoning traces) and xt,k (summaries) and concatenating them as Xt = [x1,r, x1,k, ..., xt,r, xt,k] (Eq. 1), thereby filtering noise and organizing evidence along the inferred path. The training pipeline is well-justified: Stage 1 SFT uses ChatGPT-generated references to bootstrap the rewriter (Eq. 4). Stage 2 PAQAF uses QA feedback to align the rewriter’s outputs with the downstream QA model’s needs: sample M candidates per query, select two with lowest similarity, run the QA model Q to produce a1/a2, have ChatGPT judge accuracy/relevance to pick k+ vs k−, then apply DPO with the explicit objective in Eq. 5 and ratio r(x,k)=pθ*(k|x)/pθ(k|x) in Eq. 6. The augmentation step conditions ChatGPT paraphrasing on the preferred k+ and the answer entity e, explicitly encouraging inclusion of key evidence—an actionable training design to reduce omissions.

190.human_review: The experimental results demonstrate that CoTKR significantly enhances performance across various LLMs.
190.llm_review: Experiment, Model, Performance, Result: The model design—retrieval → CoTKR (reasoning–summary alternation) → QA—is validated across settings: two datasets (GrailQA: 44k/6.8k/13k; GraphQuestions: 5,166), three knowledge rewriter LLMs (Llama-2 7B, Llama-3 8B, ChatGPT), two QA models (ChatGPT, Mistral 7B), and three retrieval methods (2-Hop with 30 triples, BM25, GS). Performance gains are concrete and often sizable. Examples: with Llama-3 rewriter and ChatGPT QA on GrailQA (2-Hop), Acc improves from Triple 57.76 to CoTKR+PA 61.51 (+3.75), and EM from 44.73 to 52.67 (+7.94). With Mistral QA on GrailQA, Acc improves from Triple 54.47 to CoTKR+PA 59.31 (+4.84), EM from 43.25 to 50.24 (+6.99). On GraphQuestions with ChatGPT QA and Llama-3 rewriter, Acc rises from Summary 54.95 to CoTKR+PA 56.37 (+1.42), EM from 40.75 to 45.26 (+4.51). CoTKR+PA also matches or surpasses using ChatGPT as the rewriter: on GrailQA with ChatGPT QA, ChatGPT-rewriter CoTKR yields 59.87 Acc, while Llama-3 CoTKR+PA reaches 61.51 (+1.64). Ablations (Table 2) show PAQAF’s contribution: on GraphQuestions with ChatGPT QA and Llama-3 rewriter, Acc improves from CoTKR 53.19 → CoTKR+PA* 54.70 → CoTKR+PA 56.37, isolating PA and showing added benefit from augmentation. The retrieval study (BM25/2-Hop/GS) indicates CoTKR’s robustness across retrievers.

191.human_review: This paper is well-presented and easy to read.
191.llm_review: Presentation: The paper explains the method precisely with equations (Eqs. 1–3 for the interleaved generation; Eq. 4 SFT; Eqs. 5–6 DPO), and clear figures (Fig. 2 pipeline, Fig. 3 training framework). Empirical evidence is organized in comprehensive tables (Table 1 main results across models/datasets; Table 2 ablation on augmentation) and analyses (Fig. 4 retrieval robustness; Fig. 5 Triple vs. natural language KR comparison). Assumptions are explicit (subject entity given in §3), and the case study (Table 3) concretely shows Summary missing “Stephen Jay Gould” while CoTKR surfaces it in the first step. Limitations and ethics sections are present and specific.

192.human_review: The experimental datasets are somewhat limited, as the experiments were only conducted on GrailQA and GraphQuestions from Freebase. GraphQuestions is constructed using fixed patterns, which means the questions are less natural and diverse.  *This limitation is not very severe given that GrailQA is one of the most representative KGQA datasets in recent years.* (please refer to suggestions 1)
192.llm_review: Data and Experiment: The scope is restricted to two datasets (GrailQA and GraphQuestions) and assumes the subject/topic entity is provided (Preliminaries §3), which simplifies the task relative to end-to-end KGQA with entity linking. On GrailQA, the dev set is used for testing, potentially conflating model selection with evaluation and inflating results. Retrieval is capped at top-30 triples for 2-Hop and relies on BM25/2-Hop/GS without reporting retrieval recall or error propagation analyses, leaving open how sensitive CoTKR is to noisier or lower-recall retrievers. The training data scale is under-specified: the number of SFT pairs |DT|, candidate samples M, and preference pairs |PN| are not quantified, nor are the costs/latency of ChatGPT calls for generating references, judging QA outputs, and paraphrasing k+. PAQAF is trained per QA model (§4.2.2), implying a separate rewriter per downstream QA; cross-QA generalization and the overhead of maintaining multiple rewriters are not evaluated.

193.key_points: Weakness: Comparison, Evaluation, Experiment, Metric, Performance
193.human_review: The experiments focus solely on the effectiveness of the rewriting module, and the choice of evaluation metrics does not follow the common computation used in complex KGQA. This makes it difficult to compare the performance of the proposed method with existing KGQA approaches (please refer to suggestions 2).
193.llm_review: Comparison, Evaluation, Experiment, Metric, Performance: Baselines omit some closely related and potentially stronger comparators. EFSUM (Ko et al., 2024) is discussed as using DPO for knowledge summarization, yet the baseline labeled “Summary” is SFT-only; a DPO-tuned summarizer baseline would strengthen claims about preference alignment. Similarly, no head-to-head comparisons are shown against ReAct-style QA systems (e.g., Keqing, KD-CoT) on the same datasets. Statistical testing and confidence intervals are absent, and gains are modest or mixed in some cells: e.g., with ChatGPT QA on GraphQuestions and Llama-2 rewriter, CoTKR underperforms Summary and Triple on Acc (51.36 vs 52.94 and 55.03), only surpassing them after PA (56.78). On GrailQA with ChatGPT QA and Llama-2 rewriter, CoTKR improves Acc over Summary by only +0.5 (58.64 vs 58.14). Metrics are limited to entity-based Acc/Recall/EM; there is no human evaluation of rewritten knowledge quality or alignment to the question’s reasoning, nor breakdowns by question type/hop depth. PAQAF’s preference labels rely on ChatGPT judging QA outputs; when ChatGPT is also the QA model, this introduces evaluator–model coupling that could bias preference selection and reported performance.

194.human_review: **Comprehensive Dataset**: The OEE-CFC dataset is extensive and well-annotated, covering a wide range of event types and argument roles, including complex and shared arguments. This makes it a valuable resource for training and evaluating event extraction models.
194.llm_review: Data and Evaluation: The authors release OEE-CFC with substantial scale and clear, role-focused coverage: 4,253 documents, 17,469 events, and 44,221 arguments (Table 3). The dataset explicitly includes phenomena often missing in prior corpora—3,644 complex arguments (8.24% of all arguments) and 5,898 shared arguments (13.34%)—and even 56 shared triggers that fire multiple events. Role distribution analysis is detailed: subject+object constitute 60.43% of arguments; situational roles collectively account for 17.57%, with time/background/scope/manner dominating 77.45% of situational roles; adverbial roles comprise 16.88%, with timeAdverb and degreeAdverb frequent (Figure 3). Multi-event density is high (docs with ≥5 events = 47.86%), contrasting sharply with ChFinAnn where single-event docs dominate (70.96%) (Figure 4). Annotation quality is quantified on a shared subset (n=100 docs): overall agreement across roles 84.88% and triggers 91.2%. Evaluation is systematic: the corpus is split 7:2:1 into 2,977/851/425 samples; head-token and span F1 are reported for identification and classification; prompt variants are compared within the same PAIE framework (Table 4). The explicit continuous prompt achieves the best Span-C F1 (63.47%), improving over the noncontinuous prompt by 2.54 points (63.47 vs. 60.93), indicating that the dataset is sensitive enough to differentiate modeling choices.

195.human_review: **Novel Methodology**: The authors developed a general open event template that includes not only common roles like subject, object, and time but also more nuanced roles such as background, manner, and scope. This comprehensive approach provides a deeper understanding of event semantics and enhances the extraction process.
195.llm_review: Method and Novelty: The paper introduces a general open event template with 21 roles spanning core (e.g., Subject, Object), situational (e.g., Background, Scope, Manner, Reason, Purpose, Result, State), and adverbial categories (degree/time/scope/place/affirmative/negative/modal Adverbs) (Table 1). This schema captures semantics that typical event templates ignore. Concrete examples in Figures 1–2 illustrate why these roles matter: the manner “分别比去年同期” is crucial to interpret the magnitude of “上涨了” (S3); background “若扣除能源和食品的价格” conditions the interpretation of “低于” (S6); result “1个百分点” disambiguates the outcome of “提高了” (S8). The template also supports events as arguments (complex entities), e.g., the first “上升” event in S5 serving as the subject of “拉动,” a prominent real-world pattern in commentary. The dataset operationalizes these novelties at scale (3,644 complex arguments; 5,898 shared arguments; 56 shared triggers), going beyond entity-only argument schemas common to ACE/RAMS-like resources.

196.key_points: Strength: Application, Data, Experiment, Prompt, Result
196.human_review: **Insightful Empirical Results**: The experiments conducted using the PAIE framework and the four designed prompts demonstrate the dataset's practical significance. The explicit continuous prompt, in particular, achieved the best performance, validating the dataset's utility in real-world applications.
196.llm_review: Application, Data, Experiment, Prompt, Result: Financial commentary is rich in causality and multi-event discourse (e.g., S2’s “引起” linking “上升/上扬,” S5’s “拉动,” S8’s 把-construction complicating argument boundaries). OEE-CFC captures these characteristics (62.92% of docs contain ≥4 events; 47.86% have ≥5), making it apt for practical applications such as event graph construction and multi-event reasoning. The authors design four prompts tailored to the template: noncontinuous role lists, explicit continuous with connective wording, general continuous with SEP symbols, and an argument quantity–based ordering that follows Figure 3’s empirical distribution (Figure 5). Results on BART-Base-Chinese PAIE show that explicit connective context aids extraction: explicit continuous outperforms noncontinuous by 1.29 Head-C F1 (69.51 vs. 68.22) and 2.54 Span-C F1 (63.47 vs. 60.93), with consistent trends on identification metrics (Table 4). The quantity-based ordering is competitive (Span-C 62.29), confirming that role ordering informed by empirical frequency can improve extraction under this open schema.

197.human_review: **Detailed Annotation Process**: The dataset setup is complex and detailed, making the annotation task more challenging than traditional event extraction tasks. It's crucial to know how annotators performed their tasks and how the quality of annotation work was controlled. This aspect requires a more detailed description.
197.llm_review: Annotation, Data, Description, Task: Several presentation and task-definition issues hamper clarity and downstream use. (1) Dataset statistics are inconsistent: Table 2 (“original dataset”) lists only 4 documents, 10 sentences, and 311 tokens, which conflicts with the later main statistics of 4,253 documents and tens of thousands of events/arguments (Table 3). The paper does not reconcile this discrepancy. (2) The notion of “meaningful events” excludes syntactically central verbs such as “受,” “是,” and “需要” (Section 1), but the criteria for exclusion are not operationalized; without measurable guidelines, trigger selection risks subjectivity across annotators and domains. (3) Domain coverage is narrow: all texts come from the Forum of 50 Economists (115 articles), limiting representativeness even within finance. (4) Articles were manually split into documents to fit model windows; while helpful for modeling, this may introduce annotator-dependent segmentation and could sever cross-sentence arguments that the guidelines permit (“event subjects can be ... token segments across sentences,” Section 2.1). (5) Despite motivating event graphs and inter-event reasoning, the dataset does not annotate event-event relations (explicitly acknowledged in Limitations), and the evaluation covers only argument extraction with triggers provided by the framework—not full open event extraction (no trigger detection, no relation extraction, limited cross-sentence evaluation).

198.human_review: **Annotation Cost**: There is no mention of the cost of the annotation work. Providing information on the time and resources required for annotation would help in understanding the feasibility of replicating or extending this work.
198.llm_review: Annotation: Although the paper states it uses kappa (Sidney, 1957), it reports agreement mostly as percentages (84.88% overall; 91.2% triggers) without specifying whether these are Cohen’s κ, F1, or raw accuracy, and without per-role breakdown. This is critical because the most subjective roles—e.g., Scope vs. Manner (S6 vs. S3), Background (S6), and the seven adverb types—are where consistency is hardest. The IAA sample is 100 documents out of 4,253 (≈2.35%); there is no description of adjudication, double-annotation coverage, or how disagreements on complex phenomena (nested/shared arguments, shared triggers, multi-valued arguments (58 in Table 3), cross-sentence spans) were resolved. While Appendix D is referenced for special cases, the main text lacks concrete, rule-based decision criteria (e.g., when “以…衡量” is Scope vs. Manner), making replication and extension challenging.

199.human_review: **Inconsistent Model Development**: The abstract mentions the development of two event extraction models, but only one is discussed in detail in the subsequent sections. Clarifying this discrepancy and providing details on both models would improve the paper's coherence and completeness.
199.llm_review: Model: The empirical study centers on a single framework (PAIE with BART-Base-Chinese) and four prompt variants. There are no comparisons to strong alternatives (e.g., DyGIE/OneIE-style span/graph models, seq2seq/generative IE, instruction-tuned LLMs), no trigger detection results, and no extrinsic evaluation (e.g., event graph construction or downstream forecasting tasks). Metrics are reported only as overall head/span F1; there is no per-role performance (e.g., whether adverbial roles like timeAdverb/degreeAdverb are harder), no specific analysis for complex entities (events-as-arguments) or shared arguments/triggers, and no cross-sentence vs. intra-sentence breakdown. Error analysis is minimal, making it hard to assess where the proposed prompts help or fail, and whether the dataset’s most distinctive phenomena are effectively learned.

200.human_review: The paper's three key contributions—SN-Caption, MatchTime, and MatchVoice—are highly valuable. MatchTime offers an intuitive yet effective solution, while the design of MatchVoice is reasonable.
200.llm_review: The paper’s contributions are concrete and multi-faceted: (i) a manually re-aligned benchmark (SN-Caption-test-align) for 49 matches (3,267 video–text pairs) that exposes severe misalignment in SoccerNet-Caption (offset range −108s to +152s; mean absolute offset 16.63s); (ii) a scalable two-stage temporal alignment pipeline that first coarsely aligns via WhisperX ASR + LLaMA-3 summarization at 10s intervals and then refines alignment with a CLIP-based contrastive model; (iii) a cleaned training corpus (MatchTime) of 422 videos (29,476 pairs; 26,058 train/3,418 val); and (iv) a tailored commentary generator (MatchVoice) that leverages aligned data to achieve SOTA scores. These pieces fit together into a coherent end-to-end system for soccer commentary generation.

201.human_review: The paper statistically highlights the misalignment issue present in existing datasets and demonstrates the impact of this issue by comparing model performance with and without proper alignment. This robust evidence strengthens the necessity for accurate alignment and solidifies the motivation for the proposed task.
201.llm_review: Strong motivation, data, model, and performance evidence: The motivation is substantiated by quantitative misalignment statistics (mean absolute offset 16.63s; only 26.29% within 10s, 60.21% within 30s in the original), and a zero-shot diagnostic showing better aligned inputs improve commentary quality. The curated MatchTime is sizable (29,476 aligned pairs), and MatchVoice is simple yet effective (frozen visual encoders; 2-layer Perceiver-like temporal aggregator with 32 learnable queries; MLP to 768-d prefix tokens; LLaMA-3 decoder). On the aligned test set, MatchVoice with Baidu features achieves BLEU-1 31.42, BLEU-4 8.92, METEOR 26.12, ROUGE-L 29.66, CIDEr 38.42, GPT-score 7.08, outperforming retrained SN-Caption and its own variants trained on the unaligned data (e.g., CIDEr +4.58 over its unaligned counterpart and +14.68 over SN-Caption on aligned data).

202.human_review: The authors provide clear and detailed guidelines for human annotation, ensuring the reliability of their dataset.
202.llm_review: Annotation and data curation are described with specific procedures that improve reliability: 20 soccer fans manually aligned 49 test matches under explicit rules—(a) watch the entire match; (b) shift timestamps 1s earlier to preserve action continuity for shots/passes/fouls; (c) for replays, mark the timestamp of the event’s first occurrence. The output (3,267 pairs) serves two roles: (1) a higher-fidelity evaluation benchmark; and (2) supervision for training/validating the fine-grained alignment model (45 matches/2,975 pairs for training; 4 matches/292 pairs for eval).

203.human_review: Table 1 clearly illustrates the significant improvements achieved through both pre-processing and alignment training, aligning well with the paper’s objectives and underscoring the value of their approach.
203.llm_review: Empirical improvements are clearly documented in tables and linked to training choices: Table 1 shows the alignment pipeline reduces Avg(|Δ|) from 13.89s to 6.89s and raises the 10s-window hit rate from 35.32% to 80.73% (and 60s from 88.07% to 98.17%) on 4 unseen matches (292 samples). Table 2 shows MatchVoice improves over baselines across visual encoders when trained on MatchTime; with Baidu features, CIDEr rises from 33.84 (trained on unaligned) to 38.42 (aligned). Table 3 finds a 30s temporal window is optimal (BLEU-4 8.92, CIDEr 38.42 with alignment), and Table 4 shows monotonic gains from coarse-only (CIDEr 37.53) or fine-only (36.13) to coarse+fine (38.42). Training details—frozen encoders, aggregator depth (2), query length (32), LR 1e−4, 100 epochs on one A100—aid reproducibility and contextualize the observed gains.

204.human_review: I believe MatchVoice to be a reasonable design. However, I am also curious about exploring whether PEFT techniques, such as LoRA or other efficient methods, could serve as alternatives to the prompt-tuning approach proposed by the authors.
204.llm_review: Prompting/technique in the coarse alignment stage is under-specified and may be brittle: The pipeline relies on LLaMA-3 to (i) summarize WhisperX transcripts into 10s event descriptions and (ii) select commentary timestamps via “sentence similarities,” but the paper omits the exact prompts, similarity computation, temperature/decoding settings, tie-breaking, and thresholds. There is no ablation on the 10s summarization interval (e.g., 5s vs 15s), no comparison across LLMs (e.g., different LLaMA-3 sizes or GPT-3.5/4), and no analysis of ASR/LLM failure modes (e.g., hallucinations, non-game chatter, multilingual broadcasts). For matches without audio, the method skips coarse alignment and directly applies the fine model, but the expected degradation is not quantified. These gaps limit reproducibility and make it hard to assess robustness of the coarse stage that underpins the large-scale data cleaning.

205.human_review: Given that the soccer game commentary application is both practical and designed for human use, incorporating evaluation metrics that capture human preferences, such as BLEURT, could provide additional valuable insights into the effectiveness of the proposed solution.
205.llm_review: Evaluation and metrics do not fully capture commentary quality or generalization: Generation quality is assessed mostly with captioning metrics (BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE-L, CIDEr) and a GPT-3.5-based score; there is no human study by soccer-savvy annotators to judge event correctness, narrative quality, or professionalism. Event-level and temporal metrics (e.g., correctness of predicted event type, precision/recall of event mentions, temporal localization error of described events) are absent. Alignment quality is validated on only 4 matches (292 samples), which is small relative to the training size. All generation results are evaluated on the authors’ own re-aligned test split, which—while motivated—can introduce evaluation bias; complementary evaluation on the original SoccerNet-Caption test or a third-party set would strengthen claims. Finally, the system uses anonymized placeholders ([PLAYER], [TEAM]); entity resolution is outside scope but limits ecological validity for live commentary use-cases.

206.human_review: It supports a large number of unique watermark IDs due to its use of vocab permutation and orthogonal perturbation methods (Section 3.3).
206.llm_review: Method: The paper proposes a training-free watermarking operator that perturbs LLM logits with two keyed components—pseudorandom vocab permutation P (seeded by hπ(µ, w_{j−n+1:j−1})) and an orthogonal perturbation F1(kp) (instantiated with Fourier basis)—applied at every generation step and verified by averaging over permutations and taking an inner product with the keyed orthogonal function (Eq. 6; Fig. 2–3). This design cleanly separates watermark signal from background because permutation-averaged logits flatten while the orthogonal function remains detectable, enabling robust detection without extracting the ID. The n-gram carrier view (embedding the same signal over many overlapping windows) makes the approach resilient to partial corruption. The framework additionally supports metadata embedding by encoding kp as a Fourier frequency and extracting it with the DFT, a capability that is uncommon in prior synonym-replacement approaches.

207.human_review: Training-free and applicable across multiple text types and languages supported by LLMs (Sections 1, 3.1)
207.llm_review: Application, Model, Training: The method is training-free and model-agnostic: it operates with off-the-shelf paraphrasers (llama-2-13b-hf for articles; Phind-CodeLlama-34B-v2 for code) and does not require modifying or retraining the generator, which greatly eases deployment. It applies to multiple text types out of the box: news-like articles (C4-realnewslike) and source code (MBJSP), using task-appropriate fidelity metrics (STS for text; Pass@10 for code). For LLM data provenance (A5), the watermark survives LoRA fine-tuning of gpt2-xl on watermarked arXiv abstracts, achieving AUROC ≈ 1.0 after ~100 black-box queries even when mixing data from up to 100 clients (Fig. 6). Verification is extremely efficient (0.035 s per document on a 16-core CPU; Table 2), enabling web-scale scanning workflows.

208.human_review: High robust verifiability even after various attacks, such as paraphrasing and translation, which are often common to LLM-generated text (Section 4.1, 4.2).
208.llm_review: Robustness: The method maintains high verifiability across diverse attacks. Pre-attack AUROC reaches 0.992 at STS 0.887 with κ=6 (Fig. 4a). Under A2 translation and paraphrasing, AUROC remains 0.951 (A2-T) and 0.881 (A2-P), substantially above M-BIT (0.567/0.363) and P-NLW (0.475/0.508) per Table 1. For overlapping watermark attacks (A3), the first watermark remains verifiable due to orthogonal signals and permutation keys, whereas both baselines are overwritten (Table 1 and Sec. 4.1). Against edit attacks (A1), AUROC shows only slight degradation even at 20% insert/delete/substitute rates (Fig. 5), contrasting the steep declines for baselines. In provenance (A5), the watermark is detectable after fine-tuning with AUROC approaching 1.0 by aggregating ~100 queries (Fig. 6), indicating signal persistence through model training.

209.human_review: Embedding and extraction of metadata, providing additional utility in verifying the provenance of text (Section 4.1, Metadata Extraction).
209.llm_review: Data: Empirical coverage is broad and uses appropriate metrics and baselines. Text ownership is evaluated on C4-realnewslike (mean length ~412 tokens) with STS fidelity and AUROC detection, comparing to M-BIT and P-NLW; code watermarking uses MBJSP with Pass@10 and compares to SRCMARKER (Table 3). The provenance setup fine-tunes gpt2-xl (LoRA) on 4,000 watermarked arXiv abstracts per topic across up to 100 topics/clients, then tests detection from 100-token generations (Fig. 6). Ablations quantify the fidelity–verifiability Pareto via κ (Fig. 4a), length effects (AUROC ≈ 0.98 at 100 tokens; Fig. 4b), metadata extraction accuracy (≈48% to ≈99% by aggregating 1 to 5 texts at κ=6; Fig. 4c; random guess 0.003125%), and ID confusion (1st percentile AUROC for 1,000 non-matching IDs: 0.976 for this method vs 0.614/0.766 for M-BIT/P-NLW). Compute profiling shows very fast CPU-only verification (0.035 s), and overall more practical verification costs than baselines (Table 2).

210.human_review: The framework may not be applicable to text types where format or style is critical, such as poetry or very short texts (Section 7).
210.llm_review: Application, Framework: (1) Applicability is constrained to content where paraphrasing is acceptable; the paper itself notes limitations for style-critical or format-critical text (e.g., poems, anthems) and very short text (Sec. 7). (2) Despite claims of generality to multiple languages or to transformations like speech or handwriting, the experiments are limited to English text and code; no multilingual or TTS/ASR round-trips are evaluated, so cross-modality robustness remains unsubstantiated. (3) Deployment aspects are only lightly discussed (Appendix L): large-scale key/ID management, threshold calibration for low false positives at web scale, and policies for legal-grade verification are not empirically demonstrated. (4) Watermarking latency is higher than M-BIT (24.8 s vs 2.97 s per document; Table 2), which could matter for high-throughput publishers unless amortized or parallelized.

211.human_review: The performance depends on the capabilities of the LLMs used for paraphrasing, which may limit its performance with less advanced models (Section 7).
211.llm_review: Model, Performance: (1) The text fidelity drops relative to synonym-based baselines: at κ=6 the method’s STS is 0.887 vs M-BIT 0.998 and P-NLW 0.942 (Sec. 4.1), and the paper reports noticeable linguistic errors for the baselines but provides no human evaluation of meaning preservation or fluency for its own paraphrased outputs. (2) For code, Pass@10 decreases from 0.984 (SRCMARKER) to 0.969 (this method) while detection improves (Table 3), but there is no deeper analysis of failure cases (e.g., which unit tests fail) or robustness across languages beyond brief Python results in the appendix. (3) The robustness suite omits strong editorial operations such as summarization/expansion, style transfer, cross-lingual paraphrasing with compression, or adversarial paraphrasers explicitly minimizing the verification score; hence real-world worst cases remain unclear. (4) There appears to be an inconsistency around A4 in-context prompting: the narrative claims the watermark remains verifiable while baselines fail, but Table 1’s A4 column is ambiguous (values shown as 0. for some rows), and no detailed setup/results are provided, making it hard to assess reliability under A4.

212.human_review: Large scale deployment studies: While the framework is designed to be scalable, actual large-scale deployment might require additional considerations for managing and verifying a large number of watermark IDs (Section 4.1, Scalability).
212.llm_review: Framework: (1) The capacity claim |F1|·|V|! (e.g., with |V|≈32k and a Fourier basis) is a combinatorial upper bound; practical capacity under finite text length, target AUROC, and stringent false-positive control across many hypotheses is not quantified. (2) The verification is presented as a single-score threshold test; there is no formal multiple-hypothesis testing or calibration procedure to control family-wise error when scanning millions of documents against many IDs. (3) Security is assessed empirically; there is no analysis of informed adversaries who can optimize paraphrases to minimize the inner product score while preserving meaning or who can exploit the deterministic dependence on hπ(µ, n−gram context). (4) Hyperparameters such as n (n-gram size) and κ (perturbation magnitude), and the choice of orthogonal basis are selected empirically without guidance or theoretical criteria relating them to detection power, text length, and target FPR, limiting reproducible deployment tuning.

213.human_review: The paper tackles an important research question. It addresses a significant gap in understanding how large language models (LLMs) encode and adapt to task-specific information through instruction tuning. It contributes by identifying distinct layers in LLMs where general to task-specific transitions occur, which extends the understanding of multi-task learning mechanisms
213.llm_review: Contribution, Model, Task: The paper makes a concrete representational contribution by identifying three functional layer regimes in an instruction-tuned Llama 2-7B (32 layers): shared layers (1–9) where CKA to single-task controls is lower for Llama 2-SFT than for the pre-trained model, transition layers (10–15) where Llama 2-SFT’s CKA sharply increases and closely matches single-task controls across many tasks, and refinement layers (16–32) where high similarity is maintained. This mapping is repeatedly evidenced in Figures 2–5 and 6 (rise then saturation), and is shown to be especially pronounced for clusters like structured-to-text, translation, and summarization that require non-trivial transformations, providing actionable guidance for where to place/adapt parameters for PEFT or MTL.

214.human_review: The paper conducts experiments across a wide range of over 60 NLP tasks, using the Flan dataset, which encompasses both language understanding and generation tasks
214.llm_review: Data, Experiment, Task: The study uses the Flan 2021 mixture spanning 60+ datasets grouped into 12 task clusters with 10 instruction templates per dataset, capped at 50k examples per cluster and a mixing rate capped at 3,000 per task to control imbalance. The experimental protocol compares a multi-task instruction-tuned model (LoRA r=8; 100k steps) against 60+ single-task controls (10k steps each) via MOSSA and linear-CKA on last-token representations across all 32 layers. Evidence is triangulated by: (i) layerwise CKA distributions for all tasks (Figure 2), (ii) per-cluster CKA (Figure 3; e.g., higher pretrain CKA for sentiment/paraphrase vs. low for coreference/translation that rises under SFT), (iii) t-SNE separability gains in layers 10–15 and beyond (Figure 4), (iv) PCA dimensionality increases around layers 10–15 for SFT (Figure 5), (v) positive correlations with readability indices peaking in 10–15 (Figure 6), and (vi) held-out unseen tasks where SFT surpasses pretrain in mid/high layers (Figure 7). This breadth across tasks and analyses substantiates the claims.

215.human_review: Figure 3 is very interesting and conveys the idea clearly.
215.llm_review: Clarity, Figure: The paper’s presentation is precise: the CKA formula and centering steps are fully specified, the modeling setup (Llama 2-7B, LoRA r=8) and data curation (cluster caps and mixing limits) are explicit, and each figure advances a specific claim. Figure 1 cleanly summarizes the 1–9/10–15/16–32 layer mapping. Figure 2’s boxplots clearly contrast pretrain vs SFT across layers. Figure 3’s cluster-wise panels show concrete differences (e.g., high SFT CKA for translation in layers 10–32). Figure 4 demonstrates increased cluster separation for SFT particularly at layers 10 and 15. Figure 5 quantifies variance with the 99% PCA component counts, peaking for SFT in transition layers. Figures 6a–b show the rise and saturation of correlations with Flesch–Kincaid and Coleman–Liau specifically between layers 10–15. Figure 7 makes the unseen-task behavior explicit. Appendix B.2’s full results and the data-size control (Fig. 10) further improve transparency.

216.human_review: Nor the acronym nor the technique were mentioned in the cited paper technique called Model-Oriented Sub-population and Spectral Anal ysis (MOSSA (MOSSA; Zhao et al. 2022),
216.llm_review: Technique: The analysis hinges on linear-kernel CKA of last-token representations to infer task-specific knowledge, which may not fully capture functional equivalence or non-linear representational relations. There is no robustness check with alternative similarity measures (e.g., PWCCA/SVCCA/CKA with RBF) or representation choices (e.g., mean-pooled token states, attention outputs). t-SNE is interpreted qualitatively without quantitative separability metrics (e.g., silhouette, Davies–Bouldin). The proposed layer mapping is not stress-tested with causal interventions such as layer ablations, layer-swapping between models, or freezing/perturbing specific layer groups. Finally, only LoRA updates are trained; without full fine-tuning or varying LoRA ranks/adapter placements, it is unclear whether the observed transitions reflect intrinsic model behavior or LoRA’s inductive biases.

217.human_review: The assumption of uniform data size and the use of single-task control models might oversimplify real-world scenarios where task datasets vary significantly in size and complexity.
217.llm_review: Complexity, Data, Model, Task: The three-phase layer partition may be specific to the 32-layer Llama 2-7B under LoRA r=8 and the Flan 2021 distribution. The data scope excludes code, long-context reasoning, and multimodal tasks; even within NLP, sampling caps (50k per cluster, 3k per task) and cluster heterogeneity could shift where transitions appear. Only seven held-out tasks are evaluated; the authors themselves note that transition layers are not identifiable for the unseen setup due to high variance, limiting universality. The readability correlations could be confounded by stylistic or length artifacts rather than task complexity per se. Without testing other sizes (e.g., 13B/70B) or families, it is difficult to claim that layers 10–15 are transition layers beyond this configuration.

218.human_review: While the study compares Llama 2-SFT with task-specific fine-tuned control models, it might benefit from additional comparisons with other state-of-the-art models or broader benchmarks to validate its findings across different settings.
218.llm_review: Benchmark, Comparison, Model: The work does not connect representational findings to standard performance benchmarks (e.g., GLUE, SuperGLUE, MTEB, WMT) to validate that higher CKA alignment with single-task controls correlates with better end-task accuracy. There are no cross-model comparisons (e.g., Mistral, GPT-NeoX) or cross-size analyses within Llama 2, and no comparison of LoRA vs full fine-tuning to calibrate the observed effects. Robustness to alternative similarity metrics (PWCCA/SVCCA) or to different input kernels is not reported, and direct quantitative comparisons to prior representation studies are limited, weakening external validity.
