The method is plug-and-play (no model retraining), and while standard MBR is O(n^2), the paper also examines lower-complexity variants (rerank and two-stage pipelines) that preserve much of the benefit. Empirically, the approach delivers consistent gains across three conditional generation tasks, with substantial improvements at practical candidate set sizes (e.g., up to +7.3 pass@1 on HumanEval, +5 LENS on SimpEval, and +1.0 COMET on WMT22 EN–CS).

286.human_review: The authors provide exhaustive empirical results to support the effectiveness of the proposed approach. I especially appreciate the wide coverage of tasks and metrics including lexical, neural, and execution-based ones.
286.llm_review: Effectiveness/Metric/Result: The effectiveness is validated rigorously across multiple utility and evaluation metrics, including reference-based (LENS, COMET) and reference-free (LENS-SALSA, COMET-QE) metrics, as well as large learned metrics (XCOMET, METRICX). Cross-metric evaluation (Table 3) shows that using one utility metric often yields improvements when evaluated by others, mitigating concerns of metric overfitting. Statistical significance tests (bootstrap) are reported for key comparisons, strengthening the credibility of the results.

287.human_review: The paper writing is clear. Figure 3 provides a good motivation of the proposal, and all the illustrations are well-polished.
287.llm_review: Figure/Motivation/Presentation: The figures strongly motivate and support the core idea. Figure 3 compellingly demonstrates that different prompts induce distinct candidate modes and that no single prompt dominates across inputs. Figure 4 connects diversity to quality as temperature varies, clarifying where multi-prompt adds value. Figures 1, 5, and 6 clearly visualize gains across candidate sizes, models, and MBR variants, making the narrative easy to follow.

288.human_review: Compared to the previous version, the authors have corrected several unfair comparison settings, clarified ambiguities in the writing, added statistical testing, and provided more comprehensive results. Overall the argument is well supported.
288.llm_review: Comparison/Presentation/Result: The paper presents broad and transparent comparisons: (i) multi-prompt vs single-prompt MBR, (ii) ablations over prompt sampling/selection (random, top-p, similarity, cluster-based), and (iii) comparisons against task-specific SOTA systems. Results are reported across open and closed models, with consistent improvements and multiple candidate set sizes, and are accompanied by significance testing and detailed appendices—facilitating fair interpretation.

289.human_review: Can you provide a comparison between human-written prompts and the prompts rephrased by GPT-4? Do you see significant performance differences between the two? If so, why not also add the human-written prompts in the prompt pool for multi-prompt MBR?
289.llm_review: Comparison/Performance/Prompt: 1) The prompt-related baselines are limited: comparisons to stronger single-prompt optimization methods (e.g., iterative LLM-driven prompt rewriting/selection, retrieval-based in-context example selection beyond simple k-NN clustering, or recent automatic prompt engineering systems) are missing, making it hard to bound how far a well-optimized single prompt could go relative to multi-prompt. 2) The prompt bank construction mostly uses paraphrasing and simple similarity heuristics; broader prompt variations (formatting, instruction structure, richer ICL retrieval strategies) are acknowledged but not evaluated, leaving open whether the gains persist or grow under more competitive prompt design. 3) Some reported gains diminish for stronger models (e.g., GPT-4), so it remains unclear how multi-prompt compares against state-of-the-art prompt optimization under high-capability regimes.

290.human_review:
This problem may be related to MBR in general, but can you talk to the budget vs. performance of MBR versus other types of decoding approaches? When scaling up the number of tokens generated per instance, does MBR has a unique advantage over approaches like self-consistency or tree-of-thoughts? [1]

[1] Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies. Wang et al., 2024.
290.llm_review: Performance: While gains are consistent, they are sometimes modest for strong models (e.g., GPT-4: +0.23 COMET EN–CS, +1.22 pass@1 on HumanEval), and cross-metric results show occasional regressions or negligible improvements (Table 3, especially with certain trained vs overlap metrics). Effect sizes often require sizable candidate sets, and performance can degrade at high temperatures, indicating sensitivity to decoding and metric choices.

291.human_review: The proposed data synthesis method is reasonable and effective. It is novel to compose two simple questions into a complex one with the constraint that the queried objects are close. The process does not need much human labor and can generate correct complex questions as shown by manual inspection.
291.llm_review: Novelty/Method/Data/Effectiveness: The paper introduces a least-to-most visual reasoning paradigm that explicitly interleaves question decomposition with tool use (Grounding, Highlight, OCR, Answer), which is a fresh and well-formalized take for VLMs. Methodologically, the bottom-up least-to-most synthesis pipeline (entity recognition → node construction → reasoning path → question synthesis) is clearly specified, modular, and relies almost entirely on open-source components, yielding a reproducible and cost-efficient way to create multi-step visual reasoning data. On the data side, the resulting 50k-example VIREO corpus includes explicit multi-step paths, aligning training signals with the proposed reasoning behavior. Empirically, the plug-and-play reasoner trained on VIREO consistently improves multiple off-the-shelf VLMs across diverse VQA tasks (GQA, TextVQA, ST-VQA, TallyQA), with especially strong gains for counting and OCR-heavy cases, supporting the effectiveness of the approach.

292.human_review: The generated sample is effective. VLMs trained with these samples achieve improvements across different datasets, especially on TallyQA.
292.llm_review: Data/Improvement: VIREO contributes a sizable and targeted dataset focused on multi-step visual reasoning with explicit intermediate steps, produced via a cost-effective, reproducible pipeline. The data spans single-entity, grouped-entity, and whole-image levels, enabling the model to learn both fine-grained and relational reasoning. The improvements are consistent across four distinct VLM backbones and several benchmarks, with absolute gains ranging from roughly 0.7 to nearly 39 points (notably large on TallyQA), indicating that the synthesized data transfers well and yields practical, architecture-agnostic gains without harming performance on unrelated tasks (MMMU, POPE).

293.human_review: The major problem is the paper neglects similar works. Visual programming also intends to decompose main questions and invoke tools to solve sub-ones. There are many works in this field and can invoke more tools such as search engines. The paper should include these works in the related section and compare their performance.
293.llm_review: Comparison/Performance/Related Work: (1) Comparison: The study lacks head-to-head comparisons against closely related tool-augmented or programmatic visual reasoning systems (e.g., MM-ReAct-style pipelines, VisProg, ViperGPT, visual CoT/ToT controllers) and against top-down GPT-4V/Gemini-generated reasoning data or controllers, making it hard to assess relative positioning. (2) Performance: While improvements are consistent, absolute performance on ST-VQA remains modest, and GQA gains are relatively small for weaker models; the choice of answer recall (instead of exact match/official metrics) for some datasets may inflate perceived improvements. LLaVA results on ST-VQA are omitted due to evaluation issues, preventing a full cross-model comparison. (3) Related Work: The discussion under-references and under-differentiates from prior multimodal CoT/ToT, program-of-thought, and modular visual reasoning literature, limiting clarity on what is fundamentally new in the problem formulation versus prior controllers and tool-use frameworks.

294.human_review: The synthesis reasoning route seems to be a chain instead of other complex structures such as tree. The tools can not use the sub-output several steps before. The minor improvements on GQA may indicate this problem.
294.llm_review: Improvement/Method: (1) Attribution of gains: Improvements may largely stem from external tools (OCR/Highlight/Grounding) rather than the decomposition policy itself; there is no thorough ablation isolating the contribution of each tool, or evaluating a decomposition-only variant without tools. (2) Methodological limitations: The data quality study is small (n=200) and reports 100% correctness across criteria, which seems optimistic; a larger, more nuanced audit would strengthen claims. The synthesis pipeline hinges on specific detectors/captioners and COCO-2014 imagery, which may inject biases and limit diversity/coverage. The approach is only "almost" open-source since Questioner/Combiner are trained from GPT-4 outputs, introducing a proprietary dependency. Inference-time overhead/latency for the plug-and-play controller is not reported, nor are robustness/sensitivity analyses to the tool set or failure recovery. Finally, improvements beyond VQA appear limited (e.g., minimal gains on MMMU), raising questions about the breadth of practical impact.

295.human_review: Well-organized and clearly written paper that provides a detailed analysis of existing attribution methods' shortcomings.
295.llm_review: Clear two-step analysis and method: the paper precisely defines context-sensitive token identification (CTI) by measuring KL divergence between Pi_ctx and Pi_no-ctx for each generated token (Eq. 1), and contextual cue imputation (CCI) via contrastive gradient saliency that subtracts gradients on p(yi) vs p(y*i) (Eq. 2). It then aggregates token-level attributions to document- and sentence-level citations (Eq. 5). The analysis includes concrete selector designs (m* calibration vs example-level m + sigma, Top-K vs Top-% CCI), and reports robustness of Top-% thresholds (3–20%) with stable agreement on XOR-AttriQA (Fig. 3), plus qualitative case studies that reveal when MIRAGE tracks actual context use versus surface similarity.

296.human_review: Introduces MIRAGE, a novel approach leveraging model internals for answer attribution, offering better interpretability and controllability.
296.llm_review: Approach, interpretation, model, novelty: MIRAGE adapts PEC ORE from MT to RAG AA and operationalizes an internals-based, plug-and-play pipeline that maps specific answer tokens to specific source tokens/documents. This yields interpretable, fine-grained evidence (e.g., Fig. 4 highlights Top-5% tokens in the correct document for predicting the numeral '9') and avoids instruction-following failures of self-citation (Table 4, where self-citation outputs [∅] while MIRAGE correctly cites Doc [1] for both sentences). The method targets faithfulness by directly leveraging the model’s computations rather than post-hoc entailment, and works across open-weight models (mT5/CORA, LLaMA 2 7B Chat, Zephyr β7B).

297.human_review: Thoroughly evaluated on multilingual datasets and against human-produced annotations, showing promising results.
297.llm_review: Strong data coverage and concrete results: On XOR-AttriQA match (142/1144 calibration/test examples), MIRAGE CAL Top 5% averages 86.7% agreement with human AA vs 84.2% for NLI MT (TRUE with MT), and vastly outperforms NLI ORIG (avg 68.0% with large language variance). The uncalibrated MIRAGE EX Top 5% averages 83.4%, showing strong performance without extra data or MT. On ELI5, using TRUE-based ALCE evaluation, MIRAGE EX Top 5% improves Zephyr β citation F1 from 30.6 (self-citation) to 45.6, with both precision (41.4 to 44.7) and recall (24.3 to 46.5) gains; for LLaMA 2, F1 rises from 26.0 to 27.6, with recall increasing from 19.8 to 29.1.

298.human_review: Efficient method that doesn't require additional training or external validation models.
298.llm_review: Method, model, training efficiency: The approach is training-free and model-agnostic, requiring only access to gradients. It eliminates the need for an 11B NLI model (TRUE) and a machine translation step used by NLI MT, and avoids instruction-following fragility of self-citation. By attributing only context-sensitive tokens (via m* thresholds), it confines gradient computations to informative positions and reduces the number of comparisons relative to entailment methods that score every sentence-document pair.

299.human_review: Demonstrates comparable performance to self-citation methods while offering finer-grained control over attribution parameters.
299.llm_review: Well-exposed parameters with demonstrated performance trade-offs: CTI thresholding offers calibrated m* vs example-level m + sigma; CCI supports Top-K and Top-% filtering. Empirically, Top-% is robust: on XOR-AttriQA EX, 3–20% yields similar agreement (Fig. 3). On ELI5, Top 5% improves over Top 3 for both models (Zephyr β F1 41.9 to 45.6; LLaMA 2 F1 25.1 to 27.6), and sentence-length analysis (Fig. 5) clarifies where MIRAGE and self-citation perform best, enabling informed parameter choices.

300.human_review: Limited innovation, as it primarily applies the PECORE method to citations without addressing significant new challenges.
300.llm_review: Application and novelty: The main technical novelty is adapting PEC ORE’s internals-based attribution to RAG AA; while useful, this is an incremental extension. The application scope is limited to QA RAG (XOR-AttriQA and ELI5), without demonstrations in other retrieval-heavy generation tasks (e.g., claims verification, long-document summarization, coding help) or user-facing verification workflows, which tempers claims about broad applicability.

301.human_review: On the XOR-AttriQA dataset, the method performs better only when using the annotated data from that dataset, but its generalizability has not been verified on other datasets.
301.llm_review: Data, generalization, and method caveats: The human-AA evaluation relies on a restricted XOR-AttriQA match subset (142 calibration / 1144 test) where the model regenerates the annotated answer, potentially biasing toward easier or more deterministic cases. The long-form ELI5 evaluation uses TRUE (an entailment model) as a surrogate for human AA, which the paper itself notes can be brittle and sensitive to surface similarity (Table 5). Generalization to noisier retrieval, multi-hop across multiple docs, and non-English long-form QA remains under-explored.

302.human_review: Lacks experiments on larger parameter models. It's unclear whether MIRAGE still has advantages over self-citation when using larger models.
302.llm_review: Experimental and model limitations: Only 7B-scale open-weight models are tested (LLaMA 2 7B Chat, Zephyr β7B), with no results for larger models (e.g., 13B–70B) or models explicitly optimized for citation. There is no systematic ablation of alternative attribution techniques (e.g., integrated gradients, attention flow, gradient x input), nor controlled studies on retrieval depth k or context-window length. The paper claims efficiency but reports no wall-clock or memory comparisons versus NLI/self-citation at scale.

303.human_review: Performance sensitivity to attribution method choice and filtering thresholds.
303.llm_review: Method and performance concerns: Gradient saliency can be diffuse or redundant; aggregation via union over context-sensitive tokens may over-cite when many tokens cross the m* threshold. On LLaMA 2, MIRAGE EX Top 5% improves recall (19.8 to 29.1) but reduces precision compared to self-citation (37.9 down to 26.2), indicating potential over-attribution. Figure 5 shows MIRAGE underperforms self-citation on very short sentences (≤10 tokens). Faithfulness is argued mainly via agreement metrics and a few case studies; stronger causal tests (e.g., input erasure, scrubbing) are absent.

304.human_review: Potential issues with duplicate information across multiple documents leading to misleading attributions.
304.llm_review: Practicality and evaluation gaps: MIRAGE requires gradient access to the LLM; this precludes many black-box RAG deployments, weakening the "plug-and-play" claim for common API-only scenarios. The key long-form results depend on TRUE-based scoring, with no human evaluation on ELI5 to validate user-perceived trust or correctness of citations, limiting evidence of real-world impact.

305.human_review: The paper raises awareness for an important issue - the lack of competence and the degradation in performance in LLMs when presented with an instruction with errors.
305.llm_review: Model- and performance-centric contribution is clear and well evidenced. Across three representative models (ChatGPT-3.5, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, Llama-2-7B-Chat) and five noise types, the paper quantifies consistent degradation patterns with concrete numbers. For ChatGPT-3.5 on MMLU, Figure 2 reports accuracy drops between 2.5% and 8.2% depending on noise type. Figure 5 shows distractive content is particularly harmful: ChatGPT-3.5 drops 3.8% (cooperative) and 7.5% (non-cooperative), with similar trends for Mistral and Llama-2. For open models, Table 2 (Mistral as target) demonstrates larger harm from OCR than ASR at similar severities (e.g., base accuracy 46.9% at ASR WER 23.7% vs 43.9% at OCR WER 24.7%), while grammatical mistakes are comparatively less damaging (47.5% at WER 21.7%) than heavy typos (42.4% at WER 35.1%). These model-specific, severity-controlled results substantively support the claim that LLMs are more resilient to grammatical noise than to OCR/typo and ASR noise, and that non-cooperative distractors are the most disruptive.

306.human_review: The methods for generating mistakes are valid and well-thought-of and the experiments include a variety of LLMs. The types of mistakes included also demonstrate thinking about the current trends of incorporating multi-modal input, though not considered as possible outputs.
306.llm_review: Experiments and methods are carefully designed and tied to the evaluated models. Noise injection is detailed and reproducible: ASR and grammar errors are learned via generators trained on paired clean/noisy data (e.g., Whisper-Tiny outputs on CommonVoice-15 and LibriSpeech-noisy; JELEG and C4-200M for grammar), stratified into four WER bins with 80,000 samples per bin; OCR errors leverage OcrAug with an expanded mapping (12 to 36 confusable groups); typos come from NLPAug combining spelling, keyboard proximity, and random replacements. Distractive content is sourced from real ShareGPT dialogs and instantiated in both cooperative and non-cooperative formats. The re-pass pipeline is evaluated with three concrete harmonizers (ChatGPT-3.5, Mistral self-correction, Llama-2-7B-Chat), yielding actionable, model-specific outcomes in Table 2: ChatGPT harmonization recovers up to +6.4% (typo WER 25.0%), while self-correction can hurt even clean inputs (−3.8%), and Llama-2 as harmonizer often degrades accuracy (e.g., clean −5.3%). The inclusion of qualitative corrections (Table 3) further clarifies model behavior.

307.human_review: The authors claim that they used GPT-4 to detect mistakes in user prompts to estimate the percentage of errors in prompts. The authors did not mention what is the performance of GPT-4 in such a task (of identifying errors of different types), did they manually check the outputs from GPT-4 to see that it indeed identified mistakes?
307.llm_review: Performance findings are confounded by insufficiently controlled prompting. The paper states zero-shot normalization in the re-pass step and mentions model-specific dialog templates for cooperative settings, but it does not document exact prompts/system messages, parity across models, or whether few-shot/chain-of-thought/format hints were used. Given known prompt sensitivity, the reported gains (e.g., ChatGPT harmonizer +5.0% at OCR WER 24.7%, +6.4% at typo WER 25.0% in Table 2) and cross-model gaps could partially reflect prompt choices. No prompt ablations (alternative templates, few-shot vs zero-shot, CoT vs direct, instruction length) or robustness to minor phrasing changes are provided, so performance and re-pass benefits may be over- or under-estimated.

308.human_review: Figure 1 does not show that more than 40% of inputs have errors because various types of errors can occur in one data point. For instance, a typo might be counted twice as a typo and a grammar mistake, or the distracting content could have spelling or grammar errors.
308.llm_review: Figures under-report uncertainty and are hard to read at a glance. Figures 3–4 plot two noise types per panel with small font and WER in parentheses on the x-axis; y-axes lack error bars or CIs, and it is unclear if accuracy is macro-averaged across the 1,000 MMLU items or weighted by subject. Figure 2 combines illustrative corrupted prompts with tiny percentages, mixing examples and aggregate effects in a single graphic. Figure 5 omits dispersion or per-model deltas beyond single numbers in the text. Given the centrality of these plots, clearer labeling (units and splits), per-noise panels, and uncertainty visualization (e.g., bootstrap CIs across 1,000 items) are needed.

309.human_review: Missing statistical analysis of results - what decrease was most significant? which model was most resilience to the different error types?
309.llm_review: Analysis is largely descriptive and limited in model/result scope. Conclusions about tokenizer-driven brittleness for OCR/typos are plausible but untested: there are no ablations with character-level models (e.g., ByT5) or alternative tokenizers, nor measures linking WER to token fragmentation (e.g., avg subwords/word). Generality is constrained by models (two 7B open-source + ChatGPT-3.5) and a single benchmark (MMLU). There is no per-subject MMLU breakdown to see if certain domains are more robust; no significance testing for differences (e.g., OCR vs ASR at matched WER, or harmonizer deltas in Table 2). The re-pass study only uses Mistral as the downstream target; we do not see whether ChatGPT-3.5 also benefits when harmonized by itself or others, which limits the strength of claims about harmonization efficacy across models.

310.human_review: The method for fixing errors by using LLMs to re-pass the prompt is very simplistic and was only demonstrated for Mistral as the mistake-fixer.
310.llm_review: Methodological realism and model coverage are limited. ASR/grammar noise is produced by a learned generator (TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat trained on 80k pairs per WER bin) rather than a full speech/user pipeline; there is no human validation to verify that generated errors match real-world distributions. OCR mappings are hand-crafted expansions (12→36 groups), and typo injection relies on NLPAug heuristics; both may misrepresent real error frequencies. Distractors are limited to a single inserted turn with no length/position ablations. In the re-pass pipeline, the self-correction path cannot no-op on clean inputs (Table 2: −3.8% for Mistral, −5.3% for Llama-2), which raises practical concerns about deploying the method. Model set is narrow (no GPT-4/GPT-4o, Llama-3, Mixtral), so it is unclear if the findings transfer to current SOTA models.

311.human_review: The paper proposes a unique solution to the problem of aligning images with long texts by integrating VLMs with LLMs, which is a substantial advancement in the field.
311.llm_review: Model: MATE cleanly instantiates a two-stage alignment that is well-matched to the problem of image–long-text retrieval. Stage 1 aligns VLM text embeddings to an LLM encoder (E5-Mistral 7B, 4,096-dim) using (i) 16M BLIP captions for pre-training and (ii) 532K MSMARCO query–document pairs for fine-tuning, with a 3-layer projection (Linear + LayerNorm + GELU) and contrastive losses. Stage 2 transfers this alignment to images by adapting the VLM image encoder (CLIP ViT-G/14) and the same projection to align image embeddings to LLM embeddings using only 585K image–caption pairs (LLaVA-alignment/CC3M). LoRA (rank=16, alpha=16, dropout=0.1) reduces adaptation cost while preserving base capabilities. Ablations on Infoseek show both text-only pretraining and query–document fine-tuning contribute: removing pretraining drops mAP@10 from 19.29 to 16.76; removing fine-tuning drops to 17.68; collapsing to a single linear mapping without ϕ further degrades to 12.92, substantiating the architectural and training choices.

312.key_points: Strength: Benchmark, Experiment, Framework, Performance, Result
312.human_review: The introduction of new benchmarks for image-long text retrieval tasks provides a robust framework for evaluating the proposed method, and the experimental results show clear performance gains.
312.llm_review: Benchmark, Experiment, Framework, Performance, Result: The paper evaluates two long-text retrieval settings with appropriate metrics: image–lengthy-caption (R@K on DOCCI and CC3M-long) and image–document (mAP@K on Infoseek and Oven). MATE achieves consistent and sizable gains. Examples: DOCCI zero-shot Caption→Image R@1: MATE 73.45 vs ALIGN 62.37, Long-CLIP 45.24, CLIP 12.16; CC3M-long zero-shot Caption→Image R@1: MATE 59.54 vs ALIGN 56.80 and Long-CLIP 54.06. For documents, Infoseek Doc→Image mAP@10: MATE 19.29 vs Long-CLIP 13.46 and ALIGN 12.06; Oven Doc→Image mAP@50: MATE 22.52 vs ALIGN 14.69 and Long-CLIP 13.00. After fine-tuning on DOCCI, MATE-448 reaches Caption→Image R@1 = 84.55, surpassing BLIP-336 (79.98) and ALIGN (70.20). The framework is further supported by alignment analyses (Mutual-KNN/CKNNA) showing stronger affinity between VLM image embeddings and LLM text embeddings, especially with long captions (e.g., DOCCI: Mutual-KNN ~0.275, CKNNA ~0.329 for ViT-G), and by ablations on encoder choice (ViT-G best) and data scaling (0.58M vs 3M image–caption pairs).

313.human_review: The multi-stage training process effectively bridges the gap between VLM and LLM embeddings without the need for extensive new data, making the approach scalable and practical for real-world applications.
313.llm_review: Application, Data, Embeddings, Training: The approach eliminates the need for scarce image–long-text supervision by reusing plentiful text-only and image–caption data to align into the LLM embedding space. Token statistics justify the focus on long texts: average lengths exceed CLIP’s 77-token limit in all evaluation datasets (e.g., DOCCI-train avg 139/139 tokens with CLIP/Mistral tokenizers; Infoseek avg 335/378). Despite training only on English image–caption pairs, MATE displays multilingual transfer on COCO-CN: Caption→Image R@1 = 33.64 and Image→Caption R@1 = 31.05, close to Chinese-trained CN-CLIP (37.63/36.44) and far above English-only baselines (e.g., ALIGN 0.40/0.93). This evidences that embedding into an instruction-tuned LLM space yields discriminative, long-text-capable representations, with practical training choices (contrastive losses, LoRA) keeping the pipeline tractable.

314.human_review: The ability to connect images with various long texts has significant potential applications in diverse fields such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and multimedia retrieval.
314.llm_review: Application: The demonstrated ability to retrieve across images and full documents (Infoseek: 1.8K documents, 9.6K related images; Oven: 3.5K documents, 37.6K images) and lengthy, human or model-authored captions (DOCCI and CC3M-long) supports use in media archives, education, knowledge bases, and high-detail domains. MATE improves with higher image resolution (DOCCI fine-tuning: MATE-336 vs MATE-448 shows R@1 gains from 81.84 to 84.55 in Caption→Image), suggesting suitability for high-resolution, detail-sensitive applications. Multilingual retrieval on COCO-CN without target-language fine-tuning further points to cross-lingual search scenarios.

315.human_review: The reliance on a projection module to align embeddings introduces additional complexity and potential challenges in maintaining semantic consistency across modalities.
315.llm_review: Complexity: The full pipeline requires substantial compute and engineering. Training uses 8×A100-80GB GPUs; the LLM embedding is 4,096-dim; and the projection ϕ has three wide layers (hidden size 4× output dim), which increases memory and latency. The multi-stage regimen (16M captions pre-training, 532K MSMARCO fine-tuning, and 585K image–caption alignment with LoRA on a ViT-G/14 backbone) imposes nontrivial cost and coordination. At inference, mapping images into the LLM space adds an extra projection step that may be expensive for large-scale galleries, potentially limiting deployment in resource-constrained settings.

316.human_review: While the method shows impressive results on curated datasets, its performance on less structured, real-world data remains to be thoroughly evaluated.
316.llm_review: Data, Evaluation, Method, Performance: Several comparisons may favor MATE. (i) Length limits: MATE (and Long-CLIP) ingest full documents, but BLIP and ALIGN are truncated to 512 tokens; on datasets where average lengths are much larger (e.g., Infoseek 335/378; Oven 271/305 tokens), truncation likely depresses baselines. (ii) Backbones/resolution: For DOCCI fine-tuning, ALIGN is restricted to 289px images while MATE and BLIP use 336/448px, and MATE’s base encoder is ViT-G/14 while Long-CLIP-L appears smaller; these choices can affect results independent of method. (iii) Pretraining overlap: Infoseek/Oven are Wikipedia-derived; E5-Mistral likely trained on Wikipedia-like corpora, possibly advantaging MATE on document retrieval. (iv) Missing baselines: No comparison to retrieval pipelines that already exploit LLM embeddings (e.g., pooling from instruction-tuned LLMs with a learned image projection) or to cross-encoders for re-ranking. (v) No efficiency report: throughput/latency/footprint is not reported, making it hard to assess performance–efficiency trade-offs.

317.human_review: The paper could benefit from more detailed explanations of how the multi-stage training improves alignment and why the chosen benchmarks are particularly suitable for demonstrating the method's strengths.
317.llm_review: Benchmark, Explanation, Training: The paper reconfigures existing datasets into two long-text benchmarks but provides limited procedural detail: how passage merging for Infoseek/Oven was performed, data cleansing/deduplication, and exact splits to ensure no leakage from training corpora (e.g., overlap with BLIP captions, MSMARCO topics, or E5 pretraining). Some methodological exposition has inconsistencies: in Section 3.2.2, the text states d = ET(t) when aligning images to LLM embeddings, which conflicts with earlier notation where d denotes E5 outputs; it is unclear whether symmetric losses are used in Stage 2. Sensitivity analyses are sparse (fixed temperature  0.02, batch sizes 4,096/512, projection depth fixed). The ablation notes performance saturation or slight degradation when scaling from 0.58M to 3M image–caption pairs (Infoseek Doc→Image mAP@10 18.82 vs 19.29), but does not explain the cause (e.g., domain mismatch, overfitting, optimization issues) or provide error analyses to characterize remaining failure modes.

318.key_points: Strength: AI, Agent, Approach, Model, Novelty
318.human_review: The paper presents a novel approach to improving business negotiations by using a remediator agent that intervenes to correct socially inappropriate language. This innovative use of LLMs for social norm enforcement significantly contributes to the field of AI and conversational agents.
318.llm_review: Novel agentic approach: The paper introduces a socially-aware remediator agent that actively rewrites norm-violating utterances to improve both task and relational outcomes in negotiation. The method is tuning-free and model-agnostic, leveraging a novel label-free in-context demonstration selection criterion (value impact) that jointly captures social and task utilities. The hierarchical traversal with early pruning for exemplar set construction is a distinctive modeling choice compared to nearest-neighbor or probability-based selection, and the multi-agent setup (buyer–seller–remediator) provides a clear AI agent framework for intervention.

319.human_review: The authors provide extensive empirical evidence across multiple negotiation scenarios, demonstrating the effectiveness of their proposed method. Using different negotiation topics and thorough analysis of the results strengthen the validity of their findings.
319.llm_review: Strong evidence of effectiveness: Across three negotiation topics, the method consistently outperforms prompt-only, vanilla ICL, RL-with-NL feedback, retrieval ICL, and SFT baselines on success rate, deal value, and social metrics (trust, relationship). Results are shown for both GPT-3.5 and an open-source 7B model, demonstrating robustness across model classes. Ablations validate the contributions of value impact, topic diversity, and hierarchical traversal, while a human study further corroborates improvements in dialogue quality and remediation helpfulness.

320.human_review: The research addresses a practical problem in business negotiations, offering a solution that can be applied in real-world scenarios. By improving both task-oriented and social goals, the approach can enhance negotiation outcomes and build better interpersonal relationships.
320.llm_review: Practicality and generality: The approach works with black-box LLMs via ICL, avoiding fine-tuning and enabling rapid deployment. By optimizing demonstrations based on downstream outcomes, it aligns model behavior with application goals in a principled manner. The planned release of code and data further increases potential impact and reproducibility.

321.human_review: Despite the notable improvements observed in the experiments, have the authors considered the time complexity introduced by their method? In real-world negotiation scenarios, the ability to respond quickly should also be an important metric.
321.llm_review: Algorithmic complexity and modest gains: The exemplar-set search is combinatorial (acknowledged as near NP-hard) and relies on simulation-based value estimates; although pruning helps, the offline compute budget and sensitivity to hyperparameters (e.g., M) are not fully quantified. Value impact is estimated with single-sample rollouts, which can be noisy and may inflate variance in selection; statistical significance of improvements is not reported. Empirically, gains over strong retrieval-ICL baselines are often modest (e.g., ~2–4% in success rate), and more thorough error/failure analysis would clarify when the added complexity is warranted.

322.human_review: If the training data for SFT and RL were increased, would their performance improve further? If so, would these better-trained models be more suitable for use in negotiations?
322.llm_review: Data and evaluation limitations tied to model and training: All data are LLM-simulated with injected violations, silver remediations are produced by GPT-3.5, and key social metrics are judged by GPT-4, introducing evaluator and simulator bias. The scope is limited to Chinese and three topics, with asymmetric violations (primarily one party), which constrains generalization. The SFT baseline relies on a relatively small pseudo-gold set and a model with weaker Chinese support, making performance comparisons less conclusive about training-based alternatives; moreover, no detection component is integrated, and the method’s performance in human-in-the-loop, real-time settings remains untested.

323.human_review: The proposed KGQA framework using LLMs to address KGQA is quite interesting; further demonstrating the LLM capabilities to address not only individual steps such as query parsing, entity and relation linking and query generation, but also working together to produce final answer
323.llm_review: Framework, Model: Triad is a coherent, end-to-end KBQA framework that explicitly operationalizes three LLM-agent roles across all four KBQA phases, and grounds them with concrete tools and indices. The G-Agent performs (i) triplet mention extraction, (ii) SPARQL template generation, and (iii) answer-type classification via few-shot prompts; the D-Agent (i) filters entity candidates with Elasticsearch and then uses the LLM to pick top-K URIs, (ii) traverses KB neighbors to collect relation candidates and LLM-ranks top-K, and (iii) constructs candidate SPARQLs from the template and URIs, prunes non-answering ones via a Virtuoso endpoint, and selects the best; the A-Agent (i) executes the chosen SPARQL over Virtuoso and (ii) falls back to LLM answering with a type-aware policy and retry when no results are returned. The design decisions are justified empirically: ablations on LC-QuAD show that downgrading the G-Agent core to older models drops F1 from 0.564 to 0.443 and 0.343; replacing D-Agent’s LLM entity selection with matching alone drops F1 to 0.274; removing A-Agent’s LLM fallback reduces F1 to 0.459–0.473. The framework is model-agnostic: swapping GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 improves LC-QuAD F1 from 0.504 to 0.564 and QALD-9 from 0.297 to 0.416, demonstrating that stronger backbones directly translate to better performance without changing the architecture.

324.human_review: The empirical study clearly demonstrates that viability of the approach
324.llm_review: Approach: The method combines KB indexing and tool-use with LLM reasoning in a way that measurably reduces error propagation. Two concrete choices are impactful: (a) generating SPARQL templates with variables and only later instantiating URIs reduces LLM calls and syntax errors compared to direct query generation; (b) pruning candidate queries by execution before final selection keeps only answer-producing SPARQLs, simplifying the LLM’s decision. The role hyperparameter study shows practical guidance: on LC-QuAD, using 3 shots for G-Agent outperforms 1–2 shots (0.564 vs 0.556/0.511), selecting too many URI candidates hurts (Top2-2 yields 0.564 vs Top2-3 0.558), and allowing more retries for A-Agent helps (1-try 0.529, 2-tries 0.561, 3-tries 0.564). The linking recall analysis pinpoints relation linking as the bottleneck: while 80.75% of gold entities survive the matching filter and 70.50% remain after LLM selection, only 52.54% of gold relations are retained by the LLM, informing where future improvements should focus. Empirically, Triad delivers large gains over pure LLMs: on LC-QuAD, GPT-4 few-shot baseline F1 is 0.340 vs Triad-GPT4 at 0.564 (+22.4 points); on QALD-9, 0.249 vs 0.416 (+16.7 points). On YAGO-QA, Triad-GPT4 reaches precision/recall of 0.690/0.664 vs GPT-4 baseline 0.193/0.190, indicating a substantial margin when the KB is effectively leveraged.

325.human_review: The paper is overall well written and easy to follow.
325.llm_review: Clarity, Presentation: The paper clearly decomposes the pipeline and formalizes each subtask with explicit function signatures and prompts (Equations 2–8). Figure 2 maps roles to phases and shows data flow from text matching and KB traversal through candidate selection to final execution, which pairs well with the narrative. Implementation specifics that aid reproducibility are included: DBpedia/YAGO triple counts and index sizes (e.g., LC-QuAD with DBpedia-04, 397M triples; Virtuoso 35.40G; Elasticsearch 1.56G), the exact backends (Virtuoso 07.20.3237, Elasticsearch 7.5.2), and the core hyperparameters with their selected values (shots=3, entity K=2, relation K=2, retries=3). The evaluation is structured with baseline families (full-shot: gAnswer, EDGQA, KGQAN; few-shot: GPT-3.5/4), role ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, and a failure taxonomy for QALD-9 with concrete categories and rates (Complex Syntax 20%, Unexploited Semantics 17%, Implicit Reasoning 5%), helping readers understand both capabilities and limits.

326.human_review: Though I liked the overall idea of using LLM agents to solve KGQA using traditional pipeline, it is not clear whether we still need to follow the standard pipeline for solving KGQA. The paper lacks the motivation for using traditional multi-step pipeline over a RAG pipeline for KGQA
326.llm_review: Agent, Motivation: The three-role decomposition is plausible but not empirically justified against simpler controllers. There is no head-to-head comparison with a single-agent tool-use baseline (e.g., a ReAct-style controller using the same Elasticsearch and Virtuoso tools) or a two-role setup that merges parsing+linking under one agent and execution+answering under another. The ablations mostly remove capabilities (e.g., replacing LLM selection with matching), but do not test alternative role splits or a unified prompting strategy with identical tools, so it remains unclear whether three roles are necessary. Additionally, the paper does not report coordination overhead or LLM call counts per question; given the multi-stage design (triplet extraction, template generation, two top-K selections, candidate execution, and possible retries), a cost/latency analysis is important to motivate the added complexity.

327.human_review: Some of the important details are missing, for instance, it is not clear what does a retry signal do when A-Agent finds no result is generated. It would be nice to elaborate more on these details.
327.llm_review: General: Reproducibility and reporting could be stronger. The study depends on proprietary GPT-3.5/4; prompts, chain-of-thought templates, and exact tool-call schemas are not fully enumerated, and code is only promised upon acceptance. Several table entries appear truncated or inconsistent (e.g., some F1 values missing decimals in Table 2; abstract claims “F1 scores of 11.8% and 20.7%,” which contradicts the main results and likely intend improvements rather than absolute scores). Statistical significance is not reported despite averaging over 5 runs; given known LLM variance, confidence intervals would add credibility. Details of text-matching thresholds and traversal depth for candidate collection are not specified, which affects the replicability and fairness of comparisons.

328.human_review: Authors should also add the results of GPT-4 numbers for LC-QuAD and QALD-9 datasets; it could be case that A-Agent uses implicit knowledge entirely ignoring the efficacy of previous phases.
328.llm_review: Data, Result: The experimental coverage is limited and may not fully support broad claims. LC-QuAD 1.0 (1,000 questions) and QALD-9 (150 questions) are small/older; YAGO-QA has only 100 questions. More challenging or contemporary datasets (e.g., LC-QuAD 2.0, ComplexWebQuestions, CFQ variants) would better test multi-hop and compositional generalization, which the error analysis identifies as weak points. Cross-system comparability is also uncertain: full-shot baselines are reported from prior papers that may use different KB snapshots and endpoints, while Triad uses DBpedia-04/10 and YAGO-4 indexed locally, making direct F1 comparisons noisy. The pure LLM baselines are implemented by the authors with post-hoc URI linking via similarity search, which could either handicap or benefit them relative to Triad’s more elaborate linking; an oracle-entity setting or shared candidate sets would clarify the true modeling gains. Finally, no per-type breakdown (Boolean vs single-fact vs multi-fact) is reported to substantiate the A-Agent’s type policy beyond anecdotal cases.

329.human_review: The radar map (Fig. 2) is clear to show the relative performance of each MLLM on this benchmark.
329.llm_review: Benchmark and Performance: The paper introduces CorrelationQA, a targeted benchmark for spurious-image-induced hallucination with concrete scale and coverage: 1,218 QA items paired with 6 visual variants each (5 spurious + 1 factual) across 13 categories (e.g., Animal, Color, Food, Plant, History, Art), totaling 7,308 text–image pairs. It includes three image modalities—natural synthetic (Stable Diffusion, 1024→512 px), plain-background typography (512 px), and a subset of realistic web images—which allows stress-testing OCR-like failure modes as well as more naturalistic scenes. The evaluation spans 9 mainstream MLLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, MiniGPT-4, mPLUG-Owl2, Qwen-VL, Idefics, GPT-4V, InstructBLIP, CogVLM) under a uniform prompt regime (“Answer in no more than five words”), with consistent scoring (accuracy and AccDrop). The results surface meaningful performance differences attributable to image condition: for instance, LLaVA-7B shows a small average AccDrop on natural images (0.02) while Qwen-VL shows a much larger drop (0.29), and typography systematically induces larger drops for most models (e.g., Qwen-VL 0.75 avg).

330.human_review: The analysis of various MLLMs, with both open and closed source models, over different categories, is comprehensive, with both qualitative and quantitative results provided.
330.llm_review: Analysis, Model, Result: The analysis is multi-angle and model-aware. By decomposing inputs into text-only, factual, spurious, random, and typography (Fig. 5), the paper shows that only text-only and factual yield comparable accuracy, whereas spurious (especially OCR-like typography) depresses accuracy across models. Per-model patterns are concrete: GPT-4V suffers non-trivial AccDrop on natural images (avg 0.32; Table 2), while LLaVA-7B/13B are comparatively robust (0.02/0.05 on natural; 0.11/0.14 on typography; Tables 2–3), plausibly linked to training exposure to knowledge-heavy VQA data. Per-category analysis (Tables 2–3) highlights tangible-entity categories as more vulnerable: e.g., for Color, AccDrop is 0.43 (Qwen-VL, natural) and 0.70 (GPT-4V, typography); for Animal, 0.53 (InstructBLIP, natural) and 0.79 (Qwen-VL, typography). Conversely, abstract categories like History/Art show smaller or inconsistent drops (e.g., GPT-4V History 0.12 natural, 0.09 typography). The findings generalize beyond synthesis: on realistic images, Qwen-VL’s spurious accuracy falls to 0.33 with AccDrop 0.34 (vs. 0.36 and 0.29 on synthetic), and LLaVA-7B remains relatively stable (0.55, 0.06 vs. 0.61, 0.02; Table 4).

331.human_review: The visualization of image-text pairs with both accurate and inaccurate answers given in Fig. 6 is clear and straightforward.
331.llm_review: Accuracy and Figure: Metrics are well-specified and tailored to the task: Accuracy is computed with an approximate match policy appropriate for short answers (≤5 words), explicitly allowing abbreviations and label-containing responses (e.g., label “Los Angeles Lakers” counts with “Lakers” or “It is Los Angeles Lakers”). AccDrop (Af − As) directly quantifies sensitivity to deception. Visualizations make these effects easy to inspect: Fig. 4 summarizes per-model Acc and AccDrop for natural vs. typography; Tables 2–3 detail AccDrop per category and model, exposing patterns like negative small drops (e.g., LLaVA-7B City −0.01, LLaVA-13B Plant −0.05) and zeroed entries marked “0*” where both accuracies are zero. Fig. 5’s condition-wise comparison clarifies that adding spurious images hurts relative to text-only, and Fig. 6’s qualitative examples align with the quantitative trends (tangible content like animals/objects induces stronger hallucinations).

332.human_review: It would be helpful for the authors to quantitatively evaluate the relevance between the question and the spurious image. Since the factual and random images could be taken as two extremes of the relevance level, it would be better to get some insights into the relevance between spurious images and questions. In other words, how do we define the spurious images that are related but do not correspond to the correct answer?
332.llm_review: Evaluation: The study over-relies on synthetic stimuli (Stable Diffusion for natural images; plain white OCR typography), with limited human validation of question quality or image–answer relationships, risking artifacts that models might exploit (e.g., generation style biases). Realistic-image evaluation is limited to two models (LLaVA-7B, Qwen-VL) and lacks a full-scale comparison across all nine models (Table 4), leaving external validity only partially supported. The benchmark constrains answers to short entities (≤5 words), omitting more compositional or multi-sentence reasoning; this is visible in category design (Table 1) and in the scoring rule that accepts label substrings, potentially inflating accuracy. Important controls are missing: (a) prompt- and decoding-sensitivity ablations (e.g., temperature, nucleus sampling, chain-of-thought, or explicit instructions to prioritize text over image), (b) mitigation baselines (e.g., a text-only or text-first decision policy, selective vision gating), (c) statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for Acc/AccDrop, and (d) systematic analysis of model calibration (e.g., self-reported confidence vs. correctness). Moreover, GPT-4 generated all QA items while GPT-4V is evaluated, creating a modest source-bias risk; a human-authored subset or cross-generator sanity check would strengthen claims. Finally, Fig. 5 shows GPT-4 text-only was evaluated on a 20% subsample (due to rate limits), making its comparability uneven with other conditions.

333.human_review: The authors need to clarify the mechanism they use to retrieve the spurious image, i.e. how to find such a spurious image that is inconsistent with the accurate answer but still relates to the questions? Given the instability in the output of diffusion models, is there any warranty mechanism to ensure that the generated spurious image is correct? Is the dataset created automatically, or the generated results have been gone through manually?
333.llm_review: Clarity, Data, Model: Several details impede reproducibility and interpretability. Data generation omits random seeds for Stable Diffusion and the exact checkpoint configuration beyond “playground-v2-1024px-aesthetic”; prompt templates are only partially shown (few-shot exemplars not fully listed), and the random-image sampling procedure is not precisely defined (e.g., same-category vs. cross-category, per-item sampling policy). The approximate-match algorithm is under-specified (case/punctuation normalization, stemming, synonym handling), yet it determines correctness. The tables include edge cases that need explanation: negative AccDrop values (e.g., LLaVA-7B City −0.01; LLaVA-13B Plant −0.05) and “0*” annotations (e.g., CogVLM History 0* in Table 2, multiple 0* in Table 3) without a clear rule for how AccDrop is computed when both factual and spurious accuracies are zero. Realistic-image acquisition lacks detail (licensing, filtering/NSFW, deduplication, number of images per item); Table 1 appears truncated in the PDF (“Total 1,218 7,”) even though the text claims 7,308 image–text pairs, and a per-category image count breakdown for realistic images is not provided. Model specs also need tightening: exact model versions/dates, decoding parameters, and API settings for GPT-4V are not stated. Releasing the full dataset, prompts, code, and evaluation scripts (including a strict-match option) would substantially improve clarity and verifiability.

334.human_review: The authors curate a new ChallengeWMT dataset using existing WMT datasets that target source texts mistranslated by multiple SOTA machine translation models. Given the increasing quality of MT-generated translations, this resource can help identify failure cases of LLMs.
334.llm_review: Data and Model: The paper contributes (i) a targeted benchmark, Challenge-WMT, and (ii) a concrete alignment pipeline, DUAT. Challenge-WMT is constructed by intersecting the lowest-COMET outputs from multiple strong systems (Google, ChatGPT, NLLB/DeltaLM) over multi-year WMT test sets for six directions (En↔Zh, En↔Et, En↔Is), yielding ~600+ sentence pairs per direction with demonstrably higher complexity (perplexity rises from 214 to 252 on average) and a large performance gap vs the full WMT (average COMET 84.5→73.6). DUAT is a modular model-agnostic process: (1) difficult-word detection via a draft translation and LLM identification, expanded by temperature sampling (K=5, T=0.5) and filtered with a dual use of token-level QE ϕ(ws|x, êy) using a threshold τ; (2) cross-lingual (target-language) interpretations for the detected spans; and (3) interpretation quality control (IQC) that ablates interpretations one-by-one and keeps those that improve sentence-level QE (wmt21-comet-qe-da), thus turning general understanding into actionable, target-side cues for translation.

335.human_review: Extensive experiments on multiple languages show that DUAT improves translation quality (as measured by COMET and BLEURT) across the board when the underlying LLM is GPT-3.5, except English-icelandic, where they conduct further experiments using GPT-4 to show that using an even powerful LLM to generate and guide the translation can be helpful.
335.llm_review: Experiment, Improvement, Model: Implemented on GPT-3.5-turbo with 8-shot ICL, DUAT-E delivers consistent gains across all six directions on Challenge-WMT: on average +1.82 COMET and +1.32 BLEURT over ICL, and +3.41 COMET and +3.33 BLEURT over zero-shot. The largest gain appears in low-resource En→Is (+3.85 COMET vs ICL). DUAT also improves over MAPS components (keywords/topic/similar demonstrations) and is robust to stronger multilingual models: on GPT-4 for En↔Is, DUAT-E outperforms GPT-4 ICL by +1.6 COMET (81.7 vs 80.1) for En→Is and +0.19 COMET (81.21 vs 81.02) for Is→En, indicating the alignment mechanism remains beneficial even when base translation quality is high.

336.human_review: Human evaluation shows that the generated translations are less literal and are driven by the general understanding capabilities of LLMs.
336.llm_review: Evaluation: The study evaluates with both automatic and human measures and contrasts multiple baselines/systems. Automatic metrics include COMET and BLEURT against ICL, zero-shot, CoT, MAPS variants, Google, NLLB/DeltaLM, and GPT-4. Human evaluation on 100 samples per direction quantifies generalization failures among mistranslations for the ICL baseline (e.g., 26% in En→Zh, 32% in Et→En), shows DUAT-E reduces these by 71%–88% (e.g., En→Zh 5→1, Et→En 17→2), and lowers literalness scores by 25%–51% (e.g., Et→En 4.46→2.60). On the full WMT22 Zh↔En, DUAT-E matches or slightly improves over ICL (Zh→En COMET 87.60 vs 87.10; En→Zh 82.75 vs 82.71), suggesting no regressions on easier data.

337.human_review: Additional ablation experiments are performed to study how the number and source of interpretations (source or target side) impact final translation quality.
337.llm_review: Ablation, Experiment, Interpretation: The ablation study isolates key components: removing the draft harms detection (−0.63 COMET En→Zh; −0.55 Zh→En), and removing IQC causes larger drops (−1.03 and −0.32 COMET respectively), showing IQC’s centrality. Difficulty-threshold (τ) sweeps reveal that more interpretations are not always better unless filtered: without IQC, adding interpretations yields unstable gains; with IQC, performance improves monotonically (e.g., En→Zh: helpful interpretations rise from 0.23 to 0.49 to 1.47 as τ decreases, corresponding to COMET 76.52→76.98→77.57). The language-of-interpretation analysis shows target-language interpretations in an implicit two-stage process outperform source-language or explicit two-stage variants (e.g., En→Zh COMET: target 77.57 > source 76.57 > explicit 75.47; similarly Zh→En: 73.25 > 72.99 > 72.22).

338.human_review: As already noted by the authors, the process is expensive as it requires prompting LLMs to generate interpretations and translations using these interpretations and it is unclear to what extent some of these steps could be made faster by a) relying on external knowledge bases; b) filtering interpretations without generating translations and c) when to ask for these interpretations. Adding some discussion on this could be helpful.
338.llm_review: Discussion: The paper acknowledges latency overhead (Limitations) because IQC ablates each interpretation sequentially, requiring |D| additional prompts per sentence, but provides no quantitative analysis of end-to-end cost (latency, tokens, throughput) or trade-offs for deployment. Although Fig. 3 recommends τ≈0.13–0.15 to balance efficiency and quality, there is no empirical measurement of wall-clock speed/cost across τ values or guidance for operational budgets, and no discussion of batching, parallelism, or early stopping to amortize IQC.

339.human_review:
There are some concurrent recent works with post-editing with LLMs given an initial translation and error explanations and it might be helpful to add that to related work discussion.

References:
339.llm_review: Discussion, Explanation, Related Work: The core claim—realigning “translation-specific understanding” to “general understanding”—is motivated with examples (e.g., Chinese 文章 meaning Wen Zhang in QA vs mistranslated as “article” in MT) and human counts of generalization failures, but the mechanism is under-explained. Why target-language interpretations specifically induce alignment (vs other scaffolds like retrieval, constraints, or specialized prompting) is argued empirically but not theoretically grounded. The dual use of token-level QE to score source spans (ϕ(ws|x, êy)) is described but not justified in detail (e.g., calibration across languages, sensitivity of τ, potential biases from QE), and alternative detectors or agreement checks are not compared.

340.human_review: Guiding Large Language Models to Post-Edit Machine Translation with Error Annotations
340.llm_review: Related Work: Positioning relative to QE-in-the-loop MT, human-in-the-loop post-editing, constrained decoding, and terminology/lexicon guidance is brief. DUAT’s pipeline resembles these strands (identify problematic spans, provide guidance, and refine), but the paper does not clearly articulate how DUAT differs from or subsumes prior QE-guided correction/refinement frameworks or constrained/terminology-aware translation approaches, nor does it provide head-to-head comparisons.

341.human_review: xTower: A Multilingual LLM for Explaining and Correcting Translation Errors
341.llm_review: Related Work: Difficult-word detection and cross-lingual interpretation closely relate to word sense disambiguation and entity-centric disambiguation in MT (the 文章/Wen Zhang case is a classic ambiguity). The paper does not engage with this literature (e.g., sense inventories, entity linking, ambiguity-aware prompting) or clarify whether DUAT is complementary to or a replacement for WSD/entity-aware pipelines, leaving unclear how much of the gain derives from better ambiguity handling versus other factors.

342.human_review: LLMRefine: Pinpointing and Refining Large Language Models via Fine-Grained Actionable Feedback
342.llm_review: Related Work: Challenge-WMT is not sufficiently situated among existing stress tests and targeted benchmarks (e.g., gender/pronoun resolution and noisy data). The construction by intersection of hard samples for multiple systems is sensible but could bias towards phenomena commonly mishandled by those systems. The paper does not compare or relate Challenge-WMT to focused sets (e.g., pronoun resolution, gender bias, noisy-input corpora) or analyze the error phenomena distribution, limiting interpretability of what kinds of difficulty the benchmark emphasizes.

343.human_review: I find the paper to be well written and that most of the design choices are reasonable.
343.llm_review: Presentation is notably strong. The paper introduces the task, data, and model in a logical order, and uses concrete scaffolding to keep the reader oriented: Figure 1 contrasts successful vs. failed negotiations with and without persona; Figure 2 summarizes the three-stage pipeline (PSFT, reward modeling, PPO). Key components are named consistently (e.g., PAR, NSCR, IPAR; Rrf, Rdc, Rd), and Equation (3) clearly specifies the supervised objective. Definitions of 17 intents, 8 strategies, and 4 phases are referenced explicitly (Tables 6–9 in the appendix), and the dataset creation pipeline is broken down into four labeled stages with clear constraints (e.g., traveler starts with Greet; negotiation deadline; phase transitions). Metrics are defined and cross-referenced to the corresponding classifiers/models (e.g., PA via Persona-NLI; NSC via NSCM; NPA via NPCM), and ablation settings are enumerated explicitly in Tables 1–2. Limitations and ethics sections are detailed (e.g., 2,048-token context limit, 40 GB GPU requirement) and aligned to the scope of claims.

344.human_review: The paper introduced a dataset with rich annotation, which could be of value to people working in this field. Also, the experimental results of using the dataset in supervised fine-tuning setting also support the effectiveness of the data.
344.llm_review: Annotation, data design, experiments, and fine-tuning are carefully specified. The dataset (DEAL) covers 20 travel packages and encodes a rich schema: 17 traveler intents (e.g., Negotiate add-X/remove-X, Negotiate price increase/decrease/no-change), 8 agent strategies (e.g., problem identification, flexible pricing), and 4 negotiation phases (relational positioning, problem solving, offer generation, decision making). Annotations were validated by three experts with inter-expert agreement > 0.83 across categories. Supporting models used for supervision and reward are reported with concrete performance: Persona-NLI accuracy 86.76% (Welleck et al., 2018), NSCM (RoBERTa-large) 91.75% accuracy / 81.34% macro-F1, NPCM 93.24% accuracy / 84.02% macro-F1, and the intent–phase generation model achieves PPL 3.71 with BLEU 0.29, METEOR 0.63, BS-F1 0.82. Fine-tuning proceeds in two stages (persona-aware supervised fine-tuning via Eq. 3, then PPO) with a composite reward separating trait-focused (persona alignment, strategy consistency, intent–phase agreement) and language-focused (fluency, coherence, diversity) terms. Experiments include both automatic and human evaluation plus ablations. Automatically, TRIP NEGOTIATOR improves over the strongest supervised baseline (PSFT) by large margins: PPL 2.13 vs. 3.67 (−41.96%), BLEU 0.35 vs. 0.28 (+0.07), METEOR 0.87 vs. 0.75 (+0.12), BS-F1 0.81 vs. 0.73 (+0.08), and trait metrics PA/NSC/NPA 82.31/84.62/81.34% vs. 74.58/78.60/74.36% (+7–10 points). Human evaluation also shows consistent gains over PSFT: PA 4.32 vs. 3.61, NSC 4.21 vs. 3.78, NPA 4.53 vs. 3.91, Win Times 88.75% vs. 75.00%, Deal Rate 82.76% vs. 71.32%, Pareto Optimality 87.24% vs. 72.48%, and language quality (Fluency 4.73, Coherence 4.71, Engagingness 4.19). Ablations removing individual rewards degrade performance (e.g., PPL increases from 2.13 to 2.51 when PAR is removed), and grouped ablations show that both trait- and language-focused rewards matter (e.g., removing all three TFR: PA/NSC/NPA drop to 77.24/79.82/78.52%).

345.human_review: The paper includes detailed comparison with previous works, the contribution of each reward components, etc.
345.llm_review: The paper articulates clear contributions and situates them against prior work with concrete comparisons. On the resource side, DEAL is distinct from distributive datasets (CraigslistBargain, AntiScam) and from general integrative settings (DealOrNoDeal, STAC), and differs from IND (Ahmad et al., 2023) by targeting tourism with multi-aspect packages (price, destination, amenities like snowboarding, farm-to-table dining). Methodologically, TRIP NEGOTIATOR combines persona-aware supervised fine-tuning with PPO and a task-specific reward suite (PAR/NSCR/IPAR + fluency/coherence/diversity), which goes beyond price-only or strategy-only approaches (e.g., He et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2023a). Empirically, comparisons span classic generative baselines (GPT-2, DialoGPT), persona-aware or strategic agents (PersRFI, INA), RL variants (ARDM, GPT-Critic), and LLM prompting (ProCoT with Llama-2-7b-chat and ChatGPT). TRIP NEGOTIATOR consistently outperforms them on both trait metrics (e.g., PA 82.31% vs. PSFT 74.58% and INA 70.28%) and language metrics (e.g., PPL 2.13 vs. ARDM 4.82; BS-F1 0.81 vs. DialoGPT 0.64). The inclusion of persona-aware PSFT as a strong baseline clarifies the incremental value of the RL-rewarded stage.

346.human_review:
**unrealistic dataset:** Since the dialogue in the dataset is mainly generated with LLM, the curated dataset is likely to be unrealistic. For instance:\
(1) The persona might not be consistent within a dialogue, which is a phenomenon that has been observed in LLMs.
(2) The dialogue flow is randomly generated, which could result in discrepancy between real-world negotiation dialogues and the generated ones. although the human intervention might be helpful in removing unnatural dialogue flows, the overall distribution will be different from real-world ones.\
It is perhaps a good idea to conduct analysis on the quality of the generated dataset, and if possible, compare the LLM-generated data to human-generated ones.
346.llm_review: Data realism and evaluation dependencies limit external validity. DEAL is largely synthetic, generated via MPT-7B with at most 4 shots due to the 2,048-token context window, and required 112 human interventions for quality—raising the risk of style artifacts from the generator. The coverage is narrow (20 travel packages), and negotiation flows and prices are governed by hand-designed constraints and concession equations (Eqs. 1–2 with k tuned by budget gap), which may not reflect organic bargaining behavior. Persona extraction relies on an automated PEM, and the core evaluation metrics (PA via Persona-NLI, NSC via NSCM, NPA via NPCM) use classifiers trained on DEAL itself, creating potential circularity: systems optimized with these signals (also used in rewards) can score highly without proving generalization. Access to the dataset is gated by an agreement, further limiting reproducibility and independent auditing. Finally, the paper does not report experiments on real user inputs or out-of-domain tourism content, so transfer beyond the synthetic setting remains untested.

347.human_review: **Persona analysis:** While "persona" is one of the main focus of this research, I do not see much discussion regarding persona (and it's affect on negotiation) in the results/analysis part. It would be nice if you can add some more analysis regarding persona.
347.llm_review: Analysis and discussion leave important questions open. Reward weights are selected heuristically and no sensitivity or robustness study is reported (e.g., no variance across seeds or PPO stability diagnostics). Ablations are binary (remove/keep), so interactions among reward terms are not quantified. The interpretation that there is a “minimal performance difference” between the full model and the variant without TFR (Rpa+Rnsc+Ripa) yet TFR are “crucial” appears inconsistent; quantifying effect sizes across metrics would clarify this point. Human evaluation lacks detail about annotator counts, agreement, and calibration, so reliability is hard to judge despite reporting Welch’s t-tests (no effect sizes are provided). Baseline LLM prompting (ProCoT) underperforms sharply (e.g., PPL 29.30–36.87), but stronger instruction-tuned comparisons (e.g., GPT-4 class models, better prompt design or few-shot exemplars aligned to the 17-intent schema) are absent, which complicates claims about superiority. Related work includes placeholders (“?” for CaSiNo and JobInterview), suggesting incomplete citation hygiene and weakening the discussion.

348.human_review: The paper introduces a unique multi-agent debate framework for hate speech detection, addressing the challenge of generalization across datasets with different labeling criteria
348.llm_review: Data, Framework, Generalization: The paper operationalizes cross-dataset heterogeneity by (i) manually refining each benchmark’s labeling criteria into an agent-specific “independent perspective,” and (ii) retrieving the three most similar labeled texts per dataset via cosine similarity to ground each agent’s stance and reason. These reasons are then stored into Hate/Non-hate reference pools. This PRE phase, followed by a DICT phase that aggregates incongruent references through a structured two-round debate and a judge’s final decision, directly targets the problem of inconsistent labeling criteria across datasets. The authors report superior cross-evaluation on five public benchmarks relative to criteria-specific and majority-vote baselines, indicating improved generalization under dataset shifts.

349.human_review: The authors conduct experiments on five different datasets, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness across various contexts
349.llm_review: Data, Effectiveness, Experiment, Framework: The framework’s effectiveness is demonstrated via cross-evaluation across five public hate-speech datasets: agents are conditioned on dataset-specific criteria and similar-context retrieval (k=3) to generate stances/reasons, then debaters combine reasons from opposing camps for two rounds before a judge issues the final label and a balanced rationale. Against baselines that either fix a single labeling criterion or aggregate by majority vote, PREDICT consistently performs better in cross-dataset testing according to the paper. The experimental design explicitly leverages dataset-grounded references (rather than generic LLM knowledge), which is a concrete, data-aware mechanism for improved transfer.

350.human_review: The debate process and final judgment provide interpretable reasoning for the hate speech classification decisions
350.llm_review: Interpretation: The method yields explicit reasoning artifacts at each step: agents produce stances and reasons grounded in their dataset-specific criteria and retrieved exemplars; debaters cite Hate vs. Non-hate references during two rounds; the judge outputs a “balanced reason” that synthesizes both sides. The qualitative analysis highlights cases where minority-agent opinions are preserved in the judge’s rationale, providing traceable evidence of how disagreements stemming from divergent labeling criteria are mediated, which improves transparency and auditability.

351.human_review: The framework incorporates different labeling criteria as independent perspectives, allowing for an improved approach to hate speech detection
351.llm_review: Approach, Framework: The paper adapts multi-agent debate to hate speech detection in a principled way: perspectives are not generic personas but are constructed from refined labeling criteria and matched contexts from each dataset; debate is structured (two rounds) and concludes with a judge that must respect arguments from both camps. This design goes beyond prior generic multi-agent methods (e.g., MAD) by tying each agent’s reasoning to dataset-specific criteria and evidence, addressing overfitting to any single annotation schema. The authors also position this as, to their knowledge, the first multi-agent simulation framework tailored to hate speech detection.

352.human_review: The authors discuss how PREDICT could be extended to other social science research topics
352.llm_review: Discussion: The work is explicitly motivated by pluralism in social science (e.g., Waseem et al., 2018; Tontodimamma et al., 2021) and frames the task as consensus-building among diverse labeling criteria. The paper argues that a judge’s balanced rationale can both respect minority stances and promote fairer outcomes. It also commits to releasing code, which, if delivered with prompts and criteria definitions, would facilitate community examination of pluralistic reasoning in sensitive content moderation tasks.

353.human_review: The study focuses only on Korean datasets, which may limit its generalizability to other languages and cultures
353.llm_review: Data, Generalization: While cross-evaluation on five public benchmarks is promising, the paper does not report generalization to other axes of shift (e.g., multilingual settings, different platforms, or temporal drift). Moreover, PRE retrieves similar examples from the same dataset to construct references; this can entrench dataset-specific distributions and biases rather than test true out-of-domain transfer. Evidence of generalization beyond the five curated datasets, or experiments using cross-source retrieval, is missing.

354.human_review: The multi-agent debate approach may be more computationally intensive and complex to implement compared to traditional classification methods
354.llm_review: Approach, Complexity, Implementation: The pipeline is complex and potentially costly: five agents (one per dataset) each retrieve k=3 exemplars, generate stances and reasons, feed Hate/Non-hate references to two debaters for two debate rounds, and finally involve a judge to issue the label and balanced reason. The approach depends on manual curation of labeling criteria by three researchers and on persona-style prompts (based on Huang et al., 2024), which introduces subjectivity. No ablations are reported on key knobs (number of agents, k in retrieval, number of debate rounds, with/without judge), leaving sensitivity and deployment feasibility unclear.

355.human_review: The performance of PREDICT relies heavily on the underlying LLMs, which may introduce biases or inconsistencies
355.llm_review: Model, Performance: The method rests on an underlying LLM to generate stances, reasons, debates, and judgments, but the paper does not analyze robustness to adversarial or noisy inputs, nor does it report calibration, abstention, or bias assessments of the judge’s decisions. There is no study of model family/size (open vs. closed LLMs) or safety guardrails to prevent propagation of harmful content in rationales—important given the domain involves offensive text.

356.human_review: The current implementation only allows for two rounds of debate, which may not be sufficient for more complex cases
356.llm_review: Implementation: Reproducibility is hindered by missing specifics in the main text: exact prompts/persona templates (Appendix D is referenced but not detailed here), the precise cosine-similarity encoder and index used for retrieval, the value k=3 justification, debate controller settings (e.g., tie-breaking, token limits), random seeds, and compute/cost budgets for running multi-agent debates. With code not yet released, it is difficult to replicate or verify the claimed improvements.

357.human_review: The paper doesn't compare PREDICT's performance with other advanced hate speech detection methods beyond majority voting and in-dataset baselines
357.llm_review: Comparison, Data, Performance: Baselines focus on criteria-specific models and majority voting, but do not cover stronger alternatives, such as multi-task/domain generalization across datasets, invariant risk minimization, instruction-tuned self-consistency, or rationale-augmented classifiers without debate. The paper also does not report statistical significance testing or ablations isolating PRE vs. DICT contributions, making it hard to attribute gains specifically to the debate mechanism rather than to increased retrieved evidence or prompt length.

358.human_review: The proposed approach to handle the knowledge graph question answering with new facts is reasonable, which first reflects the updated facts from the sentences into the knowledge graph and then perform knowledge graph question answering by generating the relation chain and the formal query executable over the knowledge graph to derive the final answer.
358.llm_review: Approach: The paper presents a concrete, end-to-end graph-augmented editing-and-reasoning pipeline that is well instantiated: (i) edited sentences are converted by an LLM into subject–relation–object triples constrained to a predefined relation set, with out-of-vocabulary relations mapped via Contriever similarity; the KG is then updated by severing prior links on the same (subject, relation) and inserting the new triple. (ii) For questions, the LLM extracts a relation chain (e.g., the 4-hop chain for “Eeyore” in the paper: Eeyore->creator->?x->child->?y->country of citizenship->?z->capital->?m), which is compiled into a SPARQL template over a Wikidata-backed KG. (iii) In parallel, LLM-based QA retrieves the top-x edited facts with Contriever and answers directly. (iv) A simple but effective arbitration favors the KG answer when it conflicts with the LLM answer. The design choices—relation normalization, explicit SPARQL execution, and conflict resolution—translate evolving edits into precise multi-hop reasoning paths, addressing the error accumulation and retrieval-noise issues that plague memory-only approaches under many edits.

359.human_review: The proposed approach outperforms relevant baselines substantially.
359.llm_review: Approach + Performance: Evidence across tables supports the claim that explicit KG reasoning stabilizes performance under many edits. On MQuAKE-CF with GPT-J-6B, accuracy at k=3000 is 49.0% for GMeLLo vs 9.8% for MeLLo; with Vicuna-7B, 41.9% vs 10.2%. On MQuAKE-T, GMeLLo also dominates: with GPT-J-6B at k=500, 81.5% vs 33.8% (MeLLo), and with Vicuna-7B at k=500, 85.4% vs 52.6%. Ablations (Table 2) show KBQA’s stability as edits grow (CF: 43.3% for GPT-J-6B and 35.9% for Vicuna-7B, invariant across k; T: 80.2% and 73.6%, invariant), while LLM-only QA collapses (e.g., CF with GPT-J-6B: 71.0% at k=1 → 12.2% at k=3000). The conflict-resolution analysis (Table 3) quantifies that the KG increasingly corrects LLM errors as k grows (GPT-J-6B CF “LLM ✖, KG ✔” rises from 8.1% at k=1 to 25.0% at k=3000; Vicuna-7B from 7.7% to 20.0%). The approach also scales to larger models: with GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct at k=3000 on CF, GMeLLo achieves 51.4% vs MeLLo’s 30.7%; with GPT-3.5-Turbo, GMeLLo reaches 66.4% while MeLLo’s prompts fail, underscoring robustness to chat-model idiosyncrasies.

360.human_review: The technical contribution of the proposed approach may be limited, as the way to perform knowledge graph question answering (e.g., generating the relation chain for the given query and then the structured formal query executable over the knowledge graph to obtain the answer) is similar to existing knowledge graph question answering methods. I acknowledge the point that the focus of this work is more advanced, since it additionally considers the setting of the evolving environment with new facts; however, considering this setting seems to be a marginal contribution.
360.llm_review: Approach + Contribution: (1) Novelty appears incremental: using LLMs to canonicalize text into KG triples and relation chains, then executing SPARQL, aligns with prior KG-augmented QA; the main additions (top-50 relation curation, Contriever-based relation matching, and a “prefer-KG” arbitration) are practical rather than algorithmically novel. (2) The reliance on a curated schema is strong: relations are filtered from the first 500 Wikidata properties and narrowed to the top 50 via GPT-3.5-Turbo frequency checks, then used everywhere (Sections 3.1–3.2, 4.1.4).
