436.llm_review: Thorough experimental validation across settings: evaluations on both EN and ZH DiaASQ (Li et al., 2023a) report recommended metrics (Micro F1, Identification F1) and compare against strong discriminative (CEC, SpERT, Span-ASTE, MvI) and generative (ParaPhrase) baselines (Table 1). Ablations isolate MGDG and SOBM (Table 2), segmentation choices are compared (TOD-BERT, TSP, SMGD, RT, TWM vs. TADS in Table 4), and debiasing is benchmarked against Set (Table 5). Implementation details are sufficiently specified for reproducibility (BART-large 440M, 10 epochs, batch size 5, lr 5e-5, 3 cross-att layers, loss ratio 1:1:1, 4×3090 GPUs), and results are averaged over multiple runs.

437.human_review: The improvements are significant, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method
437.llm_review: Demonstrated effectiveness and component-level improvements: MGDG contributes up to +8.34 Identification F1 (EN, Table 2) via word-level labeling probabilities P and utterance-level topic masks m(k) merged into cross-attention (Eq. 1–2). SOBM adds up to +5.65 Micro F1 (EN, Table 2) by enriching order diversity through segmentation-based input augmentation, and surpasses the Set debiasing baseline by up to +5.89 Micro F1 (ZH, Table 5). Overall, SADD reduces noise-induced error proportion by 31.21 points (Table 3) and yields the best quadruple extraction scores on both EN and ZH.

438.human_review: The writing in the paper could be improved. There are sections where the logical flow is disrupted, leading to confusion about the motivations behind the study. For example, the transition between lines 328 and 329 is unclear.
438.llm_review: Clarity/motivation/presentation: several presentation issues hinder readability and weaken the narrative. Examples include typos and inconsistencies (e.g., title uses “Quarduples”; “Segmentationaided” vs. “Segmentation-Aided”; “MEDG” appears once instead of MGDG), dense notation with key pieces deferred to appendices (e.g., Appendix B.2.1/B.3 for the core gap derivation), and late justification for design choices (e.g., using Targets as topics). The main text would benefit from an earlier, explicit rationale for treating target tokens as topic anchors, and a concise, self-contained walk-through of denoised attention (Eq. 1–2) with a small worked example to show how P and m(k) reweight cross-attention.

439.llm_review: Figures and related work: Figure 1 and Figure 2 are visually dense and leave some steps under-specified (e.g., how clustering-derived masks m(k) are constructed and injected layer-wise; how multiple feasible labels are paired with augmented inputs in SOBM). A step-by-step schematic with a toy dialogue and explicit mask vectors would help. On related work, the discussion on order-invariant/set prediction is narrow: beyond non-autoregressive heads and Set (Li et al., 2023b), the paper should connect to permutation-invariant learning and set prediction (e.g., Deep Sets, Set Transformers) and order-agnostic decoding/training strategies in NLG/structured prediction to better position novelty.

440.human_review: The methodology section raises a concern: it is unclear whether each word in a dialogue can have multiple roles, which might lead to confusion during the word-level denoising classification process.
440.llm_review: Method: topic-aware segmentation depends on gold targets during training (Section 4.1.2: “positions of the ‘Target’ words are determined by the ground truth”) and predicted targets at test time, creating a potential train–test mismatch and label leakage. Errors in target labeling can cascade to segmentation and the denoised attention rj, affecting both mask quality and attention weights. The paper does not quantify robustness to noisy targets or analyze error propagation; strategies like scheduled sampling, joint training with noisy target supervision, or reporting performance as a function of target labeling F1 would address this.

441.human_review: The method used to compute the proportion of errors is not specified.
441.llm_review: Method: SOBM’s order-bias mitigation hinges on reply-thread-based segmentation and permutation of segments (Section 4.2.2; Section 5.1). The assumption that segments are semantically independent may break discourse coherence or coreference when reordered, potentially inducing distribution shift. This limits portability to datasets without reply structure. While Limitations note extra training time, the overhead is not quantified (e.g., number of augmented inputs per dialogue, wall-clock and memory multiplier). A stress test on longer dialogues, ablations on the number of segment permutations, and evaluation on datasets lacking reply threads—or alternative segmentation sources—would strengthen claims of generality and scalability.

442.human_review: The paper provides a thorough and comprehensive overview of the existing methods for length extrapolation in Transformers, specifically on positional encoding ones.
442.llm_review: Method, Transformer: The paper offers a well-structured taxonomy of length extrapolation methods centered on positional encoding for Transformers, covering both absolute and relative schemes as well as LLM-era techniques (e.g., RoPE/T5-bias families, interpolation, and randomized PEs). It uses a unified mathematical framing of attention with position terms to compare methods on shared ground (e.g., decompositions of compatibility scores, Fourier/wavelength views), which clarifies design trade-offs such as shift invariance, smoothness, clipping/binning, and decay-with-distance. The survey synthesizes practical insights relevant to current Transformer practice, explaining why RoPE dominates in-distribution while bias-based RPEs often extrapolate better, and how interpolation modifies RoPE bases or indices in practice.

443.human_review: Detailed explanations and categorisations of both absolute and relative positional encodings are well-presented, which is helpful in the understanding of their impact on length extrapolation.
443.llm_review: Explanation, Presentation: The exposition is clear and accessible, with consistent notation, helpful equations, and concise highlights that summarize takeaways at the end of major subsections. Figures and the table (taxonomy, APE vs. RPE schematic, and the PE comparison table) effectively communicate differences in how positional information is injected and where trade-offs arise. The discussion section cleanly surfaces open problems (evaluation, theory, synthetic-task insights), and the limitation statement is appropriately candid about scope and evidence granularity.

444.human_review: The paper lacks empirical analysis, such as detailed experimental results comparing different methods on standardised benchmarks (this is stated in the limitation section). As a survey paper, it is a bit short.
444.llm_review: Analysis, Benchmark, Experiment, Result: (1) The survey does not provide a quantitative synthesis (e.g., a standardized re-evaluation or meta-analysis) of methods across common tasks and lengths, making it hard to compare results beyond disparate reports. (2) There is no unifying experimental benchmark or protocol proposed or executed (datasets, metrics beyond perplexity, task suite, context-length grid), so several claims (e.g., RoPE extrapolation degradation, gains from NTK-aware variants) remain qualitative or rely on heterogeneous settings. (3) Some important practical questions (efficiency trade-offs, degradation at short lengths for scaled bases, compatibility with finetuning vs. zero-shot) are discussed but not empirically validated, limiting the strength of results-oriented conclusions.

445.human_review: There is an overemphasis on positional encoding, with less attention given to other factors influencing length extrapolation, such as model architecture and pretraining.
445.llm_review: Architecture, Model, Training: The scope is narrowly constrained to positional encodings; it gives limited coverage of architectural and training dimensions known to interact with length generalization (e.g., memory-augmented attention, recurrence, sparse/global attention patterns, segment-level modeling, curriculum or data-format effects). Practical training guidance for interpolation and randomized PE (e.g., scaling schedules, stability, multi-head/base allocation, cross-attention in encoder-decoder models, multimodal extensions) is light, and there is little discussion of how behavior scales with model size or compute. This focus risks underemphasizing system-level design choices that can enable or hinder extrapolation in deployed LLMs.

446.human_review: While the need for standardised benchmarks is highlighted, the paper does not propose specific solutions or guidelines for achieving this, reducing its impact in addressing this critical issue.
446.llm_review: Benchmark, Impact: Without proposing or releasing a concrete benchmark suite and evaluation protocol (tasks, lengths, metrics, and reporting standards), the survey’s impact on practice is constrained; readers lack a turnkey way to reproduce and compare methods fairly. A curated set of long-context datasets beyond perplexity, standardized downstream tasks (e.g., retrieval QA, long summarization/code, long-reasoning), and reporting templates for failure modes would substantially increase the paper’s influence and help consolidate the field.

447.key_points: Strength: Agent, Approach, Effectiveness, Framework, Improvement
447.human_review: Iterative Improvement: The iterative nature of the framework allows for continuous enhancement of responses, guided by clear and rational evolving directions identified through multi-agent cooperation. 4. Cost-Effective: The design maximizes viewpoint diversity while minimizing the cost of agents, addressing previous challenges in multi-agent debate (MAD) approaches.
447.llm_review: Agent/Approach/Framework/Improvement/Effectiveness: The paper proposes a concrete multi-agent pipeline—debate–advise–edit–judge (with K=3 iterations and memory refresh)—and a two-stage debate strategy that first fixes opposing stances (predetermined-position) and then switches to a free debate with cross-evaluation, which increases suggestion diversity while improving reliability for the downstream advisor and editor. The judge mitigates position bias by order-switching the compared responses and avoids inconsistent LLM scoring by forcing a discrete choice (better/draw). This design translates into measurable gains across settings. For LLaMA2-7B, editing 9K randomly sampled Alpaca data with CoEvol improves MT-Bench from 2.28 (random SFT) to 4.32 and AlpacaEval from 8.31% to 43.55% (Table 1), also outperforming training on the full 52K Alpaca (Alpaca2-7B: 3.94/20.15) and an LLM-selected 9K (AlpaGasus2-7B: 2.86/8.38). For Mistral-7B with high-quality 6K DEITA-selected data, CoEvol delivers consistent improvements with different agent LLMs and data formats (Table 2): single-turn data improves from 6.26/65.49 (DEITA) to 6.75/71.43 (CoEvol-MIXTRAL), and multi-turn from 6.98/80.08 to 7.22/89.76. Ablations (Table 3) attribute gains to each agent component: edit-only (4.05/26.15) < advise+edit (4.09/30.17) < debate+advise+edit (4.17/38.25) < full CoEvol with judge (4.32/43.55), showing the judge/iteration loop adds further value. The analysis quantifies how CoEvol changes data: more samples undergo ≥2 rounds with Mixtral agents (Fig. 2a), responses become longer (Fig. 2b), and advisor suggestions most often “provide/include/incorporate/add” details (46.0%) or “enhance/enrich” explanations (17.9%), with additional emphasis/highlight (13.7%) and explore (5.6%) actions (Fig. 3). Case studies (Table 4) show the edited responses add contextual detail/examples while staying on-instruction, supporting the claim that response refinement improves IFT data quality and downstream instruction-following.

448.human_review: Concurrent Speaking: Allowing debaters to speak concurrently to mitigate the influence of speaking order might lead to overlapping arguments, making it difficult for the advisor to parse and synthesize the suggestions effectively.
448.llm_review: Several methodological and practical concerns limit the generality and interpretability of the gains. (1) The framework preferentially increases response length (Fig. 2b) and the authors acknowledge that evaluators tend to reward longer outputs; yet there is no control for verbosity or utility per token, nor analysis of hallucination or factual drift as edits add detail (e.g., Table 4’s richer content could mask subtle inaccuracies). (2) All roles are filled by LLMs, often from the same family (e.g., ChatGPT-based agents), which risks bias propagation and consensus effects; although order-switching partially mitigates judge bias, there is no cross-model adjudication or human audit to ensure edited responses are genuinely better. (3) Important baselines are missing or lightly treated: beyond DEITA selection and an SFT baseline, there are no head-to-head comparisons against established self-refinement/multi-agent editing methods (e.g., Self-Refine, Reflexion, Critic-style pipelines), nor preference-optimization baselines (e.g., DPO) that might close the gap without multi-agent overhead. (4) The paper does not provide a cost/efficiency analysis (tokens per sample, wall-clock, agent calls per round), which is essential given the multi-agent, multi-round design; practitioners cannot assess improvement-per-cost or scaling feasibility. (5) Safety/toxicity, robustness, and domain transfer are not evaluated, despite applying edits that systematically increase content and specificity, which could amplify risky outputs.

449.human_review: Evaluation Consistency: Conducting cross-evaluations between agents may lead to inconsistent evaluations if the criteria for judging arguments are not clearly defined and uniformly applied.
449.llm_review: Evaluation: The study leans almost entirely on GPT-4–based automatic judgments (MT-Bench and AlpacaEval) to establish improvements. While the judge order-switch helps within CoEvol, there are no human preference ratings, calibration against human gold standards, or independent factuality metrics to validate that the edited responses are truly better rather than longer. No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the deltas (e.g., 6.98→7.22 MT-Bench; 80.08%→89.76% AlpacaEval in Table 2), making it unclear whether some gains are robust. The authors explicitly note length preferences of evaluators (Sec. 4.2), yet do not normalize for length or report length-controlled scores. Finally, evaluation breadth is narrow: the paper does not test on factuality benchmarks or safety suites, and omits comparisons to alternative data-refinement or self-improvement pipelines on the same training/eval splits, leaving it hard to attribute improvements specifically to the two-stage debate and judge loop.

450.human_review: The dataset creation pipeline is very clearly illustrated, and is reusable to other for supervised pre-training of generative lms. This pipeline also standardized many important factors for dataset creation of this kind, e.g. the response should be either in the document or a yes-or-no choice.
450.llm_review: Clarity, Data: The paper clearly motivates the need to move beyond uniform KIE templates and documents a transparent, reproducible pipeline for building K2Q. It provides concrete dataset statistics (number of templates/questions, extractive vs. boolean mix, entities per question, question/answer lengths), explicit handling of under-specified questions and line items, careful OCR cleaning, and a validation protocol with inter-annotator agreement. The scope and constraints (English-only, licensing inherited from sources, single-/multi-page handling) are stated, and the dataset is positioned for both generative and traditional VQA-style use.

451.human_review: The uniqueness and indispensability of this dataset is clearly illustrated by comparing with existing large-scale genrative VrDU datasets.
451.llm_review: Comparison, Data: The work situates K2Q against simple-template baselines and human-authored DocVQA/DUDE via measurable dataset properties and diversity metrics. It quantifies variety (templates per dataset, questions per document) and uses perplexity and self-BLEU to show K2Q is substantially closer to human-crafted data than SD while retaining the scalability of templating. The property-level comparison to related collections (e.g., ID, UReader) clarifies how K2Q differs in being extractive, boolean, diverse, and unambiguous.

452.human_review: Experiments solidly prove that the proposed dataset reaches high quality with little labor costs, which benefits the SFT of generative backbones.
452.llm_review: Data, Experiment: Extensive experiments across five datasets and seven models (zero-shot and fine-tuned) demonstrate that training on K2Q improves ANLS over simple templates and enhances robustness to template shifts (e.g., ~40% relative gains for DocLLM when generalizing). The inclusion of mK2Q decouples size from template complexity, and the groundedness/error-type analysis provides informative diagnostics beyond ANLS. Together, the data and experiments substantiate the central claim that richer, dataset-specific templates yield more robust VRDU behavior.

453.key_points: Weakness: Data, Impact, Method, Model, Novelty
453.human_review: The impact of this paper is confined to generative methods of VrDU, which I think is limited. Also, the construction process of this dataset is not novel enough, and no new models are proposed in this paper. These issues negatively affect my overall assessment of this paper.
453.llm_review: Data, Impact, Method, Model, Novelty: 1) The contribution is principally a transformation of existing KIE corpora rather than new document content, limiting novelty and potential long-term impact to the KIE sub-area (English-only, five datasets). 2) The dataset inherits annotation noise from sources, and the overall validation shows only moderate agreement; there is no human evaluation of question naturalness or ambiguity beyond the sampled QA checks. 3) Methodologically, reliance on ANLS alone and proxy measures (self-BLEU, GPT-2 perplexity) weakly capture question realism and may not reflect downstream utility; significance testing is not reported. 4) Model coverage is incomplete: state-of-the-art OCR-free MLLMs (e.g., mPLUG-DocOwl variants) are not trained, limiting conclusions about the full modeling spectrum; multi-page questions are excluded from experiments. 5) Release is noted as partial until publication, and templates are manually authored, which may cap scalability; the paper does not yet show LLM-augmented template generation or broader task coverage beyond KIE.

454.key_points: Weakness: Comparison, Data, Model, Prompt, Training
454.human_review: The comparison in Table 7 is unfair. From my point of view, the results in this table aim to prove that prompting existing VrD-KIE datasets with well-designed (but not simple) templates helps generative VrDU training. However, all the models in this table are evaluated on K2Q, thus the question prompts of the eval dataset is only seen by models trained on K2Q/miniK2Q during training. It is suggested to validate on alternative document-VQA-like datasets with different question prompts to mitigate this exposure bias.
454.llm_review: Comparison, Data, Model, Prompt, Training: 1) Some comparisons risk confounds: trainable models are initialized from DocVQA checkpoints (potentially favoring certain approaches), while several zero-shot models likely saw related data during pretraining; contamination is acknowledged but not controlled. 2) Prompting and decoding details for zero-shot LLMs (especially GPT-4 text-only) are minimal, and choices (e.g., omitting image input for GPT-4) may understate or misrepresent capabilities. 3) Training protocols lack details on hyperparameter tuning, multiple seeds, or significance, making it hard to assess robustness. 4) Evaluations emphasize performance on the proposed templates; there is limited testing on external human-authored benchmarks beyond indirect perplexity/self-BLEU analyses, and comparisons to other instruction-style datasets (e.g., BuDDIE, ID) are not run end-to-end. 5) While mK2Q controls for size, broader ablations (e.g., template type distributions, boolean vs. extractive balance, line-item coverage) are limited, leaving open how specific prompt features drive gains.

455.human_review: The studied task is crucial for adapting LLMs to specialized domains, as it addresses the challenges of optimizing model performance in specific areas such as clinical applications.
455.llm_review: Clear application focus with concrete gains on strong open models: The work adapts Mistral‑7B and Mixtral‑8x7B to clinical QA and reports sizable, clinically relevant improvements using domain data. On Mixtral, the best configuration (continuous pretraining + NEFTune; P+N) achieves MedQA 68.34, USMLE 72.82, MMLU‑med 79.84, MedMCQA 65.34, improving over the stock Mixtral‑Instruct (52.55/65.99/75.78/53.74) by +15.8/+6.8/+4.1/+11.6 points. Against larger medical baselines (e.g., Med42 70B), Mixtral P+N is higher on all four tasks (e.g., MedQA 68.34 vs 61.52; USMLE 72.82 vs 72.01; MMLU‑med 79.84 vs 76.71; MedMCQA 65.34 vs 60.93). The study also scales to realistic data volumes (50B clinical tokens for pretraining; ~500M tokens for instruction data stated in the abstract) and reports deployment-relevant choices (no PHI, permissive licenses, Mistral/Mixtral backbones), making the contribution directly applicable to clinical NLP.

456.human_review: The proposed method demonstrates excellent performance, showing significant improvements in various clinical tasks through techniques like continuous pre-training, instruct fine-tuning, NEFTune, and complex prompt engineering.
456.llm_review: Methodologically complete pipeline with prompt-aware evaluation and task diversity: The paper evaluates four techniques—continuous pretraining on a blended corpus (50B clinical + 15B SlimPajama, 4 epochs ≈260B tokens), instruction fine-tuning on a 500M‑token dataset, NEFTune with α=5 noise at embeddings, and MedPrompt prompting with CoT, few‑shot, dynamic retrieval (Milvus + gte‑small), and an ensemble variant. Tasks span MedQA, USMLE (sample and self‑assessment), MMLU medical subset, and MedMCQA. Prompting provides substantial lift even without additional training: the authors report that MedPrompt raises Mixtral‑Instruct MedQA accuracy from 52.55% to >75% via CoT + KNN CoT ensembles (Fig. 3), while training-based methods further compound these gains across all reported tasks (Table 2).

457.key_points: Strength: Analysis, Effectiveness, Experiment, Fine-tuning, Model, Performance, Result, Technique
457.human_review: The authors provide a analysis of the experimental results, highlighting the impact of each technique on model performance and offering insights into the effectiveness of different fine-tuning strategies.
457.llm_review: Evidence‑backed analysis of technique interactions and effectiveness: The study saves multiple pretraining checkpoints and shows that non‑instructed checkpoints initially degrade QA accuracy (Fig. 2), but once instruction‑tuned, later checkpoints (exposed to more clinical tokens) steadily improve—quantifying that continuous pretraining is a foundation rather than a standalone fix. Stability evidence is provided via loss curves (Fig. 1) after applying a 1% linear LR warmup (starting at 1/10 of max LR) and mixing 50B in‑domain with 15B general tokens. NEFTune acts as an effective regularizer: on Mistral‑7B, MedQA improves from 54.28 (F) to 60.72 (N), and further to 62.69 (P+N); on Mixtral, MedQA improves from 62.60 (F) to 66.93 (N) and 68.34 (P+N). These concrete differentials substantiate the claim that noise‑augmented fine‑tuning and continued pretraining are complementary.

458.human_review: It is not clear which part of the proposed method are from prior works and which parts of the work is proposed by authors.
458.llm_review: Method novelty and positioning relative to prior work are under‑articulated: The core recipe—continued pretraining on in‑domain data, instruction tuning, and CoT prompting—is established in biomedical NLP, yet the paper does not precisely differentiate its contributions from prior continued‑pretraining efforts (beyond citing representative models like GatorTron, PMC‑LLaMA, MediTron). Methodologically, key design choices lack ablations: no study of the 50B:15B domain:general mix ratio, epochs (fixed at 4), or learning‑rate warmup schedule sensitivity; NEFTune reports that α=5 works best but shows no quantitative sweep. The pipeline omits alternative alignment methods (RLHF/DPO, safety or refusal tuning) that are widely used in clinical chat models, so it is unclear whether the reported gains are competitive with alignment‑oriented approaches under similar compute.

459.human_review: Some analysis are too shallow and are discussed in prior works, such as the usage of NEFT (L517-539), as well as the benefits of using prompt engineering (L540-L562).
459.llm_review: Prompting analysis lacks component isolation and data‑leakage safeguards, and omits critical related baselines: The dynamic few‑shot strategy explicitly retrieves the top‑5 closest training questions (embedded with gte‑small) from a Milvus store of CoTs to construct evaluation prompts. The paper does not report any de‑duplication or minimum similarity‑gap checks between retrieved exemplars and test items within the same dataset, nor cross‑dataset near‑duplicate filtering—raising a risk that near‑identical training items appear as exemplars during evaluation. Moreover, there are no ablations isolating the marginal benefit of (i) plain CoT vs (ii) static few‑shot vs (iii) dynamic retrieval vs (iv) ensemble shuffling, and no comparisons to strong prompting baselines like self‑consistency, ReAct, or Tree‑of‑Thought. Finally, the paper does not quantify prompting cost/latency (e.g., 5× generations at temperature 0.2 in the ensemble) or sensitivity to the retrieval embedding model.

460.human_review: It would be better to study the effect of different pretraining corpus (e.g. Pubmed, medical textbook) and compare their performance.
460.llm_review: Comparability, performance reporting, and training transparency need tightening: The evaluation modifies EleutherAI Harness to score the full answer text rather than option labels (a/b/c/d); many published baselines report label likelihood, so cross‑paper comparability is uncertain. No confidence intervals or multiple‑seed variance are reported for the accuracy gains in Table 2 or for >75% MedQA with MedPrompt. Compute is substantial (up to 10 nodes × 8 H100 for pretraining; 4 nodes for fine‑tuning with FSDP and bf16), yet GPU‑hours, token throughput, and cost‑normalized comparisons are not provided. Although the authors mitigate catastrophic forgetting by mixing 15B general tokens, retention is not measured (e.g., full MMLU, ARC‑C/HELM), and Fig. 2 shows early declines for non‑instructed checkpoints without quantifying general‑domain trade‑offs.

461.human_review: The dual-stage approach of KnowTuning—combining fine-grained knowledge augmentation with coarse-grained knowledge comparison—is novel and addresses a clear gap in the existing LLM fine-tuning practices.
461.llm_review: The paper proposes a clear and novel fine-tuning approach that explicitly targets knowledge awareness at two levels. The fine-grained stage selects difficult atomic facts using model perplexity and augments training with rewritten QA pairs, while the coarse-grained stage uses principled perturbations (delete/revise/shuffle) to construct preference pairs for DPO across completeness, factuality, and logicality. This decomposition is intuitive, model-agnostic, and easy to implement, and it ties the training objectives directly to the targeted knowledge qualities—an advancement over prior single-aspect fine-tuning such as factuality-only approaches.

462.human_review: The paper thoroughly evaluates the effectiveness of KnowTuning across two datasets and compares its performance with baseline models, providing both automatic and human-based evaluations.
462.llm_review: The study evaluates on both a general-domain QA set (Dolly, filtered) and a medical-domain QA set (MedQuAD), and tests two model sizes (Llama2 7B/13B). It combines reference-based GPT-4 evaluation on completeness/factuality/logicality, human pairwise evaluation against a strong baseline, and fine-grained fact-level scoring (counts and correctness rates). Across setups, the method shows consistent improvements, with win/tie/lose margins, significance tests for automatic evaluations, and ablations supporting the reported gains.

463.human_review: KnowTuning demonstrates a tangible improvement in LLMs' ability to generate answers that are not only more factual but also complete and logically structured.
463.llm_review: Model capabilities are meaningfully improved: the method increases the number of correct facts while reducing error rates, and enhances completeness, factuality, and logicality in generated answers across both model sizes. Ablations indicate both the fine-grained augmentation and the coarse-grained preference training contribute, supporting the claim that the approach strengthens models’ knowledge handling rather than merely changing style.

464.human_review: The method's reliance on filtering and rewriting QA pairs, along with constructing and training with comparison sets, may be very time-consuming and costly.
464.llm_review: Methodologically, the pipeline relies heavily on GPT-3.5 for extracting atomic knowledge, rewriting questions/answers, and generating nonfactual variants, which introduces potential label noise and bias. The notion of “difficulty” via SFT perplexity may conflate rarity and surface form with importance, and no sensitivity analysis is provided for key hyperparameters (e.g., α for difficult facts, β for deletion rate). The synthetic negatives (deleted/revised/shuffled facts) may not fully capture realistic failure modes, and details on prompts, sampling settings, and computational cost are insufficient for assessing training stability, scalability, and reproducibility.

465.key_points: Weakness: Benchmark, Evaluation, Improvement, Performance, Task
465.human_review: While the paper showcases improvements particularly in medical and generic QA tasks, it's less clear how this method performs across a broader range of knowledge-intensive tasks. A more comprehensive evaluation on knowledge-intensive tasks such as the KILT benchmark (https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.02252) is encouraged.
465.llm_review: The benchmarking is narrow—only Dolly (filtered) and MedQuAD—omitting widely used long-form, knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks (e.g., ELI5, NQ-Open, HotpotQA, TriviaQA long-form, PubMedQA). The evaluation leans heavily on GPT-4 judgments, with limited human evaluation details (sample size, protocol, inter-annotator agreement). The constructed logicality metric (via shuffling) is a weak proxy for discourse coherence, and performance is not assessed on broader tasks beyond QA. As a result, the generality of the reported improvements across tasks and stronger, more diverse benchmarks remains uncertain.

466.human_review: S1. This work effectively combines multiple findings and presents a practical approach to reducing the high computational cost of text-centric visual models.
466.llm_review: Approach/Model: The design choices are concrete and efficiency-driven. Replacing CLIP-L/336 with CLIP-B/224 (≈88M params) and using AnyRes caps visual tokens at 98–637 even for 896×676 images, compared to LLaVA-NeXT’s 1,728–2,880 tokens for 336–672 px grids. The ELVA-encoder is constructed via a two-step specialization-and-averaging recipe: (i) unfreeze the vision encoder and fine-tune a small (≈1B) VLM on text-reading datasets (OCR-IDL, PDFA, LLaVA/LLaVAR align sets) to produce multiple text-centric encoders (12 REncoders; each run ≈1.7 days on 8×V100), then (ii) uniformly average them with the base CLIP-B to form a single 88M encoder. This yields a simple, deployable stack (no resamplers, no extra expert branches) that lowers inference tokens without sacrificing high-resolution coverage.

467.key_points: Strength: Improvement, Method, Model, Performance, Training
467.human_review: S2. In particular, the method of training an image encoder with a small VLM to improve its performance for a specific task (OCR task) and averaging it with the original model would be beneficial to many readers in the community, as it has the potential to improve model performance while maintaining inference cost.
467.llm_review: Improvement/Method/Model/Performance/Training: The empirical support is strong and numerically specific. Vision encoder ablations at 3.8B (Table 2) show the ELVA-encoder (C5) raises text-centric accuracy from 40.3 to 45.7 (+5.4) and overall from 47.4 to 50.2 (+2.8) versus CLIP-B AnyRes (C1), while uniform averaging outperforms simply unfreezing CLIP (C2: overall drop to 40.9). Read-and-Reason (RR) supervision improves performance consistently (Table 3): at 7B, overall rises from 51.8 (R1) to 52.9 (R2) with text-centric +1.7 (47.5→49.2), and at 13B overall +1.4 (52.5→53.9), text-centric +1.9 (48.5→50.4). Efficiency/performance trade-offs are favorable against LLaVA-NeXT under realistic budgets (Table 5): ELVA-7B achieves 69.1 DocVQA and 61.8 ChartQA at 0.54 s/img and 14.5 GB vs LLaVA-NeXT-7B’s 68.3/51.9 at 1.01 s/img and 20 GB; ELVA-13B reaches 71.7/65.2 at 0.72 s/img, 27.0 GB vs 69.8/59.0 at 1.78 s/img, 40.1 GB. Training is transparent and reproducible: alignment/instruction datasets (~1.1M + ~1.0M), 11K steps with batch 128, plus detailed per-scale training times (e.g., 36 h for 7B, 66 h for 13B on 8×A100; Table 7).

468.human_review: S3. The authors plan to publish models ranging from 160M to 13B parameters, which could be useful for a variety of applications.
468.llm_review: Application/Model: The models target document assistants with concrete, task-aligned resources and metrics. ELVA-13B attains top or competitive scores on document- and math-centric benchmarks (Table 4): DocVQA 71.7, ChartQA 65.2, AI2D 56.8, MathVista 69.3, and HallusionBench 77.7, while maintaining single-GPU deployability (e.g., ELVA-7B at 14.5 GB VRAM, 0.54 s/img). The introduced CORD-Instruct (structured JSON/XML/Markdown outputs; 680 examples) and Parsing-Bench (LLM-as-a-judge over BID/SROIE images; ELVA-13B 59.2) directly reflect practical workflows like receipt parsing and identity document extraction. The OCR-augmented setting further boosts text-heavy performance (e.g., ELVA-13B: DocVQA 81.1, InfoVQA 44.8; Table 6), indicating a usable path for high-accuracy pipelines despite the known OCR latency trade-off.

469.human_review: W1. I am concerned about the lack of explanation about the small VLMs used when learning REncoder. There seems to be no mention of the small VLM used. It would also be better if conditions such as whether it is better to use the same series of LLMs as the subsequent LLMs or whether models of the best possible quality should be used are discussed.
469.llm_review: Explanation/Model: The mechanism by which uniform soup of 12 text-reading encoders with CLIP-B improves text-centric results while retaining general vision ability is presented empirically but not explained mechanistically. There is no probing of representation shifts (e.g., font/layout sensitivity vs. natural-object features) or attention patterns to justify why averaging works or when it fails. The trade-off against a stronger general-image baseline is only partially quantified: with CLIP-L/336 trained on their data (C6), general-image score is 58.6 vs 54.7 for ELVA-encoder (C5), a −3.9 drop (Table 2), and section 6.3 shows entity-name failures on LLaVA-Bench (e.g., 5/10 and 2/10 when names are required). A per-category error breakdown on SEED/MMStar or feature-level analyses would substantiate the claimed balance and clarify limitations in entity recognition.

470.human_review: W2. The largest improvement in Figure 1 is achieved by adding the open-source training dataset, but detailed discussion, such as data sampling strategy and the process that led to that recipe, is limited.
470.llm_review: Data/Discussion/Improvement: The new evaluation resources are small or synthetic, limiting statistical strength and external validity. CORD-Instruct contains only 680 GPT-3.5-synthesized items; Parsing-Bench is built from ≈30 images (BID, SROIE), and uses LLM-as-a-judge, which can be biased and sensitive to prompt context. The paper does not quantify inter-rater reliability or provide a human-judged subset. Although OCR-augmented improvements are sizable (e.g., ELVA-13B DocVQA +9.4, InfoVQA +10.2; Table 6), the added OCR latency (~4 s/sample with CLOVA) is not integrated into end-to-end throughput comparisons, making it hard to assess practical trade-offs. The discussion could be strengthened by (i) evaluating on larger, multilingual and standardized VDU suites, (ii) reporting end-to-end latency/accuracy (with and without OCR) under matched hardware, and (iii) adding comparisons to recent high-res LVLMs (e.g., InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD) under matched token budgets and memory constraints.

471.human_review: The method section describes the proposed method and its components in detail. Especially, each component is explained thoroughly and supported by appropriate citations.
471.llm_review: The paper’s explanation of the method is concrete and traceable from observation to design. It first quantifies that adding compositional attributes to prompts increases CLIP confidence (Fig. 1a, ImageNet-1k sample; prompts like “A photo of a [a] [cls]” shift the CLIP score distribution right). It then constructs IntCoOp to operationalize this: (i) obtain image-level attribute labels aI with a BLIP-2 VQA pipeline offline (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 1b), (ii) train a small attribute extractor A to map the CLIP visual embedding V(I) to the CLIP text-embedding space T(aI) with an L2 loss (Eq. 4, f=2), (iii) form instance-conditioned prompts via multi-head attention over the image representation (Sec. 4.2), and (iv) regularize learnable prompts toward a diverse pool of N=80 attribute-aware templates (Eq. 6, g=1). The full loss (Eq. 7) clearly decomposes into cross-entropy, attribute alignment (λ1=4), and prompt regularization (λ2=4). The authors also justify why attributes must be learned rather than generated at inference (class labels unknown), closing a common gap in prompt-based VL methods.

472.human_review: Utilizing BLIP-2 model for attribute generation is an interesting idea. This external knowledge may offer information not easily captured with only a few-shot examples.
472.llm_review: The model architecture is coherent and minimally invasive to CLIP: encoders remain frozen while adding (a) a two-layer MLP attribute extractor A: RDvl→R512 that predicts an attribute embedding aligned to CLIP’s text space, (b) deep visual prompting by appending n=4 learnable visual tokens per layer up to depth K=9 to enrich the image representation for A (Table 3 shows clear gains of deep vs. shallow prompting), and (c) a multi-head attention module that uses the shared context tokens u as queries and V(I) as keys/values to produce instance-conditioned context h(I). Prompts take the form p+(I) = [h1..hM, A(V(I)), [cls]c] (Eq. 5) with M=4; this makes the attribute embedding an explicit, interpretable component of the text input. The prompt regularizer anchors learned prompts to 80 synthetic attribute-infused templates (Radford et al., 2021), which helps control overfitting without constraining the model to a single hand-written template.

473.human_review: Both base-to-novel generalization and domain generalization experiments are conducted.
473.llm_review: Experiments are extensive and focused on generalization. In base-to-novel transfer (16-shot per base class) across 10 datasets (ImageNet, Caltech101, OxfordPets, StanfordCars, Flowers102, Food101, FGVCAircraft, SUN397, EuroSAT, UCF101), IntCoOp achieves the best average harmonic mean (HM) of base/novel accuracies: 80.75 vs. 79.48 (LFA) and 73.23 (CoOp), with clear wins on attribute-rich datasets: OxfordPets HM 97.04 (vs. LFA 95.68), StanfordCars HM 76.67 (vs. LFA 75.59), EuroSAT HM 85.77 (vs. LFA 80.83), and ImageNet HM 74.29 (vs. LFA 72.93). For domain generalization (trained on ImageNet, evaluated on V2/Sketch/A/R), IntCoOp has the strongest average 60.71, outperforming MaPLe (60.28), RPO (60.27), LASP (60.19), LFA (60.08), and ProGrad (59.08). The ablation in Table 3 shows that both deep visual prompting (K=9) and multi-head attention conditioning are necessary to reach the reported 80.75 HM, supporting the claimed design choices.

474.human_review: There is no need to limit the BLIP-2 model to generate in “one-word” because the answers from BLIP-2 will be encoded to a single embedding vector and used as a target for the Attribute Extractor. This raises the question about the necessity of ‘single-word prediction’ (which seems to be the key contribution).
474.llm_review: The contribution is incremental relative to prior prompt tuning and conditioning methods. The paper combines known components—visual prompting (Jia et al., 2022), instance-conditioned prompts (Zhou et al., 2022a), and prompt regularization toward hand-crafted templates (Yao et al., 2023)—with an attribute extractor trained on BLIP-2–generated labels. While the use of attribute-aware regularization (N=80 templates) and explicit insertion of an attribute embedding into the prompt are sensible, the conceptual novelty is modest. The interpretability claim is supported mainly by cosine similarity to an attribute-including prompt template (Fig. 3) rather than human judgments or causal probing; there is no user study or ground-truth attribute benchmark to verify that learned attributes are faithful and useful beyond performance gains.

475.human_review: The demonstration of cosine similarity (Figure 3) alone is not sufficient to show that the attribute extractor effectively extracts information predicted from BLIP-2. The performance of the ‘oracle’ setting, using BLIP-2 embeddings (i.e., the target of L_attr loss) instead of predicted ones, should be presented. Also, a direct comparison between estimated and BLIP-2 embeddings is necessary.
475.llm_review: Comparisons and embedding details leave ambiguities that affect fairness and technical clarity. First, the multi-head attention block sets Key=Value=V(I). If V(I) is CLIP’s global image embedding (a single vector), attention over a single token reduces to a learned linear transform, not a true attention over spatial tokens; if patch-level features are used, this is not specified. Second, the domain generalization table shows PLOT performing abnormally poorly (avg 41.39), far below other methods; without matching training recipes, hyperparameters, or model size/compute normalization, it is difficult to trust cross-paper reimplementations. Third, some base accuracies degrade: on ImageNet base, IntCoOp 75.99 trails ProGrad (77.02) and PLOT (77.30); on FGVCAircraft base, 38.55 is below PLOT’s 42.13 and LFA’s 41.48. These trade-offs are acknowledged only implicitly and not analyzed (e.g., whether attribute insertion shifts the bias toward novel classes). Reporting parameter counts, FLOPs, and latency (visual tokens at K=9 and added modules) would strengthen the comparisons.

476.human_review: Based on the ablation results (Table 3), adding attribute information does not appear to be a critical factor for performance improvement. In other words, visual prompting, instance conditioning, and regularization contribute significantly more.
476.llm_review: The ablations and significance analysis are incomplete for the claimed improvements. Table 3 varies prompting depth and conditioning type, but there is no main-text ablation isolating the contribution of the attribute loss (λ1) vs. the regularizer (λ2), or sensitivity to λ1, λ2, N=80 template pool size, and the chosen norms (f=2, g=1). Attribute supervision quality is only stress-tested by swapping adjectives (ImageNet HM drops from 74.29 to 63.27), but no graded noise or partial-coverage studies are provided. Gains over the strongest baseline are sometimes small: Flowers102 HM +0.24 over LFA (85.24 vs. 85.00), Caltech101 +0.12, SUN397 +0.87, and FGVCAircraft HM 37.17 is still below PLOT’s 37.46. There are no confidence intervals or statistical tests over the three random seeds, so it’s unclear if 0.1–1.0% margins are robust. Including per-dataset significance and component-wise ablations would substantiate the results.

477.human_review: Novel approach using semantic representations to improve AVQA. It uses source-wise learnable tokens to extract semantic features from audio and visual inputs and employs a source-aware semantic representation block to align audio-visual features. In addition, it also applies multi-modal spatial and temporal attention to focus on relevant regions, with integrated features using a fusion network for final answer prediction.
477.llm_review: Approach and Novelty: The paper introduces Source-wise Learnable Tokens (SLT) and a Source-aware Semantic Representation (SaSR) block that explicitly bind sound sources and visual objects to semantic categories. Concretely, the model allocates C learnable tokens GC = {gi}Ci=1 (e.g., instrument categories) and uses them in two stages: (i) self-attention to enrich audio (fr_at) and visual (fr_vt) embeddings into fs_AT and fs_VT while updating token states (Ga_C, Gv_C), and (ii) cross-attention from tokens to embeddings and back to produce fg_AT and fg_VT. Two auxiliary losses enforce token semantics: a source-presence BCE on Ga′_C and Gv′_C with ground-truth source labels p_C, and a CE regularizer Lreg to encourage each token gi to represent a distinct class. This token-centric, source-aware fusion is distinct from prior AVQA models that rely on generic cross-modal attention without explicit source-category centroids, offering a clear novelty for aligning audio-visual evidence with question-relevant entities.

478.human_review: Comprehensive experiments and comparisons with existing methods. It outperforms existing AVQA methods on the Music-AVQA dataset, especially for complex question types. It also achieves 89.9% accuracy on the AVQA-Yang dataset, surpassing previous methods. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed components.
478.llm_review: Accuracy, Comparison, Data, Experiment: On MUSIC-AVQA (45,867 QA pairs, 22 instrument classes), SaSR-Net achieves 74.21% overall accuracy, improving over A-VST (71.59%), TJSTG (73.04%), and PSTP-Net (73.52%) per Table 1. The model also attains 89.9% on AVQA-Yang, exceeding the best listed baseline HCRN+HAVF at 89.0% (Table 4). Ablations (Table 2) attribute gains to the proposed components: removing both SLT and SaSR drops accuracy to 70.31%; adding SLT alone yields 72.16% (+1.85), SaSR alone 71.78% (+1.47), and both 74.21% (+3.90). The attention modules further help (Table 3): without SA/TA the model scores 70.17%, with TA alone 72.03%, and with SA+TA 74.21%. The experimental setup is clearly stated (VGGish audio to 512D, ResNet-18 visual at 1 fps, 1 s segments, LSTM 512D question encoder, 65.1M parameters, Adam 1e-4, λ1=λ2=λ3=0.5), and results are reported on two public datasets with a broad baseline suite spanning audio-only, visual-only, video QA, and AVQA methods.

479.key_points: Strength: Attention, Figure, Interpretation, Model, Result
479.human_review: Visualization of model attention helps interpret results.
479.llm_review: Attention, Figure, Interpretation, Model, Result: The multi-modal Spatial Attention (SA) uses audio-conditioned attention over visual feature maps X^r_P to localize sounding objects and produce fsa_vt; the Temporal Attention (TA) aligns question embeddings with time-indexed fg_AT and fsa_VT to select relevant moments. Figure 3 visualizes SA heatmaps that highlight instrument regions and TA scores that peak at question-relevant timestamps, providing concrete interpretability of where (spatial) and when (temporal) the model attends. These mechanisms correspond to improvements on categories that rely on precise grounding: the paper reports notable gains over A-VST in Audio-Visual question types such as Counting (+3.55%), Localization (+9.4%), Comparative (+14.48%), and Temporal (+11.64%), aligning the design of SA/TA with the observed result improvements in tasks that require localization and temporal reasoning (Table 1 and Fig. 4).

480.human_review: The authors focused on Source-wise Learnable Tokens to extract semantically compact features from videos and employ Source-aware Semantic Representation to align these with visual and audio features. Visualizing and comparing the features in latent space would be helpful to demonstrate SaSR-Net as a better representation method.
480.llm_review: Comparison, Figure, Method: Methodological clarity and comparison scope need tightening. There are notation and definition issues that impede reproducibility: Lmatch is written as CE(fsa_vt,1) + CE(fsa_vt,0), seemingly using the matched representation for both positive and negative terms, although the text introduces a mismatched fsa_v′_t; Lsource is defined on FC(Ga′_C), FC(Gv′_C) but the prose also mentions comparisons to fg_AT and fg_VT, creating ambiguity about which signals are supervised. The cross-attention equations omit standard Q/K/V projections, making it unclear how attention weights are parameterized beyond FC layers. On comparisons, recent and relevant AVQA systems cited in Related Work (e.g., LA-VISH) are not included in Table 1, and the paper references MUSIC-AVQA v2.0 (Liu et al., 2024) but does not evaluate on it. Figures 3 and 4 are helpful but their captions do not detail quantitative localization metrics or failure cases, limiting the strength of the interpretability claim.

481.human_review: From Table 1, SaSR-Net seems to perform poorly on single-modality questions. I would like to see further elaborations on potential reasons.
481.llm_review: Performance: The improvements over the strongest baselines on MUSIC-AVQA are modest in the aggregate: 74.21% vs 73.52% (PSTP-Net, +0.69) and 73.04% (TJSTG, +1.17). Moreover, some subcategory results appear weaker than top baselines (e.g., TJSTG shows higher Audio Count 80.38% vs SaSR-Net 73.95% in Table 1), suggesting that gains are not uniform across tasks. The token design assumes a closed set of C categories; this can cap performance on open-vocabulary or out-of-domain categories and may explain why improvements concentrate on instrument-centric data rather than yielding larger across-the-board gains.

482.human_review: Computational costs should be discussed and compared for multi-modal experiments.
482.llm_review: Comparison, Experiment: Important experimental details for fair comparison are missing or underspecified. It is unclear whether all baselines are re-trained with the same backbone (ResNet-18 @1 fps) and audio features (VGGish 128D→512D), or if results are taken from prior papers with different settings. The negative-pair sampling for Lmatch (frequency, ratio per batch, and how negatives are balanced across classes) is not specified, which matters for stability and effect size. The supervision for SLT on AVQA-Yang (which lacks explicit instrument labels) is not clarified—how is p_C derived there? No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported, so it is hard to judge whether ~0.7–1.2% gains are robust. An evaluation on MUSIC-AVQA v2.0, as well as robustness studies to noise/overlapping sources, would substantially strengthen the comparative evidence.

483.human_review: The paper introduces a unique approach to TKG reasoning by addressing the asynchronous evolution of events, which has not been adequately considered in previous works.
483.llm_review: Approach and novelty: The paper proposes a natural division of the history into explicit patches (consecutive snapshots where the target entity appears) and implicit patches (where it does not), then performs dual-level aggregation. This is a clear departure from prior work that models all snapshots uniformly (e.g., RE-GCN uses GRUs over full histories; TiRGN learns periodicity and recurrence without entity-specific patching). Concretely, the method: (i) constructs connected subgraphs within patches by linking k-hop neighborhoods across timestamps; (ii) uses a relation-aware GNN with translational interaction (hl_o,i + r_i) in the attention message (Eq. 1) to capture structural dependencies within each snapshot; (iii) aggregates temporal correlations across subgraphs in a patch via a GNN (Eq. 2) to obtain local representations; and (iv) applies inter-patch cross-attention with a learnable query and position embeddings (Eq. 3) to assign adaptive weights to patches. This patch-aware, dual-level design directly operationalizes asynchronous evolution and long-range dependencies and, to my knowledge, is novel in TKG extrapolation.

484.human_review: The proposed dual-level aggregation framework is well-designed and effectively captures both local and global temporal dependencies, improving the accuracy of entity representations.
484.llm_review: Accuracy and framework: The framework yields consistent SOTA gains with clear margins. Examples: on ICEWS14, MRR 55.12 vs prior best 47.40 (L2TKG), Hits@10 77.26 vs 71.05; on ICEWS05-15, MRR 61.77 vs 57.43 (L2TKG), Hits@10 83.71 vs 80.69; on ICEWS18, MRR 38.72 vs 34.91 (RPC), Hits@10 62.46 vs 55.89; on GDELT, MRR 23.48 vs 22.41 (RPC); on ICEWS22, MRR 41.25 vs 35.86 (TiRGN); on ICEWS23, MRR 39.12 vs 34.90 (TiRGN). The modularity is supported by ablation evidence (Table 4): removing inter-patch attention drops ICEWS14 MRR from 55.12 to 53.91 and ICEWS05-15 from 61.77 to 60.01; removing the relation-aware GNN (RGNN) further reduces ICEWS14 to 52.05 and GDELT to 20.73; excluding implicit patches hurts ICEWS18 (38.72 to 36.69), showing the framework components each contribute materially to the accuracy gains.

485.human_review: Extensive experiments on six datasets show that NEDA significantly outperforms existing methods, providing strong empirical evidence for its effectiveness.
485.llm_review: Data, effectiveness, and experiment: The study spans six datasets, including four widely used ones (ICEWS14, ICEWS18, ICEWS05-15, GDELT) and two newly curated benchmarks (ICEWS22/23), evaluated under time-aware filtered MRR/Hits. Results are averaged over five runs, with code provided, enhancing reproducibility. Effectiveness is probed via: (i) ablations isolating implicit patches, connected subgraphs, inter-patch attention, position embeddings, and the relation-aware GNN; (ii) sensitivity analyses showing performance improves up to L=2 and then degrades when deeper (over-smoothing/noise from distant neighbors), and that neighbor count n in implicit patches must balance missing context (too small) vs overshadowing explicit evolution (too large); and (iii) low-data regime experiments where NEDA outperforms TiRGN even with 10–20% training data, demonstrating sample efficiency. Hyperparameters are specified (d=200, L=k=2; dataset-specific n), and inter-patch positional encoding is explicitly used to retain patch order.

486.human_review: The framework's complexity might lead to scalability issues when applied to very large TKGs. The paper could benefit from a discussion on the computational efficiency and possible optimizations.
486.llm_review: Complexity, efficiency, and framework: The pipeline is per-query and multi-stage—patch construction, per-snapshot k-hop subgraph extraction, relation-aware GNN within snapshots, temporal GNN across subgraphs, then cross-attention across patches—implying nontrivial time/memory overhead compared to snapshot-level inference (authors note this in Limitations). However, the paper provides no asymptotic or empirical efficiency analysis (e.g., training/inference time per query, GPU memory, throughput) and no scaling study vs. number of patches M, subgraph size, or degree. The smaller gain on GDELT (MRR +1.07 absolute over RPC) under 15-minute granularity and 1.7M training facts suggests practical limits when patches are dense and numerous. The framework would benefit from reporting runtime/memory on ICEWS vs. GDELT, profiling bottlenecks (subgraph sampling vs. inter-patch attention), and exploring batching/caching, sparse attention, or early pruning of low-relevance patches to improve efficiency.

487.human_review: The proposed method is evaluated only on TKG reasoning tasks. It would be interesting to see its applicability and performance on related tasks, such as temporal link prediction or temporal knowledge graph completion.
487.llm_review: Application and evaluation: Although the task definition covers both entity and relation prediction for extrapolation, experiments evaluate only entity prediction; relation prediction is not reported. The new ICEWS22/23 datasets strengthen coverage, but baseline inclusion is uneven: key recent strong baselines like RPC and L2TKG are not reported on ICEWS22/23 (Table 3 shows dashes), making it harder to compare against the best-performing methods on those sets. There is also no statistical significance testing on the reported mean improvements, and no runtime comparisons. The evaluation is limited to event-centric ICEWS/GDELT; no experiments on general-purpose TKGs (e.g., Wikidata-temporal) or domain-specific TKGs are provided, leaving generalization to other temporal regimes untested.

488.human_review: The natural division strategy for patch selection is not deeply analyzed. Further discussion on its limitations and potential improvements could strengthen the paper.
488.llm_review: Analysis, discussion, and improvement: The model’s claim to capture asynchronous evolution would be more convincing with deeper analysis. There are no visualizations of inter-patch attention weights, case studies, or error analyses illustrating how irrelevant pre-onset patches are down-weighted or how long life-cycle events are captured. The inter-patch attention uses a single global learnable query Q (Eq. 3) rather than conditioning on the specific query (s, r, t), potentially limiting adaptivity across relations or entities; this design choice is not analyzed. The patch boundary rule (entity presence/absence) is heuristic and may miss topic shifts within explicit spans; the authors acknowledge capturing only the dominant topic per patch. Sensitivity results show performance fragility to L and n, but there is no guidance for automatic selection. Improvements could include query-conditioned attention (e.g., Q derived from [h_s, r, t]), multi-topic modeling within patches (mixture attention over sub-topics), learning patch boundaries via change-point detection, gated control of implicit vs. explicit contributions, and comprehensive interpretability and failure-mode studies.

489.human_review: The proposed method effectively combines the content-based filtering capability of LLMs with collaborative filtering. It outperforms both LLM-based baselines and collaborative filtering baselines.
489.llm_review: Method, Performance: The paper proposes a concrete, training-free pipeline that combines content- and collaborative-filtering signals inside prompting. Concretely: (i) users are represented by averaged sentence-transformer embeddings of their meta-features and histories, then clustered with K-Means; (ii) for a test user, the preference generator produces concise likes/dislikes using Tlike and Tdisl templates, with a second-pass refinement; (iii) collaborative signals are injected via iterative bootstrapping that samples α similar users and their recent β interactions, summarizes them, and merges with the user’s prompt; (iv) convergence is triggered when cosine similarity between consecutive summary embeddings exceeds a threshold γ (Algorithm 1). On Amazon Beauty and Appliance, Table 1 reports that PepRec attains the best AUC and Logloss among all compared methods. For Beauty, it improves over the strongest baseline AUC (ReLLA at 0.6976) and substantially reduces Logloss (e.g., vs ReLLA at 0.7510). For Appliance, it surpasses the best baseline AUC (ReLLA at 0.7386) and achieves notably lower Logloss than DLRMs such as WD (0.4950) and TALLRec (0.4905), with the table listing Ours in the 0.4x range. These gains are achieved without training the LLM or a task-specific recommender.

490.human_review: The proposed method is tuning-free, which saves the expensive cost of fine-tuning LLMs.
490.llm_review: Fine-tuning, Method: The framework deliberately keeps the LLM fixed (illustrated by the “snowflake” icon) and forgoes any instruction tuning or supervised alignment, yet still recovers collaborative-filtering benefits by clustering users and progressively assimilating similar users’ summaries into the prompt. This contrasts with instruction-tuned baselines like TALLRec and ReLLA, which modify the LLM, but are outperformed in Table 1. The design is simple to deploy: the only learned component is the unsupervised clustering over sentence-transformer embeddings; all recommendation logic is executed through prompt construction and an early-stopping rule based on cosine similarity, eliminating fine-tuning costs and data-labeling overhead.

491.human_review: The proposed method provides better explainability to the recommendation results.
491.llm_review: Explanation, Method, Result: The preference generator produces explicit, human-readable rationales (e.g., “organic,” “healing ointments,” disfavored brands for Beauty; “white,” “30 inches,” “under cabinet,” refrigerator parts for Appliance). Figure 3 shows prediction trajectories that align with added evidence: in Beauty, the initial Pe,0 yields a neutral 0.5, and after one enhancement that highlights skincare and healing ointments from similar users, the score moves to 0.8 (true label = 1). In Appliance, the score progresses 0.28 → 0.48 → 0.58 as prompts incorporate preferences for refrigerator-compatible products, icemakers, and replacement parts, matching the target item (a filtration system). These interpretable attributions correlate with the improved aggregate metrics in Table 1 and the ablations, indicating the explanations are not post hoc but operational in the mechanism.

492.human_review: The authors conduct comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method and the necessity of each component.
492.llm_review: Effectiveness, Experiment: The ablation on Appliance (Table 2) is diagnostic and supports each design choice: using only positives (PepRec-1) performs worst (AUC 0.5740, Logloss 1.1824); adding dislikes (PepRec-2) improves AUC to 0.6689; invoking the preference generator (PepRec-3) further lifts AUC to 0.6856 and lowers Logloss; incorporating a single similar-user subset (PepRec-4) reaches AUC 0.7400 and Logloss 0.5479; the full progressive bootstrapping (PepRec) attains the best AUC and Logloss (reported as the top row in Table 2). Hyperparameter analysis reports that a small number of clusters and a modest α are sufficient, and that the backbone LLM materially affects performance. Case studies in Figure 3 concretely illustrate iterative gains that mirror the ablation trend.

493.human_review: PepRec requires a significant amount of LLM calls to predict a user's preference on one item. This is computationally inefficient and can incur a high latency. Although this is an inherent limitation of LLM-based recommendation and the authors also note this in the Limitations Section, the iterative prompt enhancement (each iteration requires two LLM calls) in PepRec makes it worse.
493.llm_review: Efficiency: Inference involves multiple GPT-4 calls per user–item pair: at least one pass to generate the user’s refined preferences plus n bootstrapping rounds, each summarizing α similar users’ β recent interactions. These prompts are token-heavy (enumerations of histories + refined summaries), and the iteration count is data-dependent, leading to variable and potentially high latency. The paper acknowledges cost/time concerns in Limitations but provides no quantitative analysis (e.g., wall-clock per 1k predictions, average n, α, β, token counts, or $/prediction across Beauty/Appliance). There is also no exploration of practical mitigations (e.g., caching per-user summaries, early stopping sensitivity to γ, prompt compression/truncation, batched inference, or replacing GPT-4 with a local smaller LLM for summaries). Without such measurements and engineering strategies, deployment in high-QPS settings remains uncertain.

494.human_review: PepRec can only capture users' recent preference given the context-length limitation of LLMs.
494.llm_review: Model: Several modeling choices may limit robustness. (i) User representations average sentence-transformer embeddings and then use K-Means, which assumes a single centroid per user and may miss multi-interest structure common in recommendation; nearest-neighbor retrieval in learned embedding spaces or mixture models could better capture user heterogeneity. (ii) Convergence relies on cosine similarity between embeddings of short textual summaries; this proxy can be sensitive to phrasing and may not reflect true information gain or downstream accuracy—no analysis is provided against alternative criteria (e.g., validation AUC gain per round). (iii) The preference generator uses only recent interactions due to token limits, risking recency bias and neglect of long-term preferences; no sensitivity to β or recency windows is reported. (iv) The method depends on GPT-4 for summarization, which raises reproducibility and hallucination concerns; while the paper notes LLM choice matters, results are not shown for smaller/open models, nor are safeguards (e.g., extractive grounding) evaluated. Together, these choices make the modeling pipeline potentially brittle across domains and LLM backbones.

495.human_review: This paper is well-written and motivated, accompanied by many nicely drawn figures and tables illustrating the major information of the paper.
495.llm_review: Motivation, figures, and presentation are strong and tightly aligned: the paper explicitly motivates two gaps—(i) identifying why LMMs fail on multimodal math (beyond binary answers) and (ii) diagnosing performance across categories (difficulty, grade, knowledge points). Figure 1 clearly visualizes the full pipeline (open-ended problems, boxed answers for outcome evaluation, and process evaluation via LMM-as-a-judge), and the worked example annotates both outcome (6 cm ≠ 4 cm) and the first error type (reasoning error). Figure 3 further clarifies the four error classes with a concrete example (e.g., misreading BF = BC as BF = 1/2 BC under “Textual condition misunderstanding”), making the error taxonomy unambiguous.

496.human_review: Fully open-ended problem evaluation instead of other formats like multiple-choice, avoiding LMM to guess an answer, which has been a serious problem in other current evaluation benchmarks.
496.llm_review: Benchmark and evaluation design are novel and detailed: MM-MATH provides 5,929 open-ended, middle-school problems with fine-grained labels across difficulty (easy/medium/hard based on student scoring thresholds >85%, 70–85%, <70%), grade (7–9), and knowledge points (e.g., Triangles, Quadrilaterals, Circles, Functions). The evaluation goes beyond binary matching: outcome scoring handles numeric tolerance (e.g., 1.414 ≈ sqrt(2) within 0.01), symbolic equivalence via SymPy for expressions (e.g., y = ax + b), interval normalization, and unit stripping; a 500-sample manual audit reports 13 outcome-evaluation errors. Process evaluation compares model steps to human solutions with GPT-4V to locate the first error and classify it into one of four categories, enabling targeted diagnosis.

497.human_review: Fine-grained meta-information annotation, including difficulty, grade level, and problem type. This information can help LMM developers better understand their model’s weaknesses.
497.llm_review: Annotations are substantive and model coverage is broad: each problem includes a human-annotated step-by-step solution and multi-dimensional metadata (difficulty, grade, teacher-defined knowledge taxonomy). The data pipeline (MathML→LaTeX via MathConverter, symbol normalization rules, GPT-4-assisted punctuation and answer boxing with manual verification) improves consistency and comparability with prior math datasets. The evaluation spans 10 models across text-only and multimodal settings, including GPT-4o, GPT-4V, Claude-3-Opus, Gemini-Pro-V, Qwen-VL-Max, InternVL-4B-Chat-1.5, Yi-34B-Chat, LLaVA-1.6-34B, and DeepSeek-VL-7B-Chat, allowing model-agnostic conclusions.

498.human_review: Process evaluation with error identification helps people know better about model’s error categories, clearly shown in Figure 4.
498.llm_review: Evaluation is evidence-rich and the figures are informative: Figures 4–6 quantify process errors across models, showing diagram misinterpretation as the dominant category (e.g., ≈56.8% for GPT-4o, ≈58.2% for GPT-4V, ≈57.0% for Claude-3-Opus), with reasoning errors as the next largest (≈36–39%). The counts highlight secondary effects (e.g., GPT-4o has 51 calculation errors vs. 29 for GPT-4V; textual-condition misunderstandings are rare across all models, <2%). The text-only vs. multimodal ablations show small gains from images—differences of 4.2% (GPT-4o), 2.7% (GPT-4V), and 0.8% (Claude-3-Opus)—supporting the claim that current LMMs underutilize visual context.

499.human_review: Comprehensive experiments on the most powerful and popular LMMs demonstrate they need help with MM-Math.
499.llm_review: Experiments are thorough and reproducible in spirit: Table 3 reports accuracy across difficulty (e.g., GPT-4o: Easy 45.8%, Medium 30.0%, Hard 10.9%) and grades (Seventh 40.0%, Ninth 36.0%, Eighth 26.0%), contrasted with a human baseline of 80.4% average (and 90.7/81.9/47.6% across difficulty). The best open-source model reported (InternVL-4B-Chat-1.5) achieves 11.6% average, while GPT-4o reaches 31.8%, quantifying a large gap to humans. Prompting and answer-format requirements (boxed answers) are standardized, and practical scoring rules (tolerance, unit handling, symbolic simplification) reduce avoidable evaluation noise.

500.human_review: Great insights with detailed examples of LMMs’ errors on the MM-Math. Example figures are clearly drawn and give reader a better deeper view of model’s behavior on the benchmark
500.llm_review: Benchmark scope, figures, and model insights are well connected: the benchmark targets open-ended, diagram-based computational problems to avoid guessing and surface reasoning chains; Figures 1 and 3 clearly illustrate the end-to-end evaluation and error taxonomy. Cross-model analyses reveal consistent patterns—e.g., closed-source models all show roughly 57% diagram-misinterpretation errors (Figure 4), suggesting common weaknesses in visual encoders; error-count figures (5–6) further separate image-comprehension deficits from reasoning/calculation issues. These model-level diagnostics demonstrate the benchmark’s utility for guiding future multimodal model and training-data design.

501.human_review: The process evaluation still requires GPT4-o in the loop. Considering the size of the benchmark (5929), running GPT4-V on all the examples of the benchmark for process evaluation can be quite expensive.
501.llm_review: Benchmark and evaluation limitations: process evaluation depends on a single closed-source judge (GPT-4V) and a first-error heuristic. The authors acknowledge ≈9% misidentification of process errors (Appendix F), and outcome scoring still has non-trivial error (13/500 manual checks). There is no inter-judge agreement, adjudication protocol, or multi-annotator validation for process labels; no statistical significance tests are reported for model differences in Table 3. Because the judge is proprietary, exact replication and longitudinal stability are uncertain. Moreover, the first-error assumption can obscure root causes when early mistakes are superficial (the authors note such cases), potentially biasing the error distribution (e.g., toward diagram misinterpretation).

502.human_review: The category of the problems in the MM-Math might be homogeneous, though Figure 2 clearly shows the detailed category. About 78% of the problems are shape-related (Properties of Shapes, Shape Transformation), thus making the tested ability in the benchmark easy to be optimize by incorporating more domain-related data.
502.llm_review: Benchmark and data concerns: coverage is restricted to Chinese middle-school computational problems from a single source (21st Century Education Network) and a single academic year (2021–2022), excluding proofs and drawing tasks, which narrows the construct of multimodal math reasoning. The transformation of multiple-choice/composite problems into open-ended items and the GPT-4 translation to English—even with manual checks—risk altering difficulty and semantics. The knowledge-point distribution is skewed (e.g., Properties of Shapes 52%, Quadrilaterals 19%, Triangles 14%, Circles 11%, Lines 8%; function subtypes: Linear 8%, Quadratic 6%, Inverse 7%), which may bias evaluation toward geometry-heavy skills. There is no reported inter-annotator agreement for knowledge tagging/grade labels, no de-duplication or train–test leakage analysis, and the paper reports inconsistent dataset size figures (5,929 in abstract vs. 5,793 later), raising questions about final benchmark composition.

503.human_review: The paper analyzes biases in sign language understanding models, covering various demographic and lexical features.
503.llm_review: Rigorous multi-level bias analysis grounded in two standard ISLR models (Analysis, Model). The paper quantifies disparities with concrete numbers across participant-, video-, and sign-level factors using I3D (Top-1 overall 0.6306; female 0.5914; male 0.6776) and ST-GCN (Top-1 overall 0.5944; female 0.5200; male 0.6838). It ties model behavior to interpretable features: e.g., videos closest to per-sign mean length achieve the best accuracy (I3D: 0.6704 for 0–1 SD vs 0.3846 for >2 SD; ST-GCN: 0.61 vs 0.4), and ST-GCN accuracy drops as right-hand pose diverges from the seed signer (Spearman ρ = −0.0289, p = 0.001).

504.human_review: It implements and evaluates multiple bias mitigation strategies, such as training on single-gender subsets, label shift approaches, and weighted resampling.
504.llm_review: Clear, reproducible evaluation and training procedures (Evaluation, Implementation, Training). The study reuses released ASL Citizen baselines and splits, reports Top-1/5/10 and parity by gender, and details mitigation training: (a) label-shift via reduction-to-binary with ST-GCN trained for 25 epochs, and (b) weighted resampling where the sampling probability decreases with the absolute per-sign z-score of video length, applied either to all videos or restricted to female-participant videos. These decisions are accompanied by explicit outcome metrics (e.g., ST-GCN Top-1: baseline 0.5238 vs 0.5488 with resampling; parity improved by 1.4–2.69%).

505.human_review: The empirical evaluation utilizes established models (I3D and ST-GCN) and performs detailed statistical analyses to understand the impact of various features on model performance.
505.llm_review: Strong linkage from analysis to measurable performance gains (Analysis, Evaluation, Model, Performance). The paper first establishes that video-quality (BRISQUE) correlates with performance (I3D Spearman ρ = −0.0367, p = 1.53e−8), that atypical speed/length hurts accuracy (e.g., I3D Top-1 drops from 0.6704 at 0–1 SD length to 0.3846 at >2 SD), and that ST-GCN is sensitive to pose dissimilarity from the seed signer (ρ = −0.0289, p = 0.001). It then validates a targeted resampling based on per-sign length deviation, improving ST-GCN Top-1 from 0.5238 to 0.5488 and increasing gender parity over baseline, demonstrating that the analyses inform effective training interventions.

506.human_review: The analysis of how various features (demographic, lexical, video-level) impact model performance enhances the understanding of model interpretability.
506.llm_review: Balanced interpretation that acknowledges confounds and model-specific mechanisms (Analysis, Interpretation, Model, Performance). The authors identify plausible drivers behind gaps—e.g., lighting confounds skin-tone detection; older participants’ longer pre/post-sign pauses inflate video length; ST-GCN’s skeleton inputs explain sensitivity to right-hand pose divergence—while also reporting null/weak effects (iconicity: ρ = 0.044, p = 0.8424). They avoid over-claiming given only 11 test participants and highlight that video-level factors show the highest mutual information with accuracy relative to demographics and lexical features.

507.human_review: The paper does not discuss the potential trade-offs between accuracy and fairness.
507.llm_review: Modest accuracy and persistent demographic gaps (Accuracy). Despite mitigation, ST-GCN’s overall Top-1 improves only from 0.5238 to 0.5488, while female Top-1 remains low (0.4406 baseline to 0.4666 with resampling) compared to male (0.6236 to 0.6476). Gender parity improves marginally (reported +1.4% to +2.69%), but remains near ~0.7. Single-gender training yields very low accuracies (male-only: male 0.292, female 0.168; female-only: female 0.206, male 0.291), limiting practical impact.

508.human_review: Why is RQ1 (How is the ASL citizen data distributed demographically and linguistically) important? This essentially reflects the data characteristics collected by the Microsoft Research Team and may not be considered a strong contribution to the work. The analysis, however, is important, but I feel it should be in a ‘Data’ section and not individually represented as a research question that the authors investigate.
508.llm_review: Data constraints limit generalizability and broader importance (Data, Importance). The dataset has 52 participants with only 11 in the test set; demographics are skewed (61.5% women; age concentrated in 20s–30s; geographic tilt toward the Northeast). Crucially, no self-reported race/ethnicity is available; skin tone is inferred via an image-based classifier that often misclassifies videos as black-and-white and yields inconsistent dominant tones when forced color vs grayscale (#81654f vs #b0b0b0), undermining conclusions about racialized fairness and reducing external impact.

509.human_review: The findings related to participant-level differences are interesting; however, the work basically uses existing models and runs them to compare scores between ASL demographics (Similarly, existing bias mitigation strategies have been used and compared) if I frame it in a simplified view, and thus it is unclear to me from the current text how or why this is new or important.
509.llm_review: Correlational findings with very small effect sizes and limited modeling breadth (Findings, Model). Many associations, while statistically significant, are tiny (e.g., phonological complexity ρ = −0.0618, p = 0.005; neighborhood density ρ = −0.0584, p = 0.01; sign frequency ρ = −0.057, p = 0.011) and not probed with multivariate or causal controls. The counterintuitive negative link between sign frequency and accuracy is noted but not investigated.
