The label-shift debiasing decreases gender parity (baseline female-to-male 0.7476 vs debiased 0.7052), and only two baseline architectures (I3D, ST-GCN) are explored, leaving model-class sensitivity underexamined.

510.human_review: A novel method named TWIST is proposed to achieve robust and scalable text style transfer in low-resource scenario.
510.llm_review: Method: The paper proposes a clear, modular pipeline that reuses LoRA weight increments via a multi-key memory and SVD-based merging, directly targeting parameter interference in interpolation for generation. Concretely, the adaptive retrieval score (Eq. 5) combines a task-level query qtask with an instance-level query qins to select source increments, and merging uses SVD-truncated AsB⊤ (Eq. 6) with top-q singular components U(q)Σ(q)V(q)⊤ to sparsify and stabilize interpolation. The ablations in Table 3 quantify each component’s effect: removing Adaptive Retrieval drops G from 65.4 to 61.9 on Genshin and from 44.2 to 42.8 on Shakespeare; removing the instance-level key (w/o Multi-key) further reduces G; replacing SVD with full AsB⊤ lowers G (65.4 → 60.9 on Genshin; 44.2 → 43.8 on Shakespeare); and discarding LoRA-based initialization hurts most (59.2/42.0), supporting the claim that retrieval and SVD truncation both contribute materially.

511.human_review: A multi-key memory network and an adaptive retrieval mechanism are designed to capture task- and instance-level information in weight increments.
511.llm_review: Task: The work squarely targets low-resource text style transfer and sets up evaluation to match that goal. It covers four datasets across nine styles—sentiment (YELP), formality (GYAFC), literary writing (Shakespeare), and six role-specific dialogues (Genshin)—and enforces an unseen-style protocol by rotating holdouts. The low-resource regime is explicitly tested by sub-sampling to {1%, 2%, 5%, 10%} of training data with three random samplings (Fig. 2), showing consistent G-score gains over small-model baselines on Shakespeare and Genshin, and over QLoRA fine-tuning on LLaMA2-7B (Fig. 2c). Human evaluation (Table 4, 50 instances per dataset, 5 raters) further indicates TWIST’s advantage on content preservation (best average rank on Content: 1.38 vs 1.76 for QLFT and 2.96 for ChatGPT-4 few-shot), aligning with the method’s motivation to reuse precise style increments while keeping content.

512.human_review: A clustering-based weight pool is constructed to identify similarities between source tasks for more effective style knowledge transfer.
512.llm_review: Method: The approach is model-agnostic and demonstrates transfer across encoder–decoder and decoder-only backbones. On T5-Large, TWIST improves the average G-score to 55.9, exceeding strong style-transfer baselines like Delete&Retrieve (49.7) and TextSETTR (45.2), and approaching B-GST’s formality strength while surpassing it on other styles (Table 1; TWIST leads on Shakespeare and Genshin with G=37.9 and 57.6). On LLaMA2-7B, TWIST achieves avg G=54.8 (Table 2), outperforming QLoRA fine-tuning (50.6) and few-shot Alpaca (44.4), and achieving style accuracy close to ChatGPT-4 few-shot (ACC within 1.9–3.0%) while delivering higher content preservation (CP 57.9 vs 43.0 on Genshin). The q-sensitivity study (Fig. 4) also shows that SVD-truncated merging can match single-task LoRA performance as q increases, while smaller q reduces interference during merging.

513.human_review: There are some unclear and imprecise parts in the Method section. (1) How should we understand the similarity and its calculation in the Multi-Keys Optimization section? q is a semantic feature, while k is a weight. Why can cosine similarity be used to measure the similarity between them? (2) How is q^{task} obtained? Why is its dimensionality c? (3)  The calculations in equation 5 are imprecise or wrong.
513.llm_review: Method: Key training mechanics are under-specified, which complicates reproducibility and raises questions about stability. For example, the key optimization update kΘ = kΘ + γ ∇kΘ cos(q, kΘ) is given, but it is unclear how this interacts with the generation loss—do gradients from L∆θt backpropagate into key parameters, or are keys updated only by the cosine objective? Are cluster keys (geometric means) recomputed during training or fixed after initialization? Retrieval is described at the task/instance level, but it is not explicit whether retrieval/merging is performed per layer or uniformly across all LoRA modules, which affects both effectiveness and cost. Finally, the reliance on a frozen BERT to compute qins is not ablated (e.g., no comparison to using the backbone’s own representations), so it is unclear how sensitive the method is to the choice of encoder for instance-level semantics.

514.human_review: The related work is not comprehensive. More PEFT algorithms should be discussed because the core of this paper is reusing weight increments.
514.llm_review: Algorithm, Related Work: While the paper cites task arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023) and touches on attention-weighted merging (Asai et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2024), it does not sufficiently situate TWIST among recent parameter-merging and adapter-fusion methods for generation. Notably absent are comparisons/discussion of Model Soups (e.g., Wortsman et al., 2022), low-rank model merging (Matena & Raffel, 2021), TIES/weight-masking merging (e.g., Yadav et al., 2023 beyond a high-level remark), and adapter fusion frameworks (e.g., Pfeiffer et al., 2021). Given TWIST’s core novelty hinges on retrieval plus SVD-truncated weight interpolation, a direct algorithmic contrast and empirical comparison with these merging/fusion baselines would clarify what is gained by the multi-key retrieval and SVD choices in sequence generation.

515.human_review: The comparison algorithms are insufficient and outdated (considering T5-Large as the backbone network).
515.llm_review: Algorithm, Comparison: Some comparisons are not aligned with the strongest contemporary baselines. For T5-Large, the paper includes classic TST systems (Delete&Retrieve, B-GST, TextSETTR), but omits recent LLM-centric supervised systems and PEFT-fusion baselines (e.g., AdapterFusion, prompt tuning with merging) that would isolate the benefit of the retrieval+SVD step. For LLaMA2-7B, comparisons are limited to QLoRA fine-tuning and few-shot Alpaca/ChatGPT-4; missing are supervised instruction-tuned LLM baselines for TST or parameter-merge baselines. Statistical rigor is also limited: although the low-resource study uses three samplings, the main tables lack standard deviations or significance tests, and the formality result where B-GST outperforms TWIST by 4.8 G (Table 1) is not analyzed. The style accuracy metric relies on in-domain classifiers trained by the authors (Appendix A), but their calibration/robustness is not reported, which could confound ACC/G.

516.human_review: The hyperparameter settings are not described. Moreover, what is the impact of the parameter r in the LoRA model? And what is the impact of different combinations of r and q?
516.llm_review: Model, Parameter: The method introduces non-trivial compute/memory overhead that is only partially quantified. The source weight pool stores LoRA increments for all layers across S styles, and even with SVD truncation each increment requires q × (dout + din + 1) parameters per module. At inference/training time, the pipeline adds (i) a frozen BERT forward to compute qins for each input, (ii) KNN-based retrieval over keys (top-W), and (iii) per-layer merging via Eq. 6. The paper relegates efficiency analysis to Appendix D and provides no latency/throughput numbers in the main text; moreover, guidance for choosing r and q is empirical (Fig. 4) and task-specific, with no principled recipe. This sensitivity implies extra hyperparameter tuning and may limit practicality as the number of styles grows.

517.human_review: The presentation needs further improvement. There are many very long sentences that affect readability. What is the 'source key'?
517.llm_review: Clarity, Presentation: Several presentation issues impede understanding. Algorithm 1 is referenced as summarizing the pipeline but is not included in the main text; key notation has inconsistencies (e.g., S denotes both the number of source tasks and appears as a summation index, C denotes both clusters and sometimes a key identifier), and Eq. (4) uses P={kC; kΘ; Δθ} without clear dimensionalities. There are typographical errors (e.g., “ScareBLEU” instead of “SacreBLEU”, “BLUE line” likely meaning “blue”), and ambiguous hyperparameters (e.g., “0.03 warmup steps” for LLaMA2 appears to be a ratio). Some figures/tables are hard to parse in the provided format (e.g., Fig. 2 axes/legends; Fig. 3 labels), and key implementation details (e.g., whether retrieval is per-layer, and when cluster keys are updated) are deferred to appendices.

518.human_review: The proposal of Incompleteness to KGQA is novel, well motivated and seems very reasonable in real-world tasks. Previous methods thoroughly tested in incompleteness setting, great ablation is performed with varying the degree of incompleteness.
518.llm_review: Ablation results directly support the paper’s novelty of combining search with LLM-based triple generation. Table 4 isolates the Generate action: on CWQ, adding Generate improves Hits@1 from 62.7 to 63.3 under CKG and from 48.6 to 50.6 under IKG-40%; on WebQSP, it improves from 74.7 to 77.9 (CKG) and 69.4 to 71.1 (IKG-40%). Figure 4 further shows that varying the number of BM25-selected related triples yields a concave performance curve on both datasets, with initial gains followed by degradation due to noise, evidencing that the proposed related-triple selection is an important lever for the method’s effectiveness. These ablations target the core novelty—LLM-as-triple-generator guided by subgraph retrieval—and quantify its contribution.

519.human_review: Despite proposed method being constructed from previously used Ideas, it is indeed novel and effective. The use of Think-Search-Generate, akin to ReACT is a powerful technique to elicit reasoning abilities of LLM, resulting in best performance across multiple settings and datasets.
519.llm_review: Effectiveness/Method/Novelty/Performance: The training-free Thinking–Searching–Generating framework treats the LLM concurrently as an agent (for KG exploration) and as a factual KG (for on-the-fly triple generation), and it yields consistent improvements under both complete and incomplete KGs. With GPT-3.5 on CWQ at IKG-40%, GoG attains 44.3 Hits@1 versus ToG’s 37.9; on WebQSP at IKG-40%, GoG reaches 66.6 vs ToG’s 61.4 (Table 2). With GPT-4, GoG reaches 75.2 (CWQ CKG) vs ToG’s 71.0 and 84.4 (WebQSP CKG) vs ToG’s 80.3, and importantly under incompleteness (IKG-40%) it obtains 60.4 (CWQ) and 80.3 (WebQSP) vs ToG’s 56.1 and 71.8 (Table 1). Cross-backbone results in Table 3 show robustness: Llama-3-70B achieves 54.6 (CWQ IKG-40%) and 74.4 (WebQSP IKG-40%), while Qwen-1.5-72B reaches 49.2 and 70.2, indicating the method’s gains are not tied to a single model. These outcomes substantiate the methodological novelty—explicitly integrating internal LLM knowledge with KG signals during reasoning—translating into measurable performance.

520.human_review: The method and motivation of paper is well described, figures help understand the paper and code is open sourced. The method is also well ablated
520.llm_review: Figures tightly connect motivation to method. Figure 1 concretely motivates the IKGQA setting using the missing triple (Cupertino, timezone, Pacific Standard Time), highlighting why conventional KGQA fails and why internal LLM knowledge must be integrated. Figure 2 situates the approach among semantic parsing and retrieval-augmented paradigms, making the distinct role of LLM-as-KG explicit. Figure 3 operationalizes the method with a step-by-step trace: Thought 1/Action 1 (Search [Apple Inc]) retrieves (Apple Inc, headquarter, Cupertino); Thought 2/Action 2 (Search [Cupertino]) fails to find a timezone edge; Thought 3/Action 3 (Generate [the time zone of Cupertino]) proposes (Cupertino, timezone, Pacific Standard Time) and verifies it, culminating in Finish [Pacific Standard Time]. These visuals make the proposed loop concrete and easy to follow.

521.human_review: IKGQA is presented as a novel task with no "datasets readily available". However, there  exist multiple papers solving the IKGQA task (without LLMs), however, they do not formulate the task "officially". Moreover, they also generate datasets based on WebQSP, however, I do not find the citations and comparison of the datasets or dataset creation process
521.llm_review: Data/Novelty: The IKGQA benchmark is synthetically constructed by randomly dropping "crucial triples" along the gold path with probabilities 20/40/60/80% (Algorithm 1), from only 1,000 samples per dataset (WebQSP and CWQ). Moreover, when a crucial triple is dropped, "all relations between these two entities will also be deleted" (Sec. 6.1), and some properties are filtered out (Algorithm 1, line 5). This procedure may not reflect real KG incompleteness (e.g., long-tail relations, type-skewed missingness, bursty gaps around specific entities) and could bias errors toward path-breaking deletions. As a result, the dataset’s novelty and external validity are limited, and the reported gains might not transfer to naturally incomplete KGs.

522.llm_review: Related Work: The discussion acknowledges prior incomplete-KG QA mainly via KGE-based methods (e.g., Saxena et al., 2020; Zan et al., 2022) but does not more fully cover adjacent strands such as rule/path mining and graph completion integrated with QA, or reinforcement-learning-based multi-hop agents over KGs that explicitly handle missing edges. A broader synthesis—beyond the cited SP and RA categories—would better position GoG relative to methods that complete, hypothesize, or verify missing facts before or during QA.

523.llm_review: Related Work: The paper briefly mentions GAG (Yu et al., 2023) as similar but provides neither a detailed conceptual comparison nor an empirical one against LLM-as-KG or text+KG hybrid retrieval methods. In the experiments (Tables 1–3), there are no baselines that augment with textual corpora (e.g., Wikipedia) or that perform graph completion plus QA, which weakens claims that the specific Thinking–Searching–Generating design is uniquely effective among LLM-based generation approaches.

524.human_review: According to ablation method heavily depends on the LLM.
524.llm_review: Ablation/Method: While Table 4 and Figure 4 are helpful, several core components lack ablations: (i) the verification step (prompts vs alternatives, error rates) is not isolated; (ii) entity linking for generated entities is not evaluated (no linking accuracy or impact on Hits@1); (iii) the number of Generate iterations n and stopping criteria are not analyzed for sensitivity or error propagation; (iv) hyperparameters such as temperature (fixed at 0.7), shot count (3 shots), and BM25 top-k are not varied except the latter in Figure 4; and (v) there is no cost/latency analysis of the agent loop versus baselines. These omissions make it difficult to assess robustness and practicality.

525.human_review: Is it not clear whether the fine-tuned approaches for comparison were run by the authors themselves or the numbers were taken from previous papers (for CKG)
525.llm_review: Approach/Comparison/Fine-tuning: Comparisons could be fairer and broader. The authors note their evaluation strategy differs from ToG (Appendix D), which can change ToG’s numbers and complicate apples-to-apples conclusions. The strongest results rely on GPT-4 (e.g., 84.4 on WebQSP CKG and 80.3 on IKG-40%), raising questions about portability to weaker or open models. Moreover, while RoG (fine-tuned) and ChatKBQA are included, there is no fine-tuned IKG-specific baseline (e.g., retraining RoG/StructGPT with IKG supervision), no hybrid SP+LLM-fallback pipeline, and only Hits@1 is reported. These factors leave the competitive landscape under IKG partially unresolved.

526.key_points: Strength: Baseline, Comparison, Method, Related Work
526.human_review: The paper is well written and clearly explains the methodology used with comparisons to popular baselines such as DPO. It effectively addresses the shortcomings of earlier methods and builds on existing literature to mitigate them.
526.llm_review: Well-chosen baselines and careful comparisons grounded in the proposed method and prior work. The paper instantiates BPO on three representative DAP objectives (DPO, IPO, SLiC) and evaluates both offline and online variants under a fixed preference budget, with three seeds and aggregate statistics (median, IQM, mean with 95% CIs). For example, on TL;DR, on-policy BPO (DPO) attains 89.5±1.4% win rate against reference text vs 77.2±0.4% for on-policy DPO and 72.0±2.4% for offline DPO (Table 1). Similar gains appear for IPO (88.6±1.7% vs 83.7±0.6%/68.5±5.3%) and SLiC (89.3±0.7% vs 82.6±0.9%/74.0±0.3%). The method-level comparison is explicitly situated against online DAP that retains a static reference and against dynamic-reference work like TR-DPO, clarifying that TR-DPO updates a reference by moving average in an offline setting, whereas BPO ties the trust region to the behavior model that actually collected the online data.

527.human_review: The dynamic adjustment of the trust region during training is a significant contribution.
527.llm_review: Focused contribution in training-time trust-region design with concrete implementation details. The core contribution is to set the KL trust region around the behavior LLM πβ that generates the preference pairs, formalized as LBPO = LDAP(x, yw, yl, πθ; πβ) with πβ updated every K steps (Algorithm 1). This directly targets the distribution shift in online preference learning and is easy to adopt: the authors fix β=0.1, run Gemma-2B with LoRA adapters, and swap πβ←πθ every K iterations. The training recipe is pragmatic: a 5-LoRA ensemble is optimized during training and merged linearly at inference, adding no inference overhead, yet stabilizing online training with a dynamic reference (Fig. 5). The contribution translates into consistent gains, e.g., on Anthropic Helpfulness BPO (DPO) improves on-policy DPO from 90.6±0.9% to 93.5±0.4%.

528.key_points: Strength: Ablation, Analysis, Comparison, Method, Model, Training
528.human_review: The authors conduct a thorough ablation of their proposed method. The analysis with variable time step intervals and comparison with a gold model provide very interesting insights. The use of ensemble LoRA to stabilise training was particularly noteworthy.
528.llm_review: Comprehensive ablations and analyses that isolate method, model, and training factors with direct comparisons. (i) Data collection frequency: with the same total data, increasing from F=1 to F=2 raises BPO (DPO) from 72.0±2.4% to 80.2±2.3% on TL;DR and from 82.2±4.4% to 89.1±1.4% on Helpfulness, already surpassing or matching on-policy DPO (Fig. 3). (ii) Reference model: even giving on-policy DPO a stronger static reference (πref=πgold trained to convergence), BPO (DPO) still dominates across training on TL;DR and Helpfulness (Fig. 4), indicating that proximity to the behavior policy, not just a stronger static πref, drives the gains. (iii) Stability: with a single LoRA, BPO training degrades within ~40 iterations; using 5 LoRAs stabilizes and improves performance (Fig. 5). An EMA reference πθ′ with τ in {1e−2, 5e−2, 1e−3, 5e−3, 1e−4} does not stabilize single-LoRA BPO (Fig. 6). (iv) Head-to-head: BPO (DPO) beats offline DPO and on-policy DPO directly (e.g., TL;DR 75.9±1.5% and 70.4±1.5% win rates respectively), corroborating pairwise superiority. All experiments use the same Gemma-2B base, fixed β=0.1, and specified steps/batch sizes, improving internal validity.

529.key_points: Weakness: Comparison, Method, Novelty, Related Work
529.human_review: Although the paper claims this to be a novel methodology using a dynamic reference policy, there has been some related work [1] that uses DPO iteratively. It would be beneficial to compare their methodology and include a citation for this work.
529.llm_review: Incremental novelty relative to behavior-regularized RL and missing direct method comparisons. Anchoring the trust region to the behavior policy is aligned with established ideas in behavior-regularized RL (e.g., BRAC/AWAC) and trust-region methods. While the paper contrasts with TR-DPO (which updates a reference via moving average offline), it does not implement a strong online dynamic-reference baseline (e.g., an online TR-DPO that updates πref via EMA or periodic copies during online data collection). The ablation with πref=πgold addresses static-reference strength but not the broader design space of dynamic-reference policies, limiting the methodological comparison necessary to substantiate novelty.

530.human_review: There is a missing citation for the use of LoRA ensembling. Additionally, it would be helpful to have a discussion on why the authors chose to use 5 LoRA weights.
530.llm_review: Discussion of limitations and broader connections is shallow. The paper notes instability with dynamic references and proposes a LoRA-ensemble fix, but it does not analyze failure cases where πβ is low-quality or biased, nor the exploration–conservatism trade-off as KL to πβ tightens. There is little connection to off-policy correction and behavior-regularization theory that could explain when constraining to πβ improves or harms learning, how to select β, or how the approach relates to importance sampling or divergence-minimization guarantees. A deeper discussion would contextualize BPO among BRAC/AWAC-style analyses and clarify boundary conditions.

531.human_review: The paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion on the computational cost of the proposed BPO method in comparison to existing techniques. This would provide a clearer understanding of its practical applicability.
531.llm_review: Limited application scope and external validity. All results are on Gemma-2B and three tasks (TL;DR, Anthropic Helpfulness/Harmlessness), with a single-turn format and no human evaluation. Both annotation and evaluation rely on the same RM-deberta preference model trained on overlapping corpora, which risks in-domain bias. There are no tests on multi-turn dialogue, larger LLMs, or cross-domain generalization, and practical considerations (training cost of 5-LoRA ensembles, wall-clock, memory) are not quantified. Claims about effectiveness with low-frequency human annotation are based on simulated annotation (F=2) rather than real human-in-the-loop studies.

532.human_review:
Since this strategy uses on-policy learning, it would be very difficult to incorporate humans in the loop for preference annotation. This could limit the applicability of the method in scenarios where human feedback is essential.

References
[1] Self-Rewarding Language Models. Yuan et al.
532.llm_review: Annotation design undermines alignment claims. The preference simulator is used both to label training pairs and to evaluate win rates, creating circularity and potential reward overfitting. There is no cross-reward validation (e.g., a second independent RM) or a small-scale human study to verify that improvements transfer to human preferences. The paper also does not report annotation noise, rater agreement, or exact Ntotal per setting beyond proportional splits (e.g., M=Ntotal/F), making it hard to assess robustness and the true cost–performance trade-off.

533.human_review: Limited exploration in the dimensions: the authors did not explore or discuss the completeness of the four criteria of retrieval, i.e. is there any possibility of existence of a new criterion, or these four criteria is complete? Further, the authors chose benchmarks specialised for these criteria, which may lead to selection bias for testing.  The authors can possibily argue by experimenting their method on a general dataset and analysize the failure cases.
533.llm_review: Benchmark/Data/Method: The paper introduces AR-Bench with four disjoint binary subtasks (intent-, knowledge-, time-, and self-aware), each containing 8,000 examples with a 1:1 positive/negative class balance and no overlap with UAR’s training data. Data sourcing is explicit and targeted: time-sensitive positives from TAQA and non-time-sensitive negatives from TriviaQA; non-knowledge-intensive instructions from Self-RAG’s GPT-4–filtered pool; and explicit retrieval intents synthesized via Self-Instruct (3,000 intents; 2k/500/500 train/dev/test). Methodologically, the approach is unified and lightweight: for each criterion, a single-layer MLP head is trained on the last token’s hidden state from a frozen Llama2 chat model, and a single decision policy (UAR-Criteria: intent → knowledge → time → self) determines retrieval timing. Because the heads share the same encoding used for generation and the base LLM is frozen, the procedure avoids full-model finetuning and adds negligible extra encoding cost in principle.

534.human_review: Classfier training: Training classifiers rather than training LoRA modules or few-shot prompting needs justification. LoRA or fewshot prompting requires little computation but may achieve comparable or better performance.
534.llm_review: Justification/Performance/Training: The motivation for multifaceted active retrieval is empirically supported by baseline behavior on AR-Bench with Llama2-13B-chat: SKR is strong on time- and self-aware (79.91 and 68.70) but weak on knowledge-aware (43.18); Self-RAG is stronger on knowledge-aware (64.85) but weak on time-aware (54.44); FLARE is uniformly low (overall 57.21). In contrast, UAR achieves high accuracy across all four (intent 92.49, knowledge 91.04, time 87.94, self 73.84) and the best overall (86.33). On downstream tasks, UAR yields the best overall average at both 7B (50.49 vs 49.23 always-retrieve, 48.50 FLARE, 47.17 SKR, 35.98 Self-RAG) and 13B (53.26 vs 52.09 always-retrieve, 50.16 SKR, 48.90 FLARE, 37.60 Self-RAG). Training is efficient: value-heads on frozen LLM states suffice, and ablating to full-model finetuning for the self-aware classifier yields only marginal gains (7B: 72.56 → 75.65; 13B: 73.48 → 76.28), supporting the design choice of lightweight heads.

535.human_review: Failure cases unaddressed in TAQA and FreshQA. Performance of UAR on TAQA and FreshQA is worse than that of Always-Ret. For these tasks, does it mean we can simply set to always retrieval and omit the classification? Especially when the retrieval rate if TAQA if UAR is near 100%.
535.llm_review: Performance: UAR’s benefits are clear and data-specific. For knowledge-irrelevant tasks, UAR avoids unnecessary retrieval and closely matches never-retrieve: Llama2-13B on DROP 58.55 (UAR) vs 58.76 (never), GSM8K 40.64 vs 40.64, while avoiding the degradation of always-retrieve (54.16 DROP, 37.68 GSM8K). For time-sensitive QA, UAR almost perfectly triggers retrieval (TAQA retrieval rate 99.6–99.7%) and attains accuracy comparable to always-retrieve with Google Search (e.g., 13B: 34.14 vs 34.20), far outperforming FLARE (25.40) and Self-RAG (15.42). For static-knowledge QA, UAR improves over always-retrieve by reducing harmful retrieval: 13B TriviaQA 71.71 (UAR) vs 71.02 (always) and WQ 59.20 vs 54.08, while using fewer retrieval calls (e.g., WQ 31.2% for UAR vs 100% for always).

536.human_review: Limited exploration in the dimensions: the authors did not explore or discuss the completeness of the four criteria of retrieval, i.e. is there any possibility of existence of a new criterion, or these four criteria is complete? Further, the authors chose benchmarks specialised for these criteria, which may lead to selection bias for testing.  The authors can possibily argue by experimenting their method on a general dataset and analysize the failure cases.
536.llm_review: Benchmark/Data/Method: AR-Bench’s balanced class design (50/50) simplifies evaluation but deviates from real-world retrieval needs, where non-retrieval often dominates. The intent-aware data rely on 3,000 Self-Instruct–generated intents seeded from only ten handwritten intents, which risks stylistic artifacts and over-regularized cues. Time sensitivity is framed via TAQA (positives) vs TriviaQA (negatives), potentially narrowing domain coverage. Methodologically, the fixed priority order in UAR-Criteria (intent → knowledge → time → self) is not empirically justified against alternatives; and the single-layer MLP over the last-token state may be under-expressive for self-awareness, consistent with the lower self-aware accuracy (e.g., 13B: 73.84) and the gap between single-criterion heads (≈99% for intent/knowledge/time) and the integrated UAR performance (overall 86.33), indicating error propagation through the decision tree.

537.human_review: Classfier training: Training classifiers rather than training LoRA modules or few-shot prompting needs justification. LoRA or fewshot prompting requires little computation but may achieve comparable or better performance.
537.llm_review: Justification/Performance/Training: Claims of negligible overhead are not substantiated with end-to-end latency/throughput numbers, even though four classifiers and a decision policy are evaluated per query. Baseline comparability is partly confounded: SKR employs an external BERT classifier while UAR uses Llama-based heads; Self-RAG is fine-tuned on Llama2-base rather than chat, leading to capability differences. For evaluation, correctness on TAQA/FreshQA is judged via ChatGPT without inter-annotator agreement or confidence analysis, and no statistical significance testing is reported across the many pairwise comparisons. The self-aware labels are constructed by sampling 10 generations per question and marking “known” only if all are correct, which can inject calibration-dependent noise and may not transfer to other decoding settings; retraining per base model is required but the data/compute cost is not quantified.

538.human_review: Failure cases unaddressed in TAQA and FreshQA. Performance of UAR on TAQA and FreshQA is worse than that of Always-Ret. For these tasks, does it mean we can simply set to always retrieval and omit the classification? Especially when the retrieval rate if TAQA if UAR is near 100%.
538.llm_review: Performance: UAR’s gains are not uniform. On DROP (7B), UAR underperforms never-retrieve (52.55 vs 57.67) and triggers retrieval about half the time (49.7%), suggesting over-triggering harms reasoning without factual knowledge. On FreshQA (13B), UAR (55.45) lags behind always-retrieve (62.05), indicating sensitivity to retrieval coverage in highly dynamic settings. The integrated UAR accuracy in AR-Bench trails the per-scenario single-classifier scores (e.g., time-aware single head 99.41 vs UAR 86.69 at 7B), consistent with decision-chain error compounding. Even where UAR is best (e.g., WQ 13B: 59.20 vs 56.20 SKR), absolute gains are modest and may fall within variance absent significance testing.

539.human_review: The experiments are well-organized and reasonably comprehensive, effectively supporting the insights and conclusions drawn in the paper. It is particularly intriguing for this reviewer to observe the efficacy of granularity expansion in achieving these positive results.
539.llm_review: Experiment: The empirical evaluation is thorough and well-controlled. The authors test on AGGRE FACT (an aggregate of 9 datasets) with both CNN/DailyMail and XSum splits and three partitions (FTSOTA, EXFORMER, OLD). They use balanced accuracy with thresholds selected on validation data following SummaC, and also report a single-threshold setting with 95% CIs (Table 2). The method attains the best overall average (71.2 balanced accuracy, Table 1) compared to strong NLI- and QA-based baselines such as AlignScore (70.1) and SummaC-Conv (69.7). The ablations are informative: removing granularity expansion (w/o GE) drops the average to 70.6, and removing atomic facts (w/o AF) to 69.7 (Table 1), while in the single-threshold analysis FIZZ averages 71.0 vs. 69.3 (w/o GE) and 64.7 (w/o AF) (Table 2). Additional analyses quantify component effects: coreference resolution yields +1.95 to +2.85 points before granularity expansion (Table 5), adaptive granularity improves XSum notably (e.g., 66.3→69.3 on XSum-FTSOTA, Table 4), and LLM choice for atomic fact generation affects performance (Orca-2 best at 71.0 avg with shorter facts; Table 3). A concrete failure case (Figure 4) and runtime trade-offs for granularity (seconds/iteration in Table 4) further substantiate the empirical narrative.

540.human_review: Although the task performance results would depend on the quality of the generated atomic facts, its impact on the task performance is not discussed.
540.llm_review: Performance, Task: The gains are modest on average and uneven across subsets. While the overall average is 71.2 (Table 1), FIZZ underperforms strong NLI baselines on several splits: e.g., CNN-EXFORMER 67.3 vs AlignScore 73.1, CNN-OLD 76.0 vs AlignScore 80.2, and XSUM-EXFORMER 72.4 vs AlignScore 80.1. Even the proposed variants sometimes outperform the full system (e.g., w/o GE: 77.6 on CNN-OLD; w/o AF: 80.4 on CNN-OLD; Table 1), which weakens the universal performance claim for atomic fact decomposition. Task coverage is narrow: all experiments are in English news summarization (AGGRE FACT), with no validation on other summarization tasks such as dialogues or biomedical reports, despite the method’s reliance on coreference and NLI that may behave differently in those domains. Practical performance is also a concern: the pipeline uses an 11B coreference model and adaptive granularity that increases inference cost (e.g., ~2.64 s/iteration at max granularity 3 in Table 4), which may limit real-time or large-scale applicability.

541.human_review: Similarly, the performance outcomes could also vary with an NLI model utilized. Nevertheless, almost no discussions are presented that makes comparisons with models other than SUMMAC and/or substantiate the adoption of SUMMAC.
541.llm_review: Comparison, Discussion, Model, Performance: Comparative fairness is partly confounded by threshold tuning. Many baselines (e.g., SummaC, AlignScore) benefit from validation-set threshold selection, whereas ChatGPT-based metrics do not, and the paper notes this asymmetry without providing calibration-insensitive comparisons (e.g., AUROC). Statistical significance against the strongest competitors is not established on Table 1 results; only Table 2 reports CIs for the single-threshold setting. On the modeling side, the pipeline tightly couples three modules—coreference (MT5), LLM-based atomic fact generation, and an NLI scorer—yet contributions are not fully disentangled: the full FIZZ is outperformed by w/o GE and w/o AF on CNN-OLD (77.6 and 80.4 vs 76.0, Table 1), suggesting brittleness. The filtering step (Algorithm 1) and scoring both rely on the same NLI model, which risks confirmation bias in what atomic facts are retained. The choice of using the minimum atomic-fact score as the final summary score is brittle; Figure 4 concretely shows a single low-scoring atomic fact (0.33) can flip an otherwise entailed sentence to inconsistent. Alternative robust aggregation (e.g., quantiles, learned calibration) is not explored, and the discussion does not quantify how often such cases occur or provide an error taxonomy.

542.human_review: The criterion for expanding the context, namely that max(e_k, c_k, n_k) ≠ e_k, may seem intuitive, but it might be overly simplistic. This hypothesis should be experimentally validated.
542.llm_review: Experiment, Hypothesis, Validation: The core hypotheses are that (i) atomic fact decomposition improves accuracy and interpretability, and (ii) adaptive granularity expansion helps multi-sentence reasoning. Ablations support (ii) clearly on XSum (e.g., 66.3→69.3 with higher granularity; Tables 2 and 4), and coreference resolution yields consistent gains (Table 5). However, validation for (i) is mixed: in Table 1, removing atomic facts improves CNN-OLD (80.4 vs 76.0), and the paper does not quantify interpretability gains with human studies (e.g., do annotators find the atomic facts faithful and useful for error diagnosis?). There is no measurement of atomic fact correctness (precision/recall against human SCUs) or filtering quality, no robustness to prompts/seeds beyond reporting average token lengths (Table 3), and no threshold-free metrics (AUROC/PR-AUC) to control for calibration. External validity is limited—only English news, no cross-domain transfer (e.g., dialogue/medical), and no multilingual tests—despite these being highlighted as future work. These missing validations make it hard to conclusively attribute the observed gains to atomic facts rather than to coreference or thresholding choices.

543.human_review: While query expansion and entity retrieval are standard techniques to enhance RAG system ability, combining these is non-trivial. MiRAG uses the K*M combinations of retrieved passages to jointly train the answer generator, passage retrieval and entity retriever.
543.llm_review: Method/Technique: The paper introduces a clear and effective multi-level RAG pipeline that first performs cross-modal entity retrieval and then uses query entity expansion to guide fine-grained passage retrieval, with answer generation conditioned on both levels. The joint training objective explicitly couples entity and passage retrievers with the generator, enabling gradients to flow end-to-end and mitigating the usual retriever–reader mismatch. The design is pragmatic—CLIP for entity retrieval, DPR-style encoders for passages, and a standard encoder–decoder generator—yet the integration via a unified RAG loss is novel for KB-VQA and technically sound.

544.human_review: Comparisons w/ existing VQA RAG baselines are fair and complete, and MiRAG achieves consistent and obvious performance improvements on ViQuAE KVQAE benchmarks. Qualitative examples in the appendix show that MiRAG is able to refer to relevant entities and generate correct answers conditioned on the augmented passage.
544.llm_review: Baseline/Benchmark/Comparison/Performance: The comparisons are thorough and fair, covering strong literature baselines (ECA, ILF, DPR v+t, PaLM) and well-constructed internal baselines (standard RAG and a multimodal score-fusion RAG). Retrieval budgets are kept comparable, and both T5-large and BLIP-2 generators are evaluated. The method achieves new state-of-the-art results on ViQuAE (e.g., EM 36.6 / F1 41.2 with BLIP-2), with consistent gains over fusion-based multimodal RAG and text-only RAG, demonstrating that entity-level signals materially improve final answer quality.

545.human_review: Ablation studies in Tables 1, 4, and Section 5.5 validate the effectiveness of enabling gradient flow (a.k.a end-to-end training) in RAG joint training, bringing significant performance gain. Multi-modal retrieval proves to be better than using the uni-modal retrieval method.
545.llm_review: Ablation/Performance/Training/Validation: The paper provides informative ablations and validations: (i) analysis of K_train and M_train showing the computation–performance trade-off and identifying K×M≈15 as a good operating point; (ii) freezing vs training the entity encoder, demonstrating that end-to-end gradients improve answer EM even if pseudo-retrieval metrics fluctuate; (iii) retrieval metrics (MRR@100, P@1/P@20) across DPR/CLIP/fusion and with entity expansion (EExp-DPR), clarifying why pseudo-relevance does not fully predict answer quality. These studies substantiate the training choices and validate the contribution of entity-driven query expansion.

546.human_review: Training Efficiency: in Section 3.5, the authors mentioned that answer generation loss has to be backward for all K$\times$M combinations, leading to the concern of training efficacy. In Appendix A, the authors do not report training GPU hours.
546.llm_review: Efficiency/Training: The multi-level retrieval and joint training introduce notable computational and memory overhead. Retrieving K entities and M passages per entity multiplies indexing and scoring costs, and the generator consumes concatenated top-N passages (M_test restricted by GPU memory), which can inflate training/inference latency. The approach also requires pretraining and maintaining a large FAISS index for millions of entities plus DPR passage indexing. While the paper discusses a K×M trade-off, it does not quantify wall-clock time, memory usage, or scalability to larger KBs, nor does it explore efficiency optimizations (e.g., dynamic K/M selection, lightweight reranking, or distillation).

547.human_review: Focuses on highly understudied topic in RAG research i.e. the importance how information is structured is also critical
547.llm_review: Importance: The paper targets a high-impact gap in RAG—LLMs missing dispersed cues and suffering from lost-in-the-middle—by restructuring retrieved content into sections that cluster related evidence. The empirical gains are substantive on multi-hop QA, where this problem is acute: with Llama2-Chat-13B, Refiner lifts HotpotQA accuracy to 67.1% and 2Wiki to 61.6% (Table 1), surpassing No-Compression (63.8/58.4) and advanced RAG baselines reported in prior work (e.g., Self-RAG-13B at 47.5/45.7; RQ-RAG at 62.6/44.8). Notably, the approach also outperforms GPT-3.5-Turbo on key benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA 67.1 vs 57.3; 2Wiki 61.6 vs 54.3; PopQA 59.4 vs 29.3), highlighting potential impact for both research and practical RAG deployments.

548.human_review: Introduces a training dataset which will be released for future research to enhance RAG models
548.llm_review: Data, Model, Training: The training pipeline is carefully engineered: Refiner (Llama2-7B-Chat backbone with LoRA rank 64, alpha 16) is SFT-trained using multi-teacher distillation (teachers: Llama2-70B-Chat, Meta-Llama3-8B/70B-Instruct, Alpaca-7B). Teacher outputs are parsed into sections/titles/contents, each sentence is verified to be verbatim from retrieved chunks and then majority-voted; only sentences backed by a majority are retained (Figure 2, Figure 4). The authors provide task-specific prompts (Table 8), an explicit pseudo-code data curation algorithm (Figure 4), and progressive training over imbalanced datasets (TriviaQA and Hotpot first, then ARC and PubHealth), with reported compute (4×A100 80GB) and optimizer choices (AdamW, linear decay, warmup). This yields a student that learns to keep necessary local context while enforcing the proposed structured format.

549.human_review: Token reduction / compression rates of Refiner upto 89% which is beneficial for reducing real-world costs
549.llm_review: The method is practical and efficient: it is plug-and-play in the post-retrieval stage and agnostic to both retrievers and downstream LMs. It substantially reduces tokens—Refiner compresses 89.1% of input tokens on average (Table 2), e.g., HotpotQA down to ~130 tokens and 2Wiki ~131 tokens—yet preserves or improves accuracy. Compared to LongLLMLingua’s ~48.9% compression and RECOMP’s higher compression (96.6%) but much lower accuracy (e.g., ARC 18.7% with Llama2-7B-Chat), Refiner offers a better quality–efficiency balance for cost-sensitive RAG pipelines.

550.human_review: The reduction and refinement into structured content also adds a notion of explainability
550.llm_review: Explanation: The output format explicitly encodes evidence structure (e.g., “1.1. ## Title” followed by verbatim content), improving interpretability, auditability, and potential citation integration. The paper quantifies verbatimness (Figure 3) at 87.4–96.8% across tasks/top-k, and analyzes common failure modes (Section 7.3: temptation to answer or to copy query options in ARC). Qualitative case studies show how sectioning disambiguates conflicting sources (e.g., PopQA’s “George Lewis” example in Table 17) and nudges the downstream LM to synthesize correctly.

551.human_review: Ablation showing resilience to adding extra content, where Refiner is still able to maintain performance partly mitigating "lost-in-the-middle" problem
551.llm_review: Ablation, Performance, Robustness: Ablations removing section structure consistently hurt performance when contexts are longer: under top-10 retrieval, mean decay is +1.6 (PopQA), +2.0 (TriviaQA), +0.7 (Hotpot), +0.8 (2Wiki) accuracy points (Table 4), indicating the structure is especially valuable in noisy/long inputs. Robustness is evidenced by stable in-task variance across downstream LMs (Table 3): for HotpotQA, std ≈ 1.77 in both top-5 and top-10; for 2Wiki, std 1.80 (top-5) and 2.98 (top-10). The system is also reported to be resilient to appended irrelevant chunks, with accuracy holding steady or even improving when 5 distractor chunks are added (Section 6.3).

552.human_review: New STOA results for multi-hop QA datasets including: HotpotQA and 2Wiki with comparable results on single-hop datasets; its worth highlighting that the gains are significantly pronounced when compared to baseline ChatGPT-3.5-Turbo for multi-hop datasets
552.llm_review: Comparison, Data, Result: The evaluation spans five public QA datasets (PopQA long-tail, TriviaQA, ARC-Challenge, HotpotQA, 2Wiki) and compares against advanced RAG (Self-RAG, RQ-RAG) and compressors (RECOMP, LongLLMLingua) using consistent retrievers and downstream LMs. Concrete wins include: with Meta-Llama3-8B, Refiner beats LongLLMLingua on multi-hop (Hotpot 67.2 vs 64.9; 2Wiki 63.7 vs 54.2) and is competitive on single-hop (PopQA 59.7 vs 59.3; ARC 71.1 vs 72.0; TriviaQA 69.3 vs 71.2). With Llama2-7B-Chat, Refiner attains 65.1/61.0 (Hotpot/2Wiki) vs LongLLMLingua’s 61.3/55.3 and RECOMP’s 47.3/58.5 (Table 1). These side-by-side results substantiate the claimed multi-hop advantage and favorable quality–efficiency trade-off.

553.human_review: The organization of paper is such that it becomes difficult to understand the methodology that is introduced by the work, e.g. sections 4.1 and 4.2 in less than a page mentions the main contribution of the paper i.e. multiple teacher KD-based dataset curations
553.llm_review: Contribution, Data, Method: (1) The core technique—extractive selection plus section-based grouping by relatedness learned via SFT—is conceptually incremental; the paper does not formalize the grouping criterion beyond instructions to teachers and does not propose a new objective or model architecture specialized for grouping. (2) Heavy reliance on teacher-generated supervision ties performance to prompt design and teacher biases; the method may inherit teachers’ sectioning idiosyncrasies. (3) Baselines miss structured post-retrieval systems that explicitly model inter-chunk relations (e.g., clustering/graph-based grouping like retrieve-cluster-summarize (Lennox et al., 2023)); the paper cites such lines but does not include them in the comparative study, making it hard to isolate the incremental benefit of sectioned restructuring over established grouping alternatives.

554.human_review: Pertaining to above, plenty of effort went into analysis where Table 3 and 4 are too redundant in terms of reporting all numbers for +5 and +10 documents across all datasets to derive a conclusion for a given ablation study
554.llm_review: Ablation, Analysis, Data: (1) While section removal ablations are provided (Table 4), there is no sensitivity study over section granularity (e.g., maximum sections), ordering policies, or the adaptive context window around quotes. (2) The multi-teacher voting threshold (> n/2) is fixed; no analysis of threshold choice, teacher set composition, or failure modes when teachers disagree widely. (3) The evaluation relies on exact-match string accuracy; ARC accuracy uses a revised regex that extracts a single letter following “is … (A–E)” (Section C.6), which improves correctness but breaks comparability to prior reports—statistical significance or agreement with human judgments is not provided. (4) The claim in Section 6.3 that adding 5 distractors can improve accuracy is plausible given the training setup, but no per-task numeric table is shown; quantifying these gains would strengthen the robustness claim.

555.human_review: Figure 4 in appendix gives detail about the training dataset construction and even it lacks several details like what is "ParseGeneratedContent" and what is "V"? similary there is a "Counter" and an "assignSection" not very clear
555.llm_review: Clarity, Data, Figure, Training: (1) There are several formatting/typo artifacts that impede clarity (e.g., stray numerals like “90447 1pairs,” “12020 English Wikipedia,” repeated “1”s in Table 7), which obscure exact training data sizes and cleaning outcomes. (2) Figure 2/4 give a high-level view of parsing/voting and section restoration, but critical edge cases (e.g., overlapping quotes, contradictory teacher section labels, tie-breaking when no majority) are not fully specified; similarly, exact retrieval top-k for training is unclear (only “TopN” pseudo-code). (3) The section format is described, but the regular expressions used to enforce verbatimness and to parse sections/titles during curation are not detailed enough to ensure reproducibility. (4) Some tables (e.g., Table 2’s token counts vs compression rate) would benefit from clarifying whether counts include section headers/titles or only content.

556.human_review: Based on these, it is difficult to assess the contribution of this work as the core contribution seems to be introducing this additional training data which is thin for a full paper
556.llm_review: Contribution, Data, Training: (1) Generalization is shown only for open-domain text QA; the authors acknowledge untested inputs (tables, domain-specific corpora). Extending the approach to non-prose sources (schemas, code, clinical notes) is non-trivial and not evaluated. (2) The fidelity risk is non-negligible: non-verbatim rates of up to ~12.6% (Figure 3) and documented tendencies to answer or copy query options (Section 7.3), which may be problematic in high-stakes settings. (3) Training supervision comes from four datasets (Hotpot, TriviaQA, ARC, PubHealth); it is unclear whether the model retains performance under domain shift (e.g., legal/biomedical RAG) without additional distillation or human-labeled structured outputs. A broader evaluation or human verification of structured outputs would solidify the claimed plug-and-play generality.

557.human_review: The proposed method is effective on in- and out-of-domain unanswerable questions when training sets include unanswerable questions while degrading scores for answerable questions. The improvement in out-of-domain unanswerable questions is significant.
557.llm_review: Improvement and method: The paper proposes a concrete training recipe that directly targets two identified issues in EQA: (a) replacing the [CLS]-span convention with a loss that does not force a phantom span for unanswerables (LQA with uniform labels over tokens for no-answer plus a token-level BCE tagging loss, LOurs = 2·LQA + 1·LTag), and (b) breaking the single-answer shortcut by adding a second synthetic span to ~20% of answerable questions. When fine-tuning on SQuAD 2.0, this yields higher overall F1 across eight test conditions (71.2 vs. 65.5 average), while maintaining in-domain SQuAD 2.0 performance (79.8 vs. 79.7 average across has/no-ans). Gains are consistent across three backbones (BERT-base, RoBERTa-base, SpanBERT-base) and averaged over five seeds.

558.human_review: The authors show that the proposed method improves the robustness to two types of adversarial attacks.
558.llm_review: Adversarial, method, robustness: Against AddOneSent and Negation attacks on SQuAD 2.0 answerables, the proposed method reduces the average performance drop from 40.7 F1 (default) to 13.2 F1, with consistent per-model improvements (e.g., RoBERTa: 41.5 → 12.4; SpanBERT: 41.7 → 10.1). When trained on SQuAD AGent, the method also reduces the drop from 30.0 to 16.2 F1. The ablation shows adversarial robustness hinges on multi-span augmentation: without synthetic spans (“no synthetic”), robustness vanishes or worsens (average ∆ rises to 41.3 vs. 40.7). This provides clear, mechanism-aligned evidence that the multi-span training counters the single-answer shortcut implicated in adversarial failures.

559.human_review: It is simple yet reasonable to use 1/n as labels for unanswerable questions, and synthetic answers to avoid overfitting to one answer.
559.llm_review: The study thoroughly evaluates robustness under distribution shift with diverse no-answer regimes: adversarial unanswerables (SQuAD 2.0 no-ans), information-seeking unanswerables (SQuAD AGent), and ACE-whQA no-ans (competitive and non-competitive). OOD gains are large and specific: +18.4 F1 on AGent no-ans (47.3 → 65.7 avg), +17.5 on ACE non-competitive (40.2 → 54.4), and +14.2 on ACE competitive (60.8 → 78.3), while preserving SQuAD 2.0 in-domain. Training dynamics further support the claim: the default method’s performance gap between SQuAD 2.0 and AGent no-ans widens across epochs, whereas the proposed loss stabilizes this gap, indicating improved OOD robustness as training proceeds.

560.human_review: No ablation study is conducted, so it is unclear from the experiments which component of the proposed method (QA loss, sequence tagging loss, synthetic answers, and inference pipeline) has an effect on the improved robustness.
560.llm_review: Ablation, experiment, method, robustness: The ablation suite is limited relative to the claims. Beyond the useful “no synthetic” condition, there is no sensitivity analysis for: (i) the proportion of synthetic spans (only ~20% is tested), (ii) how synthetic spans are constructed (choice of span location/length, overlap constraints), (iii) the loss weights (λQA=2, λTag=1), or (iv) the empty-answer decision rule (max si+ej < 0). Moreover, the two loss components (LQA vs. LTag) are not isolated via separate ablations. Because adversarial robustness almost entirely depends on synthetic spans (∆: 40.7 default vs. 41.3 no-synthetic vs. 13.2 full), a more granular ablation is needed to establish which ingredient(s) drive which robustness properties and how robust they are to design choices.

561.human_review: The motivation to use sequence tagging loss instead of the cross entropy loss is unclear to me.
561.llm_review: Motivation: The paper hypothesizes two causal drivers of brittleness—the [CLS]-span convention and the single-answer assumption—but provides limited targeted diagnostics to validate the mechanisms. For instance, the claim that the single-answer assumption encourages empty predictions under contradiction would be strengthened by error analyses quantifying the rate of empty-span predictions before/after training under Negation attacks. Similarly, the new no-answer handling parallels soft-labeling or label smoothing; showing that it specifically improves information-seeking no-ans by analyzing start/end score distributions or calibration would better support the causal link beyond the observed improvements.

562.human_review: The details about synthetic answers are omitted from the main part. I think it should be described in the main part if it is a part of the proposed method.
562.llm_review: Detail and method: Crucial implementation details are under-specified. The synthetic-span creation pipeline (Appendix B) is not described in the main text: criteria for selecting the second span, ensuring semantic validity, overlap/contiguity constraints, and quality control are unclear. For the loss, unanswerables receive uniform labels (1/n) under softmax and all-zero labels under the BCE tagger; the rationale for this combination, its training stability, and how it differs from standard label smoothing or separate null-logit approaches are not discussed. The inference thresholding for empty answers (predict empty if max si+ej < 0) also lacks justification and calibration analysis.

563.human_review: This paper may need justification for using only BERT families in the era of decoder-only large language models such as llama.
563.llm_review: Justification and model: The empirical scope is limited to base encoders (BERT-base, RoBERTa-base, SpanBERT-base). There is no evidence the method scales to stronger models (e.g., DeBERTa-v3, RoBERTa-large) or settings with longer contexts (Longformer) or retrieval/open-domain QA where unanswerability is prevalent. Given that robustness behaviors can change with scale and architecture, testing at least one larger or long-context model would better justify generality. The paper also focuses on English only, as acknowledged, leaving cross-lingual robustness untested.

564.human_review: The experiments seem to lack baseline methods. The proposed method is compared against only a default method.
564.llm_review: Comparison, experiment, method: Missing comparisons to strong, relevant baselines limits attribution of gains to the proposed method. Examples include: (i) explicit no-answer heads or null logits with tuned thresholds; (ii) confidence-based abstention/calibration (e.g., temperature scaling) for empty prediction; (iii) adversarial training with AddSent/AdversarialQA-style augmentation; and (iv) OOD evaluations on broader MRQA-style benchmarks. Although five-seed averages are reported, confidence intervals or significance tests are absent for key deltas (e.g., +18.4 F1 on AGent, −27.5 F1 attack drop reduction), making it hard to judge robustness of conclusions across runs and datasets.

565.human_review: Improving efficiency in long document tasks is an important research problem.
565.llm_review: Efficiency: The benchmark directly quantifies memory–performance trade-offs across schools with concrete compression ratios and outcomes, enabling apples-to-apples guidance for practitioners. For example, on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, KIVI-4bit achieves a 3.11× KV compression with virtually no loss in LongBench average (45.3 vs. 45.2 baseline) and perfect Needle (=100), while H2O maintains a constant-size KV cache and preserves code performance across 2×–8× (54.3/53.0/53.2/52.7 vs. 54.1 baseline). Conversely, prefill-time compression (e.g., StreamingLLM-4×) reduces LongBench average to 35.5 and Needle to 25.0, supporting OB❶ that keeping prefill uncompressed is critical for long-input/short-output tasks. The paper also distinguishes constant-KV (token dropping, prompt compression, linear-time) vs. linear-KV (quantization) regimes and notes system-level optimization support (Table 1), which is key for realizing real-world efficiency.

566.human_review: While I am not an expert in this field, it seems that the authors have surveyed, organized and implemented a comprehensive set of methods to reduce memory usage in long sequence modeling. These were applied to several LLMs (where possible) and the results seem to agree.
566.llm_review: Implementation, Method, Model: The workbench is minimalistic and open-source, and the authors follow official or endorsed implementations (e.g., H2O post-prompt eviction, KIVI per-channel quantization with sliding window, StreamingLLM/InfLLM prefill-time dropping). They dynamically adjust evicted tokens to hit target global compression ratios for comparability, and clearly record system support (e.g., custom CUDA for KIVI/FlexGen and StreamingLLM, limited support for H2O). Model coverage is representative and method-sensitive: three strong transformer baselines (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, LongChat-7B-32K) plus linear-time and hybrid families (Mamba-2.8B, RWKV-5-World-7B, RecurrentGemma-2B/9B), enabling observations like hybrids outperforming pure linear-time models on retrieval-heavy tasks.

567.human_review: The methods were evaluated on a large set of 16 long document tasks. As the compression ratios are given, the trade off between compression and performance becomes visible.
567.llm_review: Evaluation, Method, Performance: The study evaluates 10+ approaches over seven task categories (LongBench’s single-doc QA, multi-doc QA, summarization, few-shot, synthetic, code) plus a needle-in-a-haystack test, totaling 65 settings. Method-specific behaviors are backed by numbers: quantization is robust across categories (e.g., Llama-3: KIVI-4bit LongBench avg 45.3; Mistral: KIVI-4bit 43.5 ≈ baseline 43.5, Needle ~99), token dropping excels on code (e.g., Mistral H2O-2× code 53.8 > 52.4 baseline; Llama-3 H2O-2× code 54.3 ≈ 54.1), and prompt compression degrades retrieval (Llama-3 LLMLingua-8× Needle 0.0; 4× 8.3). OB❶–OB❷ are well-supported: prefill compression (StreamingLLM/InfLLM) systematically harms broad-task retention and needle, whereas quantization avoids catastrophic token loss and stays stable as context grows (with linear memory).

568.human_review: The experimental results can be useful to researchers and practitioners working with these and related methods.
568.llm_review: Experiment, Result: The paper runs multi-ratio ablations (2×/4×/6×/8×) per method and replicates trends across backbones. For token dropping, H2O shows graceful degradation on Llama-3 (LongBench avg: 44.7/44.0/43.6/43.4 vs. 45.2 baseline) and Mistral (44.6/43.7/43.2/42.8 vs. 43.5 baseline), corroborated by Figure 2’s per-category radar plots. For architectures, hybrids beat pure linear-time models: RecurrentGemma-9B-it LongBench avg 33.2 vs. Mamba-2.8B 20.7 and RWKV-5-World-7B 22.6 (Table 2), backing OB❸. Needle curves (Figure 3) reflect OB❹: KV-constant/free methods underperform—e.g., Llama-3 + InfLLM-4× Needle 42.0 vs. 100 baseline; Mamba-2.8B 10.7—while KIVI remains near-baseline across depths.

569.human_review: The analysis mostly remains on the surface.
569.llm_review: Analysis: The paper’s causal claims are not buttressed by statistical rigor or targeted ablations. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-task variance estimates. Some method-to-method differences have confounds that are acknowledged but not dissected—for instance, KIVI includes a full-precision sliding window while FlexGen-4bit does not, yet the Llama-3 gap (LongBench avg 45.3 vs. 43.9) is not explained via ablation. Similarly, prefill vs. postfill token dropping is not isolated via controlled variants on the same backbone and datasets, limiting attribution for OB❶.

570.human_review: For example, an interesting result from Figure 2 is that coding tasks seems to suffer less from compression methods than other tasks (noted in L456ff), but there is no attempt to explain this. Figure 2 itself is mentioned only once in the main text.
570.llm_review: Explanation, Figure: Several visualizations are hard to interpret without stronger guidance. The radar plots (Figure 1) compress six categories and multiple methods without uncertainty or consistent scaling, making cross-method deltas look larger/smaller than tabled values. The needle depth plots (Figure 3) do not fully define the depth metric or how word count maps to token positions, and captions do not state the exact budgets for each curve. Tables that combine multiple models and methods (Table 2) could better emphasize key comparisons (e.g., highlighting per-method deltas from each model’s baseline) and include row-level annotations about prefill vs. decoding compression.

571.human_review: While Table 2 shows results split into 7 task types, only two of them (Code and Needle) are mentioned in the main text. It would be interesting if there are other task- or instance specific phenomena that can be observed.
571.llm_review: Result, Task: The benchmark focuses on long-input/short-output settings; it does not evaluate long-generation tasks (multi-turn dialogue, story/code generation) where decoding-time compression may dominate, which the authors also note. Findings like OB❶ (avoid prefill compression) may not hold when outputs dwarf inputs. The task suite is predominantly English and does not probe multilingual or domain-shift resilience, and models are <10B parameters, limiting transferability to larger production systems.

572.human_review:
Do the results agree between the different LLMs tested?

(The authors have added analyses to their author response)
572.llm_review: Analysis, Model, Result: Cross-architecture conclusions are confounded by heterogeneous training recipes and sizes. For example, the hybrid advantage in Table 2 compares RecurrentGemma-9B-it (33.2 LongBench avg) to Mamba-2.8B (20.7) and RWKV-5-World-7B (22.6), but size (9B vs. 2.8B/7B), data, and instruction-tuning differ. Similarly, transformer baselines (e.g., Llama-3-8B) were trained on proprietary corpora, unlike open linear-time models. Without matched-scale retraining (e.g., Pythia-style controlled pretraining) or normalized deltas within the same backbone and task distribution, architectural takeaways risk over-attribution.

573.human_review: PER-PCS significantly reduces computational and storage requirements, achieving 7x faster computation and 38x less storage compared to training individual PEFTs.
573.llm_review: Efficiency and Training: The assembly stage for a target user is training-free and only records per-layer indices and composition weights, avoiding per-user fine-tuning. Sharer-side gate learning is extremely light—gates g_l are trained post-hoc for ~50 steps with all other parameters frozen (Section 2.4). The paper quantifies efficiency: compared to OPPU’s per-user training (~20 minutes on an RTX A6000 and ~17 MB per-user storage), PER-PCS achieves ~7x lower compute time for assembling a user PEFT and ~38x lower storage (Figure 7). These savings follow from not storing per-user LoRA matrices and from amortizing the one-time base task adaptation (Section 2.2, LoRA merged into the base) across all users.

574.human_review: PER-PCS maintains model ownership and fine-grained personalization for target users. It also shows robustness in terms of the number of sharers, sharer selection strategy, and the number of PEFT parameters shared.
574.llm_review: Model, Parameter, Robustness: The method defines a piece as a LoRA pair (B_l, A_l) at each linear layer and trains a piece-specific gate vector g_l per sharer while freezing (B_l, A_l). During assembly, it scores pieces as alpha_l,si = sum_{t=b}^e (g_l,si^T v_l,t) with token ranges b,e explicitly defined by |x| and |y|, then selects top-k pieces per layer and normalizes weights via softmax(alpha/√n) (Sections 2.3–2.5). This fine-grained, layer-wise composition supports robust behavior under real-world variability: (i) robustness to sharer count—Figure 3 shows stable performance and even the best MAE with as few as 30 sharers on product rating; (ii) robustness to sharer selection—Figure 4 shows movie tagging accuracy rising from ~0.268 (non-personalized) to ~0.294–0.300 across Most Active, Profile Cluster, and History Cluster selectors, and news headline ROUGE-1 improving from ~0.158 (non-personalized) to ~0.164–0.165 with similar robustness; and (iii) robustness to partial sharing—Figure 5 indicates near-saturated accuracy with only 20% of pieces shared, with RAG further stabilizing performance.

575.human_review: Extensive experiments demonstrating effectiveness and efficiency. The experiments demonstrate that PER-PCS outperforms non-personalized baselines and PEFT retrieval methods across 6 personalization tasks, with performance comparable to training individual PEFTs (OPPU) but much lower computational and storage costs.
575.llm_review: Effectiveness, Efficiency, Experiment, Performance: On LaMP (six tasks), PER-PCS improves over non-personalized and PEFT retrieval and is competitive with OPPU while being far more efficient. Examples from Table 1: (i) LAMP-2 (movie tagging) accuracy improves from 0.469 (PEFT retrieval) to 0.499 with PER-PCS+PAG, surpassing OPPU+PAG (0.467); (ii) LAMP-4 (news headline) ROUGE-1 climbs from 0.204 (PEFT retrieval) to 0.205 with PER-PCS+PAG, matching OPPU+PAG (0.205); (iii) LAMP-5 (scholarly title) ROUGE-1 reaches 0.515 with PER-PCS+PAG vs 0.509 for OPPU+PAG; (iv) LAMP-7 (tweet paraphrase) ROUGE-1 0.565 with PER-PCS+PAG equals the best baseline; and (v) LAMP-3 (product rating) MAE and RMSE at 0.262/0.558 match OPPU under some settings. Together with the measured ~7x time and ~38x storage advantages (Figure 7), the experiments substantiate both effectiveness and efficiency claims, and the ablations (Figures 3–5) show the method’s stability across sharer counts, selection strategies, and sharing ratios.

576.human_review: Overall, the manuscript is well-organized and well-written.
576.llm_review: Presentation: The paper provides a clear pipeline and concrete equations: it states the gate-augmented layer computation z_t^l = W_o^l v_t^l + B_l A_l v_t^l · σ(g_l^T v_t^l), defines history-based token ranges for scoring (b = |x|+1, e = |x|+|y|+1 for aligned pairs), and explains the per-layer top-k piece selection and weight normalization by 1/√n (Sections 2.4–2.5). Figures 1–2 visually summarize the share–gate–assemble workflow, while Table 1, Figures 3–5, and Figure 7 organize results, robustness studies, and complexity analyses. The limitations and ethics sections explicitly scope the work (single-task user histories; LoRA focus) and discuss data bias and accessibility.

577.human_review: From Figure 3, it seems that increasing the number of users who consent to share their personal PEFT will not help improve performance. I would like to see a more detailed explanation of why.
577.llm_review: Explanation, Figure, Performance: Some key choices are under-explained. The cosine-style piece scoring and the softmax(alpha/√n) scaling (borrowed from attention) lack theoretical or empirical justification specific to piece composition (no ablation on scaling vs. no scaling). The paper marks many PER-PCS entries with ‘*’ for significance in Table 1 but does not specify the statistical test, n, or p-values. Figures could be clearer: Figure 3’s axes do not state the exact top-k used during selection; Figure 4 shows baseline ROUGE-1 (~0.158) that conflicts with Table 1’s non-personalized LAMP-4 ROUGE-1 (0.175), suggesting a mismatch in subsets or preprocessing that is not explained; and Figure 6’s weight heatmaps are hard to read (small fonts, no color bar). On performance, several margins are very small (e.g., LAMP-4 ROUGE-1 0.204→0.205 over PEFT retrieval; LAMP-7 ROUGE-L ~0.517→0.519), which, without reported confidence intervals, makes it hard to judge the robustness of the gains.

578.human_review: In several tasks like LaMP-1, PER-PCS+RAG seems not to contribute and even causes a performance drop (compared with PER-PCS Base). I am curious about the potential reasons behind this.
578.llm_review: Performance: Although PER-PCS is often close to OPPU, there are cases where it underperforms when used without extra signals. For LAMP-2 (movie tagging), PER-PCS (Base) accuracy is 0.410 vs OPPU (Base) 0.463 (−0.053). In LAMP-3 (product rating), PER-PCS +RAG has worse MAE (0.272) than PER-PCS (Base) 0.262, indicating sensitivity to retrieval. The evaluation uses Llama-2-7B, BM25, and only 100 test users per task, so it remains unclear how results scale to larger user cohorts, newer base models (e.g., Llama-3), or cold-start users with sparse histories—important personalization scenarios that are not reported.

579.human_review: In the method section, why are the PEFT pieces selected in an autoregressive way? Can we directly weigh the average/merge all the left parameters with the gating score you have learned?
579.llm_review: Method, Parameter: The privacy intuition (sharing only a fraction of PEFT pieces) is not accompanied by a formal analysis of information leakage; even gate vectors g_l or partial (B_l, A_l) may encode identifiable traits. The linear aggregation ∆W_l^u = sum_s w_l^s B_l^s A_l^s could cause interference across sharers with different LoRA ranks or scales; aside from 1/√n normalization, there is no study of normalization or conflict mitigation. Several parameter choices are fixed without sensitivity analysis: per-layer top-k, LoRA ranks r, the gate training steps (~50), and cluster count K=50 for sharer selection. Despite claims of compatibility with other PEFTs (Adapters, IA3, Prefix), all experiments use LoRA; the absence of cross-PEFT validation leaves parameterization generality untested.

580.human_review: MINT offers a diverse set of IR tasks, covering a wide range of domains and document types. This ensures a representative and challenging evaluation of instruction-following abilities across various scenarios.
580.llm_review: Evaluation and Task: The benchmark targets instructed retrieval directly, spanning 100 heterogeneous IR tasks across six domains with diverse query/document types and relevance criteria. The evaluation is carefully designed to probe instruction-following via two settings (no instruction vs. +instruction), reports both overall and per-domain nDCG@10, and includes diagnostic analyses: (a) task correlation based on model performance to evidence heterogeneity; (b) a sampling effectiveness study showing >0.95 Pearson correlation at 100 queries/task with the full test, supporting efficiency without sacrificing fidelity. This breadth and rigor make the tasks and their evaluation well-suited to stress generalization and alignment to instructions.

581.human_review: The manual annotation of 776 detailed instructions provides a clear and specific guidance for each task. This allows for a more nuanced assessment of models’ ability to understand and execute complex retrieval instructions.
581.llm_review: Annotation and Task: The paper contributes 776 expert-authored instructions that specify query types, document types, and relevance criteria, with query-level instructions for tasks that require them. Instructions are reviewed and include domain-specific nuances (e.g., entity types in biomedical tasks), yielding realistic, fine-grained guidance that mirrors real user intents. This annotation quality, coupled with the wide task coverage, enables a faithful assessment of whether retrieval models can accurately interpret and follow varied instructions.

582.human_review: The paper benchmarks a variety of retrieval models, including both traditional and state-of-the-art LLM-based approaches. This allows for a comprehensive comparison of different methods and highlights the strengths and weaknesses of each.
582.llm_review: Benchmark, Comparison, Method, Model: The study benchmarks a diverse suite of methods—sparse (BM25), single-task dense, multi-task dense, instruction-tuned embedders, cross-encoder re-rankers, and LLM-based re-rankers—under consistent protocols, with and without instructions. Comparative results are substantive and actionable: instruction-tuned models benefit most from instructions (e.g., e5-mistral-7b-instruct, NV-Embed-v1), while non-instruction-tuned models often regress when instructions are added. Cross-benchmark comparison with MTEB highlights differences in generalization, offering insight into model robustness on long-tail, unseen tasks. The methodology provides a clear, reproducible yardstick for future models.

583.human_review: The paper acknowledges the importance of prompt sensitivity in LLMs but does not extensively explore this aspect. Investigating the impact of different prompts on model performance would provide valuable insights for improving instruction understanding.
583.llm_review: Model and Prompt: Prompting and instruction design are under-explored experimentally. LLM-based re-ranking is evaluated only with GPT-3.5 and a single zero-shot prompting approach, without prompt template ablations (instruction phrasing, structure, length), few-shot exemplars, or formatting studies. Likewise, the degradation observed in non-instruction-tuned embedders when instructions are added is not probed with prompt variants tailored to those models. A systematic prompt-sensitivity analysis would clarify whether performance gaps are due to model limitations or prompt design.

584.human_review: MINT primarily focuses on text retrieval tasks. Expanding the benchmark to include other retrieval types, such as image or code retrieval, would provide a more holistic evaluation of LLM capabilities.
584.llm_review: Benchmark, Evaluation, Model: While the sampling study supports reliability, the pipeline introduces potential confounds: (a) merging corpora for small tasks and random negative sampling may alter original distributions and difficulty; (b) all re-rankers depend on a single first-stage retriever, conflating re-ranker quality with upstream recall; (c) only nDCG@10 is reported, with no significance testing or robustness intervals; and (d) English-only, text-only scope limits broader applicability. Adding multiple first-stage retrievers, additional metrics (e.g., Recall@k, MAP), statistical tests, and multilingual/structured modalities would strengthen claims about generality and model comparisons.

585.human_review: TGB significantly improves the temporal grounding capabilities of MLLMs, allowing for more accurate interpretation of long-form videos by efficiently extracting and preserving relevant temporal features.
585.llm_review: Accuracy, Improvement, Interpretation: The approach delivers substantial and well-documented accuracy gains and makes the temporal reasoning more interpretable via explicit multi-span grounding. On AGQA 2.0, TGB-BLIP2 raises overall accuracy from 54.00 (BLIP2) to 61.45 (+7.45), with notable category gains such as Object-action 66.09 vs. 62.10 and Superlative 53.67 vs. 43.84. On NExT-QA, TGB-BLIP2 improves over BLIP2 from 69.6 to 72.1 overall (+2.5) and is slightly better than SeViLA (71.5). On EgoSchema (zero-shot), it achieves 41.2 with only 4 frames, outperforming Video-LLaVA’s 40.2 with 8 frames and mPLUG-Owl’s 33.8 with 5 frames. For temporal question grounding (NExT-GQA), TGB attains mIoU 19.9 (IoU@0.5 11.2), improving over IGV’s 14.0 (9.6) and FrozenBiLM’s 7.1 (4.4). The multi-span <BEGIN>/<END> selection exposes which segments support the answer, and the improved scores on relation/action and sequencing categories (AGQA: Relation-action 51.74 vs. 48.64; Sequencing 60.85 vs. 55.14) indicate better temporal interpretation.

586.human_review: The framework’s ability to handle sequences up to 16 times longer than initially trained without sacrificing performance highlights its scalability and effectiveness in real-world applications.
586.llm_review: Framework, Performance: The Temporal Grounding Bridge combines low-dimensional optical-flow features, language-guided cross-attention, and extrapolative positional encoding, yielding consistent performance gains while remaining pluggable to diverse MLLMs. It boosts multiple base models even when only TGB-grounded frames are used (AGQA: ALBEF 50.68 → 51.73; SINGULARITY 51.11 → 53.13; VIOLET 51.03 → 52.59). Efficiency–performance tradeoffs are quantified: on NExT-QA, TGB (OFs) reaches 72.1 with 2,950 GFLOPs/1,474 GMACs versus BLIP2’s 69.6 with 2,705 GFLOPs/1,350 GMACs, and is far more efficient than SeViLA (71.5 with 13,720 GFLOPs/14,357 GMACs). Length extrapolation is demonstrated: trained on 4-frame sequences, the model is reported to handle up to 16× longer input without degradation (Fig. 1B), aligning with the strong long-form results on EgoSchema.

587.human_review: TGB’s bootstrapping framework eliminates the need for explicit temporal grounding annotations, reducing the reliance on costly manual annotations and leveraging existing MLLMs for improved performance.
