587.llm_review: Framework: The design is modular and generalizable: (i) the bridge is lightweight and MLLM-agnostic; (ii) motion features are swappable (optical flow is used but the paper notes alternatives are possible); (iii) the bootstrapping pipeline generates pseudo temporal labels for both close- and open-ended settings without manual annotation; and (iv) joint optimization with Gumbel-Softmax aligns the bridge with the target MLLM. Evidence of generality includes improvements across five MLLMs and two LLMs, and zero-shot open-domain QA competitiveness (e.g., MSVD-QA 66.0 with BLIP2-3B and 71.4 with Vicuna-7B, matching or exceeding several 7B video MLLMs).

588.human_review: Could the authors provide ablation studies on the different strategies of multi-span selection that are discussed in Section D of the Appendix?
588.llm_review: Ablation: While Table 6 ablates optical flow (61.45 → 55.00 overall), fixed vs. joint bridge training (61.45 → 59.88), uniform sampling (BLIP2 54.00), and zero-shot (25.54), several critical sensitivities are not examined: (1) the number of predicted spans k and the union policy—no curves showing how grounding quality and QA accuracy vary with k; (2) the contribution of extrapolative positional encoding vs. standard positional schemes—no ablation isolating RoPE; (3) robustness to motion feature quality—no comparison across flow estimators or to learned motion tokens; (4) sensitivity of Gumbel-Softmax temperature and number of samples K on training stability and final accuracy; (5) context-length sensitivity—beyond the 4-frame training setup, it would help to report accuracy when training with 8/16 frames to confirm the extrapolation mechanism, not just the claim in Fig. 1B; (6) pseudo-label generation design—no ablation on alternative similarity metrics or thresholds for the monotonic stack selection. These would pinpoint which components drive the gains and how robust they are.

589.human_review: It is interesting to see how the number of layers of Transformer in TGB influences the tradeoff between the efficiency and performance on downstream tasks.
589.llm_review: Efficiency, Performance, Task, Transformer: Efficiency—The reported compute varies widely depending on feature choice. TGB (ViT-G features) uses 19,620 GFLOPs/9,840 GMACs for 72.3 on NExT-QA, far above BLIP2’s 2,705/1,350 (69.6). The more efficient TGB (OFs) is close to BLIP2 (2,950/1,474) at 72.1, but the paper does not include the wall-clock/throughput overhead of RAFT flow extraction end-to-end on long videos, which could be significant. Performance—Despite improvements, absolute temporal grounding remains low (NExT-GQA mIoU 19.9), and AGQA’s Duration comparison category drops relative to BLIP2 (36.99 vs. 40.39) and SeViLA (38.91). Task—Evidence is concentrated on long-form QA and TQG; it is unclear how the method scales to dense captioning, long-horizon moment retrieval at scale, or multi-event detection where recall is critical. Transformer—The 6-layer bridge may underfit multi-event, overlapping scenarios; cross-attention still scales with input length, and extrapolation is validated only up to 16× (no results for larger multipliers or failure modes on very long videos).

590.human_review: Could the performance be further improved when the size of the backbone LLMs grows larger than 7B?
590.llm_review: Improvement, Model: The magnitude of improvements depends on the base model and task. On NExT-QA, TGB-BLIP2 improves only +0.6 over SeViLA (72.1 vs. 71.5), and on AGQA some categories remain weak for generative models (e.g., Action recognition 0.00, same as SeViLA, and Duration comparison lower than BLIP2). When using only TGB-grounded frames without feeding motion features, gains for ALBEF/SINGULARITY/VIOLET are modest (+1.05 to +2.02), suggesting a substantial portion of the benefit comes from the motion bridge rather than keyframe selection alone. The bootstrapping pseudo labels are derived from the teacher MLLM and may propagate its biases/errors; the paper does not present diagnostics (e.g., teacher–student disagreement rates) to ensure the bridge learns beyond teacher artifacts.

591.human_review: The article introduces a new self-evaluation method that leverages the model's own features, avoiding dependence on external APIs and concerns about privacy leakage.
591.llm_review: Evaluation–Method–Model: The paper introduces a concrete, model-aware self-evaluation method that uses glass-box features extracted from the same Transformer model being evaluated. Specifically, it operationalizes (i) softmax-based confidence via token-level entropy (Softmax-Ent) and variance of log-probabilities (Softmax-Var), (ii) ensemble uncertainty via either random top-k decoding or prompt-pool perturbations over N=10 forward passes, and (iii) attention entropy aggregated over all decoder heads/layers via min/avg pooling. The approach requires no external evaluator or fine-tuning and only needs access to logits/attention during generation, making it applicable to off-the-shelf chat-tuned models (evaluated on LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B).

592.key_points: Strength: Accuracy, Evaluation, Experiment, Result, Validation
592.human_review: The experimental results show that the self-evaluation method based on softmax distribution achieves higher accuracy than some existing evaluation methods, validating the feasibility of this approach.
592.llm_review: Accuracy–Evaluation–Experiment–Result–Validation: Across MT-Bench and Vicuna-Bench, softmax-based features provide strong and consistent correlations with GPT-4 annotations. For LLaMA2-7B-Chat, Softmax-Var reaches Pearson r=0.561 on MT-Bench and r=0.651 on Vicuna-Bench; the simple Softmax-combo further improves MT-Bench to r=0.588, exceeding both Auto-J (0.502) and GPT-3.5 (0.434). On Vicuna-7B, Softmax-combo achieves r=0.536 on MT-Bench (higher than GPT-3.5’s 0.481) and r=0.686 on Vicuna-Bench (close to GPT-3.5’s 0.695 and above Auto-J’s 0.600). Ranking metrics show similar trends; e.g., for LLaMA2-7B-Chat on MT-Bench, Softmax-Var attains Kendall 0.470 and Spearman 0.624 versus Auto-J 0.409/0.511 and GPT-3.5 0.398/0.503. Reference-based variants further validate the signal: on Vicuna-Bench, LLaMA2-7B-Chat Softmax-Var improves from 0.651 to 0.662 with probability calibration; Vicuna-7B Softmax-Var improves from 0.615 to 0.653 (+0.038), and Softmax-Ent from 0.638 to 0.644, supporting the claim that calibration reduces evaluator bias.

593.human_review: This method is not only applicable to existing smaller models (e.g., 7B parameter models) but also holds potential for larger-scale models.
593.llm_review: Application–Model: The method is training-free and practical for deployment: Softmax-Ent/Var can be computed from the logits already produced during decoding, enabling on-device, privacy-preserving self-evaluation for models like LLaMA2-7B-Chat and Vicuna-7B without external APIs. This makes it suitable as a trigger for self-reflection or as a filter for reward modeling data selection, where a per-response confidence score is needed. The paper also demonstrates feasibility on 7B models, indicating that competitive self-evaluation need not rely on very large proprietary evaluators.

594.human_review: Simple Variants: The new metrics proposed (such as entropy and variance of the softmax distribution) are merely simple variants of existing signals, lacking in-depth analysis and explanation of their benefits and drawbacks. These variants do not demonstrate unique advantages in practical applications.
594.llm_review: Metric: The study leans heavily on Pearson correlations to GPT-4 labels without reporting confidence intervals, significance tests, or effect sizes, making it hard to judge statistical reliability. The paper also introduces a non-standard "Average" summary (coarse values like 0.6/0.5) that is not an established evaluation metric and may be misleading. Although Spearman/Kendall are reported, the paper states ranking metrics are "not fair" due to tie handling limitations, yet still uses them without robust alternatives. No calibration metrics (e.g., ECE/Brier) are reported despite claiming confidence-based evaluation, and potential confounds (e.g., response length or token frequency effects on entropy/variance) are not controlled or normalized beyond a 1/T factor.

595.human_review: Lack of Comprehensiveness: The article does not provide sufficient experimental evidence to support its conclusions. The experiments mainly focus on smaller-scale models and do not consider a wider range of models and larger datasets, which is not good for the confidence of the conclusions.
595.llm_review: Data–Evidence–Experiment: The evidence base is narrow: only two 80-question benchmarks (MT-Bench, Vicuna-Bench) and two 7B chat models (LLaMA2-7B-Chat, Vicuna-7B) are used, with GPT-4 as the sole meta-evaluator and no human annotations to validate or calibrate GPT-4’s judgments. The negative results for uncertainty estimation are based on N=10 forward passes, which is likely underpowered; no dropout-based MC sampling or larger N is tested to separate methodological failure from insufficient sampling. Key ablations are missing (e.g., sensitivity to decoding temperature/top-k, length effects, domain/task diversity, and prompt-pool composition), and there is no runtime/latency analysis to quantify the overhead vs. gains of ensemble-based methods.

596.human_review: Practical Issues: Although the self-evaluation method theoretically has certain advantages, there are still practical issues, i.e., can higher glass-box metric performance provide strong evidence that one model is better than the other on a given task. How can these general evaluations results finally affect the model development remains an issue.
596.llm_review: Evaluation–Metric–Model–Performance: Performance gains are not uniform across models/benchmarks, making the "surpass proprietary evaluators" claim too strong. For LLaMA2-7B-Chat on Vicuna-Bench, GPT-3.5 attains Pearson 0.670 vs. Softmax-Var 0.651 and Softmax-combo 0.621; for Vicuna-7B on MT-Bench, Auto-J achieves 0.567 vs. Softmax-combo 0.536. Attention-based methods are particularly weak (e.g., Vicuna-7B on MT-Bench: Attn-Ent-Avg Pearson 0.035; LLaMA2-7B-Chat on MT-Bench: 0.136), suggesting some proposed glass-box features add little value. There is also metric variability: cases where Pearson is close but Kendall/Spearman differ substantially (e.g., Vicuna-7B on MT-Bench, Softmax-combo Kendall 0.358 vs. Auto-J 0.430), and the inability to predict ties undermines rank-based comparability. These inconsistencies point to model- and benchmark-dependence and raise questions about robustness.

597.human_review: The entry point of this paper (i.e., knowledge inconsistencies) is very novel as well as important. Meanwhile, the introduction of KCA offers a systematic and highly applicable method to reduce knowledge inconsistencies in LLMs.
597.llm_review: Novelty: The paper proposes Knowledge Consistent Alignment (KCA), a data-centric alignment procedure that explicitly tests whether the foundation model already possesses the knowledge implied by alignment examples before fine-tuning. Instead of inferring inconsistency from answer correctness on the original task (as in prior QA-only approaches), KCA (a) generates an explicit reference knowledge snippet for each instruction requiring external knowledge and (b) constructs a focused multiple-choice exam (3 questions, 4 options each) from that snippet to probe the model’s knowledge boundary. The three calibration strategies (open-book appending of the snippet, discarding the instance, or converting the answer to a refusal) then operationalize different ways to avoid pushing models to learn content they demonstrably do not know. This explicit exam-based verification and knowledge-attribution step, applied to arbitrary instruction types via GPT-3.5-driven knowledge generation and classification with ICL+CoT, is a clear methodological departure from prior inconsistency-detection methods that were limited to binary QA and lacked explicit knowledge grounding.

598.key_points: Strength: Benchmark, Experiment, Model, Result, Validation
598.human_review: The paper provides extensive experimental results across six benchmarks, utilizing different foundation LLMs to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
598.llm_review: Benchmark/Experiment/Model/Result/Validation: The study evaluates four foundation models (Pythia 7B, Llama-2 7B, Llama-2 13B, Mistral 7B) trained on WizardLM-Evol-Instruct-70k and tested on six benchmarks covering both LLM-judged hallucinations (LIMAEval, VicunaEval, WizardLMEval, TruthfulQA) and metric-based tasks (MS MARCO, ACI-Bench). Across LLM-judged benchmarks, refusal tuning reduces hallucination rates substantially; for example, on TruthfulQA: Pythia 7B drops from 85.11% to 60.00% (−25.11), Llama-2 7B from 63.83% to 49.17% (−14.66), Mistral 7B from 59.57% to 52.63% (−6.94), and Llama-2 13B from 50.53% to 40.41% (−10.12). On LIMAEval, Llama-2 13B decreases from 30.34% to 25.79% (−4.55). Open-book and discard tuning often also help (e.g., Llama-2 7B on VicunaEval: 24.36% to 21.15% with open-book; discard 20.51%). On metric-based benchmarks, ROUGE-L improves meaningfully (e.g., Mistral 7B on MS MARCO: 25.05 to 27.53 with discard, +2.48; Llama-2 13B on MS MARCO: 22.35 to 25.52 with refusal, +3.17; Pythia 7B on ACI-Bench: 19.27 to 25.10 with open-book, +5.83). The paper also validates mechanisms: (i) Figure 2 shows a positive correlation between detected inconsistency percentage and hallucination rate across models/benchmarks; (ii) Figure 5 shows the subset mapped to refusal has much higher hallucination when answered by the baseline, indicating the method indeed targets high-risk items; and (iii) Table 3 confirms helpfulness is largely preserved for open-book and discard (e.g., Llama-2 13B on LIMAEval 8.48 baseline vs 8.60 open-book vs 8.55 discard), clarifying trade-offs among the three strategies.

599.human_review: The paper meticulously describes the steps involved in KCA, from knowledge requirement classification to the implementation of different tuning strategies, providing clear guidance for replication.
599.llm_review: Description/Implementation: The pipeline is specified in reproducible detail: knowledge-requirement classification uses GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613) with ICL+CoT; for each instance requiring knowledge, GPT-3.5 generates a reference snippet and exactly 3 multiple-choice questions (4 options) with CoT to label the correct answer. The foundation model’s exam score is computed by option likelihoods; instances with accuracy below tau = 0.67 (i.e., <= 2/3 correct) are marked inconsistent. Calibration is then applied by (a) appending the snippet to the instruction (open-book), (b) discarding the instance, or (c) replacing the reply with "I don’t know the factual information required to answer this instruction" (refusal). Training details include: Vicuna prompt, batch size 128, max seq length 2048, 3 epochs, greedy decoding at inference, and 8x A100 40GB GPUs (~3.5h for 7B, ~11.5h for 13B). Prompts for each stage are provided in the appendix, and the authors commit to releasing code, data, and model weights, facilitating replication.

600.human_review: The reference knowledge for an instruction is generated by a well-aligned LLM G, but G may also hallucinate and generate wrong knowledge. Hence KCA typically relies on a stronger LLM which stores broader knowledge than the foundation model M (ChatGPT-3.5 v.s. open-sourced LLMs in this paper), which restricts the scalability and makes self-improvement difficult.
600.llm_review: Model: The method’s core detection machinery depends on a single proprietary teacher model (GPT-3.5) for three stages—classifying knowledge requirements, generating the reference snippet, and authoring exam questions/answers. This creates a potential single point of failure: if GPT-3.5’s snippet is incomplete or outdated, the exam may penalize correct model knowledge or misclassify an instance as inconsistent. The exam is shallow (3 MCQs per snippet, tau = 0.67), so noise in any one question can flip the decision, especially for borderline topics. The calibration actions are coarse-grained: refusal tuning, while effective at cutting hallucinations, materially depresses helpfulness (e.g., Pythia 7B on VicunaEval drops from 6.60 to 4.63; Llama-2 13B on LIMAEval from 8.48 to 7.51), and open-book can hurt models with large inconsistent subsets (the authors note Pythia’s ~30% inconsistent portion), indicating sensitivity to dataset/model characteristics. Overall, the modeling choices risk entangling KCA’s behavior with GPT-3.5’s knowledge and with hyperparameters (3 questions, fixed tau) rather than with robust, model-internal signals.

601.human_review: When evaluating the hallucination rate, the refusal response is not considered in the calculation, so the comparison between refusal tuning and other methods may not be an apple-to-apple comparison. A comparison of different methods on the instructions with non-refusal responses should be provided.
601.llm_review: Comparison: The study does not include head-to-head baselines against the closest competing data-curation approaches for hallucination (e.g., capability disclaimers/uncertainty augmentation in Yang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023a), nor against strong training/inference alternatives like DoLA (contrastive decoding), CoVe (self-verification), Fact-RLHF, or retrieval-augmented alignment. Human evaluation is absent; LLM-as-judge (GPT-4-0613, T=0) is used for four benchmarks, and for TruthfulQA only 100 questions are sampled due to cost, limiting statistical power. Critical ablations are missing: no sensitivity study for tau, no variation of the number/quality of exam questions beyond 3, and no evaluation of different G models (e.g., GPT-4 or open-source) to test robustness to the teacher. Although the authors remove refusal outputs when computing hallucination rates for fairness, a side-by-side comparison with alternative refusal strategies or uncertainty-calibrated training is not provided, making it difficult to position KCA’s gains relative to the state of the art.

602.human_review: The analysis of over 1.2 million posts allows for robust statistical insights and the development of a well-informed model.
602.llm_review: Comprehensive pipeline with concrete, well-documented components across analysis, data, and modeling. Data: 3.8M raw Reddit posts narrowed to 1.51M (after filtering deleted/short posts) from four non-drug-related subreddits (r/unpopularopinion, r/offmychest, r/medicine, r/nursing). Relevance filtering: GPT-3.5 flagged 33,064 drug-related posts, then GPT-4 validated 16,277; a 725-post spot-check reports F1=0.86 for the validation layer. Stigma detection: 3,207 stigmatizing posts identified (1,949 directed, 1,199 self, 59 structural) using Link & Phelan’s taxonomy; an explanation layer maps phrases to labeling/stereotyping/separation/discrimination. Analysis: entity and subject–verb extraction (spaCy), emotion classification (RoBERTa-GoEmotions), and topic modeling (BERTopic/KeyBERT) uncover themes such as cannabis/legalization stigma and interpersonal/family contexts, consistent with observed substance distributions (stimulants and cannabis most frequent). Modeling: three de-stigmatization setups—baseline zero-shot (GPT-4, Llama3-70B), Informed (explicit stigma instructions), and Informed+Stylistic (adds emotion, syntax, MTLD, passive voice preservation). Human evaluation over 110 posts (660 outputs) shows Informed+Stylistic GPT-4 wins on Overall Quality (37) and Faithfulness (49), while baseline GPT-4 most reduces stigma (40) but harms faithfulness, directly evidencing the modeled trade-off and the value of the stylistic controls.

603.human_review: The use of Informed and Stylized LLMs to transform stigmatizing language into empathetic expressions is innovative and addresses a significant social issue.
603.llm_review: Clear, socially impactful framing and practical contributions. The work operationalizes Link & Phelan’s framework for both detection and generation, provides a concrete example (Table 1) of faithful de-stigmatization, and commits to releasing a labeled resource (3,207 stigmatizing posts; 1,649 de-stigmatized pairs). The linguistic analysis identifies actionable targets (e.g., derogatory labels like “junkie,” moral-judgment frames, and family-centered interpersonal stigma), and the Informed+Stylistic GPT-4 system demonstrably preserves tone (no significant LIWC differences overall; bigwords/cogproc slightly higher) while reducing harmfulness—features that make this immediately relevant for moderation aids, clinician communication training, and community guidelines.

604.human_review: The study is limited to Reddit, which may not generalize to other social media platforms where user demographics and discussion dynamics differ.
604.llm_review: Generalization is constrained by scope and tooling. The dataset is English-only and drawn from just four subreddits; results may not transfer to other platforms, languages, or community norms. The intervention targets directed stigma (1,949 cases) but does not demonstrate transfer to self (1,199) or structural (59) stigma, nor to other health-related stigmas. The pipeline depends on closed-source models (GPT-3.5/4 for filtering, labeling, generation), limiting portability to lower-resource or fully open deployments; no experiments quantify performance drop when substituting open models beyond Llama3 in generation. Finally, focusing on non-drug subreddits excludes contexts where domain slang and in-group norms differ, raising ecological validity concerns for broader deployment.

605.human_review: The manual annotation process could introduce biases, particularly in subjective interpretations of what constitutes stigmatizing language.
605.llm_review: Annotation quality and provenance are under-specified for the large-scale labels. The initial relevance pilot reports 100% agreement on 200 posts—unusually high with no details on adjudication or guidelines—which then transitions to GPT-3.5→GPT-4 labeling at scale. For stigma attributes, the human-labeled seed is small (200 posts) with only moderate agreement (k=0.67), after which GPT-4 labels the remainder. There is no systematic error analysis contrasting GPT-4 labels with a human gold set on a sizeable, stratified sample, nor per-attribute reliability for labeling/stereotyping/separation/discrimination. The reported F1=0.86 for the validation layer is computed relative to GPT-4 confirmations rather than an independent human standard, making it difficult to assess end-to-end labeling noise and its impact on downstream analysis and generation.

606.human_review: The evaluation of the de-stigmatized content might not fully capture whether the rephrased messages maintain the original intent and emotional tone of the user.
606.llm_review: Evaluation lacks statistical rigor and coverage of critical risks. Human evaluation uses 5 reviewers over 110 posts, reports only win counts (e.g., Informed+Stylistic GPT-4: 37 Overall Quality, 49 Faithfulness; Baseline GPT-4: 40 Most De-stigmatized) without inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, or significance testing. There are no ablations isolating contributions of stylistic components (emotion classifier, syntax/punctuation mirroring, MTLD, passive voice). Automatic evaluation relies on LIWC similarity with a t-test but omits effect sizes/p-values and does not measure semantic preservation or harmfulness (e.g., toxicity, bias, or stigma-specific detectors). No user-centered evaluation with people who use substances, and no stress tests for failure modes (e.g., over-smoothing, content drift, hallucinated facts, adversarial phrasing). Detection effectiveness is reported via a GPT-4 validation F1 rather than against a human-annotated benchmark.

607.human_review: Interesting observations on how the LLM refusal behavior changes by decomposing the harmful prompts.
607.llm_review: The paper introduces a clear and modular attack framework (DrAttack) that defines a new decomposition-based category distinct from prefix/suffix/hybrid approaches. The model design cleanly separates decomposition, implicit reconstruction via ICL, and synonym search, making the approach black-box, broadly applicable to both closed- and open-source LLMs, and query-efficient. The conceptual insight—that fragmenting malicious intent reduces attention on rejection tokens—offers a coherent mechanistic explanation grounded in token-probability analysis on open models.

608.human_review: The proposed method that uses semantic parsing to decompose harmful prompts appears to be a more effective jailbreaking attack. The authors also build a useful pipeline to finally decompose the harmful prompt into instruction, structure, verb and noun components.
608.llm_review: Effectiveness: DrAttack achieves strong gains on powerful closed-source LLMs (e.g., human-evaluated ASR of 80% on GPT-4) and remains competitive on open-source models, while using fewer queries than iterative baselines. Method: The decomposition + implicit reconstruction via benign ICL exemplars is well-motivated and supported by ablations showing that semantically similar, affirmative, and structured exemplars raise ASR. Prompt: The templated rule/assignment/result format and automated benign exemplar generation make the method practical and reproducible across prompts, with synonym search providing a measurable performance boost.

609.human_review: Additionally, the authors find that in-context examples are needed to make the victim LLM fall for the latent intent in these deconstructed harmful prompts. Essentially, the fragments of the harmful prompts are spread across the input to the victim LLM in an obfuscated prompt template.
609.llm_review: The paper contributes a systematic prompt engineering scheme: parsing prompts into [instruction], [verb], [noun], and [structure] phrases; using a compact RULE with ASSIGNMENT and RESULT exemplars to implicitly reconstruct malicious intent; and automating exemplar creation and synonym replacement. The ICL template is simple, benign on its face, and demonstrably effective at guiding reassembly without overtly signaling harmful intent.

610.human_review: Relies on a strong model like GPT4 to craft the attack for several key steps, including semantic parsing, synonym generation, and harmless prompt creation.
610.llm_review: Model and Prompt: (1) The pipeline depends on accurate semantic parsing and category assignment (often via GPT-4), which may be brittle for noisy, multi-sentence, or non-English inputs; errors can cascade to reconstruction. (2) The fixed phrase taxonomy ([instruction]/[verb]/[noun]/[structure]) assumes relatively clean syntax and may struggle with figurative language, ellipsis, or multi-turn contexts. (3) The implicit reconstruction step still presumes the model will follow the RULE; safety-tuned systems might increasingly learn to detect this pattern. (4) The synonym search and optional word-game steps add complexity and reliance on external embeddings and APIs, which may hinder reproducibility and robustness.

611.human_review: Is cosine similarity always sufficient to maintain faithfulness with the original intent, does the human evaluation take this into account when measuring success.-
611.llm_review: Evaluation: (1) Heavy reliance on AdvBench and limited-sized subsets of other datasets constrains coverage; some results are based on the first 100 items only. (2) Automated evaluation uses GPT judges, which can be biased, and human evaluation counts an attack as successful if any annotator flags harm—both choices may inflate ASR. (3) Many comparisons are single-run due to cost, with no statistical significance testing or variance reporting. (4) Query efficiency is analyzed in detail primarily on Vicuna-7b; broader efficiency analyses on closed-source models would strengthen claims. (5) Faithfulness is measured via cosine similarity of embeddings, which is a coarse proxy and may conflate harmful specificity with superficial lexical overlap.

612.human_review:
It is not clear if a stronger defense that looks at the prompt structure [1] instead of generic moderation classifiers will reduce the effectiveness. 


[1] The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13208
612.llm_review: Effectiveness, Prompt, and Related Work: (1) The claimed novelty of a decomposition-based category would benefit from a more thorough positioning against recent and concurrent attacks (e.g., newer 2024 methods for automated red teaming, multi-turn or decomposition-like hybrids), as well as stronger baselines beyond those reproduced in EasyJailbreak. (2) Some defense results are limited; stronger or adaptive defenses (e.g., multi-stage input sanitization, explicit segmentation detectors, or reconstruction-aware filters) may reduce effectiveness. (3) Generalization beyond English and to more diverse prompt forms (long, multi-sentence, dialogue) is not convincingly demonstrated, yet central to the method’s premise. (4) The very high ASR on GPT-4 warrants more rigorous third-party replication and sensitivity analyses (e.g., temperature, system prompts, model updates).

613.human_review: The paper studies the importance of fairness of LLMs in processing tabular data, which is of importance to society.
613.llm_review: Data, Importance, Model: The paper tackles an important, underexplored question—how the composition of in-context demonstrations affects fairness in tabular classification—and grounds it in two standard fairness-focused datasets (Adult Income and Credit Default). It evaluates five strong LLMs (Text-davinci-003, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo, Claude-3 Haiku, Claude-3 Sonnet) at temperature 0, demonstrating model-agnostic trends. On Adult (Table 1), prioritizing minority-group demonstrations with balanced labels (S2: rz=1, ry=0.5) improves both utility and fairness over zero-shot: Accuracy 0.6855→0.7328, F1 0.5882→0.7060, while Rdp 0.4063→0.6769, Reo 0.1111→0.4152, Δdp 0.2227→0.1578, and Δeo 0.3203→0.1859. Figure 2 shows consistent fairness gains on the Credit dataset across Text-davinci-003, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4, indicating the effect is not tied to a single model.

614.human_review: The paper is well-written and organized. The figures clearly present the framework.
614.llm_review: Figure, Framework, Presentation: The framework is clearly operationalized: demonstration composition is parameterized via ry (label proportion) and rz (sensitive group proportion), fairness metrics are formally defined (Equations 2–5 for DP, TPR/FPR, Δeo and Reo), and the prompting setup is made explicit (Figure 1). The perturbation workflow (Figure 3) isolates the contribution of demographic vs. label signals. The proposed FCG algorithm is presented with a step-by-step workflow (Figure 4) and concrete pseudocode (Algorithm 1). Results are accompanied by multi-seed reporting with mean ± standard error (Table 1), and ablations (Table 5) that clarify the contribution of each FCG stage, improving the paper’s readability and methodological transparency.

615.human_review: The authors conducted extensive experiments on evaluating LLM fairness on different datasets under various settings. The findings reveal the crucial factors that affect LLM fairness under the ICL settings.
615.llm_review: Data, Experiment, Findings, Model: The experimental design triangulates the main claim. (a) Across seeds {25,35,42,45,55} on Adult (Table 1), few-shot with minority-prioritized demos (S2/S3) consistently improves fairness over zero-shot while keeping or improving accuracy/F1. (b) The perturbation study (Table 2) provides causal evidence: perturbing labels degrades both utility and fairness (e.g., DataF: Accuracy 0.7480→0.6992, Rdp 0.7132→0.5054, Reo 0.3824→0.0556 when forcing ry′=0), whereas increasing the share of the minority demographic improves fairness (DataF: flipping to all male r′z=0 worsens Rdp 0.7132→0.5915 and Reo 0.3824→0.1500; Δdp and Δeo both increase). Subgroup analysis (Table 3) aligns: for gender perturbations, ΔTPR rises from 0.1250 to 0.1875 and ΔFPR from 0.1641 to 0.2656 when flipping to all male, confirming widening disparities. (c) The FCG selection further boosts performance over random selection: on Adult with K=8 and minority-balanced labels (Table 4), F1 improves from 0.5882 (zero-shot) to 0.7979, Reo from 0.1111 to 0.7021, and Δdp drops from 0.2227 to 0.0664; the ablation (Table 5) shows F1 0.7425→0.7979 and Rdp 0.7254→0.8938 when moving from random to full FCG, substantiating each component’s utility.

616.human_review: The authors only consider two datsets, which may not be necessarily sufficient for the evaluation of the framework. As there are plentiful tabular datasets, the authors should consider using more datasets.
616.llm_review: Data, Framework: The evidence base is narrow—two UCI-style datasets (Adult and Credit), both binary tasks with a single binary sensitive attribute per dataset. Intersectional fairness (e.g., gender×race), multi-attribute fairness, and multiclass classification are not covered, limiting external validity. The framework also fixes fairness metrics to DP/EqOdds variants (Rdp/Reo/Δdp/Δeo), omitting alternatives such as equal opportunity, calibration, or cost-sensitive fairness that could alter conclusions. Additionally, there is a definitional inconsistency for ry in the text/figures (Section 4 states ry=1 is all low-income; Figure 4 labels ry=1 as all high-income), which can create ambiguity when reproducing the framework.

617.human_review: The authors use various LLMs for evaluation. However, the performance of the framework on smaller LMs, such as LLaMA, could also be important and necessitates investigations.
617.llm_review: Framework, Model: The FCG objective fixes α=0.5 (equal weight to utility and fairness) and uses F1 and Reo to compute the EvolScore, but no sensitivity analysis is reported for α or metric choices. The selection process relies on dev-set feedback (Algorithm 1, CAL_SCORE), yet the paper does not quantify safeguards against overfitting to the dev split. Baselines are limited: beyond random selection (and a conceptual connection to LENS), there is no comparison to established fairness methods for tabular classification (e.g., reweighting, post-processing equalized odds, threshold optimization, adversarial debiasing) or to stronger demo-selection heuristics (e.g., facility-location, MMR, determinantal point processes). The claim of reduced iteration/time and LLM access cost for FCG is not supported with runtime or API call statistics.

618.human_review: The authors only focus on binary classification tasks. However, the fairness problems of LLMs may involve more classification tasks and even generation.
618.llm_review: Model, Task: Key modeling details for tabular-to-text prompting are deferred to Appendix C (e.g., feature normalization, handling missing values, categorical encoding order, and how many features are shown), which affects reproducibility and could influence model behavior. The scope of modeling choices is narrow: temperature is fixed at 0, K is only varied between 4 and 8 (Table 4), and no exploration of alternative prompting strategies (e.g., calibration, chain-of-thought, self-consistency) is provided. The study focuses on black-box LLMs without comparing to strong tabular baselines (e.g., XGBoost/LightGBM with/without fairness constraints), leaving it unclear how the proposed method fares against purpose-built tabular models for this task.

619.human_review: The paper does a thorough analysis of the memory and time complexity providing insights into how the method scared with increasing datasets and label numbers
619.llm_review: Analysis/Complexity/Data/Method: The paper provides a concrete, data-grounded analysis of a distributed ensemble method (random label forests) that subsamples labels and trains tree-based linear submodels in parallel. It explicitly derives per-machine time and space complexity when using two-level trees: training time changes from O(K m c~ n̄ R + (K + c m/K) n̄ l) for all labels to O(K r m c~ n̄ R + (K + c r m/K) n̄ l) under label subsampling rate r, and model size per machine from O(K n + m ñ) to O(K n + r m ñ). This analytical prediction is corroborated by measured model sizes (Table 4): e.g., on amazon-3m the per-machine model shrinks from 135.89 GB (full tree) to 12.69 GB at r = 0.1 (≈10.7× reduction, close to 1/r); on wiki-500k, 161.37 GB to 13.65 GB (≈11.8×). Methodologically, the paper identifies a critical training detail unique to label subsampling: retaining “empty-labeled” instances in each submodel to avoid distorted level-1 probability estimation (Sections 3.2 and Fig. 2), and formalizes training and prediction (Algorithm 1, averaging probabilities over submodels that contain a label).

620.human_review: The papers conducts comprehensive experiments across datasets and baseline comparison.
620.llm_review: Comparison/Data/Experiment: The empirical study spans six public XML datasets ranging from thousands to millions of labels (eur-lex-4k, wiki10-31k, amazoncat-13k, amazon-670k, amazon-3m, wiki-500k). Comparisons include OVR, a tree with all labels (K = 100), and the proposed method, plus careful ablations of distributed settings (Table 2). The ablations show that the ensemble with label subsampling and bypassing level-1 estimation improves over random partitions: on amazon-670k, random 10 partitions vs random label forests-A yields P@3 36.43 → 40.28 and P@5 32.30 → 36.70; random label forests-B further matches/exceeds the full-label tree (eur-lex-4k P@1 82.29 → 83.08; amazoncat-13k P@3 79.55 → 80.17). The main table (Table 3) shows random label forests consistently outperform the full-label tree on four datasets (e.g., amazon-670k P@1 44.58 → 45.19; amazon-3m P@1 47.48 → 48.69) and approach OVR where OVR is available.

621.human_review: The evaluation metrics and computational requirements clearly highlight the benefit of the proposed techniques
621.llm_review: Evaluation/Metric: The paper uses standard XML ranking metrics (Precision@1/3/5) and justifies metric choices, noting that P@1 is less discriminative on wiki10-31k due to many single-label instances. It reports mean±std over 10 runs for datasets where K-means randomness matters (eur-lex-4k, wiki10-31k, amazoncat-13k, amazon-670k), demonstrating stability: e.g., eur-lex-4k P@3 for random label forests is 69.90 ± 0.08, and amazon-670k P@5 is 36.65 ± 0.01. Complementary evaluation of model size (Table 4) substantiates the claimed memory benefits per machine, providing a balanced view of accuracy vs. resource usage.

622.human_review: Impact of sub-sampling and negative sampling is highlighted and considered during the formulation of random label forests
622.llm_review: The paper includes clear procedural details (Algorithm 1, two-level tree example, precise treatment of probability estimation via Eq. (10) and the hinge-based transform in Eq. (5)), and documents practical choices (K = 100 for partitioning, uniform subsampling with r = 0.1 and N = 100 submodels) alongside limitations (Sec. 6), making the approach easier to reproduce with standard linear solvers (e.g., LIBLINEAR) and existing tree-based XML toolchains.

623.human_review: In the XML , the paper does not study or highlight the impact on long-tail distribution .
623.llm_review: Data/Impact: On data with strong hierarchical label correlations, the method underperforms the full-label tree and may have limited impact. On wiki-500k, the tree with all labels achieves P@1/P@3/P@5 = 68.39/48.90/38.00, while random label forests drop to 64.37/45.83/36.09 (Table 3). Even increasing the subsampling rate from r = 0.1 to 0.15 only improves to 65.45/46.84/36.92 (Sec. 6.1), still below the full-label tree. The authors attribute this to uniform subsampling breaking label hierarchies (e.g., Wikipedia categories). The paper does not evaluate label-aware subsampling or hierarchical variants, leaving applicability uncertain in taxonomy-heavy domains.

624.human_review: The paper does not highlight any hyper-parameters and sensitivity of the algorithm towards the same. Details for experimental setup is not-adequate for a fair comparison
624.llm_review: Algorithm/Experiment/Parameter: Key hyperparameters are fixed with limited sensitivity analysis. The main experiments use r = 0.1, K = 100, and N = 100; while Sec. 6.1 reports a single alternative (r = 0.15) on wiki-500k, there are no systematic sweeps over r, K, depth, or K-means iterations R, nor calibration of how overlap (subset vs. partitioning) and N affect accuracy and coverage. OVR results are missing on the largest datasets (amazon-3m, wiki-500k) due to runtime, which hinders assessing how closely the proposed method approaches the strongest linear baseline at extreme scale. More comprehensive ablations (e.g., P@k vs r, N; depth vs accuracy; K vs training time) would strengthen the empirical support.

625.human_review: Table 6 highlights reduction in training time, but does not highlight number of distributed compute used and total compute used to train the proposed algorithm
625.llm_review: Algorithm/Training: The paper argues that removing empty-labeled instances harms level-1 probability estimation (illustrated by Fig. 2 and Eq. (13)), but does not quantify the training-time and memory trade-off of retaining them (e.g., wall-clock with vs. without removal, calibration quality). The method also cannot predict labels never sampled by any submodel; although the authors suggest this is rare, they provide no coverage guarantees or measurements (e.g., the probability that a label is unsampled is (1−r)^N; for the main setting r = 0.1, N = 100 this is ~2.7e−5, but the actual fraction is not reported). Each submodel requires running K-means, increasing total training cost; alternatives (e.g., shared partitions, approximate K-means, or label-aware negative sampling) are not explored.

626.human_review: The proposed method introduces complexity which is not clearly explained  in the distributed training and label sub-sampling techniques. With the release of the code, it would be hard for the paper to be re-produced.
626.llm_review: Complexity/Method: The complexity analysis focuses on per-machine scaling and assumes ample parallelism. While per-machine model size reductions match r in Table 4 (e.g., ~10× at r = 0.1), the paper does not analyze the aggregate compute and memory across N submodels, orchestration overheads, or communication in ensembling, nor provide end-to-end time-to-accuracy comparisons in the main text (training times are deferred to Appendix E). Claims like “training time … is much faster … if computers are enough” (Sec. 3.3) hinge on strong assumptions (e.g., no stragglers, no K-means bottlenecks) and hide constants introduced by repeating K-means and tree training N times.

627.human_review: Paper lacks theoretical proofs/guarantees to support the correctness or covergence of random forest labels method.
627.llm_review: Method/Theory: The probability estimation within trees uses a heuristic transform of the square-hinge margin (Eq. (5)) and multiplicative decomposition (Eq. (10)), while cross-submodel aggregation is a simple average over submodels containing the label. There is no theoretical analysis of bias, calibration, or consistency of these estimates under label subsampling and overlap, nor bounds on approximation error vs. OVR or on tail-label recall. The paper’s rationale for keeping empty-labeled instances is intuitive but lacks formal guarantees, leaving the method’s theoretical underpinnings primarily empirical.

628.human_review: The paper offers a valuable critique of the current research trajectory in AES, encouraging the community to reconsider the emphasis on performance metrics.
628.llm_review: Metric and performance treatment is precise and actionable. The paper explains QWK beyond a namecheck (Section 2.2): it notes QWK’s 0–1 range, possibility of negative values, and its squared-error weighting that differentiates near vs. far misses. Building on this, Section 3 recommends concrete performance analyses that go beyond a single averaged QWK: per-genre/per-prompt breakdowns (e.g., persuasive vs. narrative vs. source-dependent), trait-level discrimination analyses (e.g., whether ORGANIZATION is better separated), and minority-class sensitivity checks. It also points to emerging explainability work (He et al., 2022; Fiacco et al., 2023) as tools to connect performance to model behavior. These specifics make the critique of metric-only reporting credible and give readers an immediate checklist for stronger evaluations.

629.human_review: By advocating for a broader outlook, the authors promote a more sustainable and impactful direction for AES research, which could lead to more robust and generalizable solutions.
629.llm_review: The paper squarely targets generalization and articulates concrete levers for impact. Section 4 argues that ASAP’s composition (U.S. Grades 7–10, mostly native speakers; three essay types; time-restricted setting) limits external validity and explicitly recommends evaluating on at least one additional corpus with different properties, naming CLC-FCE (ESL; holistic plus error tags) and ICLE (time-unrestricted; multi-trait annotations). Section 5 dissects cross-prompt AES: it identifies that many within-prompt models ignore prompts/rubrics, and shows why Ridley et al.’s leave-one-prompt-out setting mixes essay types and rubrics, undermining transfer. It proposes using prompt and rubric as inputs, leveraging LLMs to elicit prompt-specific knowledge, and aligning training/test by essay type/rubric. Section 6 adds a trait-centric, prompt-independent representation to support transfer, and Sections 7–9 broaden impact via essay-pretrained models, LLM-assisted corpus creation/annotation, and integration with tutoring systems. These are specific, feasible directions that, if adopted, would materially improve out-of-domain robustness and downstream educational utility.

630.human_review: The writing level is relatively clear and the writing quality is good.
630.llm_review: The presentation is well-organized and concrete. Section 2 methodically surveys corpora (ASAP/ASAP++, TOEFL, CLC-FCE, ICLE, AAE, and non-English datasets), the evaluation metric (QWK with an accessible explanation), and system families (heuristic, classic ML with explicit feature types, and neural with named architectures like R2BERT, hierarchical models, and attention pooling). Sections 3–9 each culminate in explicit, numbered recommendations (#1–#7) with concrete actions (e.g., multi-corpus evaluation in #2, prompt/rubric-aware cross-prompt modeling in #3, trait-based interpretability/generalization in #3 [traits], corpus/model releases in #5, LLM-assisted workflows in #6). A Limitations section candidly notes subjectivity and survey incompleteness, and an Ethics Statement clarifies the intent behind shifting focus beyond leaderboard gains.

631.human_review: I think some of the methods you mentioned in your article, such as heuristic or ML baseline , have already been mentioned in the previous work. You don't have to spend a lot of space describing this part. You need to describe more emphatically the evaluation and optimization methods of AES in the era of pre-trained models or even LLM.
631.llm_review: The paper stops short of specifying actionable baselines, methods, or training protocols for its proposals, limiting reproducibility and uptake. For cross-prompt modeling, it argues that prompts and rubrics should be inputs and that training/test should be essay-type/rubric aligned, but does not describe a reference architecture (e.g., how to encode rubrics, losses for aligning trait/holistic predictions, or domain adaptation objectives) or concrete data splits. For trait-based holistic scoring, it does not provide a trait set definition, scoring scales, or a pipeline to combine trait scores into holistic predictions (linear vs. nonlinear aggregation, calibration). For LLM-based trait scoring, it lacks prompt templates, few-shot selection strategies, or training details for using noisy LLM outputs as supervision (e.g., filtering, confidence thresholds, or teacher–student distillation). For multi-corpus evaluation, it does not propose standardized splits or baseline systems to anchor comparisons. These omissions across baseline specification, methodological description, and training details hinder direct testing of the recommendations.

632.human_review: As a review article, the way the paper is written is too subjective (such as Line 523-559 and Line571-580), contains a lot of speculation, and does not give enough papers and evidence to support it. In addition, the descriptions of existing papers are too brief, which does not allow readers to fully understand the existing work (such as line 561-569).
632.llm_review: Several key claims rely on plausible but unsubstantiated assertions or open questions rather than evidence. Section 4 questions ASAP’s generalizability (e.g., asks what fraction of ASAP persuasive essays actually contain persuasive arguments) but provides no analysis of ASAP distributions or error types to support overfitting concerns. The statement that essay length is a confounder in time-restricted corpora is not quantified (no correlations, partial correlations, or controlled experiments). Section 6 asserts that LLM-scored traits, even if noisy, could improve holistic scoring after fine-tuning, but offers no pilot study or ablation to demonstrate gains from noisy trait supervision. Section 8 proposes LLM-assisted corpus creation/annotation and claims potential efficiency benefits, yet presents no measurements of reviewer time saved, agreement with human raters (e.g., QWK/κ), or quality filtering efficacy. Without such evidence, the recommendations read as well-argued hypotheses rather than empirically grounded guidance.

633.human_review: This paper tackles a novel and important problem of prompt optimization in multi-step tasks.
633.llm_review: Novelty/Prompt/Task: The paper tackles a largely unexplored problem—automatic prompt optimization for multi-step agent tasks—where prompts are long, structured, and must guide long-horizon decisions. PROMST is novel in combining human-designed feedback rules with LLM-driven prompt generation and a learned heuristic to navigate the large discrete prompt space. The work is tightly aligned with prompt engineering needs in complex, multi-step environments and demonstrates clear task relevance across 11 diverse agent settings.

634.human_review: The proposed method, PROMST, is well-motivated by important problems of multi-step prompt optimization, such as the difficulty of prompt engineering and automatic reasoning over errors.
634.llm_review: Method/Prompt: The framework is methodologically well-motivated and modular. It separates roles for TaskLLM and PromptLLM, introduces a Summarizer (SumLLM) to distill diverse error feedback into concise guidance, and uses a Generator (GenLLM) to propose new prompt candidates. The learned score prediction model (fine-tuned Longformer) provides an explicit, conservative filtering criterion (variance- and error-aware thresholding) to balance exploration and evaluation cost. The prompt optimization is conducted offline across trials, and the method remains orthogonal to online dynamic approaches (e.g., Reflexion), which underscores its flexibility and composability. The design choices are coherent with the unique constraints of long, multi-component prompts.

635.human_review: The experimental results are satisfactory in quality and quantity, as the authors provide results on multiple tasks and LLMs compared to a sufficient number of baseline methods.
635.llm_review: Experiment/Model/Result: The experimental evaluation is broad and generally strong. The authors test across 11 multi-step tasks and five LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Mixtral-8x7B, Mixtral-Large), compare against six representative baselines, and consider two TaskLLM/PromptLLM configurations. PROMST typically achieves the best scores, with notable average gains over strong baselines (e.g., 0.69 vs 0.61 using GPT-4/ GPT-4; 0.32 vs 0.27 using GPT-3.5/GPT-4). Ablations show the score model improves efficiency and convergence, SumLLM adds measurable gains, and human-feedback templates are robust to paraphrasing. Additional studies cover cross-LLM transfer and combination with Reflexion, reinforcing the empirical claims.

636.human_review: The formatting for both the text and the visualizations has room for improvement. I have described a few of them in the suggestions, and I would suggest carefully reviewing the paper to fix them.
636.llm_review: Figure: Several figures would benefit from clearer quantitative presentation. For instance, in Figure 4a the binning/definition of distribution/ratio of prompt scores is not fully specified, and Figure 4c lacks detailed axis annotations and uncertainty visualization beyond a color legend. Figure 5a could include error bars or confidence intervals to contextualize the difference between GPT-4 few-shot and the fine-tuned model. Figure 2s feedback templates are illustrative but small and hard to parse; adding a structured legend or zoomed examples per error type would aid readability. Overall, clearer axis labels, units, and consistent plotting conventions would improve interpretability.

637.human_review: It seems that some descriptions and experimental results solely rely on the Appendix, which may confuse the readers of this paper.
637.llm_review: Description/Experiment/Result: Important experimental and reporting details are under-specified. The main text provides limited description of the human-designed feedback rules per task (delegated to the appendix), making it difficult to assess generality and ease of transfer. The scoring function R and the sub-goal vs. completion trade-offs are discussed but not systematically quantified (e.g., how sensitive are rankings to metric choice across all tasks?). The compute budget and evaluation cost (number of API calls per task/iteration, wall-clock time) are not explicitly reported, hindering reproducibility and fairness comparisons. Some hyperparameters (e.g., the generation s_d when the score model activates) are referenced but not fully detailed. Statistical significance and variance across trials are not consistently presented, and the decision to give baselines random feedback instances (without human rules) may disadvantage methods designed around learned/self feedback. Results on some tasks show small margins, making stronger significance or confidence reporting important.

638.human_review: Some explanations on tasks that PROMPST underperforms baseline methods would be helpful.
638.llm_review: Explanation/Performance/Task: While the paper offers some exploratory analyses (e.g., longer prompts tend to perform better), the explanatory depth remains limited. Performance variations across tasks are not fully accounted for, and in a few cases PROMST underperforms strong baselines (e.g., ScienceWorld with GPT-3.5/GPT-4, GridWorld2 with GPT-3.5), without a thorough task-specific diagnosis (e.g., which error types or prompt components fail). The reliance on human-crafted scoring functions and feedback rules raises questions about bias and generality; claims of preference alignment via score function changes are suggestive but would benefit from user studies or broader task families. The observed correlation between prompt length and performance may be confounded by content density or component structure; more controlled studies would clarify causal factors.

639.human_review: Introduction of the PrideMM dataset fills a critical gap in multimodal meme analysis, particularly for LGBTQ+ related content.
639.llm_review: Analysis and Data: The paper provides concrete, reproducible evidence about the dataset and annotations. PrideMM contains 5,063 text-embedded images collected from Facebook, Twitter, and Reddit (2020–2024) with explicit deduplication (dupeGuru, difPy), OCR (Google Cloud Vision), and text cleaning steps (removal of non-alphanumeric characters and @handles). The 3-phase annotation protocol (dry-run 50, revision 200, consolidation 50 per annotator) yields improved Fleiss’ κ from dry to final: Hate 0.66→0.74, Target 0.68→0.81, Stance 0.62→0.75, Humor 0.60→0.74. Label distributions are clearly reported (e.g., Hate 50.97/49.03, Humor 67.57% positive, Target: Community 46.90% vs Individual 10.03%), which is valuable for downstream analysis and method design.

640.human_review: The dataset is well-annotated for multiple aspects, including hate speech, targets, stance, and humor, offering a holistic approach to meme classification.
640.llm_review: Data: PrideMM fills a clear gap by offering a multimodal, multi-aspect meme dataset centered on LGBTQ+ discourse, annotated for four tasks: Hate (5,063), Target (2,482 hateful memes only), Stance (5,063), and Humor (5,063). The dataset spans multiple platforms and recent years, and includes predefined 85/5/10 splits. Given prior multimodal datasets often cover a single aspect (e.g., HMC), this multi-aspect labeling (hate, target, stance, humor) within memes is a substantive resource contribution.

641.human_review: Effective use of the pre-trained CLIP model helps in preserving valuable knowledge and improving classification performance.
641.llm_review: Model, Performance, Training: MemeCLIP is a well-motivated CLIP adaptation that freezes ViT-L/14 encoders, adds per-modality linear projections to 1024 for SAI compatibility, uses dual feature adapters with residual blending, and a cosine classifier initialized with CLIP textual prompts ("A photo of {LABEL}"). It trains end-to-end in a single stage and consistently improves over strong baselines: on PrideMM Hate, it achieves Acc 76.06/AUC 84.52/F1 75.09 vs HateCLIPper’s 75.53/83.12/74.08; on Humor, it reaches F1 77.21 vs ISSUES 75.73; on HarMeme, it tops Acc 84.72/AUC 92.07/F1 83.74 vs HateCLIPper’s 83.68/90.83/83.31.

642.human_review: MemeCLIP is designed to be robust against imbalanced data, a common issue in real-world datasets, through the use of feature adapters and a cosine classifier.
642.llm_review: Data and Robustness: The target task is both smaller (2,482 samples) and imbalanced (Community 46.90%, Individual 10.03%), yet MemeCLIP attains Acc 66.12/AUC 81.66/F1 58.65, outperforming prior frameworks on Acc and AUC while maintaining competitive Macro-F1. Cross-dataset validation on HarMeme further supports robustness (Acc +1.04 and AUC +0.09 over the strongest baseline), and the reported standard deviations over three seeds are small (e.g., Hate Acc ±0.23), indicating stable training.

643.human_review: Extensive benchmarking against unimodal and multimodal baselines establishes strong performance standards for future research.
643.llm_review: Benchmark and Performance: The paper offers a comprehensive and careful benchmark suite: unimodal (BERT, CLIP-text, ViT-L/14, CLIP-img), multimodal (CLIP, CLIP-Adapter, MOMENTA, HateCLIPper, ISSUES), three metrics (Accuracy, Macro-AUROC, Macro-F1) with mean±std over three seeds, and a stepwise ablation (projections, adapters, cosine classifier, SAI). The ablation on Hate shows steady gains from CLIP baseline (Acc 72.39) to full MemeCLIP (76.06), isolating each component’s additive value.

644.human_review: Although the PrideMM dataset is novel, its size (5,063 images) might still be insufficient for training highly complex models without risk of overfitting.
644.llm_review: Data, Model, Novelty, Training: Methodological novelty is incremental and largely compositional: projections (as in HateCLIPper), adapter-based tuning (Gao et al., 2024), cosine classifier (Liu et al., 2020), and SAI (Shi et al., 2023), with a simple fusion (element-wise multiplication) and frozen CLIP encoders. On the data side, reliance on OCR text without explicit noise-robust modeling (e.g., no character/word-level noise augmentation, confidence-weighted training) is a risk, especially since text cleaning removes symbols that may convey meaning in memes. The topical scope is constrained to LGBTQ+ memes (2020–2024), limiting broader novelty from a data perspective.

645.human_review: The focus on LGBTQ+ related content may limit the generalizability of the findings to other domains or types of memes.
645.llm_review: Generalization: Beyond HarMeme, there is no out-of-distribution or robustness testing—no time-split evaluation (e.g., training on 2020–2022, testing on 2023–2024), platform-held-out splits (train on Twitter/Reddit, test on Facebook), OCR-perturbation stress tests, or adversarial edits (e.g., font changes, overlays). No zero-shot or few-shot transfer experiments are reported (e.g., using SAI-only without fine-tuning on PrideMM), leaving open questions about deployment readiness under domain shift.

646.human_review: While qualitative analysis of misclassified samples is provided, a more detailed quantitative analysis could offer deeper insights into the model’s performance.
646.llm_review: Analysis, Model, Performance: The error analysis is limited to two qualitative examples and lacks per-class confusion matrices, rare-class F1 (e.g., Target=Individual at 10.03%), or calibration metrics. On stance detection, MemeCLIP underperforms HateCLIPper on Accuracy (62.00 vs 63.24) despite higher AUC/F1, but the paper does not analyze the source of this gap (e.g., stance-specific cues, sarcasm) nor propose targeted modifications (e.g., stance-aware prompts or loss weighting). Statistical significance beyond mean±std is not reported.

647.human_review: The heavy reliance on CLIP might limit the exploration of other potentially effective multimodal representations and frameworks.
647.llm_review: Framework: The architecture treats tasks independently and does not exploit cross-task dependencies (e.g., hate→target constraints, humor→stance ambiguity). The fusion is simplistic (element-wise), with no cross-modal attention to align OCR text spans with image regions or to capture irony. CLIP is fully frozen; there is no exploration of partial unfreezing, LoRA, or adapter depth, nor sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters (e.g., residual ratio α, cosine scaling σ), which could materially affect outcomes.

648.human_review: Comparison with similar existing dataset is missing.
648.llm_review: Comparison and Data: The comparative study omits strong recent VLMs (e.g., BLIP-2/InstructBLIP, LLaVA, Florence-like models) that are competitive on multimodal tasks, and does not include other meme datasets such as Hateful Memes (HMC) or Russia–Ukraine memes for broader cross-domain testing. There is no data-scaling or label-efficiency analysis (e.g., performance vs % of training data), nor human performance baselines to contextualize difficulty.

649.llm_review: Prompt: The GPT-4 comparison uses a safety-framed, binary prompt ("I am trying to build a website with safe images... 0/1") on only 100 PrideMM test images and only for Hate, without prompt variants, few-shot exemplars, temperature/reporting settings, or multi-aspect prompts. It also ignores OCR text as an input to the LLM pipeline. The reported metrics (Acc 68.00, F1 69.23) on this tiny sample are insufficient for a robust comparison and underrepresent what prompt-engineered or tool-augmented VLMs could achieve.

650.human_review: The paper introduces a unique method of globally explaining neural relevance models by constructing a "relevance thesaurus," which is innovative and addresses limitations of local explanations.
650.llm_review: The paper proposes a clear and novel method–model combination for global explanations in IR: PaRM, a two-stage Partial Relevance Model distilled from a cross-encoder to infer term–term relevance without explicit alignments. The first stage trains on attention-guided partial query–document views to learn coarse alignments; the second stage calibrates word-pair scores to [0,1] for direct use as a thesaurus. This design targets text-pair relevance directly (rather than single-text classification), avoids perturbation pitfalls, and scales to very large candidate spaces, yielding a principled pathway to interpretable global explanations.

651.human_review: The proposed method is practically implemented by integrating the relevance thesaurus into BM25 scoring functions to enhance ranking effectiveness and fidelity.
651.llm_review: Effectiveness is convincingly demonstrated and the implementation is well specified. BM25T (PaRM) achieves statistically significant gains over BM25 on MS MARCO Dev/DL’19/DL’20 and improves on 7/12 BEIR datasets, with consistent fidelity improvements to several neural rankers (cross-encoder, SPLADE, TAS-B, Contriever(+M)). The method is practical: it integrates seamlessly with BM25/QL via a simple replacement/translation logic, uses public models (MiniLM cross-encoder, BERT-base-uncased), specifies key settings (sequence lengths, Lucene+Krovetz tokenization, candidate vocabularies, thresholding), and keeps implied matches bounded under exact term matches to preserve interpretability and stability.

652.human_review: The proposed method identifies and demonstrates the existence of biases (e.g., brand name bias, temporal bias, encoding errors) in ranking models.
652.llm_review: The explanation logic and model are well aligned: a global thesaurus of query–document term pairs is integrated into BM25 and QL to approximate neural ranker behavior while remaining transparent. Evaluating fidelity against diverse neural architectures shows the model captures behavior shared beyond the teacher cross-encoder. Importantly, the thesaurus enables actionable global insights (e.g., brand-name, temporal, and encoding biases), illustrating the method’s capacity to surface systematic behaviors that local explanations often miss.

653.human_review: The paper concludes that the relevance thesaurus is effective for models trained on similar data. However, this suggests the method may not perform as well across different domains or datasets, potentially limiting its generalization ability and practical applicability.
653.llm_review: Application and generalization remain limited. The thesaurus is distilled from MS MARCO and restricted to frequent terms (top-10k queries, top-100k documents), leaving long-tail vocabulary, multiword expressions, and phrase-level semantics undercovered. Zero-shot BEIR gains are mixed, with notable degradations on some datasets, suggesting domain sensitivity. The approach relies on English-centric preprocessing choices (Lucene+Krovetz) and is only demonstrated for passage retrieval; there is no evidence for transfer to document-level retrieval, multilingual or morphologically rich languages, or real user-facing applications, so practical generalizability is uncertain.

654.human_review: Although the paper identifies various biases, it lacks a detailed analysis of the real-world impact of these biases on retrieval performance.
654.llm_review: Analysis and performance could be strengthened. The bias findings, while compelling, are primarily qualitative and limited in scope; a systematic, controlled study of ranking impact across contexts and mitigation strategies is missing. Performance-wise, a sizable gap to the cross-encoder remains; QLT is underexplored (not tuned to the thesaurus), and comparisons to stronger translation-model baselines are sparse. Key ablations (e.g., attention-based masking vs. alternatives, candidate vocabulary sizes, score thresholding, two-stage necessity, calibration choices) are absent, making it difficult to attribute gains and assess robustness and sensitivity.

655.human_review: The paper introduces a detailed benchmark for evaluating the resilience of language models against subtle and complex shortcuts. This framework categorizes shortcuts into three main types: occurrence, style, and concept.
655.llm_review: Benchmark/Framework/Model/Robustness: The paper proposes a three-tier framework (occurrence, style, concept) with seven instantiated shortcut types, several of which are underexplored in NLP robustness (e.g., synonym occurrence and concept correlation). The benchmark operationalizes this with three datasets (Yelp 5-class ratings, GoEmotions reduced to 4 emotions, Beer palate ratings) and two test regimes (normal vs anti-test) that invert shortcut-label associations, plus a tunable strength parameter λ∈{1.0,0.8,0.6}. This design surfaces model robustness differences in a controlled manner: for example, as λ decreases, macro-F1 gaps consistently shrink (Fig. 3), and BERT exhibits large anti-test drops across all shortcut families (e.g., GoEmotions single-term: accuracy ∆≈0.712; Table 1), while A2R nearly neutralizes the category occurrence shortcut on Yelp (macro-F1 ∆=0.004; Table 3).

656.human_review: The paper provides a well-organized review of related literature, positioning the current study within the broader context of research on spurious correlations and model robustness.
656.llm_review: Model/Related Work/Robustness: The work advances beyond prior studies focused on explicit, trivial triggers by testing subtler cues—synonyms (15 phrases like "to be honest", "frankly speaking"), stylistic rewrites (formal vs casual; Shakespeare vs Hemingway), and concept-level co-occurrence/correlation (Beer palate with aroma). This yields model-level robustness insights grounded in evidence: Llama3-8B is not universally robust, with large drops on GoEmotions author-style (∆=0.367*) and Beer concept-correlation (∆=0.226*), while being relatively robust on Yelp synonyms (∆=0.010*), and A2R shows strong resistance to category shortcuts on Yelp (∆=0.004) yet fails on style (∆=0.320) (Tables 2–3).

657.human_review: The study evaluates a wide range of models, including traditional small LMs, LLMs, and state-of-the-art robust models.
657.llm_review: Evaluation/Model: The experimental protocol is careful: models are trained and evaluated over 5 runs with averaged metrics; both accuracy and macro-F1 are reported; statistical significance is marked (e.g., many LLM drops with p<0.05 in Table 2). The evaluation spans distinct model families—BERT-base, Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3-8B, and three robust methods (A2R, CR, AFR)—revealing concrete, model-specific patterns such as Llama2-7B being more robust than Llama2-13B on Yelp style-register (∆=0.030* vs 0.100*), while Llama3-8B is better on Yelp synonyms (∆=0.010*). The λ-sweep (Fig. 3) demonstrates that robustness degrades monotonically as shortcut strength increases, lending credence to the causal role of shortcuts rather than noise.

658.human_review: The benchmark and experiments are focused solely on text classification tasks, specifically sentiment analysis and emotion prediction. This limits the generalizability of the findings to other NLP tasks, such as machine translation or question answering.
658.llm_review: Benchmark/Experiment/Generalization/Task: The benchmark is limited to sentiment/emotion classification (Yelp stars, GoEmotions reduced to neutral/amusement/joy/excitement, Beer palate with ratings in {0.4,0.6,0.8,1.0}). Shortcuts are injected via templates and LLM rewrites—for example, inserting "honestly" with base probabilities tied to labels (0/25/50/75/100%) and adding "I wrote this review in [Country/City]" to the text. Anti-test sets reverse these distributions. While effective for stress testing, this construction may not reflect naturally occurring shortcuts in tasks like NLI, QA, or IE, and may exaggerate spurious effects. Moreover, style shortcuts are produced by Llama2-70B without quantitative validation of label preservation or style fidelity, and the authors acknowledge possible label shifts and only manual spot checks (Limitations), which constrains external validity.

659.human_review: The use of LLMs to rewrite text for creating style shortcuts may introduce noise or alter the original meaning of the text.
659.llm_review: Model: Model coverage is narrow. On encoders, only BERT-base is tested—omitting stronger and widely used baselines such as RoBERTa-large or DeBERTa-v3. On decoders, only Llama2-7B/13B and Llama3-8B are included, with no instruction-tuned/chat variants or alternative architectures (e.g., Mistral, Mixtral). The robust set is limited to A2R/CR/AFR, leaving out invariance-based and distributionally robust training methods (IRM, GroupDRO). These omissions make it difficult to generalize the reported robustness rankings across modern model families.

660.human_review: The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of the quality of the modified datasets. Although manual checks were performed, a systematic quantitative evaluation would strengthen the validity of the conclusions.
660.llm_review: Analysis/Data/Evaluation: The interpretability analysis is restricted and does not match the breadth of the data interventions. SHAP is applied only to 100 Yelp instances for occurrence shortcuts, yet not to style or concept cases. Even within occurrence, analysis is narrow; while Table 4 usefully shows large SHAP contributions for the single-term token toward label 4 (e.g., +1.579) and against label 0 (e.g., −0.851) for BERT at λ=1, there is no parallel quantification for register/author shortcuts or concept correlation. Additionally, there is no quantitative quality audit of LLM rewrites (style fidelity, label preservation), no per-group performance breakdowns, and no calibration/causal counterfactual checks, limiting what can be inferred about mechanisms vs artifacts.

661.key_points: Weakness: Evaluation, Method, Model, Novelty, Robustness
661.human_review: While the paper evaluates existing robust models, it does not propose new methods to improve robustness against the identified shortcuts. Introducing novel techniques or strategies would add significant value to the study.
661.llm_review: Evaluation/Method/Model/Novelty/Robustness: Some shortcut instantiations remain stylized or overt (e.g., inserting a separate sentence "I wrote this review in [Country/City]"; author styles confined to highly distinctive extremes like Shakespeare vs Hemingway), which complicates the claim of subtlety and novelty over prior synthetic-trigger work. The anti-test protocol flips correlations completely, yielding large deltas that may overstate brittleness compared to real OOD. Methodological coverage of robust training is narrow (A2R/CR/AFR), missing stronger causal/invariance or DRO baselines; likewise, LLMs are only evaluated under fine-tuning, not zero-/few-shot prompting where shortcut reliance might differ. Consequently, conclusions such as "none are universally robust"—while empirically true here—offer limited guidance on which families/strategies would work under more realistic shifts.

662.human_review: The study could explore the impact of different hyperparameter settings on model robustness.
662.llm_review: Model/Parameter/Robustness: Robustness conclusions may be sensitive to heterogeneous training hyperparameters and limited sensitivity analyses. λ is fixed to {1.0,0.8,0.6} for train and 1.0 for test without justification for range selection; A2R follows original settings except 100 epochs on GoEmotions; CR picks best validation accuracy; AFR uses a two-stage overfitting/reweighting regime; LLM fine-tuning details are deferred to the appendix. Without matched training budgets and comprehensive sweeps (seeds, learning rates, early stopping), it is hard to disentangle intrinsic robustness from tuning effects—for example, Llama2-13B underperforms Llama2-7B on Yelp style-register (∆=0.100* vs 0.030*; Table 2), which could reflect suboptimal hyperparameters rather than a size-robustness tradeoff.

663.human_review: This paper provides a method to balance two critical aspects (quality & diversity) of dataset curation, which is crucial for improving the robustness of language models in following instructions.
663.llm_review: The paper proposes a clear, data-driven method (QDIT) that jointly optimizes instruction-response quality and instruction diversity by combining a facility-location diversity term over instruction embeddings with a quality score via a tunable alpha. Methodologically, this gives principled control over the quality–diversity trade-off while remaining practical through greedy selection and standard accelerations. On the robustness front, the study carefully targets worst-case behavior (bottom 10% by reward or win rate) and shows that increasing data diversity substantially improves worst-case performance without harming best-case, e.g., aggregated gains of +5.2% in worst-case HH score and +6.26% in worst-case winning score over quality-only selection.

664.human_review: This paper offers detailed experiments on how quality and diversity inference the instruction tuning process. It's beneficial for potential researchers in data selection areas.
664.llm_review: The experimental design leverages multiple and diverse data sources (Ultrachat 1.3M, LMSYS-Chat 1M, a Mixed 270K set, and smaller Alpaca 52K and Dolly 15K), with consistent subset sizes (e.g., 10K for large sources, ~5% for small) to isolate selection effects. Evaluations span five instruction-following suites via LLM-based pairwise comparison and a reward model (HH score), and report average, worst-case (bottom 10%), and best-case (top 10%) metrics. The authors further probe evaluator sensitivity (Claude-2/2.1, GPT-3.5/4), perform ablations (alpha sweep, data size, selection variants), and report statistical significance (paired t-test) and multiple seeds, yielding a credible, data-centric picture of the method’s impact.

665.human_review: The authors conduct extensive experiments across multiple datasets and models to validate QDIT's effectiveness and versatility. These experiments clearly demonstrate QDIT's superior performance in various scenarios, particularly in improving the worst-case instruction-following capability.
665.llm_review: Effectiveness is demonstrated across experiments and models: compared to quality-only selection, QDIT consistently improves worst-case metrics and often improves average metrics (e.g., Ultrachat 10K shows worst 10% HH 3.497 vs. 3.405; LMSYS 10K shows worst 10% HH 3.551 vs. 3.391), while leaving best-case largely unchanged. The method transfers across base models (LLaMA-1 7B and Llama-2-13B) and even shows gains on several general benchmarks (MMLU/BBH/ARC/DROP/LAMBADA/SCIQ), with higher average scores in most settings. Use of multiple evaluators and a human check strengthens the validation that improvements are not artifacts of a single judge.

666.human_review: This paper only compares QDIT with random, quality, and QDIT variant settings, lacking comparisons with other instruction data selection methods such as CaR and DEITA.
666.llm_review: Comparisons are limited primarily to random and quality-only selection, plus two in-house diversity variants (thresholding and clustering). The study does not compare against well-known alternative subset selection methods for diversity/coverage (e.g., determinantal point processes, k-center/coreset selection, other submodular objectives), nor does it probe alternative similarity backbones (beyond sentence-transformer cosine) or non-linear quality–diversity combinations. This narrows the methodological and data-selection comparison space and leaves open how QDIT stacks up against other established coverage/diversity techniques.
