741.llm_review: Clarity, experiments, and presentation: The paper is explicit about the retrieval–generation pipeline and evaluation. It details (i) first-stage retrieval with DPR, (ii) silver passage selection from the top-100 candidates using multiple strategies (DA match; LFA lexical/semantic/perplexity; combined LFA&DA), (iii) BERT-based re-ranking (Nogueira & Cho, 2019), and (iv) Vicuna-13B fine-tuned for 1 epoch on ASQA to generate long-form answers from the top-5 passages. Metrics are well matched to goals: Direct Answer Recall and Wikipage Recall for retrieval; ROUGE-L and D-F1 (with an MRC model) on ASQA and C-F1 on CONVMIX for answer quality; and token-level Groundedness w.r.t. retrieved passages. The ablation table (Table 1) directly compares all supervision variants; notably, simple LFA lexical matching yields DR 35.0, semantic similarity 34.1, LLM perplexity 34.0, and the combined SILVER is best at 35.5, making the contribution and trade-offs transparent. Qualitative examples (Table 3) show concrete groundedness gains (e.g., Grandpa Joe: 0.61→0.94; Sopranos episodes: 0.23→1.00) and a per-turn recall plot (Fig. 1) clearly visualizes conversational drift and SILVER’s consistent advantage over DPR.

742.human_review: The generalization of the proposed method might be limited. The proposed method is only based on the ASQA dataset with annotated long-form answers (LFAs) and direct answers (DA). When annotated long-form answers are not available, it is still a fundamental challenge to obtain the training data for the retriever.
742.llm_review: Data, generalization, and training: Evidence is limited to Wikipedia-centric datasets (ASQA and CONVMIX) and a DPR first-stage retriever trained on NQ, leaving generalization to other domains/corpora untested (e.g., ELI5, QAMPARI, news, biomedical, or web). The silver labeling relies on LFA text being available; where only short answers or distant supervision exist, the proposed scheme may be inapplicable or weaker. Because silver positives are primarily selected via lexical overlap with LFAs and DAs, and groundedness is computed as token overlap with retrieved passages (stopwords removed), there is a risk of metric–supervision alignment inflating gains in groundedness and ROUGE-L independently of actual factual support. Training choices appear narrow: the generator is a single LLM (Vicuna-13B, 1-epoch fine-tuning); the first-stage retriever is fixed (DPR); and key hyperparameters like k (number of silver passages) and negative sampling details are not quantified in the main text. Together, these limit claims about robustness and portability beyond the current setup.

743.key_points: Weakness: Comparison, Effectiveness, Experiment, Improvement, Method
743.human_review: The improvement of the proposed method is marginal, with about 1-2% improvement. In addition, the experiments do not compare with other reranker models, making the effectiveness of the proposed method under-measured.
743.llm_review: Comparison, effectiveness, experiments, improvement, and method: While the ablations compare weak-supervision strategies, baseline coverage for retrieval/reranking is dated. There are no comparisons to stronger contemporary first-stage and hybrid retrievers (e.g., Contriever, GTR/T5, SPLADE, ColBERTv2/hybrids) or competitive cross-encoder rerankers (e.g., monoT5, E5 rerankers) or LLM-based reranking. Effect sizes are modest in the controlled comparison with DPR (Table 1): DR improves +1.2 absolute (34.3→35.5), ROUGE-L +0.9, D-F1 +1.3; and the incremental benefit of combining LFA&DA over LFA-lexical alone is small (DR 35.5 vs. 35.0; Wikipage recall 0.516 vs. 0.501; Groundedness 0.858 vs. 0.851). On CONVMIX, despite follow-up answer recall gains (0.260→0.306), end-to-end C-F1 remains flat (20.8 vs. 20.8 for LFA-lexical and only +0.6 over DPR’s 20.2), which weakens the claim that the method translates into better conversational QA quality. The paper reports no statistical significance tests, and provides no sensitivity analyses for k (silver passages), top-5 vs. larger retrieval depths, or alternative first-stage retrievers. As the strongest variant is largely driven by lexical matching, additional controls (e.g., human evaluation of long-form quality, robustness to paraphrase-heavy references) are needed to substantiate effectiveness claims.

744.human_review: The paper introduces PsyGUARD, an automated system for suicide detection and risk assessment in psychological counseling, showcasing advancements in fine-grained taxonomy development, dataset creation, and benchmark establishment.
744.llm_review: Strong combination of Benchmark and Data: The paper contributes PsyGUARD, a large-scale Chinese dataset (14.8k utterances) with 11 fine-grained, action/thought-aware classes and limited multi-labeling, aggregated from multiple sources (Weibo, Zhihu, Yixinli, and open-source counseling dialogues). The annotation pipeline is carefully designed (initial training, iterative labeling, adjudication, quality control) with substantial agreement in large batches (Fleiss’ kappa > 0.7). Alongside, the authors provide comprehensive benchmarks spanning zero/few-shot LLMs and fine-tuned encoder models, enabling reproducible comparisons and establishing a solid baseline for counseling-oriented suicide risk detection.

745.human_review: Empirical results provide valuable insights into the performance of automated systems in detecting suicide risk, contributing to understanding the capabilities and limitations of such technologies in personalized risk assessment.
745.llm_review: Performance and Result are clearly reported and compelling: Fine-tuned models substantially outperform prompting. ChatGLM2-6B with LoRA reaches about 92% accuracy (best ~91.99%), and RoBERTa-large achieves ~91.7%, while the best prompting baseline (GPT-4 zero-shot) attains ~75%. Results include micro and macro metrics plus an error analysis (e.g., sensitivity to suicide-related terms, confusion between exploration and intent), providing a transparent picture of strengths and failure modes.

746.key_points: Strength: Benchmark, Data, Framework, Method, Related Work
746.human_review: The paper's clear organization, including sections on related works, taxonomy construction, data collection processes, benchmarks, and risk assessment frameworks, aids technical readers in comprehending the research context and methodology.
746.llm_review: Coherent integration across Benchmark, Data, Framework, Method, and Related Work: The paper is well-situated in prior taxonomies (e.g., C-SSRS, 4-level, binary), articulates why counseling-specific, fine-grained labels are needed, and proposes a theory-informed 11-class taxonomy. It delivers the PsyGUARD dataset, methodologically diverse baselines (prompting, full fine-tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning), and a practical risk assessment framework for triage. Together, these elements form a clear, end-to-end research pipeline that advances the area and is useful to both practitioners and researchers.

747.human_review: Limited dataset diversity may hinder the generalizability of the proposed system, impacting its scalability and effectiveness across different demographics and cultural backgrounds.
747.llm_review: Data, Effectiveness, and Generalization limitations: A large portion of the corpus derives from Chinese social media and open-source counseling dialogues, which may not fully reflect real, diverse counseling sessions. The work does not evaluate end-to-end effectiveness (e.g., counselor outcomes, response time, safety events), and there is no assessment of cross-demographic, cross-lingual, or cross-platform generalization, limiting confidence in real-world impact.

748.human_review: Absence of tailored models for fine-grained suicide prevention in counseling services poses a challenge, potentially limiting the system's precision and adaptability in real-world scenarios.
748.llm_review: Adaptation and Model gaps: Although the target is counseling, the core modeling is largely single-utterance classification without conversation-level context, personalization, or clinician-validated calibration. The risk assessment component is presented as a rule-guided/LLM prompting template rather than a trained, integrated module, making adaptation to varied counseling workflows and sustained supervision less convincing.

749.human_review: Issues with data format and biases in existing datasets raise concerns about the dataset's robustness and representativeness, affecting the reliability and reproducibility of the study's results.
749.llm_review: Data and Robustness concerns: The dataset is highly imbalanced (e.g., very few ‘Suicidal Preparatory Act’ cases), yet the training regime does not explicitly address imbalance, and per-class results are not reported. Robustness to figurative language, sarcasm, typos, code-switching, or adversarial phrasing is not tested, leaving uncertainty about stability under noisy, real counseling inputs.

750.human_review: Lack of a holistic risk assessment framework for diverse suicide categories may restrict the system's predictive accuracy and practical utility in counseling interventions.
750.llm_review: Accuracy and Framework risks for safety-critical use: While micro-level metrics are high, macro F1 is notably lower (around 70% for the best fine-tuned models), and the analysis does not quantify false negatives in the most critical classes. There is no calibration analysis, precision–recall trade-off study, or thresholding strategy. The proposed risk assessment framework lacks empirical validation of escalation criteria, alert latency, and operator burden—key requirements for safe deployment.

751.human_review: While insightful, the study's perceived impact within computational linguistics and mental health support systems may be constrained, potentially affecting its visibility and significance among the readers.
751.llm_review: Significance is moderate: The taxonomy extends known schemes, the benchmarks use standard models, and the resource is limited to the Chinese setting. Without stronger clinical validation, deployment studies, or cross-lingual extensions, the impact is more incremental than transformative for the broader *ACL community.

752.human_review: Innovative Approach: The paper's proposal of an iterative selection mechanism that integrates zero-shot CoT reasoning represents a significant advancement in the area of in-context learning.
752.llm_review: Approach and novelty: The paper introduces a simple, training-free retrieval scheme that selects in-context demonstrations by matching training examples to the model’s zero-shot chain-of-thought (reasoning path) for the test query, rather than to the raw input. This reasoning-aligned retrieval is an original angle that operationalizes the long-discussed trade-off between similarity and diversity: the CoT-driven similarity anchors demos to the test case, while iterative updates to the reasoning path naturally inject diversity across iterations. The method is model- and parameter-agnostic (no logits or gradients), requires only a lightweight embedding model for KNN, and integrates seamlessly with standard prompting and majority voting, making it broadly applicable.

753.human_review: Empirical Validation: The method has been robustly tested across multiple tasks, showing that it not only improves accuracy but also effectively balances diversity and similarity in the selection process.
753.llm_review: Accuracy, method, and validation: IDS consistently outperforms strong baselines across six benchmarks (BoolQ, GSM8K, MATH, CommonsenseQA, LogiQA, AGNews), with an average accuracy of 69.8% vs. 68.1% for the best baseline (Top-k-Consistency), and notably larger gains on reasoning-heavy datasets (e.g., GSM8K 78.5 vs. 76.1; MATH 37.5 vs. 35.6). The evaluation is careful: five seeds to reduce randomness, matched numbers of iterations/decoding paths across baselines, and comparisons against both classical and recent selection methods (e.g., Vote-k, MMR, G-fair-Prompting, Skill-KNN). Robustness is shown across model families and scales (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Llama-2-chat 7B/13B/70B), indicating the method’s reliability beyond a single API.

754.human_review: Detailed Quantitative Analysis: The inclusion of detailed quantitative analyses, such as the comparison of average similarity scores between selected demonstrations and test samples, provides a strong empirical basis for the claimed improvements.
754.llm_review: Analysis: The paper provides clear diagnostics on why the approach works. It first motivates the task-specific nature of the diversity vs. similarity trade-off with pilot results, then shows IDS achieves a middle ground in similarity scores between random and top-k methods. Additional analyses explore iteration count effects (q=1,5,7), model robustness (GPT-4, open-source Llama-2), and qualitative case studies illustrating how iterative selection avoids misleading similar demos and corrects earlier mistakes. Appendices further examine the number of shots, embedding models, and Zero-shot-CoT triggers, painting a well-rounded picture of behavior and robustness.

755.human_review: Need for Ablation Studies: Despite detailed analyses, the paper could be strengthened by including comprehensive ablation studies that delineate the contribution of each component of the IDS methodology to the overall performance. This would offer deeper insights into the essential elements of the approach and validate the necessity of each iterative step.
755.llm_review: Ablation, method, and validation: While the paper includes several analyses, it lacks targeted ablations to isolate the contribution of each component. In particular: (1) a direct comparison of selecting demos via the reasoning path vs. via the original query under identical decoding and voting would clarify the source of gains; (2) an ablation of iteration mechanics (one-time selection with multiple samples vs. reselecting every round) would quantify the value of iterative re-retrieval; (3) removing majority voting or reasoning generation during inference would show their marginal contributions; (4) a study of alternative rationale strategies (e.g., manual-CoT, shorter rationales, or no-CoT selection) would test dependence on rationale quality. From a validation standpoint, results rely on subsampled test sets due to cost; adding statistical significance tests and a cost/latency breakdown (API calls, context length growth, retrieval time) would strengthen claims about efficiency and practical reliability.

756.human_review: Generalization Concerns: The paper primarily focuses on a single model architecture (GPT-3.5), and while it hints at broader applicability, demonstrations of effectiveness across a range of models or further validation on open-source models could enhance the paper's impact and generalization claims.
756.llm_review: Application, architecture, generalization, and model: Practical deployment may be hindered by iterative reasoning generation, which increases API calls and latency and could stress context windows when demonstrations and rationales are long. The approach assumes models produce useful zero-shot CoT; weaker or non-CoT-friendly models, multilingual settings, or domains with noisy rationales may degrade selection quality. The retrieval backbone uses general-purpose SBERT embeddings and a single KNN strategy; domain shift, long-document inputs, or structured generation tasks are not evaluated. Although results span multiple LLMs, applications beyond English short-form QA/classification and arithmetic/logic reasoning remain untested, and no guidance is provided for adapting the method to long-context or non-text tasks where memory and retrieval strategies might need architectural adjustments.

757.human_review: The proposed reverse instructions generation process, though a simple idea, seems to  be empirically effective for long text generation task.
757.llm_review: Effectiveness: Strong, repeatable gains across long-form generation benchmarks with concrete margins. On the LongForm-C test, LongForm-LLaMA-7B achieves 24.8 METEOR vs. Alpaca-7B 15.2, FLAN-T5-11B 12.5, and OPT-30B 12.3 (Table 2). Out-of-domain, it averages 19.7 METEOR on RGen, ELI5, and WP vs. the best baseline (Alpaca-7B) at 14.6 (Table 3). These results show that instruction tuning on LongForm-C yields sizable improvements over both instruction-tuned baselines and a 10x larger untuned model.

758.human_review: Authors addressed the previous concerns raised by reviewers by including the ablation study demonstrating the effectiveness of reverse instructions.
758.llm_review: Ablation, Effectiveness: The subset ablations isolate the contribution of Reverse Instructions (RI). With the same LLaMA-7B backbone, NLG METEOR rises from 13.6 (NLP-only) to 19.9 with NLP+RI (+6.3), while MMLU remains roughly stable (35.4 to 35.5). Adding SC to NLP alone yields 18.6 METEOR but does not match the gains from RI (Table 5). This pinpoints RI as the main driver of long-form generation improvements.

759.human_review: The paper is overall well written and well organized.1. Though ablation study shows that RI helps, but it only helps in NLG but not NLU. This raises the question on effectiveness of the RI generation process specifically for the NLU task.
759.llm_review: Ablation, Effectiveness, Presentation: The paper separates evidence cleanly across settings: in-domain (Table 2), OOD (Table 3), data-collection comparison with FLAN on the same backbone (Table 4), and subset ablations (Table 5). It also flags potential confounds in Table 3 († noting RGen appears in FLAN/Tk-Instruct training), aiding interpretation. This clear structuring makes it easy to trace which dataset components (RI vs. SC vs. NLP) produce the observed gains.

760.human_review: With the recent updates in LLMs generation capabilities, I am skeptical whether the proposed  reverse instructions is still needed and its overall effectiveness. It would be nice to try out on newer versions of similar sized LLMs such as Llama2.
760.llm_review: Effectiveness, Model: Benefits generalize across model families and sizes. LongForm-T5-XL (3B) scores 24.3 METEOR on LongForm-C test, outperforming T0++, Tk-Instruct, and FLAN-T5—all 11B models (Table 2). Decoder-only variants also improve substantially (LongForm-OPT-6.7B: 24.2; LongForm-LLaMA-7B: 24.8). The paper reports that a smaller LongForm-OPT-2.7B surpasses untuned OPT-30B on long text generation, and highlights a simple but effective modeling choice ([EOI] token) that helps autoregressive models separate instruction from output.

761.human_review: Though ablation study shows that RI helps, but it only helps in NLG but not NLU. This raises the question on effectiveness of the RI generation process specifically for the NLU task.
761.llm_review: Ablation, Effectiveness, Task: While subset ablations show RI’s importance, they do not dissect RI’s internal design choices. RI uses three instruction styles (formal 50%, chatbot 30%, search 20%) and length-control prompts applied to 30% of samples, but there is no ablation quantifying each factor’s impact on NLG or NLU. Task-wise, OOD evaluation covers only three datasets (RGen, ELI5, WP) with automatic metrics (METEOR main; BLEU/ROUGE relegated to appendix) and no human assessment of coherence, planning, or factuality of outputs. The only human study (97/100 instruction relevance) validates instruction–document alignment, not generation quality. Also, corpus mining choices (C4 filtered by Reddit upvotes; k-means center selection) may bias topics; the authors note occasional overlong answers to simple prompts, but there is no targeted evaluation to quantify this failure mode.

762.human_review: With the recent updates in LLMs generation capabilities, I am skeptical whether the proposed  reverse instructions is still needed and its overall effectiveness. It would be nice to try out on newer versions of similar sized LLMs such as Llama2.
762.llm_review: Effectiveness, Model: Some comparisons conflate data and model differences. Baselines vary in backbone (T5-11B vs. LLaMA-7B vs. OPT-30B) and training pipelines, and Alpaca is reimplemented by the authors—potentially affecting its strength. The one controlled backbone study (Table 4) uses LLaMA-7B to compare FLAN vs. LongForm-C vs. both, but similar controlled comparisons are missing for T5 and OPT, and there are no multiple-seed runs to assess variance. Stronger claims about parameter efficiency and generality would benefit from holding the backbone fixed across more families and isolating instruction data as the only variable.

763.human_review: The question examined is an important one, as more modern automatic speech recognition systems are applied in language documentation of endangered languages (which are frequently morphologically complex).
763.llm_review: Clear, well-scoped question with concrete cross-architecture evidence: the paper asks whether multilingual ASR models trained without polysynthetic languages are robust to complex morphology, then shows (i) significantly lower CER for non-isolating vs. isolating languages across both models (Table 2: r ≈ -0.8 to -0.9, p ≤ 0.001), and (ii) higher WER degradation for morphologically complex languages under increased OOV pressure (Figures 6–7), with token–type ratio emerging as a key predictor. This framing, tied to concretes like the absence of polysynthetic languages in Whisper/XLSR pretraining (0% in Table 1), makes the contribution relevant to endangered-language ASR.

764.human_review: The authors explore several combinations of indicators of morphological complexity and performance metrics in trying to tease out the underlying cause.
764.llm_review: Complexity–metric–performance linkage is explicitly operationalized and statistically grounded. The study: (a) quantifies complexity using four measures (average word length, type–token ratio, Morfessor-derived morphemes/word, morpheme length); (b) perturbs OOV via a maxsplit procedure (700 utterance swaps to maximize type OOV); and (c) evaluates WER, CER, and an OOV-robustness metric (correct OOVs / total OOVs). Key results include significant correlations between higher type–token ratio and larger degradation for Whisper in both WER (r=0.75, p=0.01) and CER (r=0.77, p=0.009). For XLSR, after identifying domain-driven outliers (Cree/Yupik), WER degradation correlates very strongly with type–token ratio (r=0.94, p=0.0004), and CER correlates with average word length (r=0.89, p=0.003) and morpheme-based measures (r≈0.77–0.78, p=0.02). These effects tie specific complexity metrics to measurable performance changes.

765.human_review: In doing so, they come up with ingenious ways of comparing ASR performance between languages in spite of the complex landscape of varied morphologies, amounts of data, quality of recordings, and contents diversity.
765.llm_review: Valuable dataset curation across typological diversity and practical performance insights. The paper assembles 10 languages spanning isolating (e.g., Namakura 2h18m, East Uvean 2h9m, Bambara 7h11m) to polysynthetic (e.g., Hupa 9h12m single speaker; Enenlhet 5h17m; Kunwok 1h03m; Plains Cree 2h04m Psalms; St. Lawrence Yupik 33h32m Bible), none seen in pretraining for Whisper/XLSR. Consistent fine-tuning for 30 epochs on both Whisper-medium and XLSR-53 (CTC with a trigram LM for XLSR) enables comparisons that surface actionable observations: isolating languages have substantially higher CER across both models (Table 2), Whisper tends to transcribe OOVs more accurately than XLSR for most languages (Figure 5; exceptions: Hupa, Bambara), and WER degradation is generally larger for morphologically complex languages under OOV stress (Figures 6–7).

766.human_review: In the end the authors succeed at least in establishing an impact of morphological complexity on the performance of modern ASR systems, but without being able to identify a precise cause or mechanism.
766.llm_review: Complexity–performance claims are sensitive to data confounds and outlier handling. (1) The standout language-specific factors undermine clean attribution to morphology: Hupa’s single-speaker corpus yields an anomalously low type–token ratio and atypical behavior (low WER degradation for Whisper but the highest for XLSR), while Cree and Yupik draw from Bible readings, driving them to behave as outliers for XLSR; the strongest XLSR WER result (r=0.94, p=0.0004) requires excluding these two languages. (2) OOV-robustness shows no significant correlation with any complexity measure for either architecture, weakening the central hypothesis that complex morphology (and higher OOV rates) should degrade the ability to produce unseen words. (3) Opposite CER–OOV trends across models further blur the story: for Whisper, higher subword/subtype OOV rates correlate with lower CER (r=-0.67, p=0.03; r=-0.78, p≈0.00), whereas for XLSR, higher token/subword OOV rates correlate with higher CER (r=0.86, p=0.001; r=0.68, p=0.03). These inconsistencies make it hard to isolate morphology as the driver rather than domain, speaker diversity, data size, or recording conditions.

767.human_review: It turns out that type-to-token ratio comes out as the main factor that influences degradation of WER and CER for morphologically complex languages, however properly estimating type-to-token ratio is not trivial and the method used  is not presented in enough details given its importance in the conclusion.
767.llm_review: Methodological limitations constrain rigor and comparability. (1) No development set is used and the last checkpoint is selected for all runs; this can bias results toward noise in later epochs and differs by language/data size. (2) Sample size is small (n=10 languages) yet many correlation tests are reported without multiple-comparison correction; several p-values sit near 0.05–0.08 (e.g., Whisper correlations for word length and morpheme length on WER/CER), making findings fragile. (3) Decoding setups differ across architectures: XLSR uses a trigram LM trained on the training transcripts, while Whisper appears to rely on its decoder without a matched LM; this asymmetry can affect OOV handling and CER/WER in opposite directions and complicates cross-model conclusions. (4) The OOV maximization procedure (700 utterance swaps) is under-specified with respect to controlling for other distributional shifts (e.g., phonetic content, speaker, domain), and OOV is defined at the surface type level without orthographic normalization; Morfessor is trained on small, heterogeneous transcripts, likely yielding language-dependent segmentation quality that directly affects morpheme-based complexity metrics. Together, these choices reduce causal interpretability and reproducibility.

768.key_points: Strength: Data, Experiment, Model, Result, Robustness, Task
768.human_review: The paper provides thorough experimental results across multiple datasets, demonstrating the robustness and effectiveness of CasCoD on both IND and OOD tasks. The authors also conduct the ablation study on model and data sizes to validate the scalability and adaptability of this method. Overall, this is a sound and solid work.
768.llm_review: Data/Task: The paper evaluates on a well-chosen in-domain task (BBH with a clear 4:1 train/test split) and multiple out-of-domain multiple-choice reasoning suites (BB-sub, AGIEval, ARC-E/C), providing a diverse set of reasoning tasks. Experiment: The study compares against strong and relevant baselines (Std-CoT, MT-CoT, Step-by-step, SCOTT, Answer-SFT) and includes thorough ablations on model size (1.1B/7B/13B), training data size (12.5%–100%), loss weighting, and a single-step variant, as well as a faithfulness analysis (LAS). Model: A practical teacher–student framework (ChatGPT → LLaMA2 with LoRA) and a simple, reproducible cascading objective (q→r, q⊕r→a) that aligns training and inference. Result: CasCoD improves accuracy over distillation baselines on both IND and OOD settings and reaches a substantial fraction of teacher performance; it is competitive with Answer-SFT on OOD while retaining the ability to generate CoTs. Robustness: Gains persist across model sizes and with substantially less training data, and OOD performance is relatively insensitive to loss-weight α. Task: The approach directly targets reasoning with CoTs and demonstrably increases generalization across unseen multiple-choice reasoning tasks.

769.human_review: The paper is well-formulated, with a clear structure that is easy to follow. The flow of writing and thinking is logical and coherent.
769.llm_review: Presentation: The paper is clearly structured with a motivating example, an intuitive figure contrasting standard and cascading distillation, and precise training objectives with equations. The training–inference alignment is well explained, datasets and setups are described in sufficient detail, and ablations are easy to follow. Limitations and ethical considerations are explicitly acknowledged, which improves readability and transparency.

770.human_review: The novelty and contribution of this work are a little incremental and limited. The paper builds on existing CoT distillation methods by introducing a two-step process, which, although effective, may not be seen as a large progress from current techniques.
770.llm_review: Novelty: While the cascaded conditioning (q→r followed by q⊕r→a) is a neat reorganization, the core idea overlaps with prior work that separates rationale and answer objectives (e.g., Step-by-step, MT-CoT). The incremental difference—conditioning answer prediction on the generated rationale and training both steps jointly—may be perceived as a modest extension rather than a fundamentally new distillation paradigm.

771.key_points: Weakness: Analysis, Effectiveness, Explanation, Generalization, Method
771.human_review: The analysis of the method primarily focuses on generalizability. A deeper exploration of the effectiveness and explanation of the method would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the advantages of the methods.
771.llm_review: Analysis/Effectiveness/Explanation/Generalization/Method: (1) The central claim that spurious question–answer correlations drive poor OOD generalization is plausible but not directly tested; there are no controlled diagnostics (e.g., counterfactuals, answer shuffling, correlation probes) to establish causality beyond aggregate performance gaps. (2) Effectiveness versus the simplest baseline (Answer-SFT) is mixed on some OOD sets (e.g., AGIEval and ARC-E/C), tempering the claim of broadly superior generalization. (3) Methodologically, delimiter-based rationale–answer splitting can be brittle across tasks/teachers, and the two-pass training introduces exposure bias (answer is trained on gold rationales, but inference uses generated ones) without mitigation (e.g., scheduled sampling or self-refinement). (4) Generalization is evaluated primarily on multiple-choice tasks that are still close to BB/BIG-Bench distributions; broader domains (open-ended reasoning, math/code with free-form answers) are not assessed. (5) The study would benefit from deeper analyses to isolate components (e.g., masking out answer tokens in single-step training as a control; sensitivity to noisy/incorrect rationales; error propagation from r to a) and statistical significance reporting.

772.human_review: Logical Design. This paper analyzes the complex issue of clickbait and designs a multimodal model based on the causal representation framework. The model extracts a wide range of multimodal information and makes predictions based on the invariant and causal factors.
772.llm_review: Analysis, Framework, Model: The paper presents a concrete causal modeling framework tailored to multimodal clickbait disguised with non-bait content. It explicitly disentangles three latent factors by: (i) extracting an invariant factor ic via an invariance mask m optimized with an IRM-style objective (Eq. (1): gradient-norm penalty over empirical risk across scenarios plus L2 regularization on m); (ii) estimating scenario structure by alternation—training scenario predictors Φ_s on the variant part vc = (1−m)⊙x with Eq. (2) and reallocating samples by Eq. (3)—so that invariance is learned relative to discovered spurious correlations; and (iii) separating scenario-specific causal signals with a Gumbel-Softmax mask γ over ξ(vc), retaining k_d dimensions for sci, and designating the remainder as non-causal nfi. The causal graph in Fig. 3(c) guides the design by isolating IC from confounding and constraining scenario effects to flow via SC, and the final predictor uses [ic; sci] (Eq. (5)). Compared to CCD (causal intervention limited to cross-modal misalignment) and VLP (generic multimodal pretraining), the proposed combination—IRM-based invariance, unsupervised scenario discovery on vc, and contrastive dissociation of sci from nfi—directly targets the evolution of disguised clickbait and its spurious co-occurrences. The model is anchored in rich multimodal inputs (Swin-T visuals with face/object detectors, BERT text with OCR for thumbnails, CTTransformer for cross-modal relations, six linguistic/style features, and creator profile features), which makes the causal decomposition operational rather than purely conceptual.

773.human_review: Sufficient Experiments. Experimental evaluations have been conducted on multiple datasets of varying scales, demonstrating the efficiency of the proposed algorithms.
773.llm_review: Data, Efficiency, Evaluation, Experiment: The evaluation spans three standard datasets with clear sizes—CLDInst (4k bait/3k non-bait), Clickbait17 (9k/29k), FakeNewsNet (5k/17k)—and uses 20-run averages with oversampling to mitigate class imbalance and t-tests (p < 0.005). The method consistently outperforms strong multimodal and causal baselines. From Table 1, accuracy gains over VLP are +3.23 (88.79 vs 85.56) on CLDInst, +4.13 (92.83 vs 88.70) on Clickbait17, and +3.54 (91.56 vs 88.02) on FakeNewsNet, with corresponding F1 gains of +4.88 (88.94 vs 84.06), +6.78 (93.52 vs 86.74), and +6.11 (92.85 vs 86.74). PR curves in Fig. 4 show uniformly higher precision across recall, supporting better bias-resilience. Ablations quantify each component’s necessity: removing the IRM-based invariant factor (w/o EICF) yields the largest drops (ACC/F1: −5.62/−6.03 on CLDInst, −7.22/−8.06 on Clickbait17, −6.62/−7.07 on FakeNewsNet), while removing multimodal features (w/o MF) also harms performance materially (e.g., ACC −5.23 on Clickbait17). Additional ablations (w/o ESCF, w/o ENF) validate the contributions of scenario-specific causal and non-causal handling. Case studies (Fig. 5) show that ic clusters samples without separating scenarios, sci separates scenarios but needs ic for class discrimination, and nf captures scenario-unique but label-weak noise—empirically aligning with the intended factor roles. A manual audit reports disguised-post prevalence of ~23/26/27%, matching the larger gains on Clickbait17/FakeNewsNet where disguise is more common. The social-metadata-based augmentation leverages historical signals (share frequency, viewing time) for pseudo-labels to improve label efficiency while keeping test-time inputs content-only.

774.human_review: The model diagram is not sufficiently appropriate. It is stated that five types of features across multiple modalities are extracted, however, Figure 2 only illustrates the extraction of four features, omitting the interaction between textual and visual features, which may lead to confusion.
774.llm_review: Figure, Model: While Fig. 3(c) asserts that backdoor paths from C and S to Y through NF are cut, the training objectives do not provide an explicit independence constraint between NF and Y. The only mechanism is Eq. (4), which sets a non-clickbait target for predictions on nfi across the training data; this does not guarantee NF ⟂ Y (e.g., it lacks an MI penalty or adversarial head to decorrelate NF from Y), nor does it prevent leakage through shared parameters between F and F_ξ. Similarly, the confounder C and scenario S are depicted but not operationalized in loss terms beyond the scenario alternation; there is no explicit modeling or estimation of C, making the claim that IC is isolated from C largely dependent on the IRM penalty’s effectiveness. The iterative scenario estimation loop (Eqs. (2)-(3)) is susceptible to circularity: Φ_s is trained on vc determined by m, and m is optimized given scenario splits produced by Φ_s; no convergence diagnostics or failure modes are discussed, and Fig. 2 does not depict this alternation, the stopping criterion, or kd selection. Finally, the contrastive design forces all nfi to predict 0 (Eq. (4)), which may bias the classifier’s calibration on negative evidence and is not justified in the graphical model; the figure does not clarify how this aligns with the stated “backdoor cutting.”

775.human_review: Lack of technical details introduction. The meaning of the dashed lines in Figure 3 should be explained in detail to facilitate the reader's understanding.
775.llm_review: Detail, Figure: Important implementation and experimental details are missing or are deferred to appendices without specifics, undermining reproducibility. Examples include: concrete values or search ranges for α and β in Eq. (1), the number of scenarios |S| and how it is chosen, kd and the projection dimension of ξ, the number of alternation rounds T and stopping criteria, optimizer/schedule, learning rates, batch sizes, and how trivial masks (m≈0 or m≈1) are avoided beyond the L2 term. The pseudo-label augmentation is described only at a high level (share frequency, viewing time)—thresholds, selection rules, and noise-control strategies are not reported, yet augmentation materially affects data efficiency. For evaluation, it is unclear whether the ± values in Tables 1–2 are standard deviations or standard errors over 20 runs, and oversampling details (strategy, per-class multiplicity) are not provided. Figures could better support the claims: Fig. 2’s training vs inference paths, mask application points, and alternation loop are not visually separated; PR curves in Fig. 4 are dense with small fonts/legends; t-SNE plots in Fig. 5 lack axis scales and a legend mapping colors/markers to scenarios and labels, making it hard to verify the described separations.

776.human_review: The task are well defined, though there are no previous benchmarks they have worked on.
776.llm_review: Benchmark and Task: The paper introduces a concrete cross-task benchmark for conversational task-switching that spans five distinct tasks—Gigaword summarization, MMLU Abstract Algebra (MCQ), MMLU Human Aging (MCQ), TweetQA (QA), and Rotten Tomatoes sentiment (classification)—and evaluates 15+ switch pairs. Evidence: (a) Target-task switch matrices per model (Tables 17–20) report percentage performance deltas across all CH-task → Tt combinations; (b) zero-shot baselines for all target tasks and models are provided (Appendix B, Tables 5–9); (c) conversation histories are built from each task’s train set and the (L+1)-th turn is evaluated on the test set (Appendix A), enabling controlled construction of history and switch. This scope and documentation make the benchmark reproducible and extensible.

777.human_review: A good message to practioners as well as LLM creators. They should be careful about the context they condition on. In fact, those creating apps should probably weight the context in attention based on the task classification.
777.llm_review: Attention and Task: The study explicitly formalizes the desired conditional independence rL+1 ⟂ h | uL+1 (Eq. 2) for distinct tasks and measures violations via a task-switch sensitivity metric τ (Eqs. 3–5) tied to the autoregressive attention over the full history. Evidence that attention to prior-task content modulates outcomes: as conversation length L grows, accuracy shifts amplify (e.g., Figure 2 for MMLU AA target shows larger deviations with L, particularly for 7B models), indicating that additional attended history from a different task can increasingly bias the next-turn prediction despite the new prompt.

778.human_review: The performance problem seems to be across model sizes as per certain tables provided. Hence, it is an important problem.
778.llm_review: Importance, Model, Performance: The work demonstrates that prior-task interference can materially degrade performance across both small and large models, highlighting a reliability risk for deployed assistants. Specific examples: with Tt = MMLU AA and CH-task = Gigaword, GPT-3.5 drops −12.12% and GPT-4 drops −8.74%; Llama-7B and Mistral-7B drop −18.75% (τ = 5.23) and −21.74% (τ = 3.13), respectively (Table 2). With CH-task = Rotten Tomatoes and Tt = MMLU AA, GPT-4 drops −8.20%; Llama-7B drops −12.50% with very high sensitivity τ = 9.91 (Table 2). These results show the phenomenon affects frontier and smaller models alike.

779.human_review: There is a lot of work to be done in this area. This work takes the first step. It would have been great if the work was a bit more comprehensive. 4 tasks with 4 switches is a simple work, and possibly needs extension to become a major benchmark. Having said that, the work in the current form is good.
779.llm_review: Benchmark: The paper contributes a well-documented evaluation suite: standardized prompt templates per task (Appendix D, Table 10, including answer-tag constraints for classification), ablations over conversation length L (Figures 3–7), multiple seeds for open 7B models with variance bands (Appendix C.3, Figures 11–12), and explicit tracking of format-failure rates that can confound classification metrics (Figures 8–10). The inclusion of both open (Llama-7B, Mistral-7B) and closed (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) models and full switch matrices (Tables 17–20) increases external validity and practical utility.

780.human_review: Some of these points are known. But it is good to see numbers behind claims like multi-turn with wrong context degrades performance.
780.llm_review: Performance: The results clearly separate within-task in-context gains from cross-task switch degradations. Within-task gains: with Tt = RT and CH-task = RT, all models improve (GPT-3.5 +3.00%, GPT-4 +1.74%, Llama-7B +2.54% with τ = 4.02, Mistral-7B +3.17% with τ = 2.65; Table 3). Cross-task degradations: with Tt = MMLU AA and CH-task = TweetQA, GPT-3.5 −19.19%, GPT-4 −8.20%, Llama-7B −12.50% (τ = 6.37), Mistral-7B −7.25% (τ = 2.78; Table 2). The paper also nuances that some cross-task switches can help (e.g., CH-task = RT → Tt = MMLU AA for Mistral-7B: +11.59% with low τ = 0.83), and investigates formatting-induced failures (Figures 8–10) to interpret metric shifts.

781.human_review: A paper like this should be a dataset paper. They should release their dataset and provide the initial benchmark for others to improve on.
781.llm_review: Benchmark, Data, Improvement: Despite covering five tasks, parts of the benchmark are small and synthetic, reducing ecological validity. For example, the MMLU AA subset uses only 14 train and 99 test items; MMLU HA uses 26 train and 222 test (Appendix A, Table 4). Conversation histories are teacher-forced with ground-truth responses, and there are no real conversational logs with naturally occurring multi-intent/task switches. Improvements: expand to larger and more diverse datasets (including multilingual), incorporate real chat transcripts with organic task switches and longer histories, and evaluate beyond the current token-length constraints to observe very long-range effects.

782.human_review: The experiments show mixed results. So I find an improvement in performance in some cases and a decrease in performance in other cases. In fact all of this might be within error bars. Therefore it would be *very* helpful to know the standard deviation of some of the metrics reported.
782.llm_review: Experiment, Metric, Performance, Result: The primary sensitivity metric τ relies on the zero-shot response r* and model token probabilities, which the authors cannot access for closed models (asterisks in Tables 2–3), limiting cross-model comparability and preventing sensitivity analysis exactly where performance is strongest (GPT-3.5/4). τ can also misalign with performance deltas; e.g., with Tt = RT, CH-task = Gigaword, Mistral-7B shows a small −0.79% change but a relatively high τ = 3.04 (Table 3), suggesting confidence shifts that are not reflected in accuracy. The study reports few statistical tests; significance of modest deltas (±1–3%) is unclear, and uncertainty is only visualized for 7B models (Appendix C.3). Recommendations: add significance testing across seeds, report calibration/confidence metrics, evaluate alternative sensitivity definitions (Appendix E) alongside accuracy, and use stricter answer-format enforcement or logit-based classification for open models to reduce format noise.

783.human_review: What do we know about noisy multi-turn conversations? What if we filled the context with noise? Does it degrade performance? Can the authors divide the sections into classes of tasks, and for each class what is the correlation of performance improvement or degradation?
783.llm_review: Performance: Many observed degradations are small in deployment-relevant settings. For Tt = RT (where zero-shot is already high: 86.68–91.80%, Appendix B, Table 7), most cross-task deltas for GPT-3.5/4 are between −1.0% and +3.0% (Table 3), making practical impact ambiguous without user-level error analysis or cost-of-error estimates. The paper does not test mitigations (e.g., context filtering, system prompts, task-segmentation) or quantify their potential gains, so performance implications remain preliminary.

784.human_review: Figure 2 shows a fluctuation with performance for different number of turns. Does this suggest that there is a lot of noise with little signal? I couldn't really interpret the results for GPT4.
784.llm_review: Figure, Interpretation, Performance, Result: Several plots hinder precise interpretation. Figures 6–7 explicitly clip y-axes at +75%, which can mask large positive shifts and distort relative effects; y-axis ranges also differ across panels/models, complicating direct comparisons. Uncertainty (CIs or error bars) is absent for GPT-3.5/4, and variance is only shown for 7B models (Appendix C.3). Additionally, the paper discusses a link between negative accuracy change and high τ, yet mixed cases exist (e.g., Tt = RT, CH-task = RT yields positive accuracy but τ remains >2 for 7B models; Table 3), reinforcing the need for scatter/correlation plots between τ and performance and consistent axes to support claims.

785.human_review: The ASC method represents a significant contribution to the field of information retrieval by enhancing the efficiency of sparse document retrieval.
785.llm_review: Contribution, Efficiency, Method: The paper introduces ASC, a two-parameter (mu, eta) thresholding scheme with segmented cluster-level maximum term weights that tightens cluster bounds and enables adaptive, probabilistically safe pruning at both cluster and document levels. This methodological refinement directly translates into substantial efficiency gains on CPUs (e.g., multi-x speedups with <=0.1% MRR@10 loss) while incurring modest memory overhead (~9%), making it a practical contribution for high-throughput sparse retrieval.

786.human_review: The paper validates the efficacy of the ASC method using established benchmarks such as MS MARCO and BEIR. These comprehensive experiments not only confirm the method’s capability in improving relevance scores and reducing latency but also offer a thorough comparison with existing methods, thereby solidifying the practical advantages of ASC.
786.llm_review: Benchmark, Comparison, Experiment, Validation: The empirical evaluation is broad and careful: MS MARCO Dev and TREC DL’19/20 with SPLADE, plus zero-shot BEIR, and additional models (uniCOIL, LexMAE). ASC is compared against strong DAAT/SAAT baselines (MaxScore, Anytime Ranking, IOQP), reports both mean and P99 latencies, includes recall along with MRR/nDCG, uses significance testing, and presents ablations (mu sweeps, segmentation strategy random vs. k-means). Results consistently show that ASC attains comparable or better effectiveness with sizable speedups, validating the approach under diverse settings.

787.human_review: A formal analysis providing a probabilistic guarantee on rank-safeness is a strong point of the paper. This rigorous mathematical backing is essential, as it substantiates the reliability and effectiveness of the new retrieval method under various operational conditions.
787.llm_review: Analysis, Method: The paper provides formal analysis for the method: (i) segmentation tightens cluster bounds (Theorem 1); (ii) an adaptive pruning rule using MaxSBound and AvgSBound regulates aggressiveness based on bound tightness (Theorem 2); (iii) rank-competitiveness within a factor mu without time budget (Theorem 3); and (iv) a probabilistic safeness guarantee within factor eta under random segmentation (Theorem 4). The empirical correlation between AvgSBound/MaxSBound and bound tightness supports the theoretical design.

788.human_review: The paper is well-written, presenting complex ideas in a structured and accessible manner, which makes it easy for readers to understand and follow the proposed method and its implications.
788.llm_review: Method, Presentation: The method is presented with clear formulas and a step-by-step flow (two-level pruning conditions, cluster traversal order, document-level bounds), a worked example, and practical guidance (default hyperparameters, cluster/segment choices, quantization, space overhead). The limitations section is candid and situates ASC relative to block-based pruning frameworks and potential integrations, improving readability and practical uptake.

789.human_review: The paper could improve the accessibility and clarity of its data presentations. Tables and figures should ideally be placed at the top of the page using the ‘[t]’ placement specifier in LaTeX, rather than ‘[h]’, to ensure they appear at the beginning of pages. This would enhance readability and make it easier for readers to reference these visual aids as they navigate through the text.
789.llm_review: Clarity, Data, Presentation: (1) The definition of (mu, eta)-approximate retrieval is somewhat unconventional (average of top-k' rank scores and expected values), and the choice of k' is not emphasized, which may hinder interpretability for practitioners; the claim of being "probabilistically safe" depends critically on random segmentation and may feel stronger than warranted in non-ideal conditions. (2) While the dense retrieval comparison is discussed as out of scope, the absence of empirical dense baselines limits the data-driven perspective on end-to-end tradeoffs; sensitivity analyses on the number of clusters/segments and space-time trade-offs are only partially explored. (3) Presentation of some tables/figures is dense and occasionally hard to parse (shorthands like C%/Re, split equations/labels, minor typos), which can obscure key takeaways.

790.human_review: My other concerns in the last submission have been tackled. Please continue to improve the presentation of the paper as I have suggested.
790.llm_review: Presentation: Notational and formatting issues detract from clarity: mixed use of theta/mu/theta-eta thresholds without an algorithm box, figure/table layouts that blend examples and decisions, and scattered references to settings (e.g., mu choices across k=10 vs. k=1000) that require cross-referencing appendices. A concise pseudocode or algorithm listing, more consistent notation, and streamlined figure captions would significantly improve readability.

791.human_review: Confidence calibration with black-box techniques is an important area of research right now, so the author's method will likely help future works in this direction
791.llm_review: Method/Technique: The paper proposes a principled decomposition of confidence into Uncertainty(Q) and Fidelity(ai), and combines them as Conf(Q, ai) = (1 − Uncertainty(Q)) * F(ai) (Eq. 7). Uncertainty is computed as normalized entropy over sampled answer frequencies (Eq. 6), which is appropriate for closed-set QA with K samples and M options. Fidelity is elicited via a hierarchical chain formed by iteratively replacing an option with the statement "All other options are wrong" and observing the model’s next-best choices under greedy decoding (Sec. 3.2). The fidelity of each chain position is weighted by τi and normalized (Eq. 4), with τ tuned around 2 (Table 4) to avoid overconfidence. The ablation in Table 4 shows Fidelity is the key driver (e.g., on LLaMA2-13B-Chat, dropping Fidelity increases ECE10 from 0.069/0.070/0.043/0.121 to 0.675/0.614/0.704/0.677 on ARC/MMLU/CSQA/TruthfulQA), while Uncertainty adds complementary signal (dropping it yields 0.122/0.184/0.115/0.202). This provides concrete evidence that the decomposition is technically meaningful and useful.

792.human_review: I think the proposed technique, specifically decomposing confidence into two more specific aspects (fidelity and uncertainty) is an interesting way to think about confidence calibration
792.llm_review: Technique: The fidelity-chain mechanism is simple and effective for black-box LMs: replacing an option’s content with a canonical phrase elicits a rank ordering among options without logits, and greedy decoding makes the chain largely temperature-invariant. The paper quantifies this robustness: Figures 4 and 7 show UF Calibration achieves the lowest or near-lowest ECE across temperatures compared to Sampled/Token/Verbalization baselines. The weighting scheme (τ ≈ 2) is justified empirically (Table 4: setting τ to 4–5 worsens ECE10 on LLaMA2-13B-Chat, e.g., CSQA from 0.043 to 0.075/0.094), indicating the design is interpretable and tunable rather than ad hoc. The call budget is practical: K = 10 samples for uncertainty plus ~2–3 additional calls for fidelity chains per question (Fig. 3, Table 8), and accuracy is preserved because the final answer is the mode of samples (e.g., GPT-3.5-Turbo ARC accuracy 79.266 for both Sampled and Ours in Table 1).

793.human_review: The method performs well across LLMs and datasets in multiple-choice tasks
793.llm_review: Data/Method/Model/Performance: The study evaluates 6 RLHF LMs (GPT-3.5/4-Turbo; Baichuan2-13B-Chat; LLaMA2-Chat 7B/13B/70B) on four MCQA datasets (ARC-Challenge 1,172 Q; MMLU with 1/8 subjects subsampled; CommonSenseQA 1,221 Q; TruthfulQA 817 Q). UF Calibration yields consistent calibration gains across metrics and settings: for GPT-4-Turbo on TruthfulQA, ECE10 improves from 0.091 (Sampled) and 0.056 (Verb) to 0.042 with Ours, with CE10 increasing from 0.478 (Sampled) to 0.764 and IPR10 decreasing from 0.178 (Sampled) to 0.044 (Table 1). On GPT-3.5-Turbo for CommonSenseQA, Ours reduces ECE10 from 0.135 (Sampled) to 0.073 and improves CE10 from 0.782 (Sampled) to 0.812 (Table 1). On LLaMA2-13B-Chat, Ours achieves the best ECE10 on 3/4 datasets (0.069 ARC, 0.070 MMLU, 0.043 CSQA, 0.121 TruthfulQA) versus the best competing methods (0.135, 0.225, 0.142, 0.238 respectively; Table 4). On LLaMA2-70B-Chat, Ours improves CE10 dramatically (e.g., CSQA CE10 0.918 vs Token 0.339) while keeping ECE10 competitive (0.094 vs Token 0.093; Table 3). Temperature and parameter scaling analyses (Figs. 4–5) show UF Calibration remains strong as sampling temperature and model size vary, supporting robustness beyond a single configuration.

794.human_review: There is still a missing discussion on why "All of the other options are incorrect" is a valid approach for quantifying fidelity. Many MCQA questions have answers that depend just on the remaining answers (e.g. "which of these animals is the largest?")
794.llm_review: Discussion: While the paper introduces IPR (Eq. 8) and CE (Eq. 9) to complement ECE, their theoretical grounding is limited. CE is the normalized entropy of bin densities and depends on the arbitrary choice of 10 equal-size bins; there is no sensitivity analysis to bin count or adaptive binning. IPR also depends on binning and does not connect to established notions like reliability, resolution/sharpness, or proper scoring rules. For instance, in Table 1 (GPT-4-Turbo, ARC), Ours has higher ECE10 (0.127) than Sampled (0.067) but better IPR10 (0.083 vs 0.200) and CE10 (0.757 vs 0.221); the paper asserts a balance among metrics but does not justify how to trade these off or whether higher CE10 aligns with desirable sharpness without harming reliability. Although Brier scores are mentioned (Table 7, Appendix), they are not analyzed in the main text, and no confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported for ECE/IPR/CE. Failure modes (e.g., when Sampled outperforms Ours on ECE, as above) are not examined, weakening the normative claim about "Truly Well-Calibrated Confidence."

795.human_review: This approach also can only be used on multiple-choice settings and not long-form generation, where confidence calibration is often more important. The authors should qualify the scope of their claims to note that this approach has only shown to work for multiple choice tasks. This is brought up in the limitations but should be clearly explained in the main paper as well
795.llm_review: Approach/Task: The method is restricted to closed-set tasks (MCQA/classification), as acknowledged, and hinges on a specific prompt transformation ("All other options are wrong"). This may induce distribution shift or encourage process-of-elimination heuristics rather than measuring genuine fidelity to the original content; sensitivity to option order, paraphrasing, or label permutation is not evaluated. The uncertainty estimate relies on a small sampling budget (K = 10) without a study of how K affects ECE/variance; no cost-accuracy-calibration trade-off curves are provided despite multiple extra calls per question (~2–3 for fidelity chains). Baseline coverage is incomplete: for open-source models with logits, standard post-hoc calibrations (temperature scaling tuned on validation, isotonic/Dirichlet/beta calibration) are not included; for black-box settings, stronger self-consistency ensembles or conformal prediction (only in Appendix B.1, not in main tables) are not compared head-to-head. These gaps leave open whether UF Calibration remains superior under stronger or better-tuned baselines and under common perturbations to task formatting.

796.human_review: The proposed method operates as a post-processing step, which means it does not require retraining the individual models. This can be advantageous in practical applications where retraining can be computationally expensive.
796.llm_review: Training: The approach is fully post-hoc and training-free, allowing heterogeneous MLMs to be fused without finetuning or architectural alignment. This is evidenced by the use of per-choice likelihoods from off-the-shelf models and simple algebraic combinations (Eqs. 2–7), with no optimization or additional training. The paper shows that this property yields practical gains under limited training budgets: for weaker models, self-composition (debias) delivers large improvements, e.g., LLaVA-7B on MMVP improves by +12.08% (Table 1, text) and LLaVA-13B on MMBench improves by +4.39% (41.58 to 45.97 with debias, α=0.1, Table 1). The post-hoc fusion also scales over multiple models: mix-composition with weighted majority-vote boosts MMVP by +13.42% over weighted majority-vote (23.49 to 36.91, Table 2), again without any training.

797.key_points: Strength: Clarity, Contribution, Method, Related Work
797.human_review: The paper is well-organized and clearly written, with a logical flow that makes the proposed method easy to understand. The related work section is thorough and positions the contributions in the context of existing research.
797.llm_review: Clarity, Contribution, Method, Related Work: The paper clearly defines a unified likelihood composition framework, partitioned into self-composition and mutual-composition (Fig. 1), and gives concrete, reproducible formulations: debias uses Y = (1+α)Y_simple − αY_noimg (Eq. 2, Fig. 2 prompts), highlight uses Y = (1+α)Y_positive − αY_negative (Eq. 3, Fig. 3 prompts), ensemble averages likelihoods (Eq. 4), majority-vote uses a mask on argmax positions with optional likelihood weights (Eq. 5), and mix-composition combines self- and mutual-operations (Eqs. 6–7). The contribution lies in organizing prior ideas (e.g., ensembling; Dietterich, 2000; majority voting/CoT-SC, Wang et al., 2022; contrastive/negative prompting, O’Brien & Lewis, 2023; Niu et al., 2021) into a coherent, method-agnostic fusion framework and empirically validating that simple mixes outperform vanilla ensemble/majority baselines across 9 VQA datasets and 10 MLMs. Prompts and α-sweeps are described, and analyses include inter-model heatmaps (Fig. 5) and model-count ablations (Fig. 6), supporting clarity and reproducibility.

798.human_review: The ensemble methods used, such as debiasing, highlighting, majority-vote, and traditional ensemble strategies, are well-known and commonly used in the field. The paper does not introduce fundamentally new techniques or methodologies in model ensemble.
798.llm_review: Method, Model, Novelty, Technique: The methodological novelty is incremental. Debias is effectively subtracting a no-image likelihood baseline; highlight is negative prompting contrasted with a standard prompt—akin to contrastive decoding with prompt variants. Mutual-composition uses classical ensemble and majority vote; mix-composition linearly combines these signals (Eqs. 6–7). Importantly, the method does not address cross-model calibration beyond per-model softmax normalization (Sec. 3, footnote 2), which may be insufficient for heterogeneous models with different tokenizers and output scales. The choice to compute each option’s likelihood via the option letter (Sec. 3, footnote 3: “each option’s likelihood is actually the corresponding option letter’s likelihood”) risks introducing spurious biases unrelated to the semantic content of the answers. Empirically, highlight can substantially harm performance, suggesting instability: e.g., LLaVA-1.6-7B on MMBench drops from 71.30 (baseline) to 51.61 with highlight at α=1.0 (Table 1), and LLaVA-1.6-13B drops from 74.05 to 70.37 (Table 1). Stronger fusion baselines (temperature scaling or logit calibration per model, learned stacking/meta-ensembles, Bayesian model combination) are absent, so it remains unclear whether the gains are specific to the proposed composition or largely due to generic averaging.

799.key_points: Weakness: Analysis, Framework, Method, Result, Theory
799.human_review: The paper lacks a deep theoretical analysis explaining why the proposed combination of common ensemble methods yields better results. Incorporating a more rigorous theoretical framework could strengthen the understanding of the method's advantages.
799.llm_review: Analysis, Framework, Method, Result, Theory: The framework lacks a theoretical account of when subtractive debiasing or highlight improves decision quality across heterogeneous models. Analyses are primarily heuristic: α sweeps (Fig. 4) and inter-model heatmaps (Fig. 5) offer qualitative insights but no guarantees or principled selection rules. Statistical soundness is underreported: tables show point accuracies (or aggregate scores like MME) without variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing, so claims such as “self-composition brings a consistent improvement” are not fully supported—e.g., LLaVA-1.6-7B on MMBench drops slightly with debias α=0.1 (71.30 to 71.14, Table 1), and highlight frequently degrades results across models/datasets (Table 1). The inter-model analysis uses α=1.0 universally and observes that benefits appear when models are similar, but does not explain why or explore counter-examples. Claims of generality extend only to multiple-choice VQA; no theoretical or empirical bridge is given to other tasks.

800.key_points: Weakness: Benchmark, Data, Experiment, Method, Robustness, Validation
800.human_review: There is a concern that the method may be overly fine-tuned to specific benchmarks. It would be useful to include experiments on out-of-sample datasets or unseen tasks to validate the robustness of the approach.
800.llm_review: Benchmark, Data, Experiment, Method, Robustness, Validation: While coverage across 9 VQA datasets (MME, MMBench, VSR, POPE, MMVP, VQAv2*, VizWiz*, GQA*, OKVQA*) and 10 MLMs (six LLaVA variants plus Yi-VL, Qwen-VL, InternVL, InternLM-Xcomposer) is broad, all evaluations are on multiple-choice VQA. There are no tests on open-ended multimodal generation, captioning, or grounding, limiting external validity. Robustness checks are missing: no option-order shuffling, no distractor re-weighting, no prompt paraphrase or instruction variants beyond the specific positive/negative prompts, and no sensitivity to decoding settings. The reliance on option-letter likelihoods is not stress-tested against letter bias or format changes. Data contamination risks (e.g., overlap between training corpora of base MLMs and MME/MMBench) are unaddressed. Compute/budget fairness is unclear: mix-composition can require multiple prompts per model; with N=6 models and two prompts (positive/negative) this implies up to 12 forward passes per example, yet there is no budget-matched comparison to a stronger single model or to calibrated ensembles. No ablations isolate the impact of the softmax normalization step or explore learned per-model weights.

801.human_review: The construction of a dataset of 472 moral scenarios based on Chinese moral words adds empirical depth and gives a robust evaluation of LLMs.
801.llm_review: Data, Evaluation, Model: The paper assembles a focused, sizable Chinese dataset of 472 moral scenarios derived from 514 negative moral words in the Chinese Moral Dictionary (CMD), each scenario containing a moral question, two mutually exclusive options, and explicit mappings from options to one or two moral principles. Scenarios are further rewritten into male/female variants to probe gender effects. Evaluation spans word-level polarity judgments (two prompts: “Is X moral?” vs. “Is not X moral?”) and scenario-level choices with firmness scores (1–3). The study reports concrete rates at the word level (overall proportion of words judged immoral: ChatGPT 0.93, Gemini 0.85, ChatGLM 0.74, Ernie 0.69; with family > individual across all models) and cross-level consistency DL (ChatGPT 0.77, Gemini 0.68, ChatGLM 0.52, Ernie 0.42). Cross-model comparisons are grounded in similarity to a human baseline (30 Chinese university students): scenario-choice consistency with SCU is highest for ChatGPT (0.82) and Gemini (0.78), lower for ChatGLM (0.68) and Ernie (0.56), highlighting model-specific patterns under a common Chinese evaluation setting.

802.human_review: The paper introduces a unique three-module framework for evaluating the moral beliefs of LLMs
802.llm_review: Framework, Model: The three-module pluralistic framework—(i) moral choice with firmness scoring, (ii) moral rank via Best-Worst Scaling and Iterative Luce Spectral Ranking (BWS+ILSR), and (iii) two-round moral debate—enables complementary probing of preferences and their stability. It yields model-level insights anchored in results: rank correlations show ChatGLM aligns best with human moral-principle priorities (SROCC with SCU = 0.26), while ChatGPT’s rank correlation is slightly negative (−0.07), and Gemini/Ernie are near zero (~0.03). Combined with scenario-choice similarities (ChatGPT/Gemini closer to SCU decisions) and firmness distributions (Gemini score-3 = 0.89; ChatGPT score-3 = 0.52), the framework supports nuanced claims about individualistic vs. collectivist tendencies and confidence levels across models.

803.human_review: The study employs rigorous methods, including moral ranking through Best-Worst Scaling and Iterative Luce Spectral Ranking, and robustness checks through repeated experiments and parallel experiments.
803.llm_review: Experiment, Method, Robustness: The study incorporates multiple robustness levers: (a) dual prompts at the word level (DQ consistency: ChatGPT 0.84, Gemini 0.68, ChatGLM 0.58, Ernie 0.53), (b) option-order flipping to mitigate positional bias, (c) three repeated runs (Appendix B.2), (d) 2-shot examples to calibrate firmness scoring, and (e) pre/post-debate reassessment. The gender-rewriting yields DG consistency measures (ChatGLM 0.87 vs. Ernie/ChatGPT 0.96 and Gemini 0.92), quantifying gender sensitivity. Debate analyses (Figure 4) quantify pre/post choice changes by pairing models as debaters, and Appendix C.3 links higher firmness to lower change rates, consistent with observed distributions (e.g., Gemini’s high score-3 share coincides with greater choice stability).

804.human_review: The study deliberately provides minimal context in moral scenarios to avoid randomness, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world moral decision-making.
804.llm_review: Complexity: The pipeline layers LLM-generated scenarios (from ChatGPT, plus Ernie augmentation), manual filtering, option-to-principle mapping, BWS+ILSR ranking over principles (which are further mapped to Kohlberg stages), and two-round debates. Each stage introduces potential error/bias and compounds upstream choices. For instance, Appendix A.3 notes recurring occupations in generated scenarios, signaling distributional bias; the principle and stage assignments (e.g., Table 4) are pivotal but lack inter-annotator agreement statistics, making downstream rankings sensitive to early annotation or generation artifacts. This depth of abstraction can obscure where effects originate and complicates attribution for observed cultural or gender differences.

805.human_review: Assigning and evaluating "immoral" stances in debates may ethically charge the LLMs' training processes and output. The paper does not sufficiently address how these ethical risks are mitigated or the potential long-term effects on the models' behavior.
805.llm_review: Evaluation, Model, Training: Cultural claims are confounded by running English-centric models entirely in Chinese, blending language proficiency, RLHF policies, and cultural priors (e.g., ChatGPT/Gemini show higher word-level accuracy—0.93/0.85—but this may reflect overall capability or Chinese proficiency rather than culture). The human baseline is small and homogeneous (n=30 Chinese university students), and only the default scenarios were annotated by humans—the man/woman rewrites lack human judgments, limiting conclusions about gender bias. The dataset is derived from negative moral words only, and many scenarios are generated by ChatGPT, risking test-set priors leakage. Key evaluation details are under-specified or deferred to appendices (e.g., exact Gemini version, seeds, statistical significance tests, effect sizes, temperature control across all experiments), and data/code are promised “later,” weakening reproducibility and the strength of statistical claims.

806.human_review: The construction of the moral scenarios and the binary choices presented may inherently bias the models' responses. The study does not adequately discuss how it ensures that these scenarios are balanced or how it handles the ambiguity inherent in moral decision-making.
806.llm_review: Model: The comparison spans only four heterogeneous LLMs: two proprietary, large English models (GPT-3.5-turbo-16K, Gemini pro) and two smaller Chinese models (ChatGLM2-6B-32K, Ernie-Bot-turbo). Differences in size, RLHF, safety layers, and general capability plausibly drive observed patterns (e.g., firmness distributions where Gemini gives score-3 = 0.89 vs. ChatGLM score-1 = 0.43), independent of moral beliefs. There is no capability-matched control or ablation (e.g., similarly sized Chinese/English models, or same-base models with/without RLHF), and debate pairings likely advantage stronger models, further conflating moral stability with raw capability. Broader coverage (e.g., Qwen, Baichuan, Llama-3-instruct Chinese, GPT-4-class baselines) would make model-level conclusions more credible.

807.human_review: The paper is clearly presented and easy to follow, and the inventory of 10 logical patterns is illustrated in a clear and concise manner.
807.llm_review: The paper is easy to follow and well organized. The task is introduced with concrete, testable criteria for template design (comprehensive, expressive, simple; §3.1), and the task formulation is crisply decomposed into two subtasks (template selection and slot-filler extraction; Figure 1, §3.3). The annotation protocol is described in operational detail: 7 vetted MTurk workers, three calibration rounds with feedback incorporated into guidelines, 3 annotators per CA, MACE aggregation with a 0.8 threshold yielding 469 high-confidence CAs, and expert verification of 872 sentences from the remaining 309 CAs. Reporting specific quality checks (Krippendorff’s α = 0.50 on single-template data; expert agreement of 88.0% on 50 sampled CAs; 78.5% inter-expert agreement on 50 expert-verified CAs; slot-filler spot check 38/43 correct) strengthens credibility. Clear dataset statistics (778 CAs, 5,172 sentences; train/dev/test = 516/128/134 CAs) and release of data and scripts further support reproducibility.

808.human_review: The author provides detailed examples in the body and appendix to illustrate the rationality of the 10 logical pattern designs. In particular, Figure 4 explains the possibility of multiple reasonable interpretations using different logical patterns for the same IA-CA pair.
808.llm_review: Figures effectively anchor the contributions. Figure 1 walks the reader through a concrete IA–CA pair for the Alternative pattern, with x/y/z placeholders and red arrows that localize the attacked component (causality, value, or conclusion), making the notion of “attack points” tangible. Figure 2 specifies the exact model I/O contract (list of template IDs aligned to CA sentences, plus a dictionary mapping template IDs to extracted slot-fillers), which materially reduces ambiguity for anyone reimplementing the experiments. The alignment between Figure 1’s subtask framing and Figure 2’s I/O example clarifies how the annotation labels translate into modeling targets.

809.human_review: In Table.1, Mig and Alt patterns are relatively easy to understand. However, examples are lacking to illustrate the distinction and necessity of MM1 and MM2 logical patterns. In MM1, x promotes z and z promotes y, which is used to explain that x does not suppress y. In MM2, it is explained that x promotes z and z suppresses y, which means x promotes y. I believe that x can also suppress y here. Is there a more reasonable explanation to illustrate this?
809.llm_review: Key distinctions among templates and reporting choices need clearer, example-driven explanation. For instance, Alternative vs. Another true cause both posit a z that suppresses y; the paper’s textual gloss differentiates them by prioritization (Alt) versus causal attribution (ATC), but without minimal pairs showing when a sentence like “the true cause is z, so reduce z instead of x” should be Alt or ATC. Similarly, Missing mechanism #1 (x promotes z; z promotes y) vs. #2 (x suppresses z; z suppresses y) encode different causal chains but yield the same net effect (x promotes y); readers need contrasting, real CA snippets to reliably disambiguate them. Coverage is reported as 86.5% in the abstract but 87.5% in §4.3; reconciling this discrepancy and explicitly defining how “Not Applicable” is decided (e.g., rhetorical moves outside Argument from Consequences, meta-comments, or off-topic content) would improve interpretability. Finally, segmentation and multi-template handling remain under-specified: §4.2 labels “consecutive sentences with same template label” as segments, but it is unclear how overlapping templates across adjacent sentences or multiple templates within a single sentence are recorded beyond the expert pass; an illustrative edge-case annotation would help.

810.human_review: The CA logical structure analysis task involves two sub-tasks: template selection and slot filling. When the template selection is ambiguous in the first sub-task (multiple logical pattern templates may be selected), there is a lack of further processing of slot-fillers in the second sub-task, which may also be due to conflicts in template understanding by LLMs (e.g., GPT-4), leading to poor performance.
810.llm_review: The performance and analysis section does not yet diagnose failure modes commensurate with the reported difficulties. Template selection F1 tops out at ~0.60 (GPT‑3.5‑turbo, Table 2), with other models around 0.49–0.56, while slot-filler precision is effectively zero across models (Table 2 prints “0.” for all), yet there is no ablation to test simpler pipelines (e.g., sentence-level multi-label classification for templates; span extraction or sequence tagging for slots) versus the single generative setup that jointly predicts both. No per-template confusion or performance by attack point (causality/value/conclusion) is reported, so we cannot see which patterns are inherently harder. The training/test mismatch likely matters: models are trained only on single-template sentences (516 train CAs) but evaluated on multi-template sentences (134 test CAs), which could depress F1; this is not analyzed. Evaluation choices are not stress-tested: the RougeL threshold for slot correctness is deferred to Appendix H, with no sensitivity analysis or semantic matching (e.g., exact-span vs. paraphrase) despite the near-zero precision. Few-shot (20-shot, same-IA examples) vs. fine-tuning comparisons lack per-model variance or significance tests, and there is no cross-topic generalization (e.g., train on DP/HW, test on part-time jobs) to assess task robustness.

811.human_review: Is the use of RougeL in the Precision score too strict? Slot-filler extraction may be paraphrased after LLM.
811.llm_review: Methodologically, several choices constrain generality and may introduce bias. The template inventory is limited to Argument from Consequences and evaluated on only three topics (Death Penalty, Homework, Part-time Jobs), which bounds external validity; even the authors note there are 60+ schemes. The annotation pipeline starts with a single-template-per-sentence assumption and attempts to recover multi-template cases via expert verification, but only 872 sentences are reviewed and 134 CAs end up with any multi-template sentences, leaving open how many were missed. The reliability assessment is not broken down by template (no per-template α or confusion), making it hard to know which categories are stable. MACE thresholding is fixed at 0.8 without comparison to alternatives, and Footnote 6 states experts reviewed the bottom 20% entropy cases, which (if entropy means uncertainty) would paradoxically target the most confident items rather than the ambiguous ones—this needs clarification to rule out selection bias. Finally, modeling jointly generates template IDs and slot spans, scored with lexical-overlap RougeL; without validating span extraction against a token-level method or adding semantic matching, the chosen metric may undercount correct extractions and skew method conclusions.
